paragraphs.text: PAULUS OROSIUS
THE FIRST BOOK OF THE HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS

I have obeyed your instructions, most blessed father Augustine, and I only wish I had done so as effectively as I did it willingly. Still, I am hardly troubled either way over the question of whether I have done well or not.

For you have already taken on the work of judging whether I was capable of what you instructed; I, for my part, am content with the testimony of obedience alone, provided I have graced it with goodwill and effort.

For in the great house of a great householder there are many animals of various kinds that are useful in helping to run the household, yet the care of the dogs is not the least of these. To them alone nature has given the instinct to press eagerly toward the task for which they are trained, and, through a kind of inborn habit of obedience, to hold themselves back solely in expectation of disciplined fear, until they are released by a nod or a signal and allowed to carry it out.
For they have qualities of their own which raise them above the brute beasts and bring them close to rational creatures: namely, to discern, to love and to serve.

For, discerning between their masters and strangers, they do not hate those they chase but are zealous for those they love; and loving their master and his house, they keep watch not as though from a natural fitness of body, but stay watchful out of the awareness of an anxious love.
Hence also, with a mystical meaning in the Gospels, the Canaanite woman was not ashamed to say, nor was the Lord too proud to hear, that the little dogs eat the crumbs under their masters' table.
Blessed Tobias too, following an angel as his guide, did not disdain to have a dog as his companion. So, bound to your love for all by a special love of my own, I have willingly obeyed your wish.

For since my submission owes the deed to the command of your fatherhood, and since my work, which came from you and returns to you, is wholly yours, I have added more to it in this one respect alone that is mine: that I did it gladly.

You had instructed me to answer the empty-talking perversity of those who, being strangers to the City of God, are called "pagans" from the crossroads and villages (pagi) of country places, or "gentiles" because they are wise in earthly things. Since they do not seek the things to come, and either forget or do not know the things that are past, they slander the present times as more beset with evils than ever before, for this reason alone: that Christ is believed in and God is worshipped, while idols are worshipped less.

You had instructed me, then, to set out in a brief and orderly volume whatever I could find, in all the records of histories and annals now available, from ages gone by that were burdened with wars, ravaged by plagues, grim with famine, terrible with earthquakes, extraordinary for floods, fearful for eruptions of fire, cruel with strokes of lightning and storms of hail, or wretched even with parricides and crimes.

It was especially unfitting that your Reverence should be taken up with a slight little work while you are pressing on to complete the eleventh book against these very pagans — of which the first ten, like rising rays of light, have shone over the whole world as soon as they were raised from the watchtower of the Church's
brightness. And your holy son Julian of Carthage, a servant of God, was demanding that his request on this matter be satisfied with the same confidence with which he had made it.
So I set to work, and at first I was overwhelmed with confusion, for as I kept turning the matter over, the disasters of the present times seemed to have boiled over beyond all measure.

But I found that past days were not only just as heavy as these, but more cruelly wretched in proportion as they were further removed from the remedy of the true religion. So this inquiry has rightly made it plain that death, greedy for blood, reigned while the religion that would restrain men from bloodshed was unknown; that as this religion began to dawn, death was struck dumb; that death is being confined now that religion prevails; and that it will be utterly gone when religion alone reigns.

Excepted, of course, and set apart are those last days at the end of the world, at the appearing of Antichrist or even at the final judgment, for which the Lord Christ foretold through the holy Scriptures, and by his own testimony as well, distresses such as there have never been before.

Then, by that same standard which holds both now and always, but with a plainer and heavier distinction, through the unbearable tribulations of those times testing will come upon the saints and destruction upon the wicked.

Nearly all those men, both among the Greeks and among the Latins, who have devoted themselves to writing and have handed down in words the deeds of kings and peoples for lasting memory, have begun their writing with Ninus son of Belus, king of the Assyrians —
men who, in their blind opinion, would have us believe that the origin of the world and the creation of humankind had no beginning, and yet who lay it down that kingdoms and wars began with him,
as though the human race had lived until then in the manner of cattle, and only then, shaken and roused as if to a new kind of foresight, had first come awake.
I, however, have resolved to trace the beginning of human misery from the beginning of human sin, touching only on a few points and those briefly.
From Adam, the first man, to Ninus, the "great" king as they call him, in whose time Abraham was born, there are 3,184 years, which all the historians have either left out or not known.

From Ninus, or Abraham, to Caesar Augustus — that is, to the birth of Christ, which took place in the forty-second year of Caesar's rule, when peace was made with the Parthians, the gates of Janus were closed and wars ceased throughout the world — [?] years are reckoned, and in them all the leisure and labour of men of action and of writers has been spent.

The matter itself therefore requires that I touch, as briefly as possible, on a few things from those books which, speaking of the origin of the world, have won belief for what is past by foretelling what was to come, and afterwards by the proof that followed.
Not that I would seem to force their authority on anyone; but it is worthwhile to recall the common opinion which we share with everyone.

First, if the world and man are directed by divine providence, which is just as well as good; and if man, who through the changeableness of his nature and the freedom of his will is both weak and stubborn, must be governed with tenderness when he needs help, and must also be justly corrected when he is unrestrained in his freedom,
then anyone who sees the human race through himself and in himself perceives that this world has rightly been exercised by alternating good and evil from the beginning of mankind.

Next, we are taught that sin and the punishment of sin began with the first man himself; and moreover, even these writers, who begin in the middle of time and nowhere make mention of earlier ages, have described nothing but wars and disasters —

and what else are wars to be called but evils falling now on one side, now on the other? And evils of this kind, as they were then and as they are now insofar as they exist, are without doubt either open sins or hidden punishments for sins.

What, then, prevents us from laying open the head of that matter whose body they have depicted, and from showing, even by the slightest account, that those earlier ages, which we show to have been far more numerous, suffered similar miseries?

I am therefore about to tell of the conflicts of the human race from the founding of the world to the founding of the City, then up to the principate of Caesar and the birth of Christ, from which time the dominion of the world has remained under the power of the City, or even up to our own day, so far as I
am able to bring them to knowledge; and to show, as from a watchtower, a world set ablaze by the torch of greed and burning with evils in its various parts. For this
I think it necessary
first to set out the world itself, which the human race inhabits, as it was divided into three parts by our forefathers and then marked out into regions and provinces,
so that, when the disasters of wars and plagues in particular places are shown, every diligent reader may gain a knowledge not only of events and times but also of places.

Our forefathers held that the whole circle of the earth, encircled by the border of the Ocean, was three-cornered, and they called its three parts ASIA, EUROPE AND AFRICA, though some have thought there were two, namely Asia, and then Africa, which they considered should be counted as part of Europe.
ASIA, bounded on three sides by the Ocean, stretches across the whole breadth of the East.

Toward the west, on its right it touches Europe, which begins beneath the northern pole, and on its left it leaves Africa; while below Egypt and Syria it has our sea, which we generally call the Great Sea.
EUROPE begins, as I said, in the northern region, at the river Tanais, where the Riphaean Mountains, facing away from the Sarmatian Ocean, pour forth the river Tanais.

This river, flowing past the altars and boundary markers of Alexander the Great set in the territory of the Rhobasci, feeds the Maeotic Marshes, whose vast overflow enters the Euxine Sea far and wide near the city of Theodosia.
From there a long strait is sent out near Constantinople, until it is received by this sea which we call Our Sea.
Europe's boundary in Spain is the western Ocean, especially at the Gades Islands, where the Pillars of Hercules are seen and the tide of the Ocean pours in through the mouth of the Tyrrhenian Sea.
AFRICA begins at the borders of Egypt and of the city of Alexandria, where the city of Paraetonium lies on this Great Sea, which washes between all regions and lands of the middle world.

From there it runs through the places the inhabitants call Catabathmon, not far from the camp of Alexander the Great and above Lake Chalearzus, then along the borders of the Upper Auasitae, and stretching crosswise through the deserts of Ethiopia it reaches the southern Ocean.
Africa's boundaries to the west are the same as Europe's, that is, the mouth of the Strait of Gades.
Its farthest limit is Mount Atlas and the islands they call the Fortunate Isles.
Since I have briefly given the general divisions of the threefold world, I shall also take care, as I promised, to describe the regions of the parts themselves.

ASIA has, at the middle of its eastern front, the mouths of the river Ganges on the Eastern Ocean; on the left, the promontory of Caligardamana, off which to the southeast lies the island of Taprobane, from which the Ocean begins to be called the Indian Ocean;
on the right it has the promontory of Samara on Mount Imaus, where the Caucasus ends, below which to the north lie the mouths of the river Ottorogorra, from which the Ocean is called the Seric Ocean.

Within these limits is INDIA, which has on the west the river Indus, which is received by the Red Sea, and on the north Mount Caucasus; the rest of it, as I said, is bounded by the Eastern and the Indian Ocean.
It contains forty-four peoples, not counting the island of Taprobane, which has ten cities, and not counting a great many other inhabitable islands.
From the river Indus, which lies to the east, to the river Tigris, which lies to the west, are these regions: ARACHOSIA, PARTHIA, ASSYRIA, PERSIS AND MEDIA, a mountainous and rugged country.

They have Mount Caucasus to the north, and to the south the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, while through the middle flow the principal rivers, the Hydaspes and the Arbis. In them are thirty-two peoples.
But the whole is generally called Parthia, although the Holy Scriptures often call it all Media.
From the river Tigris to the river Euphrates is MESOPOTAMIA, which begins in the north between Mount Taurus and the Caucasus.
To the south it is followed by Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and lastly Arabia Eudaemon, which stretches eastward in a narrow tract of land between the Persian and the Arabian Gulfs.
In these are twenty-eight peoples.

From the river Euphrates, which lies to the east, to Our Sea, which lies to the west; then from the north, that is, from the city of Dagusa, which lies on the border of Cappadocia and Armenia not far from the place where the Euphrates rises, to

Egypt and the farthest end of the Arabian Gulf, which stretches westward from the Red Sea, that is, from the Ocean, toward the south in a long, narrow channel crowded with rocks and islands, the land is generally called SYRIA. Its largest provinces are Commagene, Phoenicia and Palestine, not counting the Saracens and the Nabataeans, whose peoples number twelve.

At the head of Syria is CAPPADOCIA, which has Armenia on the east, Asia on the west, the Themiscyrian plains and the Cimmerian Sea on the north, and on the south Mount Taurus, below which lie Cilicia and Isauria, as far as the Cilician Gulf, which faces the island of Cyprus.

The REGION OF ASIA, or, to speak properly, Asia Minor, is surrounded on all sides by sea except on its eastern side, where it extends toward Cappadocia and Syria: on the north by the Euxine Sea, on the west by the Propontis and the Hellespont, and on the south by Our Sea. There is Mount Olympus.
LOWER EGYPT has Syria Palaestina on the east, Libya on the west, Our Sea on the north, and on the south the mountain called Climax, and Upper Egypt, and the river

Nile, which seems to rise from the shore where the Red Sea begins, at the place called the Mossylon trading post; then, flowing westward for a long way and forming in its midst an island called Meroe, it finally bends northward and, swollen by its seasonal floods, waters the plains of Egypt.
Some authors say that it has its source not far from Atlas and immediately sinks

into the sands; then, after a short distance, it overflows into a vast lake, and from there it glides eastward through the Ethiopian deserts as far as the Ocean, and bending again to the left, it comes down to Egypt.

It is indeed true that there is a great river of this kind, with such a source and such a course, and that it truly produces all the monsters of the Nile; near its source the barbarians call it Dara, while the other inhabitants call it Nuhul.

But this river, in the region of the peoples called the Libyo-Egyptians, not far from the river which we said bursts forth from the shore of the Red Sea, is received into an immense lake and swallowed up,
unless perhaps it discharges by a hidden channel into the bed of the river that comes down from the east.
UPPER EGYPT stretches a long way to the east.
On its north is the Arabian Gulf, on its south the Ocean. On the west it begins from Lower Egypt, and on the east it is bounded by the Red Sea. There are twenty-four peoples there.
Now that we have described the southern part of all Asia, it remains to set out the part that is left, from the east to the north.

MOUNT CAUCASUS first rises between the Colchians, who live above the Cimmerian Sea, and the Albanians, who live by the Caspian Sea. All the way to the farthest east it appears to be a single ridge, but it has many names.
Many would have this ridge believed to be that of Mount Taurus, because in fact Mount Parcohatras in Armenia, lying between the Taurus and the Caucasus, is thought to join the Taurus to the Caucasus.

But that this is not so is shown by the river Euphrates, which, pouring out from the foot of Mount Parcohatras and making its way south, keeps that mountain on its left and shuts off the Taurus on its right.
So the Caucasus itself, between the Colchians and the Albanians, where it also has gates, is called Mount Caucasus;
from the Caspian Gates to the Armenian Gates, or to the source of the river Tigris, between Armenia and Iberia, the mountains are called the Acroceraunian Mountains;
from the source of the Tigris to the city of Carrae, between the Massagetae and the Parthians, it is Mount Ariobarzanes;
from the city of Carrae to the town of Cathippus, between the Hyrcanians and the Bactrians, it is Mount Memarmali, where amomum grows; the ridge next to it is called Mount Parthau;
from the town of Cathippus to the village of Safris, between the Dahae, the Sacaraucae and the Parthyenae, it is Mount Oscobares, where the river Ganges rises and silphium grows;
from the source of the river Ganges to the sources of the river Ottorogorra, which lie to the north, where the mountain-dwelling Paropanisadae live, it is Mount Taurus;
from the sources of the Ottorogorra to the city of Ottorogorra, between the Chuni Scythians and the Gandaridae, it is Mount Caucasus.
The last, between the Eoae and the Passyadrae, is Mount Imaus, where the river Chrysorhoas and the promontory of Samara are received by the eastern Ocean.

So from Mount Imaus, that is, from the lowest end of the Caucasus, and from the right-hand side of the east where the Seric Ocean stretches, to the Boreum promontory and the river Boreus; from there along the Scythian Sea, which is to the north, to the Caspian Sea, which is to the west; and as far as the long ridge of the Caucasus, which is to the south, there are forty-two peoples of Hyrcanians and Scythians, who wander far and wide because the land spread out before them is barren.

THE CASPIAN SEA rises from the Ocean in the northern region; both its shores near the Ocean are deserted and uncultivated. From there it stretches southward through a long narrow strait, until, having widened out over a great expanse, it ends at the foot of Mount Caucasus.

So from the Caspian Sea, which is to the east, along the coast of the northern Ocean to the river Tanais and the Maeotic Marshes, which are to the west, along the shore of the Cimmerian Sea, which is to the southwest, to the head and gates of the Caucasus, which are to the south, there are thirty-four peoples.
But in general the nearer region is called Albania, and the farther one, below the Caspian Sea and mountain, the land of the Amazons.
The boundaries of Asia have been set out as briefly as possible. Now I shall range with my pen over EUROPE, so far as it is granted to human knowledge.

It begins from the Riphaean Mountains, the river Tanais and the Maeotic Marshes, which are to the east, and runs along the shore of the northern Ocean to Gallia Belgica and the river Rhine, which comes down from the west,
and then to the Danube, which they also call the Hister, which lies to the south and, running eastward, is received by the Pontus. To the east is Alania,
in the middle is Dacia, where Gothia also lies, and then Germany, the greater part of which is held by the Suebi. Of all these there are fifty-four peoples.
Now I will set out everything that the Danube separates from barbarian territory, down to Our Sea.

MOESIA has on the east the mouths of the river Danube, on the southeast Thrace, on the south Macedonia, on the southwest Dalmatia, on the west Histria, on the northwest Pannonia, and on the north the Danube.

THRACE has on the east the gulf of the Propontis and the city of Constantinople, which was formerly called Byzantium; on the north part of Dalmatia and a gulf of the Euxine Sea; on the west and southwest Macedonia; and on the south the Aegean Sea.

MACEDONIA has on the east the Aegean Sea, on the northeast Thrace, on the southeast Euboea and the Macedonian Gulf, on the south Achaea, on the west the Acroceraunian Mountains at the narrows of the Adriatic Gulf (these mountains lie opposite Apulia and Brundisium), on the west Dalmatia, on the northwest Dardania, and on the north Moesia.

ACHAEA is surrounded by sea on almost every side. On the east it has the Myrtoan Sea, on the southeast the Cretan Sea, on the south the Ionian Sea, on the southwest and west the islands of Cephalonia and Cassiope, on the north the Corinthian Gulf, and on the northeast a narrow ridge of land by which it is joined to Macedonia, or rather to Attica. This place is called the Isthmus, and on it stands Corinth, which has not far off to the northeast, in Attica, the city of Athens.
DALMATIA has on the east Macedonia, on the northeast Dardania, on the north Moesia, on the west Histria, the Liburnian Gulf and the Liburnian islands, and on the south the Adriatic Gulf.

PANNONIA, NORICUM AND RAETIA have on the east Moesia, on the south Histria, on the southwest the Pennine Alps, on the west Belgic Gaul, on the northwest the source of the Danube and the frontier that separates Germany from Gaul between the Danube and Gaul, and on the north the Danube and Germany.

THE LIE OF ITALY stretches from northwest to southeast. It has on the southwest the Tyrrhenian Sea and on the northeast the Adriatic Gulf. The part of it which borders on and touches the mainland is shut off by the barrier of the Alps.
These rise from the Gallic Sea above the Ligurian Gulf and first close off the territory of the people of Narbonensis, then Gaul and Raetia, until they come to rest at the Liburnian Gulf.

BELGIC GAUL has on the east the frontier of the river Rhine and Germany, on the southeast the Pennine Alps, on the south the province of Narbonensis, on the west the province of Lugdunensis, on the northwest the British Ocean, and on the north the island of Britain.
LUGDUNENSIAN GAUL, drawn out lengthwise and bent round in a narrow strip, half encircles the province of Aquitania.
It has on the east Belgica and on the south part of the province of Narbonensis, where the city of Arles is situated and where the river Rhône is received into the Gallic Sea.

THE PROVINCE OF NARBONENSIS, part of THE GAULS, has on the east the Cottian Alps, on the west Spain, on the northwest Aquitania, on the north Lugdunensis, on the northeast Belgic Gaul, and on the south the Gallic Sea, which lies between Sardinia and the Balearic Islands. Off its coast, where the river Rhône flows into the sea, lie the Stoechades Islands.
THE PROVINCE OF AQUITANIA is bent into a curve by the slanting course of the river Loire, which for the most part forms its boundary.

On the northwest it has the ocean, which is called the Aquitanian Gulf, and on the west the Spains; on the north and east it borders Lugdunensis, and on the southeast and south the province of Narbonensis.
SPAIN as a whole is triangular in shape, and since it is surrounded by the Ocean and the Tyrrhenian Sea it is almost an island.
Its first angle, facing east, hemmed in on the right by the province of Aquitania and on the left by the Balearic Sea, thrusts into the territory of Narbonensis.
The second angle points toward the northwest. There Brigantia, a city of Gallaecia, raises a very tall lighthouse, one of the few works worth recording, looking out toward Britain.
Its third angle is where the islands of Gades, facing southwest, look across an inlet of the Ocean toward Mount Atlas.

Hither Spain begins in the east, and the Pyrenean range carries its northern side as far as the Cantabri and the Astures; from there, passing through the Vaccaei and the Oretani, whom it has on the west, it is bounded by Carthage, which lies on the shore of Our Sea.

Further Spain has on the east the Vaccaei, the Celtiberians and the Oretani, on the north the Ocean, on the west the Ocean, and on the south the Gaditanian strait of the Ocean, through which Our Sea, called the Tyrrhenian, flows in.
And since the Ocean contains islands called Britain and Ireland, which lie off the far side of the Gauls, facing Spain, they will be briefly described.

BRITAIN, an island of the Ocean, stretches lengthwise toward the northeast; on the south it has the Gauls. Its nearest shore is reached by those crossing over at a city called Rutupiae Harbor, from which it looks out toward the Menapii and the Batavi, who are situated not far from the Morini to the south.
This island is eight hundred miles long and two hundred miles wide.
Behind it, where it lies open to the boundless Ocean, it has the Orkney Islands, of which twenty are uninhabited and thirteen are inhabited.
Then there is the island of Thule, which is separated from the others by an immense distance and lies toward the northwest in the middle of the Ocean; it is known to scarcely any.
THE ISLAND OF IRELAND lies between Britain and Spain, and stretches over a long distance from southwest to northeast.

Its nearer parts, facing the Cantabrian Ocean, look out across a wide stretch of sea toward Brigantia, the city of Gallaecia, which faces it from the southwest toward the northwest; this is especially true of the promontory where the mouth of the river Scena lies and where the Velabri and the Luceni live. This island is nearer to Britain and smaller in area, but more productive because of its mild climate and soil; it is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.
Very near to it lies the island of Man, which is itself of no small size and has good soil; it too is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.
These are the boundaries of the whole of Europe.
As I have said, when our forebears described AFRICA as to be reckoned the third part of the world, they followed not the measurement of areas but the logic of the divisions.
For this Great Sea, which rises from the Ocean in the west, bends more toward the south and so has made the territory of Africa narrower, squeezed as it is between the sea and the Ocean.

For this reason some, recognizing that although Africa is equal to Europe in length it is much narrower, thought it unseemly to call it a third part; they assigned Africa instead to Europe and preferred to call it a portion of the second part.

Moreover, much more land in Africa lies uncultivated and unknown because of the heat of the sun than in Europe because of the severity of the cold, since nearly all creatures, whether animals or plants, endure the extreme of cold more patiently and easily than the extreme of heat. This, of course, is why Africa appears smaller in every respect, both in extent and in population: by its very nature it has less space, and because of its harsh climate more of it is desert. Its description by provinces and peoples is as follows:
LIBYA CYRENAICA AND PENTAPOLIS is the first region in Africa after Egypt.

It begins at the city of Paraetonium and the Catabathmon Mountains, and from there extends along the sea as far as the Altars of the Philaeni. Behind it, as far as the southern Ocean, it has the peoples of the Libyo-Ethiopians and the Garamantes.
On the east it has Egypt, on the north the Libyan Sea, on the west the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes (opposite whom is the island of Calypso), and on the south the Ethiopian Ocean.

THE PROVINCE OF TRIPOLITANIA, which is also called Subventana or the region of the Arzuges, where the city of Leptis Magna is (although the name Arzuges is applied generally along the whole long frontier of Africa), has on the east the Altars of the Philaeni between the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes; on the north the Sicilian, or rather the Adriatic, Sea and the Lesser Syrtes; on the west Byzacium as far as the Lake of the Salt-pans; and on the south the barbarian Gaetulians, Nathabres and Garamantes, who reach as far as the Ethiopian Ocean.
BYZACIUM, ZEUGIS AND NUMIDIA. We find that Zeugis was formerly the general name not of a single district but of the whole province.

Byzacium, then, where the city of Hadrumetum is, Zeugis, where Great Carthage is, and Numidia, where the cities of Hippo Regius and Rusicade are, have on the east the Lesser Syrtes and the Lake of the Salt-pans; on the north Our Sea, which faces the islands of Sicily and Sardinia; on the west Mauretania Sitifensis; and on the south the Uzara Mountains and, beyond them, the peoples of the Ethiopians, who roam as far as the Ethiopian Ocean.

THE MAURETANIAS, SITIFENSIS AND CAESARIENSIS, have on the east Numidia, on the north Our Sea, on the west the river Malva, and on the south Mount Astrixis, which separates the fertile land from the sands that stretch as far as the Ocean. Over these sands wander the Gangines Ethiopians.

TINGITANIAN MAURETANIA is the last part of Africa. It has on the east the river Malva; on the north Our Sea as far as the Strait of Gades, which is narrowed between the two facing promontories of Abenna and Calpe; on the west Mount Atlas and the Atlantic Ocean; toward the southwest Mount Hesperius; and on the south the peoples of the Autololes, who are now called the Galaules, reaching as far as the Hesperian Ocean.
This is the boundary of all Africa. Now I will measure out the positions, names and extents of the islands that lie in Our Sea.

THE ISLAND OF CYPRUS is bounded on the east by the Syrian Sea, which is called the Gulf of Issus; on the west by the Pamphylian Sea; on the north by the Cilician Strait; and on the south by the sea of Syria and Phoenicia. Its extent is one hundred and seventy-five miles in length and one hundred and twenty-five miles in width.

THE ISLAND OF CRETE is bounded on the east by the Carpathian Sea, on the west and north by the Cretan Sea, and on the south by the Libyan Sea, which is also called the Adriatic. It is one hundred and seventy-two miles long and fifty wide.

THE CYCLADES ISLANDS, of which the first on the east is Rhodes, on the north Tenedos, on the south Carpathos and on the west Cythera, are bounded on the east by the shores of Asia, on the west by the Icarian Sea, on the north by the Aegean Sea, and on the south by the Carpathian Sea. There are fifty-four Cyclades in all. They extend five hundred miles from north to south and two hundred miles from east to west.

THE ISLAND OF SICILY has three promontories. The first, called Pelorus, faces northeast, and the city of Messana is nearest to it. The second, called Pachynum, below which lies the city of Syracuse, faces southeast. The third, called Lilybaeum, where a city of the same name is also situated, points west.

From Pelorus to Pachynum is one hundred and fifty-nine miles, and from Pachynum to Lilybaeum one hundred and eighty-seven. It is bounded on the east by the Adriatic Sea; on the south by the African Sea, which lies opposite the Subventani and the Lesser Syrtes; on the west and north it has the Tyrrhenian Sea; and from the northeast round to the east the Adriatic strait, which separates the people of Tauromenium in Sicily from the Bruttii in Italy.

THE ISLANDS OF SARDINIA AND CORSICA are separated by a narrow strait, twenty miles wide. Of these, Sardinia has on the south, facing Numidia, the people of Caralis, and facing the island of Corsica, that is, toward the north, it has the people of Ulbia.

Its extent is two hundred and thirty miles in length and eighty miles in width. It has on the east and northeast the Tyrrhenian Sea, which faces the port of the city of Rome; on the west the Sardinian Sea; on the southwest the Balearic Islands, which lie far off; on the south the Numidian Gulf; and on the north, as I have said, Corsica.

THE ISLAND OF CORSICA is jagged with many promontories. It has on the east the Tyrrhenian Sea and the port of the City; on the south Sardinia; on the west the Balearic Islands; and on the northwest and north the Ligurian Gulf. It is one hundred and sixty miles long and twenty-six miles wide.

THE BALEARIC ISLANDS are two, the Greater and the Lesser, and each contains two towns. The Greater faces Tarraco, a city of Spain, and the Lesser faces Barcelona, toward the north. Below the Greater lies the island of Ebusus. Further, they face Sardinia on the east, the Gallic Sea on the northeast, the Mauretanian Sea on the south and southwest, and the Iberian Sea on the west.
These are the islands situated throughout the whole Great Sea from the Hellespont to the Ocean that are held to be the most famous, both for their cultivation and for their place in memory.

I have surveyed briefly, as best I could, the provinces and islands of the whole world. Now, so far as I am able, I will set out the particular miseries of each people, how they have arisen without ceasing from the beginning, and how they came about for each.

After the making and adorning of this world, when man, whom God had made upright and without blemish, and consequently the human race, had been corrupted by lusts and befouled by sins, just punishment at once followed unjust licence.

The sentence of God, the Creator and Judge, was appointed for sinful man, and for the earth on man's account, and will last as long as men inhabit the earth. All of us, however unwillingly, either prove it by denying it or endure it while confessing it; and on obstinate minds, whom Scripture has not persuaded to believe, their own weakness brands it as a witness against them.

Then the sea poured back over all the earth and the Flood was sent; and when the whole world was covered, so that sky and sea formed a single expanse, the entire human race was destroyed, apart from a few who were preserved in the ark through the merit of their faith to renew its stock. This the most truthful writers teach most clearly.

Yet that it happened has been attested even by those who, though ignorant of past times and of the very Author of time, have nevertheless learned it by inference from the evidence of the stones we often see on remote mountains, encrusted with shells and oysters and often hollowed out by water.

And although we could still bring forward other things of this kind, both worth telling and of assured credibility, let these two, as the principal ones, suffice: the transgression of the first man and the condemnation of his descendants and his life, and then the destruction of the whole human race;
only so that, if the pagan historians have in any order touched upon matters of ours, these may be set out more fully along with the rest in the very order in which they come up.

In the year 1300 before the founding of the City, Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was the first, as they themselves maintain, to carry his arms abroad out of a lust to extend his dominion, and for fifty years he led a bloody life of war throughout all Asia.

Setting out from the south and from the Red Sea, he devastated and subdued the Euxine Sea in the far north, and he taught the barbarous Scythians, who were till then unwarlike and harmless, to rouse their dormant savagery, to know their own strength, to drink no longer the milk of their flocks but the blood of men, and in the end to conquer even as they were being conquered.

Finally he defeated in battle and killed Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, who is also said to have been the inventor of the magic arts. Afterwards he himself, while besieging a city that had revolted from him, was struck by an arrow and died.

On his death he was succeeded by his wife Semiramis, a man in spirit who dressed as her son. For forty-two years she kept her peoples, already greedy for blood by habit, busy with the slaughter of nations.

Not content with the borders which she had inherited, won by her husband, then the only warrior, over fifty years, this woman added to her empire Ethiopia, crushed by war and drenched in blood. She also made war on the Indians, whose land no one but she and Alexander the Great ever entered.

To hunt down and slaughter peoples living in peace was at that time all the more cruel and grievous than it is now, because in those days they had neither the fires of war abroad nor such indulgence of greed at home.

Burning with lust and thirsting for blood, amid ceaseless debaucheries and murders, she would kill every man whom she had summoned like a queen, kept like a harlot and enjoyed in bed. At last, having shamefully conceived a son, impiously exposed him and incestuously lain with him, she covered her private disgrace with a public crime.
For she decreed that between parents and children no reverence for nature should be observed in seeking marriage, but each should be free to do as he pleased.

In the year 1160 before the founding of the City, the region bordering on Arabia, which was then called Pentapolis, was utterly consumed by fire from heaven. Among others Cornelius Tacitus records this, saying:

"Not far from there are plains which, they say, were once fertile and inhabited by great cities, but were burned up by the stroke of thunderbolts; traces remain, and the very soil, though solid in appearance, has lost its power to bear fruit."
And though at this point, as if ignorant, he said nothing about the cities being burned on account of men's sins, a little later, as if forgetting his intention, he adds:
"While I would grant that cities once famous were consumed by fire from heaven, I think that the land is tainted and corrupted by the exhalation of the lake."

By saying this he admitted, however unwillingly, that he both knew of and conceded the burning of the cities, which without doubt were consumed for the guilt of their sins, and he plainly revealed that it was not knowledge that he lacked but the will to declare his belief. This I will now set out more fully.
On the border of Arabia and Palestine, where the mountains slope down on either side and give way to the plains below, there were five cities: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Zoar.

Of these Zoar was small, but the others were large and great, for they enjoyed a fertile soil, and the river Jordan, spreading across the plains and divided into channels most conveniently, was spent on increasing their abundance.

For this whole region, which made bad use of good things, its very abundance was the cause of its evils. For out of abundance grew luxury, and out of luxury foul lusts, to such a degree that men, committing shameful acts with men, rushed into them without regard even for place, circumstance or age.
So God in his anger rained fire and brimstone on this land, and burned up the whole region with its peoples and cities, condemning it to everlasting destruction as a future witness to his judgment,

so that even now the shape of the region can be seen, but a region of ash is what one finds, and the valley in the middle, which the Jordan used to water, is now covered by a sea that has spread over it.

So greatly was the divine wrath kindled over what are thought to be small matters that, because those people misused good things and made the fruits of God's mercy into the food of their lusts, the very land that had held these cities was first burned by fire and then overwhelmed by water, and so perished from common sight in everlasting damnation.

So now, if they please, let those who, as far as in them lies, spit upon Christ, whom we have shown to be the Judge of the ages, distinguish between the causes of Sodom and Rome and compare their punishments. I need not go over these again, chiefly because they are known to all.
And yet how gladly I would hear their opinions, if only they would honestly confess them as they really hold them.

Still, since only a few mutter about Christian times, and that in corners, I do not think it should be taken too hard, when the feeling and the talk of the whole Roman people, expressed with one voice and one judgment, are well known.

For that people has most unmistakably testified that its accustomed pleasures were checked only briefly by a small and slight disturbance, so that it cried out freely: "If it got the circus back, nothing had been done to it"; that is, the swords of the Goths had done nothing at Rome, provided the Romans were allowed to watch the circus games.

Unless perhaps, as happens with many people especially at this time, who after long repose think even a little trouble that arises an unbearable hardship, they rank these most merciful warnings, by which all of us are touched at one time or another, above the punishments of others that they have heard and read about.
These people, at least, I warn by this very end of Sodom and Gomorrah, so that they may learn and understand how God has punished sinners, how he is able to punish them, and how he will punish them.

In the year 1070 before the founding of the City, the Telchines and the Caryathii fought a stubborn battle against Phoroneus, king of the Argives, and the Parrhasians, with uncertain hopes and no fruit of victory.

A little later the same Telchines, defeated in war and driven from their homeland, ignorant of the world and believing that they were withdrawing entirely from contact with all human habitation, took the island of Rhodes, formerly called Ophiussa, as though it were a safe possession.

In the year 1040 before the founding of the City, there was a savage flood in Achaea which laid waste almost the whole province. Because it poured forth in the time of Ogyges, who was then the founder and king of Eleusis, it gave his name to the place and the period.

In the year 1008 before the founding of the City, there was in Egypt first an extraordinary abundance, more than could be wanted, and then a long and unbearable famine, which Joseph, a just and wise man, relieved through divine foresight. So the historian Pompeius and his abridger Justin relate; among other things
he says: "Joseph was the youngest of the brothers. His brothers, fearing his outstanding abilities, seized him and sold him to foreign merchants.

Carried off by them into Egypt, he learned the magic arts there with his shrewd intelligence and soon became very dear to the king himself. For he was most skilled in interpreting portents and was the first to establish the understanding of dreams, and nothing of divine or human law seemed unknown to him,

so much so that, foreseeing many years in advance a coming barrenness of the fields, he had gathered in the crops; and so remarkable were the proofs of his skill that his answers seemed to come not from a man but from God.

Joseph's son was Moses, who was commended not only by inheriting his father's knowledge but also by the beauty of his appearance. But when the Egyptians were suffering from scabies and leprosy, they were warned by an oracle and drove him out of the borders of Egypt together with the sick, so that the plague should not spread to more people."
So says Justin.

But since this same Moses, whom these writers attest to have been wise and learned, wrote of these things more fully and more truly, as deeds done by himself and his people, the ignorance of these writers must first be supplemented by his trustworthiness and authority, which even they acknowledge,

Next, the deceitful malice of the Egyptian priests must be refuted. Either out of cunning, which is the more obvious explanation, they tried to erase from memory the evident wrath and mercy of the true God by a confused and piecemeal account, so that they would not have to show, to the shame of their idols, that he deserved to be worshipped by whose counsel, as they would have had to admit, these evils were foretold and by whose help they were escaped; or perhaps, to take it more charitably, they simply forgot.

For through the foresight of our Joseph, who was a servant of the true God and was devoutly and attentively concerned for his Lord's creation, they themselves, being priests, had grain in abundance; but because they were false priests, they felt no grief with the others who were starving. Indeed, the one who is comfortable forgets; the one who suffers remembers.

Yet although histories and annals are silent about the events of that time, the land of Egypt itself stands as its own witness. Brought under royal control at that time and then restored to its cultivators, it has paid, down to the present day, an unceasing tax of a fifth of all its produce.
This great famine, then, took place under a Diospolitan king of the Egyptians named Amosis, at the time when Baleus ruled the Assyrians and Apis the Argives.

Before the seven years of famine there had been seven other years of plenty. Their abundance, which would have been squandered all the more carelessly the more richly it had been produced, our Joseph gathered and stored by his skill, and so preserved the whole of Egypt.

He acquired all the money for Pharaoh and glory for God, rendering by a most just administration tax to whom tax was due and honour to whom honour was due. He took in the herds, lands and property of everyone; but those who had sold themselves along with their lands in return for an allowance of food he set free on a fixed agreement to pay a fifth part.

Who would believe that this Joseph, whom God appointed as the author of the Egyptians' survival, could have slipped so quickly from their memory that a little later they consigned his sons and his whole kindred to slavery, afflicted them with hard labour, and destroyed them by slaughter?

It is no wonder, therefore, if even now some are found who, having turned aside the sword hanging over their necks by holding up the Christian name, either hide or slander the very name of Christ, by which alone they have been saved, and claim that they are oppressed by the times of those through whose merits they are set free.

In the 810th year before the founding of the City, Amphictyon, third in line from Cecrops, reigned at Athens. In his time a flood of waters destroyed the greater part of the peoples of Thessaly, a few being saved by taking refuge in the mountains, chiefly on Mount Parnassus, in whose region Deucalion then held the kingship.
He took in those who fled to him on rafts, and sheltered and fed them on the twin peaks of Parnassus; and for this reason, it is said, the human race was restored by him.
At that time also, as Plato bears witness, a great many plagues and dreadful diseases raged in Ethiopia, almost to the point of leaving it a desert.

And lest anyone should think that the times of God's wrath and the times of war's fury are separate, in that same period Father Liber subdued India, drenched it in blood, filled it with slaughter and defiled it with lust — a nation, mind you, that had never been subject to anyone and was content simply with its own native peace.

In the 805th year before the founding of the City, Pompeius and Cornelius testify that unspeakable evils and unbearable plagues fell upon the Egyptians. Both of them set out to relate these things in connection with the Jews, but their disagreement has troubled me somewhat.

For Pompeius, or Justin, speaks as follows: "When the Egyptians were suffering from scabies and leprosy, they were warned by an oracle and drove Moses, together with the sick, beyond the borders of Egypt, so that the disease would not spread to more people. Having thus become the leader of the exiles, he stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians; and the Egyptians, trying to recover them by force of arms, were driven back home by storms."

Cornelius, on the other hand, says this about the same matter: "Most authors agree that when a wasting disease that disfigured the body had broken out throughout Egypt, King Bocchoris went to the oracle of Ammon to seek a remedy, and was ordered to purge his kingdom and to carry that race of men off to other lands as hateful to the gods.

So the multitude was sought out and gathered together, and after it had been abandoned in desolate places, while the rest lay stupefied in tears, Moses, one of the exiles, urged them not to look for any help from gods or men, but to trust themselves to a heavenly leader, by whose help they had first driven off their present miseries."

So Cornelius says that the Jews were driven out into the desert under compulsion from the Egyptians themselves, and then he incautiously adds that by the help of Moses their leader they had driven off their miseries in Egypt. This shows that certain things vigorously accomplished through Moses have been concealed.

Justin likewise asserts that Moses, expelled along with his people, stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians, and that the Egyptians, attempting to recover them by force of arms, were checked and driven back by storms and returned home. Here too he has revealed something more, though not the whole of what the other concealed.
Therefore, since both of them have borne witness to Moses, that great leader, let the events be set out from Moses himself, just as they were both done and recorded by him.

When the Egyptians were tormenting with hard labour the people of God — that is, the race of Joseph, by whose help they themselves had been saved — oppressing them with slavery and, worse still, forcing them by a cruel decree to kill their own offspring, God commanded through Moses, his messenger, that his people be set free to serve him.
Scorned, he punished the obstinate with the harshest penalties; and they, weighed down and crushed by ten plagues, at last forced those whom they had refused to release even to hasten away.

AFTER the waters were turned into blood, offering to those burning with thirst remedies worse than the punishment itself; AFTER the hideous filth of frogs crawling over everything, clean and unclean alike; AFTER the stinging gnats, impossible to escape anywhere, as the whole air quivered with them;

AFTER the dog-flies, darting about with horrid movements even through the inward parts of the body and cruelly inflicting torments as painful as they were shameful; AFTER the sudden ruin and universal destruction of all the flocks and beasts of burden; AFTER the seething blisters and running sores and, as they themselves preferred to call it, the scabies and leprosy breaking out over their whole bodies;

AFTER the hail mixed with fire, crushing men, herds and trees on every side; AFTER the clouds of locusts, which, when everything else had been consumed, went after even the very roots of the crops; AFTER the darkness, dreadful with apparitions,

so thick it could be touched, deadly in its long duration; and finally, AFTER the same death of the firstborn throughout all Egypt and an equal storm of bereavement falling on everyone — those who had not yielded to God when he commanded yielded to him when he punished. But soon, in a most wicked change of heart, they dared to pursue those they had released, and paid the final penalty for their abominable obstinacy.

For their king led the entire army of Egypt, equipped with chariots and cavalry, against the wandering people. We can estimate its size chiefly from this one fact: that six hundred thousand men feared it and fled.

But God, the protector of the oppressed and the avenger of the obstinate, suddenly divided the Red Sea, and, widening the edges on either side, held up the walls of stiffened waves like the face of a mountain, so that, lured on by the hope of an unobstructed path, the godly entered a way of salvation they had despaired of, and the ungodly a pit of death they had not expected.

And so, while the Hebrews walked safely over dry ground, the masses of standing water poured back behind them, and the whole multitude of Egypt was overwhelmed and killed together with its king; and the entire province, already tormented by the plagues, was emptied by this final slaughter.

Most certain memorials of these events survive even now. For the tracks of the chariots and the ruts of the wheels can be seen not only on the shore but also in the deep, as far as the eye can reach; and if they happen to be disturbed for a time, whether by chance or by curiosity, they are immediately restored by divine power to their former appearance by the winds and waves,
so that whoever is not taught the fear of God through zeal for the religion he has revealed may be terrified of his wrath by the example of the vengeance he once took.

In these times, too, so unremitting and severe a heat blazed that the sun, carried off its course, is said not to have warmed the whole world but to have scorched it with fire; the Ethiopian could not bear the heat bearing down on him, which was greater than usual, nor could the Scythian, who was unused to it. From this, certain people, unwilling to grant God his ineffable power and searching for empty little explanations, have spun the ridiculous fable of Phaethon.

Likewise, in the 775th year before the founding of the City, fifty murders of kin were committed in a single night among the children of the brothers Danaus and Aegyptus. Then Danaus himself, the contriver of such great crimes, was driven from the kingdom he had acquired by so many outrages and withdrew to Argos. There, having shamefully persuaded the Argives to join in his crime, he drove from the kingdom Sthenelas, who had taken him in as a destitute fugitive, and reigned in his place.

At that time in Egypt there was the cruel hospitality and the still crueller religion of Busiris, a most bloodthirsty tyrant, who offered the blood of innocent guests as a drink to the gods who shared in his crimes. This was without doubt abominable to men; I should like to know whether it seemed abominable to the gods themselves as well.

At that time also the murder of a kinsman was added to the incest of Tereus, Procne and Philomela, and, more abominable than either, a banquet of unspeakable food, when, because her sister's chastity had been ravished and her tongue cut out, the mother killed her little son and the father ate him.

In those same times Perseus crossed from Greece into Asia, where he subdued the barbarian nations in a hard and long war, and finally, as victor, gave his name to the conquered people: for from Perseus they came to be called Persians.

But I am now forced to confess that, for the sake of reaching my end, I am passing over a great many of the evils of the world that surround me on every side, and abridging everything. For I could never get through so dense a forest unless I sometimes flew over it in frequent leaps.

For since the kingdom of the Assyrians lasted 1,160 years, down to Sardanapalus, through nearly fifty kings, and almost never rested from waging or suffering wars until that time, what end will be found if we try to record them by listing them, not to say by describing them?

Especially as the wars of the Greeks are not to be passed over, and those of the Romans above all must be reviewed. Nor do I need to recount now the shameful deeds of Tantalus and Pelops, and the still more shameful stories told about them.

Of these two, Tantalus, king of the Phrygians, having most shamefully carried off Ganymede, son of Tros king of the Dardanians, kept hold of him in a still fouler contest that broke out over him, as the poet Phanocles affirms, who records that a very great war was stirred up for this reason;

or else, as the poet would have it, this same Tantalus, as a hanger-on of the gods, procured the abducted boy for Jupiter's lust in his role as a familiar pander — the same man who did not hesitate to serve up even his own son Pelops at Jupiter's banquet.

I am weary even of recounting the struggles of Pelops himself against Dardanus and the Trojans, however great; because they are commonly celebrated in the fables, people listen to them with little attention.
I also pass over what Palaephatus writes about Perseus, Cadmus, the Thebans and the Spartans, through endless recurrences of alternating evils.

I say nothing of the outrages of the Lemnian women; I omit the pitiable flight of Pandion, king of the Athenians; I leave aside the hatreds, rapes and murders of kin committed by Atreus and Thyestes, hateful even to heaven.

I omit Oedipus, killer of his father, husband of his mother, brother of his sons, stepfather to himself. I prefer to keep silent about how Eteocles and Polynices strove against each other in combat, so that neither of them should fail to be the murderer of a brother.

I do not wish to recall Medea, wounded by savage love and rejoicing in the slaughter of her little children, or whatever else was perpetrated in those times: one may guess how men endured things from which even the stars are said to have fled.

In the 560th year before the founding of the City there was a most savage conflict between the Cretans and the Athenians, in which, after both peoples had suffered wretched losses, the Cretans exercised a still bloodier victory.

They cruelly handed over the sons of noble Athenians to be devoured by the Minotaur — whether I should more properly call it a savage man or a human beast I do not know — and fattened that misshapen monster on the torn-out eyes of Greece.
In those same days the Lapiths and the Thessalians fought in all too famous battles.

But Palaephatus, in the first book of his Incredible Tales, reports that the Thessalians themselves were thought by the Lapiths to be Centaurs, and were so called, because as horsemen dashing about in war they looked like a single body of horse and man.

In the 480th year before the founding of the City, Vesozes, king of Egypt, eager either to embroil in war or to unite in one kingdom the south and the north, regions separated by almost the whole of the sky and sea, was the first to declare war on the Scythians, first sending envoys to dictate terms of submission to the enemy.

To this the Scythians replied to the envoys that the immensely wealthy king had foolishly undertaken a war against the poor, a war which he himself, on the contrary, ought rather to fear, since the outcome of war was uncertain and it offered no rewards and obvious losses. Moreover, they would not wait for him to come to them, but would go out of their own accord to meet their plunder.

There was no delay, for deeds followed words. First they forced Vesozes himself to flee in terror back into his kingdom; then they attacked his abandoned army and seized all its equipment of war; and they would have ravaged the whole of Egypt as well had they not been hindered by the marshes and driven back.

Turning back from there at once, they subdued Asia with endless slaughter and made it pay tribute. After lingering there for fifteen years without peace, they were at last called home by the demands of their wives, who declared that unless they returned they would seek children from their neighbours.

Meanwhile, among the Scythians, two young princes, Plynos and Scolopetius, driven from home by a faction of the nobles, took a great host of young men with them and settled on the coast of Pontic Cappadocia near the river Thermodon, making themselves masters of the Themiscyrian plains. There, after plundering all their neighbours for a long time, they were treacherously slaughtered through a conspiracy of the neighbouring peoples.

Their wives, stirred by exile and widowhood, took up arms; and so that all might share the same spirit from the same condition, they killed the husbands who had survived. Then, inflamed against the enemy by the blood of their own, they took vengeance for their slain husbands by destroying their neighbours.

Then, having won peace by arms, they took foreign men as partners, promptly killed the male children born to them, and carefully reared the females, burning off the infants' right breasts so that their shooting of arrows would not be hampered; hence they were called Amazons.
They had two queens, Marpesia and Lampeto, who divided their forces into two parts and took turns by lot in conducting the war and guarding the homeland.

So when they had subdued the greater part of Europe and had captured a number of cities in Asia, and had themselves founded Ephesus and other cities, they sent the main part of their army home laden with very rich spoils; the rest, left behind to hold their dominion in Asia, were slaughtered together with Queen Marpesia in an onslaught of the enemy.
Her daughter Sinope took her place, and crowned her singular glory in valour with lifelong virginity.

Such admiration and dread had seized the nations roused by their fame that even Hercules, when he was ordered by his master to bring back the queen's arms, as if he had been sent to certain danger, gathered all the choice and noble youth of Greece and prepared nine warships; and yet, not content with this great swarm of strength, he chose to attack without warning and to surround them unawares.

Two sisters were then ruling the kingdom, Antiope and Orithyia. Hercules, arriving by sea, overwhelmed them while they were unwary, unarmed and idle in the carelessness of peace. Among the very many who were killed or captured, two sisters of Antiope were taken: Melanippe by Hercules and Hippolyte by Theseus.
Theseus took Hippolyte in marriage, while Hercules returned Melanippe to her sister and received the queen's arms as the price of her ransom.
After Orithyia, Penthesilea gained the throne; we have heard of the most illustrious proofs of her valour among men in the Trojan War.

Alas, how shameful is human error! Women who were fugitives from their homeland entered, overran and laid waste Europe and Asia, that is, the largest and strongest parts of the world, and held them for almost a hundred years, overthrowing many cities and founding others; and yet the misery of mankind was not blamed on the hardship of the times.

But now those Getae who are now also called Goths — whom Alexander declared should be avoided, whom Pyrrhus dreaded, whom even Caesar shunned — having left and emptied their own homes, have entered the Roman provinces all together with their entire strength, and, though long held up as a terror, now seek by entreaty a place in an alliance with Rome which they could have claimed by force of arms.

They ask for a small place to live, not of their own choosing but at our judgment, though the whole earth lay subject and open to them, free to take as much as they pleased; they offer themselves for the defence of the Roman realm, they whom alone unconquered kingdoms feared.

And yet blind paganism, since it does not see that these things were accomplished by Roman valour, will not believe that they were obtained by Roman good faith; nor, though it understands, will it consent to confess that it is by the benefit of the Christian religion — which unites all peoples in a kindred faith — that the men of that race have been made subject to it without a battle, whose women destroyed the greater part of the world with immense slaughter.

Then, in the 430th year before the founding of the City, comes the celebrated story of the abduction of Helen, the confederacy of the Greeks and the gathering of a thousand ships, then the ten-year siege and finally the famous destruction of Troy.

In that war, waged most bloodily for ten years, what nations and how many peoples that same whirlwind swept up and afflicted, Homer, the foremost of poets, has made plain in his splendid poem; nor is it our business to go over it again in order now, since it would be long for this work and seems to be known to everyone.

Nevertheless, let those who have learned of the length of that siege, the atrocity of the destruction, the slaughter and the captivity, consider whether they are right to be offended by the present state of affairs, whatever it may be, when by the hidden mercy of God enemies who could pursue them in war across all lands with equipped forces instead follow them across every sea, offering hostages for the sake of peace; and lest they should perhaps be thought to do this out of love of quiet, they offer themselves and their own lives at risk against other nations for the peace of the Romans.

A few years later, what arms were stirred up by the arrival in Italy of Aeneas, the fugitive from Troy, what wars it aroused for three years, how many peoples it entangled and afflicted with hatred and destruction, has been branded on our memory too by the lessons of the grammar school.

Moreover, in the middle of these times lie the exiles and shipwrecks of the Greeks, the disasters of the Peloponnesians, broken at the death of Codrus, the Thracians, previously unknown, rising up in new wars, and a general upheaval at that time throughout all Asia and Greece.

In the 64th year before the founding of the City, Sardanapalus reigned as the last king of the Assyrians, a man more corrupt than a woman. He was seen among flocks of harlots, dressed as a woman and working purple wool on a distaff, by his prefect Arbatus, who was then governor of the Medes, and was held in loathing; soon afterwards, when the peoples of the Medes had been roused, he was challenged to war, and on being defeated he threw himself onto a burning pyre. Thereafter the kingdom of the Assyrians passed to the Medes.

Then, amid many battles breaking out on every side, which it seems by no means fitting to discuss in order, it passed through various fortunes to the Scythians and the Chaldaeans, and returned again by a similar path to the Medes.
In this brief account one must weigh how great were the ruins and disasters of nations, and how many wars poured forth, when so many such kingdoms changed hands so often.
After this Phraortes ruled the Medes, and spent the twenty-two years of his reign in constant wars with the Assyrians and the Persians.
After him reigned Diocles, a man highly experienced in arms and always engaged in wars, who at his death handed on to Astyages an empire greatly enlarged.
Astyages, who had no male offspring, had a grandson, Cyrus, born among the Persians. But as soon as Cyrus grew up, he gathered a band of Persians and declared war on his grandfather.

Now Astyages had forgotten the crime he had long before committed against Harpalus, when he killed his only son, a little boy, and served him up to his father to eat, and, so that no merciful ignorance might lessen the most unhappy man's bereavement, taunted him with the infamous meal by showing the father the boy's head and hands

— forgetting this deed, then, he entrusted the supreme command of the war to Harpalus himself, who promptly handed over to Cyrus by treachery the army he had been given. On learning this, Astyages hastily gathered his forces, marched in person against the Persians and renewed the struggle more fiercely, having declared to his men that if anyone tried to withdraw from the battle out of fear, he would be met with the sword.

Under this compulsion the Medes fought hard, and when the Persian line, driven back once again, was gradually giving way, their mothers and wives ran out to meet them and begged them to return to the battle. When they hesitated, the women lifted their garments and exposed their private parts, asking whether they wished to take refuge in the wombs of their mothers or their wives.

Ashamed at this, they returned to the battle and, making a charge, forced those from whom they had been fleeing to flee in turn. There Astyages was captured; Cyrus took nothing from him but his kingdom, and set him over the very great nation of the Hyrcanians. As for Cyrus himself, he did not wish to return to the Medes. This was the end of the empire of the Medes.
But the cities that had been tributary to the Medes revolted from Cyrus, and this became for Cyrus the cause and origin of many wars.
At that time Phalaris of Sicily, having seized tyrannical power, was ravaging the people of Agrigentum.
Cruel in mind and crueller still in his inventions, committing every wickedness against the innocent, this unjust man at last found someone he could justly punish.

For a certain Perillus, a worker in bronze, seeking the tyrant's friendship and thinking it a gift well suited to his cruelty, made a bronze bull, in whose side he skilfully fitted a door through which the condemned could be thrust inside. When someone shut in there was roasted by fires set beneath, the hollow bronze would amplify the cries wrung from him and give out, with a deathly resonance, a bellowing suited to the image, so that in this wicked spectacle it would seem to be the lowing of a beast and not the groaning of a man.
But Phalaris, welcoming the work while cursing its maker, provided material both for vengeance and for cruelty: he punished the craftsman himself with his own invention.

A little earlier there had also been a king among the Latins, Aremulus, who grew in crimes and impieties for eighteen years and was at last cut off by divine judgement with a thunderbolt, paying a timely penalty at an untimely age.

Let the Latins and the Sicilians now choose, if they please, whether they would rather have lived in the days of Aremulus and Phalaris, who wrung the lives of the innocent from them by torture, or in these Christian times, when the Roman emperors, governed above all by religion itself, having crushed tyrannies for the good of the state, do not exact vengeance even for the wrongs the tyrants did to themselves.

Thirty years before the founding of the City, a very great war was fought with all their strength and spirit between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, in which mutual slaughter drove them to the point that, as though both were defeated, they withdrew from each other and abandoned the war.
At that time, too, a sudden invasion of Asia by the nation of the Amazons and by the Cimmerians caused very great devastation and slaughter far and wide for a long time.

Twenty years before the founding of the City, the Lacedaemonians, warring with unwearied fury for twenty years against the Messenians because their maidens had been slighted at a solemn sacrifice of the Messenians, entangled the whole strength of Greece in their own ruin.

They had bound themselves by great curses and sworn oaths never to return home unless Messene were taken; and after ten years, worn out by the long siege yet having gained no fruit of victory, they were being called back, moved moreover by the complaints of their wives, who protested at their long widowhood and the danger of childlessness.

Having held a council, they feared that if the hope of offspring were cut off, this persistence would breed ruin for themselves rather than for the Messenians. So they sent back to Sparta those men in the army who had come as reinforcements after the oath was sworn, and allowed them to lie promiscuously with all the women: a licence shameful enough, and yet of no use.

They themselves, holding to their purpose, took the Messenians by treachery and crushed the conquered under slavery. But the Messenians, after long enduring a bloody domination amid lashes and chains, shook off the yoke, took up arms and renewed the war. The Lacedaemonians chose Tyrtaeus, an Athenian poet, as their leader in battle.
Routed in three engagements, they made up the army they had lost by calling a band of slaves to freedom.

But when even so they thought they should abandon the contest for fear of danger, they were fired up again by a poem composed by Tyrtaeus, their poet and general, and recited before the assembly, and soon rushed into battle; and they clashed with such force of spirit that rarely has a bloodier battle ever blazed up. In the end, however, victory went to the Lacedaemonians. A third time the Messenians

renewed the contest, and the Lacedaemonians did not delay; both sides brought many forces to their aid. The Athenians, meanwhile, prepared to attack the Lacedaemonians from the other side while they were occupied elsewhere.

Nor did the Lacedaemonians rest: being themselves occupied with the Messenians, they sent in the Peloponnesians to meet the Athenians in battle. The Athenians, having sent a small fleet to Egypt, were outmatched in strength and easily beaten in a naval engagement. Then, when the fleet had returned and they had been strengthened by a force of soldiers as well, they challenged the victors to battle.

The Lacedaemonians too left the Messenians and turned their arms against the Athenians. For a long time there were shifting and heavy battles, with victory in the balance, and at last both sides withdrew with the outcome undecided.
It must above all be understood, however, that Sparta is the same city as Lacedaemon, and that the Lacedaemonians are therefore called Spartans.

So the Lacedaemonians, recalled from there to the war with the Messenians, and not wishing to leave the Athenians at leisure in the meantime, made a pact with the Thebans to restore to them the rule over the Boeotians, which they had lost at the time of the Persian War, if they would take up the war against the Athenians.
Such was the fury of the Spartans that, though entangled in two wars, they did not refuse to take on a third, provided they could win enemies for their foes.

The Athenians, alarmed by so great a storm of wars, chose two generals, Pericles, a man of proven valour, and Sophocles, the writer of tragedies. Dividing the army, they laid waste the territory of the Spartans far and wide and added many cities of Asia to the Athenian empire.

From then on, for fifty years, war was waged by land and sea with victory ever uncertain, until the Spartans, their resources diminished and their good faith ruined, became a disgrace even to their allies.

Yet that these things weighed upon Greece through so many ages is reckoned of little account; whereas now it is not to be borne that pleasures should sometimes be interrupted and lusts hindered for a little while.

And yet there is this difference between the people of that time and of this: they bore these unbearable things patiently, because they had been born or brought up among them and knew nothing better; whereas these, accustomed all their lives to an unbroken clear sky of tranquillity and delights, are disturbed by every cloud of anxiety that gathers, however slight.
If only they would pray to Him who drives away even this slight disquiet, by whose gift they have enjoyed this continuous peace, unknown in other times!
And since I remember promising, when I marked out the order of my account by certain divisions, as it were, that I would tell of events from the founding of the world to the founding of the City,

let this be the end of this volume, which we have unfolded from the founding of the world, so that the following book may begin from the founding of the City. It will contain the more closely woven evils of those times, since men were by then more practised and better schooled in wickedness.
HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS
BOOK TWO

I think there is no one now who can be unaware that God made man in this world. Hence, too, when man sins the world is rebuked, and to curb our intemperance this earth on which we live is chastised by the failure of the other living creatures and the barrenness of its crops.

Therefore, if we are God's creation, we are rightly also under God's governance. For who loves more than he who made? And who rules in better order than he who both made and loves? And who can order and rule what has been made more wisely and more powerfully than he who both foresaw what was to be made and accomplished what he foresaw?

Therefore that all power and all ordering come from God is perceived by those who have not read and acknowledged by those who have. And if powers are from God, how much more so kingdoms, from which the other powers proceed;

and if there are various kingdoms, how much more fittingly some one supreme kingdom, to which the whole power of the other kingdoms is subject, such as was the Babylonian at the beginning, then the Macedonian, afterwards also the African, and finally the Roman, which remains to this day;

and by the same ineffable ordering, at the four cardinal points of the world four principal kingdoms stand out in distinct stages: the Babylonian kingdom in the east, the Carthaginian in the south, the Macedonian in the north, the Roman in the west.

Between the first and the last of these, that is, between the Babylonian and the Roman, as between an aged father and a little son, the African and the Macedonian came, brief and intermediate, like a guardian and a trustee, admitted by the power of circumstance and not by right of inheritance. Whether this is so, I shall take care to set out most plainly.

The first king among the Assyrians who was able to rise above the rest was Ninus. When Ninus was killed, his wife Semiramis, queen of all Asia, restored the city of Babylon and made it the capital of the Assyrian kingdom.

The kingdom of the Assyrians stood long with unshaken power; but when Arbatus, whom others call Arbaces, governor of the Medes and himself a Mede by nation, had killed his king Sardanapalus at Babylon, he transferred the name and supremacy of the kingdom to the Medes.

Thus the kingdom of Ninus and Babylon passed to the Medes in the same year in which Procas began to reign among the Latins. He was the father of Amulius and Numitor and grandfather of Rhea Silvia, who was the mother of Romulus.

And to show fully that all these things were arranged by ineffable mysteries and the deepest judgements of God, and did not come about by human strength or uncertain chance: all ancient histories begin with Ninus, and all Roman histories take their rise from Procas.

Further, from the first year of Ninus' reign to the time when Babylon began to be restored by Semiramis, sixty-four years intervene; and from the first year of Procas, when he began to reign, to the founding of the City by Romulus, there are likewise sixty-four years. Thus in the reign of Procas the seed of the future Rome was sown, though the shoot did not yet appear; and in the same year of Procas' reign the kingdom of Babylon came to an end, though Babylon itself still stood.
When Arbatus departed to the Medes, the Chaldaeans kept part of the kingdom in their own hands and claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes.

Thus power over Babylon lay with the Medes, and possession of it with the Chaldaeans; but the Chaldaeans, out of regard for the ancient dignity of the royal city, preferred to call themselves its people rather than to call it theirs.

Hence it came about that Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him down to Cyrus, though we read that they were powerful through the strength of the Chaldaeans and famous under the name of Babylon, are nevertheless not counted in the number and succession of illustrious kings.

So Babylon was dishonoured under the governor Arbatus in the same year in which Rome, to speak precisely, was sown under King Procas. And Babylon was finally overthrown by King Cyrus at the very time when Rome was first freed from the domination of the Tarquin kings.

For at one and the same coincidence of times the one fell and the other rose. The one then first suffered the domination of foreigners, the other then first spurned the arrogance even of its own. The one then, as if dying, left its inheritance, and the other, coming of age, then recognized itself as heir. Then the empire of the East fell and the empire of the West arose.
And not to linger longer over words, I commit myself to the teeth of madmen, but in the confidence that I shall be freed by the protection of truth.
Ninus reigned fifty-two years. He was succeeded, as I said, by his wife Semiramis, who herself reigned forty-two years and in the middle of her reign founded Babylon as the capital of the kingdom.

Thus Babylon, about 1,164 years after its founding, was despoiled of its wealth and its kingdom and deprived of its very king by the Medes and by Arbatus, their king but its own governor; yet it remained unharmed for some time afterwards.
Likewise Rome too, after just as many years, that is, about 1,164, was broken into by the Goths and their king Alaric, who was also its own count, and despoiled of its wealth,

but not of its kingdom; it still remains and reigns unharmed. And yet by hidden decrees the pattern of correspondence between the two cities has been kept so completely that there its governor Arbatus seized the kingdom, and here this city's prefect Attalus attempted to reign; although in this city alone, by the merit of a Christian emperor, the impious attempt came to nothing.
