I have thought these things should be recorded chiefly for this reason: so that, with so great a mystery of God's ineffable judgements partly laid open, those who foolishly grumble about Christian times may understand that one God ordered the times, both for the Babylonians at the beginning and for the Romans at the end; that it is owing to his mercy that we live, and to our own intemperance that we live wretchedly.

See: Babylon and Rome had a similar rise, similar power, similar greatness, similar times, similar blessings and similar evils; yet not a similar end or a similar fall. For the one lost its kingdom, the other keeps it; the one was bereaved by the killing of its king, the other is secure with its emperor unharmed. And why is this?

Because there the foulness of lust was punished in the king, while here the most restrained equity of the Christian religion was preserved in the king. There, with no reverence for religion, the licence of fury sated the greed for pleasure; here there were Christians who spared, Christians who were spared, and Christians for whose memory's sake and in whose memorial shrines mercy was shown.
Therefore let them stop tearing at religion and provoking the patience of God, thanks to which they may have even this left unpunished, if they ever stop.

Let them indeed recall with me the times of their ancestors: most turbulent with wars, accursed with crimes, foul with dissensions, unbroken in miseries. They may rightly shudder at those times, because they happened, and they must needs pray that they may not come again;

and let them pray to the one God alone, who then by hidden justice allowed them to happen and now by open mercy grants that they do not. These things I shall now set out more fully from the very beginning of the City, going through the histories in order.

In the 414th [?] year after the overthrow of Troy, and in the sixth Olympiad (the Olympiad is celebrated with contests and games at Elis, a city of Greece, every fifth year, after four full years have passed in between), the city of Rome was founded in Italy by the twins Romulus and Remus.

Romulus at once stained its kingship with the murder of kin, and with cruelty equally successful he gave the Sabine women, carried off against all custom and joined in shameless marriages, the blood of their husbands and parents as a dowry.

Thus Romulus, after killing first his grandfather Numitor and then his brother Remus, seized power and established the City. He consecrated his grandfather's kingdom, his brother's walls and his father-in-law's temple with blood, and gathered a band of criminals with a promise of impunity.
His first field of war was the City's forum, a sign that foreign and civil wars, mingled together, would never be lacking.
He seized the women of the Sabines, whom he had lured with a treaty and games, as shamefully as he wickedly defended the deed.
Their leader Titus Tatius, an old man pressing honourable claims of family duty, he long drove back by arms, and soon after taking him into partnership in the kingship, he killed him.
A battle was fought with the Veientes, still of small name but already of great strength. The town of the Caeninenses was captured and destroyed.

Once they had taken up arms there was never any rest, for they feared shameful want and foul hunger at home if ever they settled into peace. From here on I shall touch as briefly as possible on the ceaseless contests, each always as grievous as the strength engaged in it:

how Tullus Hostilius, the founder of military discipline, trusting in his well-trained young men, made war on the Albans, and after a long struggle in which the hope on both sides was uncertain but the slaughter certain, at last cut short its dreadful course and doubtful outcome by the combat of the triplets;
how, when the peace was broken again, Mettius Fufetius,

who had held back in suspense during the war with Fidenae and had even plotted treachery, was torn apart by chariots driven in opposite directions, paying for the guilt of a double mind with the penalty of a divided body;

how the Latins were often engaged under the leadership of Ancus Marcius and sometimes overcome; how Tarquinius Priscus cut down all his neighbours and the twelve peoples of Tuscany, then powerful, in countless conflicts; how the Veientes, pressed hard by Servius Tullius, were defeated but not subdued;

how the kingship of Tarquin the Proud was gained by the crime of murdering his father-in-law, kept by cruelty towards the citizens, and lost through the outrage of the violation of Lucretia; and, amid his vices at home and the virtues that shone out abroad, the strong towns in Latium that he captured, Ardea, Oricolum and Suessa Pometia, and whatever he achieved against Gabii, whether by his own deceit, by his son's punishment, or by the strength of Rome.
But how great were the evils the Romans endured during those 353 years of unbroken rule by kings is shown not only by the expulsion of one king but also by their forswearing the royal name and power.
For if his arrogance alone had been at fault, it would have been enough to expel him alone, preserving the royal dignity for better men.

So, when the kings had been driven from the City, the Romans, thinking it better to take counsel for themselves than to let anyone lord it over their freedom, created consuls; and under them the now adult age of the growing state was exercised in bolder undertakings.

In the 244th year after the founding of the City, Brutus, the first consul among the Romans, strove not only to equal Rome's first founder and king in the murder of kin but even to surpass him. For he dragged before the assembly his own two young sons and as many brothers of his wife, the young Vitellii, who were accused of a plot to bring the kings back into the City, had them beaten with rods, and struck them down with the axe.
He himself then, in the war with the Veientes and the Tarquinienses, fell together with Arruns, son of Tarquin the Proud, who met him in combat and died with him.

Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, a most powerful champion of the royal name, sought to force Tarquin back upon the Romans, and for three continuous years he terrified, hemmed in and besieged the trembling city. Had the enemy not been moved, either by Mucius with his steadfast endurance in letting his hand be burned or by the maiden Cloelia with her wonderful daring in crossing the river, the Romans would surely have been forced to endure either captivity, overcome by the besieging enemy, or slavery, subjected to the restored king.

After this the Sabines, scraping together forces from every side, marched on Rome with great preparations for war. Dismayed by this fear, the Romans created a dictator, whose authority and power would take precedence over the consul's; and this measure brought very great advantage in that war.

There followed the secession of the plebs from the patricians when, while the dictator Marcus Valerius was conducting a levy of soldiers, the people, goaded by various injustices, occupied the Sacred Mount in arms. What could be more dreadful than this destruction, when the body, cut off from the head, was planning the ruin of that by which it drew breath? And it would have been all over with the Roman name through ruin from within, had not a speedy reconciliation crept in before the secession itself became aware of what it was.

Besides those open disasters of war, a hidden destruction pressed hard and loomed over the City in wretched succession: for in the consulship of Titus Geganius and Publius Minucius, two of the very greatest abominations among all evils, famine and pestilence, seized the weary City. There was a brief pause in the battles, but no pause in the deaths.

The Veientes, Etruscans and formidable enemies, rising in war with the forces of their neighbours joined to their own, were met by the consuls Marcus Fabius and Gnaeus Manlius. There, after the sworn oath by which the Romans had vowed not to return to camp except after victory, the battle was so fierce and the condition of vanquished and victors so alike that, with very much of the army lost and the consul Manlius and the former consul Fabius killed in the fighting, the consul Marcus Fabius refused the triumph the senate offered him, because mourning was owed rather than celebration for such great losses to the state.

That family of the Fabii, most glorious in numbers and strength, took the war against the Veientes as its own; how great a bereavement its fall inflicted on the state is witnessed, under names infamous to this day, by the river that destroyed them and the gate that sent them out.

For when three hundred and six Fabii, truly the brightest lights of the Roman state, had asked that a war against the Veientes be assigned to them alone, they confirmed by their first successes the hopes of an expedition rashly undertaken. Then, drawn into an ambush and surrounded by the enemy, they were all slaughtered there, only one being spared to report the disaster, so that their country might suffer more wretchedly in hearing of their loss than in the loss itself.

Nor were such things happening only at Rome: every province was burning with its own fires, and what the foremost poet described of one city I would say of the whole world: “Everywhere cruel grief, everywhere fear, and death in many a form.”

At that same time, then, Cyrus, king of the Persians, whom I mentioned earlier for the sake of setting out the history, was ranging with his armies through Asia, Scythia and the whole East, while Tarquin the Proud, as king or as enemy, was crushing the City with slavery or with war.

Cyrus, as I have said, having subdued everyone against whom he had marched, made for the Assyrians and Babylon, at that time the richest nation and city of all. But his advance was checked by the river Gyndes, second in size only to the Euphrates.

One of the royal horses, outstanding for its whiteness and beauty, was tempted by confidence that it could swim across. But where the current, striking the shallows, threw up whirlpools along the rushing channel, it was seized, swept headlong and drowned.

The king, enraged, resolved to take vengeance on the river, swearing that the river which had just swallowed his splendid horse would be left so that women could wade across it barely wetting their knees. Nor was he slow to carry it out: for a full year, with all his forces, he cut up the river Gyndes and drew it off through great ditches, breaking it into four hundred and sixty channels.
With diggers trained by this work, he also diverted the Euphrates, by far the most powerful river, which flows through the middle of Babylon.

Thus, where the shallows could be waded and parts of the riverbed lay open and dry, he made a way through and took the city, though among mortals it was almost equally incredible that it could have been built by human labor or could be destroyed by human strength.
For many have recorded that Babylon was founded by the giant Nimrod and restored by Ninus or Semiramis.

It was visible from every side across the level plain, in a most fertile natural setting, laid out in a square like a military camp, with walls of equal length. The strength and size of its walls are almost beyond belief: fifty cubits wide and four times as high.
Its circuit is four hundred and eighty stades. The wall is built of baked brick bonded with bitumen, and a broad moat runs around it outside in place of a river.

Along the front of the walls are a hundred bronze gates. The width of the wall at the top, where the battlements are, has quarters for the defenders arranged evenly on both sides, and the space between them can take swift four-horse chariots. Inside, the houses, four stories high, are remarkable for their menacing height.
And yet that great Babylon, the first city founded after the restoration of the human race, was now conquered with almost no delay at all, taken and overthrown.

Croesus, king of the Lydians, famous for his wealth, had then come to help the Babylonians; defeated, he fled anxiously back to his kingdom. Cyrus, after he had invaded Babylon as an enemy, overthrown it as a conqueror and set it in order as a king, carried the war into Lydia, where he overcame with no trouble an army already terrified by the earlier battle. He even captured Croesus himself, and having captured him granted him both his life and his inheritance.

There is no need at this point to dwell on the unstable condition of changeable things. For the capture of Babylon confirms that whatever is made by labor and by hand slips away and is worn out by age. Just as its empire was the first and the most powerful, so it was also the first to give way, so that, as if by some right of the succeeding age, the inheritance due might be handed on to those who came after, who would themselves keep the same rule of handing it on.

So great Babylon and vast Lydia gave way at the very first assaults of the advancing Cyrus; the mightiest arms of the East, together with their head, fell in the course of a single battle. And yet our people complain with heedless anxiety if the massive structure of the once most powerful Roman state now trembles, shaken more by the weakness of its own old age than by the strength of others.

Next, then, the same Cyrus, following up his success, made war on the Scythians. Queen Tomyris, who then ruled that people, could have prevented him from crossing the river Araxes, but she let him cross: first out of confidence in herself, and then because of the advantage of having the enemy shut in by the river at his back.

So Cyrus entered Scythia and pitched his camp far from the river he had crossed. Then, by a ruse, he stocked the camp with wine and food and abandoned it, as if he had fled in fear. On learning this, the queen sent a third of her forces and her young son to pursue Cyrus.
The barbarians, as though invited to a banquet, were overcome by drunkenness; and soon, when Cyrus returned, they were all cut down together with the young man.

Tomyris, having lost her army and her son, prepared to wash away her grief as mother and as queen with the blood of the enemy rather than with her own tears. She feigned a loss of confidence, as if in despair after the defeat inflicted on her, and by gradually withdrawing lured the arrogant enemy into an ambush.

There, having laid an ambush among the mountains, she destroyed two hundred thousand Persians together with the king himself. What made the affair more astonishing than anything else was that not even a messenger survived to report so great a disaster.

The queen ordered Cyrus's head to be cut off and thrown into a skin filled with human blood, and taunted him in no womanly fashion: "Glut yourself," she said, "on the blood you thirsted for, the blood of which you went on insatiable for thirty years."
In the 245th year from the founding of the City, some time after Cyrus had been killed among the Scythians, Darius obtained the kingdom by lot.
For in between them reigned Cambyses, Cyrus's son. After conquering Egypt, he loathed the whole religion of Egypt and did away with its rites and temples.
After him the Magi also dared to steal into the kingship under the name of the king they had killed; but they were soon detected and crushed.

So Darius, one of those who had put down the audacity of the Magi by the sword, was made king by common consent. After he had recovered by war the Assyrians and Babylon, which were breaking away from the Persian empire, he made war on Antyrus, king of the Scythians, chiefly for this reason: that he had sought the king's daughter in marriage and had not obtained her.

A great necessity indeed, that seven hundred thousand men should be exposed to the danger of death for the lust of one man! With incredible preparations he entered Scythia with seven hundred thousand armed men, but the enemy gave him no opportunity for a regular battle,

and moreover kept tearing at the rear of his forces with sudden raids. Fearing that his return would be cut off if the bridge over the river Danube were broken, he fled in alarm, having lost eighty thousand fighting men. Yet he did not even count this number of the lost among his losses: a host that scarcely anyone would have dared aspire to possess, he did not feel the loss of.

From there he attacked and subdued Asia and Macedonia. He also defeated the Ionians in a sea battle. Then he launched an attack on the Athenians and turned his arms against them, because they had given help to the Ionians against him.

The Athenians, when they learned that Darius was approaching, had asked the Spartans for help. Nevertheless, having found out that the Persians were held up by the idleness of a four-day religious observance, they seized hope from the opportunity, and with only ten thousand citizens under arms and a thousand Plataean auxiliaries they burst out onto the plains of Marathon against six hundred thousand of the enemy.

Miltiades was then in command of that war. Relying more on speed than on strength, he advanced so briskly that he closed with the enemy hand to hand before he could be driven back by a free volley of arrows.
So unequal was the fighting in that battle that on one side there seemed to be men ready to kill, on the other cattle made ready to die.
Two hundred thousand Persians fell on the plains of Marathon on that occasion.
This loss Darius did feel: for, beaten and routed, he seized his ships and fled back to Persia.

But while he was renewing the war and striving to take vengeance on the victors, he died in the very midst of his preparations, in the seventy-fourth Olympiad, that is, in the 275th year after the founding of the City. At that time in Rome the virgin Popilia was buried alive for the crime of unchastity.

Xerxes, succeeding his father Darius on the throne, spent five years preparing the war against Greece that his father had undertaken. Demaratus the Spartan, who happened at that time to be living in exile at Xerxes' court, betrayed this to his own people by means of tablets that were first written on and then covered with wax.

Xerxes, then, is said to have had seven hundred thousand armed men from his own kingdom and three hundred thousand from his allies, as well as twelve hundred beaked warships and three thousand transports. It has rightly been recorded that for such an unheard-of army and boundless fleet the rivers were scarcely enough to drink, the lands scarcely enough to march over, and the seas scarcely enough to sail.

This host, so incredible in our own times that its number is harder to believe now than it was to defeat then, was withstood by Leonidas, king of the Spartans, with four thousand men in the narrow pass of Thermopylae.

Xerxes, scorning the handful set against him, ordered the battle to begin and the fighting to be joined. Those whose kinsmen and comrades had fallen on the plains of Marathon were the first both into the fight and into the slaughter.

Then a larger and more sluggish mass took their place. Since it was no longer free to charge, nor unhampered to fight, nor ready to flee, and stood propped up only by its own dead, for three days on end it was not a battle between two peoples but the slaughter of one.

On the fourth day, when Leonidas saw that the enemy was pouring around him on every side, he urged his allied auxiliaries to withdraw from the battle, escape to the mountaintop and save themselves for better times; but he and his Spartans, he said, must meet a different fate: he owed more to his country than to his life.

Having sent the allies away, he reminded the Spartans that they should hope for a very great deal of glory and nothing of life; they must not wait for the enemy or for daylight, but must seize the chance of night to break into the camp, cross weapons with the foe and throw his ranks into confusion; nowhere could victors die more honorably than in the enemy's camp.

Persuaded, then, to prefer death, they armed themselves to avenge the death to come, as though they were both exacting and avenging their own destruction. Marvelous to tell, six hundred men broke into the camp of six hundred thousand.

Uproar broke out through the whole camp. The Persians themselves even helped the Spartans by slaughtering one another. The Spartans, looking for the king and not finding him, cut down and laid low everything, roamed through the whole camp, and among the dense heaps of bodies could barely find a few men left to pursue: victors beyond all doubt, had they not chosen to die.

The battle went on from the beginning of the night through the greater part of the day. At last, worn out with conquering, each of them, as his limbs failed and he felt himself sated with vengeance for his own death, fell there, exhausted, among the obstacles of corpses and on ground quivering with thick, half-clotted blood, and died. Xerxes, twice beaten on land, prepared for a battle at sea. But

Themistocles, the Athenian commander, when he learned that the Ionians, by helping whom in the earlier war he had drawn the Persians' attack upon himself, were bringing a fleet they had fitted out to help Xerxes, resolved to win them over to his side and draw them away from the enemy.

Since there was no opportunity of speaking with them, he ordered messages to be set up and fixed to rocks in places where the Ionians seemed likely to put in with their ships. In them he rebuked them with fitting reproach as men who had once been his allies and partners in danger but were now unjustly standing idle; he urged them with solemn exhortation to return to the obligations of their ancient treaties, and above all he advised them, once battle was joined, to back water as though giving way and take themselves out of the fight.

So the king, keeping part of the fleet with him, stayed on the shore as a spectator of the battle. Artemisia, on the other hand, queen of Halicarnassus, who had come to help Xerxes, threw herself into the fighting most fiercely among the foremost commanders, so that, roles reversed, one saw womanly caution in the man and manly daring in the woman.

While the battle hung in the balance, the Ionians, as Themistocles had instructed, began little by little to withdraw from the fight. Their defection persuaded the Persians, who were already looking about for a way to flee, to flee openly.
In that panic many ships were sunk or captured; but more of them, fearing the king's cruelty as much as the enemy's savagery, slipped away to their homes.
Mardonius approached the king, anxious after so many misfortunes, and advised him that the king ought to return to his kingdom before bad news stirred up revolution at home;

as for himself, if the remaining forces were handed over to him, he would both exact vengeance from the enemy and ward off disgrace at home; or, if the fortunes of war continued adverse, he would indeed give way to the enemy, but without dishonor to the king.

The plan was approved, and the army was handed over to Mardonius. The king set out with a few men for Abydos, where he had built his bridge as if he were master of the sea. But finding the bridge broken up by the winter storms, he crossed over in alarm in a fishing boat.

It was truly a sight that the human race ought to have looked upon and lamented, measuring the changes of fortune by this contrast above all: that he should be content to hide in a tiny boat, he beneath whom the very sea had once lain hidden, and who had made it bear the yoke of its captivity when he joined it with a bridge;
that he should need the humble service of a single slave, he to whose power, as mountains were cut through, valleys filled and rivers drained, nature itself had yielded.

The land forces too, which had been entrusted to the commanders, wasted away so badly from toil, hunger and fear, and, as disease grew fierce, such a plague and such a foulness of the dying arose, that the roads were filled with corpses, and even dreadful birds of prey and ravening beasts, lured by the bait of food, followed the dying army.
Mardonius, however, to whom Xerxes had entrusted what remained of the war, was at first puffed up by a brief success, but soon was cast down to the depths. He stormed Olynthus, a town of Greece.

He tried by various inducements to lead the Athenians to hope for peace; but when he saw that their freedom could not be overcome, he burned part of their city and led his whole war apparatus into Boeotia.

There a hundred thousand Greeks followed him as well. Joining battle without delay, they destroyed his forces and forced Mardonius to flee with a few men, stripped bare as if from a shipwreck. They took his camp, which was crammed with royal wealth, though at no small cost to their old-time diligence: for after this booty was divided, Persian gold was the first thing to corrupt the virtue of Greece.

So utter ruin, once begun, pressed hard upon the wretched Persians. For by chance, on the very day on which Mardonius's forces were destroyed in Boeotia, part of the Persian army was fighting a naval battle in Asia beneath Mount Mycale.

There a new rumor suddenly filled the ears of both fleets and both peoples: that Mardonius's forces had been wiped out and the Greeks had emerged victorious. Wonderful is the ordering of divine judgment: the battle was joined in Boeotia at sunrise, and it was announced in Asia at midday on the same day, across such great stretches of sea and land!

This rumor contributed above all to the outcome, because the Persians, on hearing of their allies' disaster, were gripped first by grief and then by despair, so that it left them neither ready for battle nor fit for flight. And so the enemy, made more resolute by the success of his good fortune, fell upon them in their dismay and routed them.
Xerxes, having become contemptible to his own people after his unsuccessful war in Greece, was trapped in his palace by Artabanus, his prefect, and killed.

O times most worthy of longing and remembrance! O those days of unbroken calm, which are held up to us to look back upon as though out of darkness! In them, within a very short span, three wars under three successive kings snatched away one million nine hundred thousand men from the vitals of one kingdom, to say nothing of Greece, most unhappy at that time, which in its dying surpassed this whole number at which we now stand stupefied.

In that war against Xerxes, which was the last both for himself and for the enemy, that most famous Leonidas of the Spartans spoke to his six hundred those celebrated words of encouragement: "Eat your breakfast as men who will dine in the underworld"; yet to the auxiliaries, whom he was ordering to leave the fight, he compassionately [?] that they should [?] themselves for better times.

See: whereas he promised that better times were to come, these people assert that the better times are past. Since each side detests its own present, what else can we conclude except that times are either always good but unappreciated, or never better at all?

But at Rome, to return to the point from which I digressed (for I am not compelled by any pause in miseries to pass on to other peoples; rather, just as evils once boiling up everywhere were bound together in the events themselves, so they are also related intermingled, since my purpose is to compare the times of the whole world with one another, not to mock the

sufferings of any one part of it): at Rome, then, in the year [?] after the founding of the City, when war had been suspended for a little while, a severe plague, which there always either cut short the rare truces or forced them to be made, blazed violently through the whole city. Fittingly, as a portent beforehand, the sky was seen to be on fire, when the capital of the nations was burning with so great a fire of disease.
For in that year the plague carried off both consuls, Aebutius and Servilius, wiped out the greater part of the military forces, and destroyed many nobles and above all the common people
with a loathsome wasting, even though a pestilence that had broken out four years earlier had already ravaged the same people.
Then in the following year exiled citizens and runaway slaves, led by Herbonius, a Sabine, seized and set fire to the Capitol.

There the young men, under Valerius as consul and commander, resisted most bravely; but the struggle of the battle was so fierce and grave that the consul Valerius himself was killed there, and so he further stained, by his own death, a victory over slaves that was unworthy in itself.

The following year saw a consul besieged with his defeated army. For the Aequi and Volsci defeated the consul Minucius in battle and, as he fled, hemmed him in on Mount Algidus with hunger and the sword; and it would have ended disastrously had not Quintius Cincinnatus, that outstanding dictator, crushed the enemy and broken the tight siege.

He was found in the countryside and summoned from the plough to the fasces. Taking up the office and raising an army, he soon emerged the victor; he put a yoke of oxen on the Aequi and, holding victory as though it were a plough-handle, was the first to drive the subdued enemy before him.
In the year next before the three hundredth from the founding of the City, while envoys sent to the Athenians to bring back the laws of Solon were awaited, famine and plague held Roman arms in check.

In the three hundredth year itself, that is, in the ninety-fifth Olympiad, the power of the consuls was handed over to the decemvirs for the purpose of establishing the Attic laws, and this brought great ruin upon the state.

For first of the decemvirs, while the others stepped down, Appius Claudius alone prolonged his own command, and at once a conspiracy of the others followed. Disregarding the custom by which the insignia of command lay with one man while the power was shared, they all did everything according to their own whims.
So, among the other things they all presumed to do with the utmost insolence, they suddenly appeared in public each with twelve fasces and the other insignia of command.

And in this new undertaking of a wicked order of things, with the reverence due to the consuls set aside, a band of tyrants burst forth. They added two tables of laws to the ten earlier ones, did a great many things with the most insolent arrogance, and on the day when it was customary to lay down office they appeared in public with the same insignia.

The lust of Appius Claudius above all increased the hatred against them. In order to violate the virgin Verginia, he first brought a suit claiming her as a slave. Because of this her father Verginius, driven by grief for her freedom and by shame at the disgrace, struck down his daughter in full view of the people as she was being dragged off into slavery, a dutiful parricide.

The people, stirred by the atrocity of this necessity and warned of the danger to their freedom, took up arms and occupied the Aventine Hill. Nor did they cease defending their freedom by arms until the conspiracy of the plotters had resigned its very offices.

In the third and fifth Olympiad after the hundredth, there were such frequent and such severe earthquakes in Italy, throughout almost the whole year, that Rome was wearied by constant reports of countless shocks and of the collapse of country houses and towns.
Then there followed so continuous and scorching a drought that it took away all hope of the earth bringing forth crops

for that year and the next. At the same time, when the Fidenates, enemies made formidable by a band of very large auxiliary forces crowding around them, were threatening the citadel of Rome, Aemilius, dictator for the third time, barely captured Fidenae itself and so warded off and remedied a great mass of evil.

So great among them was the contention of evils and of passions that either wars pouring in from outside blotted out the disasters at home, or, when truces were granted after the losses of war, various plagues blazing from sky and earth wasted them with ceaseless assault.

From the beginning Sicily was the homeland of the Cyclopes, and after them it was always the nurse of tyrants and often the captive of slaves as well. The first of these fed on human flesh, those in between on torture, and the last on deaths. And this is not counting that in foreign wars it was treated either as plunder or as prize.

To put it as briefly as I can, this island has known no rest from evils except now. Indeed, to show the difference between the times more plainly: just as formerly, alone among all lands, it always suffered tumults either from within or from without, so

now, alone out of all, it never does. For even Etna itself—to say nothing of how long that calamity lasted which weighed on it, or, by contrast, how long the peace has lasted which it now enjoys—Etna, which then seethed with frequent eruptions to the ruin of cities and fields, now merely smokes harmlessly, as a witness to the truth of the past.

So, leaving aside the tyrants for the moment (among whom the one who was the avenger soon became the successor), in the intervening time, that is, in the 335th year from the founding of the City, when the people of Rhegium in Sicily were troubled by discord and the city was split into two parties by dissension, one party called in veterans from Himera, a city of Sicily, to help them.

These men first drove out of the city those against whom they had been called in, and soon afterward slaughtered also those whom they had come to help. Then they seized the city together with the wives and children of their allies, daring a crime that no tyrant could match:

for it would have been better for the people of Rhegium to suffer anything at all than to invite of their own accord men to whom they themselves, as exiles, would leave their homeland, wives, children and household gods as plunder.

The people of Catana too, finding the Syracusans oppressive and hostile, asked the Athenians for help. But the Athenians sent a fleet to Sicily equipped more for their own interests than their allies', since they were scheming to extend their own empire and feared that the Syracusan fleet, recently built, might be of use to the Spartans.
And since the Athenians who had been sent made a successful start by defeating the enemy, they brought larger forces and a stronger army back to Sicily under the generals Laches and Chariades.
But the Catanians, weary of the war, made a treaty with the Syracusans and rejected the Athenians' help.

Later, however, when the Syracusans broke the terms of peace with designs of domination, they again sent envoys to Athens, who, with unkempt hair and beards and dressed in mourning, begged for pity and help by both their words and their appearance.

So a great fleet was fitted out under the generals Nicias and Lamachus, and Sicily was attacked again with such great strength that even those who had obtained it began to fear what they had asked for.
The Athenians at once fought two land battles with success, shut up the worn-out enemy in their city, surrounded them with a blockading fleet, and hemmed them in by land and sea.

The Syracusans, their affairs broken and exhausted, asked the Spartans for help. These soon sent Gylippus, a single man, but one who was held to be worth every kind of reinforcement. On arriving he heard that the war was already turning against them, so he gathered auxiliaries, partly in Greece and partly in Sicily, and seized positions favorable for the war.
Then, though defeated in two battles, he was not dismayed: in the third engagement he killed Lamachus, put the enemy to flight and freed his allies from the siege.
After this the Athenians, beaten on land, turned to trying their fortune at sea and prepared to fight a naval battle. Learning of this, Gylippus summoned a fleet fitted out by the Spartans.

The Athenians likewise sent Demosthenes and Eurymedon with reinforcements to replace the general they had lost. The Peloponnesians too, with the agreement and by the decree of many cities, sent huge forces to aid the Syracusans.

So under the guise of a war on behalf of allies they pursued their own quarrels at home, and both sides fought with all their might, as though the struggle had been moved from Greece to Sicily by agreement.
The Athenians were defeated in the first engagement, and also lost their camp with all their money, both public and private, and all the equipment for a long campaign.
Their strength was broken and reduced to straits, and Demosthenes urged that, while their affairs were not yet wholly lost, however battered they might seem, they should go home and leave Sicily.
But Nicias, made more desperate by shame at his bad conduct of affairs from the start, insisted on staying.

They renewed the naval fight, and soon, drawn through inexperience into the narrows of the sea off Syracuse, they were surrounded by an enemy ambush. Eurylochus [?], the general, was the first to be killed, and eleven ships were burned. Demosthenes and Nicias abandoned the fleet, thinking they could flee more safely by an overland march.

Gylippus first seized their hundred and thirty abandoned ships, then set out after the fugitives themselves and captured and killed a great many. Demosthenes escaped the disgrace of slavery by a voluntary death, while Nicias crowned an unworthy and shameful life with the disgrace of captivity.

So the Athenians, after two years of struggle in Sicily, not without loss to the Spartans, were beset by other evils at home. For Alcibiades, who had earlier been named general against Syracuse, was soon detained for trial on a certain charge,

and going into voluntary exile he betook himself to Sparta and urged the Spartans to press on with a new war against the Athenians while they were in disarray, and not to give them any breathing space that might keep them from being crushed.
All Greece agreed with this undertaking, as though forces were being pooled for the public good to put out a fire that threatened everyone.

Darius too, king of the Persians, remembering his father's and grandfather's hatred of this city, made a treaty with the Spartans through Tissaphernes, governor of Lydia, and promised them the costs of the war and troops.

Wonderful to tell, the Athenians had such great resources at that time that, though the forces of Greece, Asia and the whole East were launched against them—that is, against a single city—they seemed to have been worn down by fighting often and never yielding, rather than conquered.
For at the start Alcibiades drove all their allies to desert them for the Spartans; but then, attacked by plots among the Spartans too out of envy, he fled and went over to Tissaphernes in Media.

He quickly became intimate with him through his adaptable nature and the charm of his fitting eloquence, and persuaded him not to help the Spartans with such lavish resources: rather he ought to become the arbiter and spectator of this struggle, and keep the strength of Lydia intact for use against the victor.

For this reason Tissaphernes ordered only part of his fleet, with a moderate force, to be sent to the Spartans, so that they would neither fight in safety at another's risk because they had help in abundance, nor give up the war they had begun because they were wholly abandoned.

Among the Athenians, meanwhile, after they had long been torn by internal discord, with danger looming the supreme power was transferred to the senate by the will of the people. For discords are nourished by leisure, but when necessity presses, private causes and hatreds are set aside and men take counsel for the common good.

But since this very arrangement proved ruinous because of the arrogance inborn in that people and the tyrannical lusts of its leaders, Alcibiades, the exile, was at last recalled by the army and made commander of the fleet.

On learning this, the leading men first tried to betray the city to the Spartans; then, when that scheme came to nothing, they went into exile of their own accord. So Alcibiades, having freed his country, led the fleet against the enemy.

Battle was joined and the Athenians won the victory. The greater part of the Spartan army was cut down, nearly all their generals were killed too, and eighty ships were captured, not counting those that were burned and sunk in the fighting.
The war was moved back to land, and went just as badly for the Spartans. Broken by these events, the Spartans asked for peace, but could not obtain it.

Moreover, the Syracusan forces were recalled to Sicily when news came of the threat of war from Carthage. So Alcibiades with his victorious fleet ranged over all Asia, plundering and laying everything waste with war, fire and slaughter; and he captured and recovered a great many cities that had earlier broken away from the alliance.
Having thus won a great name, Alcibiades entered Athens as a victor, to the admiration and joy of all.
After a short interval he increased his forces, enlarged his army and fleet, and made for Asia again. The Spartans, for their part, put Lysander in command of their fleet and of the war.

Cyrus too, the brother of Darius, who had been put in charge of Ionia and Lydia in place of Tissaphernes, strengthened them with great resources and auxiliaries. So Lysander, with a sudden attack, overwhelmed Alcibiades' army while it was intent on plunder and therefore scattered and straggling everywhere; he defeated it without a real battle and cut it down as it fled.

This was a great disaster for the Athenians, and they received a far crueler wound than the one they had inflicted not long before. On learning of it the Athenians supposed that Alcibiades had taken care to avenge the old grievance of his exile by this crime of treachery,
and so they appointed Conon in his place, and entrusted to him what remained of their forces and the supreme command of the war.
Wishing at least to fill up his depleted forces in number, he enlisted old men and boys and enrolled an army.

But a force of that kind did not hold up the war, for war is usually decided by strength, not numbers. So this unwarlike band was at once either captured or slaughtered, and so great was the carnage in that battle that not only the dominion but even the very name of the Athenians seemed to have been wiped out.

But they, in their desperate situation, resolved to grant the city to foreigners—so that those who a little before had ruled all Asia might now, with this rabble, at least defend their walls and their freedom—and although even by their own judgment they were not equal to defending these, even with walls before them, they nevertheless prepared to try a naval battle once again.
Fury devoid of judgment mistakes resentment for courage, and whatever anger plans, recklessness promises.

So, with all of them either captured or killed, nothing at all was left even of the remnants. Only the general Conon survived the war and his people, and, fearing the cruelty of his fellow citizens, he went over to King Cyrus.

Then Evagoras, the Spartan general, took all their cities from them and left the Athenians nothing but an empty city; nor did they keep even this for long, for afterward he surrounded the city itself with a siege. Inside, famine, desolation and disease harried the besieged,
and when, after every abomination of misery, things it is horrifying even to speak of, no hope remained to them but death, they asked for peace.

Then there was a great debate between the Spartans and their allies. Most declared that this most restless city should be razed to the ground and this most hostile people wiped out together with its very name,

but the Spartans said they would not allow one of the two eyes of Greece to be put out. Moreover, they even promised peace if the long walls running from the harbor of Piraeus to the city were torn down, if the Athenians surrendered their remaining ships of their own accord, and if they then accepted thirty chosen men as their rulers.
When the Athenians submitted and yielded to these terms, the Spartans appointed Lysander to lay down laws of obedience in the city.
This year was notable for the capture of Athens, the death of Darius king of the Persians, and the exile of Dionysius tyrant of Sicily.

So the thirty rulers appointed over the Athenians turned into thirty tyrants. First they surrounded themselves with three thousand bodyguards, and soon also posted seven hundred soldiers from the victorious army at their sides.
They inaugurated the general slaughter that was to follow everywhere by killing Alcibiades, who, while fleeing, was shut up in a bedroom on his journey and alive

was burned. With him dead, as though their avenger had been removed, they drained the wretched remnants of the city without fear through murders and plunder. They also slew Theramenes, one of their own number, whom they perceived to be displeased with these things, as an example to terrify the rest.

So everyone fled the city in all directions; but since by the Spartans' prohibition the exiles were refused hospitality throughout Greece, they all betook themselves to Argos and Thebes. There they were cherished with such kindly hospitality that they not only eased their grief at the loss of their homeland but even began to contemplate the hope of recovering it.

Among the exiles was Thrasybulus, an energetic man, distinguished among his people by the nobility of his family; he was the one who led them to dare for their country. So the exiles gathered and seized Phyle, a fortress on the borders of Attica, and gained strength with the help of the resources of many cities. Lysias too, the Syracusan orator, sent them five hundred soldiers with their pay, as if to help the city that was the common homeland of eloquence.

That battle was fierce, but since the one side was fighting for the freedom of its homeland and the other for dominion over a land not its own, the battle itself also passed judgment on their spirits and their causes. For the tyrants were defeated and fled back into the city, and all those Athenians whom they had earlier chosen as their bodyguards, now suspected of treachery, they removed from guarding the city.

They even dared to try to bribe Thrasybulus himself. When that hope proved vain, they summoned help from Sparta and rushed into war again. In that battle two of by far the cruelest of all the tyrants were slain.

When Thrasybulus realized that the rest, beaten and put to flight, were for the most part Athenians, he went after them with shouts, held them back with a speech and bound them with entreaties, setting before their eyes whom they would be fleeing from and to whom they would be fleeing: he had undertaken war against thirty masters, not against his wretched fellow citizens. Rather, all who remembered that they were Athenians ought to follow the avengers of Athenian freedom.

This exhortation had such an effect on them that they soon returned to the city and forced the tyrants to leave the citadel and withdraw to Eleusis. After they had received back into the fellowship of the city their fellow citizens, until then exiles, these stirred the tyrants to war out of jealousy, for to them the freedom of others seemed like their own slavery.

Then, when battle had been declared, the tyrants first came together as if for a parley, and were trapped in an ambush and slain like sacrificial victims for peace. Thus the Athenians, brought back together into one body, after endless tears of great joy, laid these first foundations of their recovered liberty: they bound themselves by a solemn oath that past discords and hostilities should be consigned to perpetual oblivion and everlasting silence.

This kind of pact, by which they shaped as it were a new way of life and a new happiness for their state, they called an amnesty, that is, an abolition of evils. It was a most wise provision of the Athenians, especially after such great lessons of misery—if only human affairs could somehow hold firm, as they are ordained, with men's agreement enduring.

But this very agreement was broken almost while its words were being spoken, so that scarcely two years later Socrates, that most famous of philosophers, driven by their ill treatment, was forced to take his own life among them by poison; and then, scarcely forty years later, to say nothing of other things, these same Athenians, wholly stripped of their freedom, were slaves under Philip, king of the Macedonians.

Nevertheless the Athenians, wisest of all, sufficiently taught even by their own misfortunes that by concord the smallest things grow and by discord the greatest fall, and that all things, good or even bad, that are done abroad are rooted in and spring from beginnings at home, wiped out hatreds at home and suppressed wars abroad. They left their descendants an example from their ruin and counsel from their recovery—if only, given the most frail fickleness of the human mind, what is resolved in adversity were kept in prosperity.

At about the same time a civil war, or rather more than a civil war, which was scarcely ended short of fratricide, was being waged among the Persians. For when King Darius died and his sons Artaxerxes and Cyrus disputed the kingdom, at last they fought it out with great preparations, and with ruin to provinces and peoples on both sides.

In that conflict, when chance had brought the two brothers face to face as they charged from opposite sides, Artaxerxes was the first to be wounded by his brother, but escaped death thanks to the speed of his horse. Cyrus, however, was soon overwhelmed by the royal guard and so put an end to the contest. Artaxerxes, then, gaining both the spoils of his brother's expedition and his army, secured the power of the kingdom by fratricide.
Thus all Asia and Europe were thrown into confusion with deaths and crimes, partly each within itself, partly against one another.

See how, in a very small page and in very few words, I have not so much unfolded the deeds of so many provinces, peoples and cities as I have wound up great tangles of misery. For who could unfold in words the disaster of that time, its deaths, or match its sufferings with tears?

And yet these very things, because they have faded through the long passage of the ages, have become for us exercises for the wit and entertaining stories. Still, if anyone were to apply his mind more closely, and with the whole feeling of his heart immerse himself almost in those very causes and wars, and then, standing as it were on the height of a viewing place, weigh each period by its own character, I would readily say that he would judge that those times could not have been so wretchedly disturbed and confused unless God was angry and turned away, nor these times so settled unless He was favorable and merciful.
Then in these times Sicily was shaken by a very severe earthquake, and was laid waste besides by the fires and hot ashes boiling out of Mount Etna, with very great damage to fields and farmsteads.

At that time too the city of Atalante, adjoining Locris and connected to the mainland, was cut off by a sudden onrush of the sea and left desolate as an island. Plague also attacked the pitiable remnants of the Athenians and ravaged them for a long time.

In the 355th year from the founding of the City, the siege of Veii, lasting ten continuous years, wore down the besiegers more than the besieged. For the Romans were often crushed by sudden sallies of the enemy, and were also forced to wage war in winter quarters, to winter under hides, and finally to endure hunger and cold in sight of the enemy.
In the end they took the city by tunnels and stealthy infiltration, without any proof worthy of Roman valor.
This victory, more useful than glorious, was followed first by the exile of the dictator Camillus, who won it over the Veientes, and then by the invasion of the Gauls and the burning of the City.
Let anyone dare, if he can, to compare any disturbances of our time with this disaster—although the injury of the present does not weigh the same as the story of a past evil.

So the Senonian Gauls, under their leader Brennus, with a large and very strong army, were besieging the city of Clusium, in the region now called Tuscia, when they saw Roman envoys, who had come at that time to make peace between the two sides, fighting against them in the battle line. Stung by indignation at this, they abandoned the siege of the town of Clusium and marched on Rome with all their forces.

The consul Fabius met them with an army as they rushed on in this way; yet he did not stop them. Rather, that enemy onslaught cut him down like dry grain, laid him low and passed over him. The river Allia bears witness to this disaster of Fabius, as the Cremera does to that of the Fabii. For one could not easily recount a similar ruin of Roman arms, even if Rome had not also been burned besides.

The Gauls entered the city, which lay open, and slaughtered the senators as they sat stiff as statues in their seats; and burning them in the fire of their houses, they buried them under their own collapsing roofs.

All the rest of the young men, who are known to have numbered barely a thousand at that time, they shut up under siege as they hid in the citadel on the Capitoline Hill; and there they wore down, subdued and sold those unhappy remnants through hunger, disease, despair and fear.

For a thousand pounds of gold was agreed upon as the price of the Gauls' departure—not because Rome was of small repute among the Gauls, but because they had already worn it down so much that it could no longer be worth more.

When the Gauls departed, there remained within the City's former circuit a foul heap of shapeless ruins, and everywhere the echo of voices, as people wandered through obstructed ways, strangers among their own surroundings, answered back and kept their anxious ears in suspense. Horror shook their minds; the very silence terrified them—for emptiness in wide spaces is a source of dread.
Hence they considered, approved and attempted moving their home, living in another town, and even being registered under another name.

Here are the times by comparison with which the present is weighed; here are the times for which memory sighs; here are the times that strike people with regret over the religion they chose, or rather neglected.

Truly these two captures are comparable, and may be set side by side: that one raged for six months, this one passed in three days; the Gauls, having destroyed the people and razed the City, hunted down even the very name of Rome in its last ashes, while the Goths, abandoning their purpose of plunder, drove crowds who knew not where to go to refuges of safety, that is, to the holy places; there scarcely a senator was found who escaped even by being absent, here scarcely one is missed

who perhaps perished in hiding. I could quite rightly make this comparison: the number of those saved there was the number of those lost here. Plainly, what the facts reveal must also be confessed: in this present disaster God raged more and men less, since by accomplishing himself what they had not carried out, He showed why He had sent them.

For since it was beyond human strength to set bronze beams on fire and bring down the masses of great buildings, the Forum, with its vain images which by a wretched superstition counterfeit either a god or a man, was struck down by bolts of lightning; and all those abominations that the flames set by the enemy did not reach, fire sent from heaven overthrew.
And since this is a rich subject for discussion that can by no means be concluded in this book, let this be the end of the present volume, so that we may pursue the rest in those that follow.
THE THIRD BOOK OF THE HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS OF PAULUS OROSIUS.

I declared in the previous book, and must now repeat, in keeping with your instruction about the past conflicts of the world, that not everything can be set out, nor every detail of what was done and how it was done, since these things are great and countless. They have been written about at very great length and by very many authors. Those writers had the same events before them, though not the same purpose, for they were recounting wars, while we are recounting the miseries of wars.

Besides, this very abundance I complain of puts me in a difficult position and hems me in with a still more tangled anxiety. If for the sake of brevity I leave some things out, it will be thought either that I did not know of them or that they never happened at that time. But if I try to indicate everything without spelling it out, and gird it up in a compressed brevity, I will make it obscure, and for most readers it will be said in such a way that it seems not to have been said at all,

especially since we, on the contrary, take care to convey the force of events and not merely their outline. Brevity and obscurity, or rather brevity, which is always obscure, may offer an outline of knowledge, but it takes away the strength of understanding. Since I know that both faults must be avoided, I will do both things, so that each may in some way temper the other, if it appears that not much has been left out and not much has been squeezed together.

In the 364th year from the founding of the City, a year that Rome felt as most grievous because of a captivity unknown to her before, and that Greece found splendid because of an unaccustomed peace, at the very time when the Gauls held Rome captured and burned and were selling it, Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, sent envoys commanding all Greece to lay down its arms and rest in peace, and warned that anyone who opposed the peace would be attacked in war.

The Greeks could surely have scorned such an order as steadfastly as they had often bravely conquered, had they not so gladly seized an opportunity, offered from whatever quarter, that they had so eagerly longed for.

For they showed how grudgingly and wretchedly they had carried on until then the wars they laid down so easily, even on shameful terms. What could be more shameful for free and brave men than to lay down their arms and submit to peace at the command of an enemy far away, often beaten, still an enemy and threatening besides? Yet so it was: at the mere sound of peace announced, the sickly zeal for war had wasted away in everyone's heart, and after long vigils of toil an unexpected rest had relaxed them as they yawned in a stupor, before their own will could arrange that rest by treaty.

Why so great a weariness had crushed the hearts and bodies of all the peoples throughout Greece, and so easily persuaded those savage spirits to settle into a leisure unknown to them, I will show as briefly as I can.
The Spartans, being men, and Greek men at that, desired more the more they had. Once they had made themselves masters of the Athenians, they swallowed all Asia in their hope of domination.

So, stirring up war against the whole East, they chose Dercylidas as general for this campaign. Seeing that he would have to fight against two very powerful satraps of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes, he adopted a plan suited to the moment in order to escape the weight of a double engagement: he declared war on one and attacked him, and held the other in check by making peace.

Pharnabazus denounced Tissaphernes as a traitor to Artaxerxes, then king of both, above all because he had negotiated terms of a treaty with the enemy in wartime. He urged the king to appoint in his place the Athenian Conon, who happened then to be living in exile on Cyprus, as commander for the war at sea. So Conon, after receiving five hundred talents of silver, was summoned through Pharnabazus and put in command of the fleet.

When the Spartans learned this, they too sent envoys to ask Hercynion, king of Egypt, for help in the naval war. From him they received a hundred equipped triremes and six hundred thousand measures of grain, and they also gathered great support from their allies on every side.

By common consent they appointed Agesilaus commander of this campaign, a man lame in the foot, but they preferred, in the most difficult state of affairs, that their king should limp rather than their kingdom. Rarely have commanders so evenly matched in every kind of energy come together in a single war. Worn out by the bitterest battles against each other and smeared with much blood, they parted as though neither had been beaten by the other.

Conon, then, having received pay from the Great King a second time, this time in person, returned to the fleet. He invaded the enemy's lands, stormed towers, forts and other strongholds, and like a storm let loose he flattened everything wherever he fell.

The Spartans, beset by troubles at home, ceased to covet what lay abroad and cast away their hope of domination as the danger of slavery loomed over them. They recalled Agesilaus, whom they had sent with an army into Asia, to help their homeland.

Meanwhile Pisander, whom King Agesilaus had left in command at Sparta, had fitted out a very large and very well equipped fleet. Moved by rivalry with Agesilaus's prowess, he wanted to roam the coast on naval raids himself while Agesilaus was conducting his campaign on land.

Conon, having taken on this task, devoted a double care to it, owing diligence to his allies and loyalty to his homeland, so that he might show his country his natural devotion and give his allies his energy. He was the more devoted to his fellow citizens in that he was spending the risk of other men's blood for their peace and freedom, and was fighting against most insolent enemies at the king's peril and for his homeland's reward.
So they joined battle at sea, the Persians under Conon, the Spartans under Pisander. Soldiers, rowers and the commanders themselves were swept with equal fury into mutual slaughter.

The size and savagery of this war is revealed by the condition of the Spartans, which declined from then on for ever after. For from that time the hope of the Spartans was seen to ebb and slip backward, until, rising with difficulty and falling back wretchedly, it was worn out and lost both its power and its name.

For the Athenians, on the other hand, this same battle was the beginning of recovering their power, just as for the Spartans it was the beginning of losing theirs. The Thebans, then, supported by Athenian help, were the first to attack the Spartans, who were wounded and fearful from their earlier defeat. The Thebans were greatly emboldened by the courage and energy of their general Epaminondas, with whom they thought they could easily win the rule of all Greece.

So a battle was fought on land, and the Thebans won with very little effort. In this encounter too Lysander was defeated and killed. Pausanias, the other Spartan commander, was accused of treason and sent into exile.

Having won the victory, the Thebans gathered the forces of their whole army and marched on Sparta, thinking they would enter without any trouble a city stripped of its defenders, since they had already destroyed almost all its forces together with the king himself and saw that it had been abandoned by all its allies.

Driven by the danger to their city, the Spartans held a levy of untrained soldiers, of whatever sort they could, and went out to meet the enemy. But men who had once been beaten had neither the courage nor the spirit to stand against their conquerors.

When the slaughter was falling almost entirely on one side, King Agesilaus, recalled from Asia, suddenly arrived unexpectedly at the battle. He attacked the Thebans, who were by now more elated and more careless from the success of their double victory, and defeated them without difficulty, especially since his own forces were still almost intact. Agesilaus himself, however, was seriously wounded.

When the Athenians learned that the Spartans had been raised up by this unexpected victory, they were terrified by fear of their former servitude, from which they had scarcely begun to breathe again. They gathered an army and joined it to the Boeotians as reinforcements, entrusting it to the general Iphicrates, who was quite young, barely twenty years old, but who fortified the weakness of his age with maturity of mind.

Conon too, an Athenian but the commander of a Persian army, on hearing of Agesilaus's return, came back to lay waste the lands of the Spartans. So the Spartans, shut in and terrified by the din of enemies sounding all around them, wasted away in what was almost utter despair.

But Conon, once he had had his fill of ravaging the enemy's soil far and wide, went on to Athens. Amid the great joy of the citizens he himself was sad, seeing that the city, once splendidly adorned with people and refinement, was now worn down in the wretched squalor of ruin and desolation.

So he wrought a great monument of devotion and compassion in rebuilding it. The city the Spartans had emptied he filled again with Spartan plunder, and the city the Persians had burned down he restored with the Persians building it.

Meanwhile Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, as was said at the beginning, sent envoys commanding all the peoples of Greece to lay down their arms and settle into peace. He did so not out of compassion for their exhaustion, but so that, while he was occupied with wars in Egypt, no invasion of his kingdom would be attempted.

So while all the Greeks were relaxed in the peace they had so longed for and were growing sluggish in leisure at home, the Spartans, more restless than vigorous, and unbearable more for their madness than for their courage, after laying wars aside attempted war by stealth.

Watching for a time when the Arcadians were away, they broke into one of their forts in a sudden attack. The Arcadians, roused by the wrong, joined the Thebans to them as allies and sought to win back by war what they had lost by stealth.

In that battle Archidamus, the Spartan commander, was wounded. Seeing his men being cut down as though already beaten, he asked through a herald for the bodies of the slain for burial, which among the Greeks is customarily taken as a sign that victory has been conceded.
The Thebans, satisfied with this admission, gave the signal to spare them and put an end to the fighting.

Then, after a few days of truce had passed, when the Spartans had turned to other wars, the Thebans under their general Epaminondas grew confident of invading Sparta, thinking it unguarded and abandoned. They came to Sparta silently in the dead of night, but did not find it as careless or undefended as they had supposed.

For the old men, armed together with the rest of the crowd too old or too young for war, had learned in advance of the enemy's approach and threw themselves into the narrow passages of the gates. Barely a hundred men worn out with age charged out against fifteen thousand soldiers. While they were holding up so great a weight of war, the young men arrived and resolved without hesitation to engage the Thebans in open battle.

Battle was joined, and when the Spartans were being beaten, Epaminondas, the Theban general, fighting too recklessly, was suddenly wounded. As a result, fear arose in the Thebans from their grief, and stupefaction in the Spartans from their joy, and both sides withdrew as if by silent agreement.

Epaminondas, gravely wounded, when he had learned of his men's victory and had kissed his shield, removed the hand with which he had closed the wound, opening a way out for his blood and a way in for death. His death was followed by such a ruin of the Thebans that they seemed not to have lost their leader but to have perished with him themselves.

I have woven a tangled wickerwork of disordered history, and, following step by step the words of the accounts, I have entangled in it the uncertain cycles of wars waged this way and that in frenzied madness; for, as I see, the more I have kept to the order of events, the more disorderly my writing has become.

The shameless lust of the Spartans for domination: among how many peoples, in what cities, in which provinces did it stir up what kinds of hatred, and how many causes of conflict? Who could set this out by number, by order or by reason? Indeed, they themselves are said to have been afflicted no more by wars than by the confusion of wars.

For this war was dragged on without a break for several generations, and Athenians, Spartans, Arcadians, Boeotians and Thebans, and finally Greece, Asia, Persia and Egypt together with Libya and the islands, fought immense battles by sea and land alike in confused movements back and forth. I could not report the thousands of men slain even if I were to count the wars.

So let anyone now find fault with these times and praise those times who does not know that all the peoples of these cities and provinces now grow old in nothing but games and theaters, just as then they wasted away above all in camps and battles.

That most flourishing city of the Spartans, which at that time aspired to rule the whole East, could barely muster a hundred old men; so beset was it by unceasing evils that it wretchedly spent its lives before their time.

And do men complain now, whose cities, full of boys and old men, are enriched by their young men traveling abroad in safety, and who earn the wages of pleasure at home through peaceful pursuits? Unless perhaps, since in human fickleness everything present usually seems mean, life itself has become tiresome to those whose ears itch for novelty.
In the 376th year from the founding of the City, a most violent earthquake shook all Achaea, and two cities, Bura and Helice, were swallowed up when the ground split open into chasms.

I, on the other hand, could now tell of similar things in our own day at Constantinople, now likewise the chief city of the nations, things foretold and begun but not carried through. After a terrible warning, and while the city's conscience foreknew its own guilt, the earth was shaken from its foundations and trembled below, and fire poured out from heaven hung overhead, until God, moved by the prayers of the emperor Arcadius and the Christian people, turned aside the destruction that was upon them,

proving that he alone is both the preserver of the humble and the punisher of the wicked. But out of modesty I would let these things be mentioned rather than explained, so that whoever knows them may recall them, and whoever does not may look into them.

Meanwhile the Romans, who for seventy years had been subdued and worn down, exhausted by constant wars with the city of the Volscians, and besides with the Faliscans, the Aequi and the people of Sutrium, finally, at the time described above, captured these same cities under the command of Camillus and put an end to a struggle that kept coming back to life.
At the same time, too, they defeated the Praenestines, who had come right up to the gate of Rome fighting and killing, at the river Allia, with Titus Quinctius in command.
In the 384th year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Lucius Genucius and Quintus Servilius, a great plague seized all Rome.

It was not of the usual kind, when the balance of the seasons is disturbed more or less than ordinary, that is, by an untimely drought in winter, a sudden heat in spring, an unseasonable wetness in summer, or the unwholesome lure of a rich autumn, and when, on top of this, a corrupting breeze breathed out from the forests of Calabria brings sudden bouts of acute illness that soon pass.

Rather, it was severe and long-lasting, sparing no sex and no age, and for two years it steadily wore everyone out with a general wasting, so that even those it did not drive to death it left drained and broken by a shameful emaciation.

At this point, I think, the detractors of the Christian era would complain if I happened to pass over in silence the ceremonies by which the Romans of that time appeased the gods and calmed the diseases.

As the plague grew fiercer day by day, the pontiffs advised that stage plays be put on, since the gods demanded them. So to drive off a temporary plague of the body, an everlasting disease of the soul was brought in.

This is indeed a rich occasion for me to lament and rebuke. But since Your Reverence has already exercised your zeal for wisdom and truth on this subject, it is not right for me to venture to say more about it. Let it be enough that I have mentioned it, and that I have referred the reader, whatever his purpose, to the full treatment in that work.

This wretched plague and its still more wretched expiation were followed the next year by a quite grim portent. Suddenly the ground split open in the middle of the City, and through a vast chasm the gaping underworld was suddenly laid open.
For a long time the shameless pit remained there with its gaping abyss, a spectacle and a terror to all, and, as the gods' interpreters declared, it demanded the wicked burial of a living man.

Marcus Curtius, a man of equestrian rank, in full armor, satisfied those insatiable jaws by casting himself headlong, and fed the cruel earth an unhoped-for fill. It was not enough for it to receive through the graves the dead from so great a plague; it also had to split open and swallow the living.

In the 388th year from the founding of the City, a terrible flood of Gauls again settled by the river Anio, four miles from the City. Without doubt they would easily have seized the panic-stricken city by the weight of their numbers and the eagerness of their courage, had they not grown sluggish through idleness and delay.

There Manlius Torquatus began a most savage battle in single combat, and Titus Quinctius the dictator finished it in a most bloody engagement. Very many of the Gauls fled from this battle, but when they had restored their forces and were rushing into war again, they were defeated by the dictator Gaius Sulpicius.
A little later there followed a battle with the Etruscans under Gaius Marcius. How many men were slain there may be guessed from the fact that eight thousand Etruscans were taken prisoner.

For a third time in those same days the Gauls spread out to plunder through the coastal districts and the plains lying below the Alban hills. Against them, after a new levy of soldiers had been held and ten legions enrolled, sixty thousand Romans marched out, since the Latins had refused them help.

Marcus Valerius finished this battle with the help of a raven, from which he was afterward called Corvinus. For when the Gaul who had issued the challenge was killed, the enemy were terrified, scattered in flight and were slaughtered in great numbers.

I think that among the evils must also be counted that first treaty concluded with the Carthaginians, which took place at this same time, especially since from it arose evils so grievous that they seem to have begun from then.
For in the 402nd year from the founding of the City, envoys were sent from Carthage to Rome and concluded a treaty.

That this entry of the Carthaginians into Italy would be followed by a hailstorm of evils and the unbroken darkness of continual miseries is attested by the unanimous reliability of the histories, by the infamy of the places and by the abhorrence of the days on which those things were done.
At that time, too, night was seen to stretch over the greater part of the day, and hail of stone fell from the clouds and pelted the earth with real stones.
In those days, too, Alexander the Great was born, truly a whirlpool of miseries and the most savage hurricane of the whole East.

At that time, too, Ochus, also called Artaxerxes, after finishing a very great and long war in Egypt, drove a great many of the Jews into exile and ordered them to live in Hyrcania by the Caspian Sea.
It is believed that they remain there to this day, with their race greatly increased, and that someday they will break out from there.

In the storm of this same war, as he swept through, he destroyed Sidon, the wealthiest city of the province of Phoenicia, and Egypt, though he had earlier been defeated there, he now subdued, crushed with the sword and made subject to Persian rule.

From this point on, the Romans immediately took up wars against the Samnites, a people strong in wealth and arms, on behalf of the Campanians and the Sidicini. The Samnite war, fought with uncertain fortunes, was followed by Pyrrhus, perhaps the greatest enemy of the Roman name, and the war with Pyrrhus was soon followed by the Punic war.

And although the gates of Janus, standing always open, show that there was never any respite from the disasters of war after the death of Numa, yet from that time on the heat of evils blazed up, as though pressing down from the whole sky at midday.

Moreover, once the Punic war had begun, whether wars, slaughter, ruin and every kind of unspeakable death ever ceased before the reign of Caesar Augustus, let anyone who thinks the Christian era should be defamed inquire, find out and declare.

Except, however, for that one year during the Punic wars, which passed like the flight of a bird flying by, when, because the gates of Janus were closed, the Romans, amid the fevers and diseases of the state, were enticed by this very brief sign of peace as by a tiny sip of cold water, only to burn up again for the worse and be afflicted far more severely and violently.

But it is established beyond all doubt that under Caesar Augustus, after the peace with Parthia, the whole world for the first time laid down its arms, put an end to its quarrels, was settled in a general peace and a new tranquility, and obeyed Roman laws; that it preferred Roman justice to its own arms, and, scorning its own leaders, chose Roman judges;

and finally, that all nations, all provinces, countless cities, innumerable peoples and all lands had a single will, to devote themselves freely and honorably to peace and to take counsel for the common good, something that before then not even a single city or a single people of citizens, or, what is more, a single household of brothers, could have maintained for long.
If, moreover, these things came about in the reign of Caesar, and it is shown by the clearest proof that in the very reign of Caesar the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ dawned upon this world,

then those whom envy was driving to blasphemy will be forced, however unwilling, to recognize and admit that this peace of the whole world and this most tranquil calm came about not through the greatness of Caesar but through the power of the Son of God, who appeared in the days of Caesar; and that the world itself, in a general acknowledgment, obeyed not the emperor of one city but the Creator of the whole world, who, as the rising sun floods the day with light, so at his coming mercifully clothed the world in a widespread peace. This will be set out more fully when, by the Lord's own doing, we come to that point.

So in the 409th year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Manlius Torquatus and Decius Mus, the Romans made war on the Latins, who had rebelled. In this war one consul was killed and the other became the murderer of his own son.

For Manlius Torquatus put to death his own son, a young man and a victor, who had killed Metius of Tusculum, a noble horseman and at that time the enemy who was most conspicuously challenging and taunting them.
The other consul, when in a second engagement he saw the wing he commanded being cut down and overwhelmed, of his own accord threw himself into the thickest of the enemy and fell.
