Manlius, although victorious, did not deserve the welcome by the noble young men of Rome that is customarily given at a triumph, for he triumphed as the murderer of his own son.
In the year after this, Minucia, a Vestal Virgin, was condemned for having committed unchastity and was buried alive in the field that is now called the Accursed Field.

But after a short interval of time, I shudder to relate what took place. In the consulship of Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Flaccus, the matrons of Rome burst out in an unbelievable frenzy and passion for crime.

It was indeed a foul and pestilent year. Corpses were already being carried out in heaps on every side, and still everyone simply believed that the air had been corrupted. Then a certain slave woman came forward as an informer and proved the charge. First, many matrons were forced to drink the poisons they had brewed, and as soon as they had swallowed them they perished.
So great, moreover, was the number of matrons who shared in these crimes that three hundred and seventy of them are reported to have been condemned at one time.

In the year 422 from the founding of the City, Alexander, king of the Epirotes and uncle of the famous Alexander the Great, brought his forces over into Italy. While he was preparing war against the Romans and busying himself with wars among the cities neighbouring Rome, eager to strengthen his army and either to win allies for himself or to draw them away from his enemies, he was defeated and killed in Lucania in a very great battle by the Samnites, who were supporting the Lucanian people.

But since I have gone some way in reviewing the disasters of Rome, and since I am reminded by the mention of this Alexander, I shall go back a very few years and gather together, as briefly as I can, great matters in a small compass concerning Philip, king of the Macedonians, who had as his wife Olympias, sister of this Alexander of Epirus, and by her fathered Alexander the Great.

In the year 400 from the founding of the City, Philip, son of Amyntas and father of Alexander, obtained the kingdom of the Macedonians and held it for twenty-five years, during which he heaped up all these piles of cruelties and whole mountains of evils.
He had first been given as a hostage to the Thebans by his brother Alexander, and for three years he was educated in the house of Epaminondas, a most energetic general and an outstanding philosopher.

When Alexander himself had been killed through the crime of their mother Eurydice—who had already committed adultery, had first killed another of her sons, and, having made her daughter a widow, had bargained for marriage with her son-in-law at the price of her husband's death—Philip was compelled by the people to take up the kingdom, which he had been guarding for the young son of his murdered brother.
Worn down abroad by the onslaught of enemies rising against him on every side, and at home by fear of plots that were often discovered, he waged his first war against the Athenians.
Having defeated them, he turned his arms against the Illyrians, and after slaughtering many thousands of the enemy he captured Larissa, a most renowned city.
From there he invaded Thessaly, not so much from love of victory as from ambition to possess the Thessalian cavalry, so that he might add their strength to his own army.
So, having taken the Thessalians by surprise and brought them under his power, he joined together the bravest squadrons of horse and companies of foot and made his army invincible.

Then, after defeating the Athenians and subjugating the Thessalians, he married Olympias, sister of Arybbas, king of the Molossians. Arybbas thought that by forming an alliance with the Macedonians through kinship with their king he would enlarge his own dominion; but by this very means he was deceived, lost it, and grew old as a private man in exile.
Next, while besieging the city of Methone, Philip lost an eye to an arrow. The city itself, however, he soon stormed and took.

After this, having first outwitted almost all of Greece by his schemes, he subdued it by force. For while the cities of Greece each wished to rule, they all lost their rule, and while they rushed without restraint into mutual ruin, they realized only when at last crushed and enslaved that what each was losing singly was being lost by all.

Philip watched their mad dealings as if from a watchtower, and, a cunning craftsman of deceit, always fed their quarrels—the kindling of wars—by offering help to the weaker side, until he had made victors and vanquished alike subject to himself.

The opportunity to win mastery over the whole of Greece was given him by the unbounded domination of the Thebans. They had defeated the Lacedaemonians and the Phocians and worn them out with slaughter and plunder, and, having moreover burdened them in the common council of Greece with a fine so large that they could in no way pay it, they drove them to take up arms.

So the Phocians, under the leadership of Philomelus and supported by Lacedaemonian and Athenian auxiliaries, joined battle, routed the enemy, and took the Theban camp. In the following battle, amid immense slaughter on both sides, Philomelus was killed; in his place the Phocians made Onomarchus their leader.

The Thebans and Thessalians, for their part, set aside a levy of their own citizens and of their own accord sought as their leader Philip, king of Macedonia, whom they had earlier struggled to drive off as an enemy. Battle was joined, the Phocians were cut down almost to the point of extermination, and the victory went to Philip.

But when the Athenians heard the outcome of the war, they seized the pass of Thermopylae to prevent Philip from crossing into Greece, in the same way as they had once done when the Persians were advancing.

So when Philip saw that he was shut out from entering Greece because Thermopylae had been blocked, he turned against his allies the war he had prepared against his enemies. The cities whose leader he had been shortly before, which opened their gates to welcome and receive him, he attacked as an enemy and cruelly

plundered; and, utterly casting off every sense of alliance, he sold the wives and children of all of them into slavery and also overthrew and despoiled every temple. Yet in twenty-five years he was never defeated, as though the gods were angry with him.

After this he crossed into Cappadocia and waged war there with the same treachery: he captured the neighbouring kings by deceit, put them to death, and subjected the whole of Cappadocia to Macedonian rule.

Then, after the slaughter, burning, and plundering carried out in allied cities, he turned to the murder of his own kin, setting out to kill his brothers, born to his father by a stepmother, because he feared them as co-heirs to the kingdom.

When he had killed one of them, the other two fled to Olynthus. Philip soon attacked it as an enemy, and that most ancient and flourishing city he filled with slaughter and blood and emptied of wealth and people; his brothers too he dragged off and put to torture and death.

Next, elated by the destruction of his allies and the murder of his brothers, he thought he was permitted to do anything he had in mind. He seized the gold-bearing districts of Thessaly and the silver mines of Thrace, and, so as to leave no law human or divine unviolated, he took control of the sea, scattered his fleet, and set about practising piracy as well.

Moreover, when two brothers, kings of Thrace, who were in dispute over the boundaries of their kingdom, had by mutual consent chosen him as their judge, Philip, true to his character, came to the judgment as if to a war, with his army in battle order, and deprived the unsuspecting young men of their lives and their kingdom.

The Athenians, who had earlier blocked Philip's entry by fortifying Thermopylae, now of their own accord sought peace with him and even warned that most treacherous enemy that the guard on the pass had been neglected.
The other cities of Greece as well, so that they might devote themselves more fully to their civil wars, voluntarily submitted to foreign domination under the guise of peace and treaty,

especially when the Thessalians and Boeotians were demanding that Philip show himself the leader against the Phocians that he had professed to be and carry on the war he had undertaken, while the Phocians, together with the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, were striving with bribes and entreaties to have the war either postponed or called off.

Philip secretly promised contrary things to each: to the Phocians he confirmed by oath that he would grant them peace and pardon, while to the Thessalians he pledged that he would soon be at hand with his army; yet he forbade both sides to prepare for war.
So Philip, with his forces drawn up, entered the pass of Thermopylae without any danger, occupied it, and fortified it with garrisons placed at intervals.

Only then did not the Phocians alone but all Greece realize that it had been taken captive. For Philip broke his word, trampled on his oath, and gave the Phocians first over to unspeakable butchery; then he ravaged the cities and territories of all, and by his bloody presence made sure that he would be feared even when absent.

When he returned to his kingdom, he moved peoples and cities about at his whim, just as herdsmen drive their flocks now through summer pastures, now through winter ones, according as each place seemed to him to need filling or emptying.
Everywhere a pitiful sight met the eye and a most dreadful kind of misery: to suffer destruction without invasion, captivity without war, exile without crime, subjection without a conqueror.

Amid the goads of injustice an overwhelming dread weighed upon the wretched people, and their grief grew in the very act of hiding it, sinking all the deeper the less they were allowed to voice it, for they feared that even their tears might be taken as defiance.

Some peoples he tore from their homes and settled on the borders of the enemy; others he placed at the furthest bounds of his kingdom; some, out of jealousy of their strength, lest they be able to do what they were believed capable of, he split up to repopulate exhausted cities.
Thus that once most glorious body of flourishing Greece, its liberty first extinguished, fell apart into many mangled fragments.

When he had done these things throughout a number of the cities of Greece and yet still kept them all in the grip of fear, he reckoned the wealth of all from the plunder of a few. To complete an equal devastation of them all, he judged that a coastal city would be necessary and profitable, and he decided that Byzantium, a renowned city, was the most suitable to become his base by land and sea; and when it resisted him he at once laid siege to it.

This Byzantium was founded long ago by Pausanias, king of the Spartans, and later was enlarged by Constantine, the Christian emperor, and named Constantinople; it is now the seat of a most glorious empire and the capital of the whole East.

After a long and fruitless siege, Philip turned to piracy, so as to recover by plunder the money he had used up in the siege. He captured one hundred and seventy ships laden with merchandise, sold off their cargoes, and so gave his gasping poverty a little relief.

Then he divided his army, part to gather plunder and part to carry on the siege. He himself set out with his bravest men, took many cities of the Chersonese, crushed their peoples, and carried off their wealth. He also crossed into Scythia with his son Alexander with the aim of plunder.

At that time Atheas was king of the Scythians. Hard pressed in a war with the Histrians, he asked Philip for help through the people of Apollonia; but when the king of the Histrians died soon afterwards, freed both from fear of war and from the need for help, he dissolved the treaty he had made with Philip.

Philip abandoned the siege of Byzantium and turned to the Scythian war with all his forces. Battle was joined, and although the Scythians were superior both in numbers and in courage, they were defeated by Philip's trickery.

In that battle twenty thousand boys and women of the Scythian nation were captured and a great quantity of livestock was driven off, but no gold or silver was found; this indeed first gave proof of the poverty of the Scythians. Twenty thousand thoroughbred mares were sent to Macedonia to improve the breed.

But as Philip was returning, the Triballi met him in battle, in which Philip was wounded in the thigh so severely that the weapon passed through his body and killed his horse. Since everyone thought he had been killed, his men turned to flight and lost the plunder. Then for some little time, while he was recovering from his wound, he remained at rest in peace.

But as soon as he had recovered he made war on the Athenians. Placed in such great danger, they enlisted the Lacedaemonians, once their enemies but now their allies, and wearied the cities of all Greece with embassies, urging them to attack the common enemy with their common strength. So a number of cities joined the Athenians, while fear of war drew others over to Philip.
When battle was joined, though the Athenians had a far greater number of soldiers, they were nevertheless defeated by the valour of the Macedonians, hardened by continual wars.

The outcome itself showed that this battle was far more terrible than all earlier wars, for this day put an end, throughout all Greece, both to the glory of the dominion they had won and to the condition of their most ancient liberty.

Afterwards Philip used his victory over the Thebans and Lacedaemonians most bloodily: some of the leading men of their cities he beheaded, others he drove into exile, and all he stripped of their property.

Those who had earlier been banished by their fellow citizens he restored to their homelands, and out of these exiles he appointed three hundred as judges and governors, so that, salving their old grievance with new power, they would not let the unhappily oppressed peoples breathe again in hope of liberty.

Besides this, he held a great levy of soldiers from all Greece in support of his royal plans, and prepared two hundred thousand foot and fifteen thousand horse, apart from the Macedonian army and a countless horde of barbarian peoples, intending to send them on a Persian expedition into Asia.

He chose three generals, namely Parmenion, Amyntas, and Attalus, to be sent ahead against the Persians. And while the forces mentioned above were being gathered from Greece, he decided to celebrate the wedding of Alexander, joining to him his daughter Cleopatra. This Alexander was the brother of his wife Olympias, and was later struck down by the Sabines in Lucania; Philip had made him king of Epirus as payment for the sexual abuse he had inflicted on him.

On the day before he was killed, Philip was asked what end a man should most wish for, and he is said to have answered that the best was one that could befall a brave man, after the glories of his achievements, while reigning in peace: sudden and swift, by an unexpected blade, without bodily struggle or disgrace of mind. This very thing soon happened to him.
Nor could the angry gods—whom he had always held of little account and whose altars, temples, and images he had overthrown—prevent him from obtaining what seemed to him the most desirable death.

For on the wedding day, as he was making his way to the magnificently prepared games between the two Alexanders, his son and his son-in-law, he was surrounded in a narrow passage, without his guards, by Pausanias, a young Macedonian noble, and killed.

Let them now assert these things and extol them with many words as the praises of brave men and happy deeds—they for whom the bitterest calamities of others turn into pleasant tales—provided, however, that they themselves never bewail in sadder narration the injuries by which they are at times afflicted.

But if they want others who hear their own complaints to be as moved as they themselves felt in suffering them, let them first compare not past with present, but deeds with deeds, and judge both from hearsay, as though arbiters of other people's affairs.

For twenty-five years the treachery, ferocity, and tyranny of a single king drove on the burning of cities, the destruction of wars, the subjugation of provinces, the slaughter of men, the plundering of wealth, the seizure of flocks, the sale of the dead, and the enslavement of the living.

These deeds of Philip that have been recalled to our memory would suffice as an example of miseries, even if Alexander had not succeeded him on the throne. His wars—or rather, the evils of the world that followed in order under his wars—I set aside for a little while, so that at this point I may insert Roman affairs in keeping with the chronology.

In the year 426 from the founding of the City, a notable disgrace of the Romans made the Caudine Forks quite celebrated and famous. In the previous war twenty thousand Samnites had fallen when Fabius, the master of the horse, engaged them in battle; so now the Samnites, with more watchful care and better-prepared equipment, took up position at the Caudine Forks.

There, when they had shut in the consuls Veturius and Postumius and all the Roman forces by the narrowness of the ground and by their arms, their leader Pontius was so carried away by the security of his victory that he thought he should consult his father Herennius as to whether to kill the trapped men or spare them once they had been brought under the yoke. He chose, however, to keep them alive for disgrace.
For it was well known that the Romans had very often before been defeated and killed, but had never been captured or forced to surrender.

So the Samnites, masters of the victory, ordered the whole Roman army—shamefully captured, stripped even of arms and clothing, allowed only a single cheap garment each to cover their private parts, sent under the yoke, and reduced to servitude—to lead a long procession.
Six hundred Roman knights they took as hostages, and they sent the consuls back laden with disgrace and empty of everything else.

Why should I labour with words to magnify the stain of this most shameful treaty, when I would rather have kept silent? For today the Romans either would not exist at all or would be slaves under Samnite dominion, if they, when subject to the Samnites, had kept the good faith of the treaty that they will not allow their own subjects to break.

The following year the Romans broke the pact they had concluded with the Samnites and forced them into war. It was fought under the urging of the consul Papirius and caused great slaughter on both sides.

With anger at their recent disgrace spurring on the one side and the glory of their latest victory the other, the Romans at last won by stubbornly dying; and they did not cease alike to be slain and to slay until they had conquered the Samnites, captured their leader, and laid the yoke on them in their turn.

Then the same Papirius drove the Samnite garrison out of Satricum, stormed the town, and took it. This Papirius was held at that time among the Romans to be so warlike and energetic that, when it was said that Alexander the Great was planning to come down from the East, seize Africa by force, and cross from there into Italy, the Romans considered that, among the best generals they then had in their state, he above all would be the one able to withstand Alexander's onslaught.

So in the year 426 from the founding of the City, Alexander succeeded his father Philip on the throne. He gave the first proof of his spirit and valour by swiftly crushing the uprisings of the Greeks, whose instigator in revolting from Macedonian rule had been the orator Demosthenes, bribed with Persian gold.

Accordingly, when the Athenians begged him to spare them from war, he let them off and even freed them from the fear of a fine. The Thebans he wiped out, destroying their city and selling the survivors into slavery; the other cities of Achaea and Thessaly he made tributary; and soon afterwards, shifting the war there, he subdued the Illyrians and Thracians as well.

Then, as he was about to set out for the Persian war, he killed all his relatives and kinsmen. In his army there were thirty-two thousand foot, [?] thousand five hundred horse, and one hundred and eighty ships. With so small a force, whether it is more amazing that he conquered the whole world or that he dared to attack it is uncertain.

In his first engagement with King Darius there were six hundred thousand Persians in the battle line, and they turned their backs, overcome no less by Alexander's skill than by the valour of the Macedonians. There was therefore a great slaughter of the Persians. In Alexander's army only one hundred and twenty horsemen and nine foot soldiers were lost.

Next he besieged, stormed, and took Gordium, a city of Phrygia which is now called Sardis, and gave it over to plunder. Then, when news was brought to him of Darius's approach with great forces, fearing the narrow ground in which he found himself, he crossed the Taurus range with amazing speed, covering five hundred stades at a run in a single day, and came to Tarsus. There, when he had gone down into the ice-cold river Cydnus while sweating, he went stiff, and with his sinews contracted he came very close to death.

Meanwhile Darius advanced into battle with three hundred thousand foot and one hundred thousand horse. This multitude of enemies alarmed even Alexander, chiefly in view of his own small numbers, although, having already overcome six hundred thousand enemies with the same small force, he had learned not only not to fear battle but even to hope for victory.

So when both armies had halted within a spear's throw, and the commanders, riding up and down, were rousing with various incitements the hosts that stood waiting for the signal for battle, the fight was joined with great spirit on both sides.
In it both kings, Alexander and Darius, were wounded, and the struggle remained in doubt until Darius fled; from then on a slaughter of the Persians followed.

There eighty thousand foot and ten thousand horse were slain, and forty thousand were captured. Of the Macedonians, one hundred and thirty foot and one hundred and fifty horse fell. In the Persian camp much gold and other wealth was found. Among the captives in the camp were Darius's mother, his wife, who was also his sister, and his two daughters.
When Darius failed to obtain their ransom even by offering half his kingdom, he gathered all the forces of the Persians and the auxiliaries of his allies and renewed the war for the third time.

But while Darius was doing this, Alexander sent Parmenion with forces to attack the Persian fleet, and he himself set out for Syria. There, of the many kings who came out to meet him of their own accord wearing the fillets of suppliants, some he took into alliance, some he replaced, and some he destroyed. Tyre, a most ancient and flourishing city, which resisted him trusting in its kinsmen the Carthaginians, he crushed and captured.

From there he overran Cilicia, Rhodes, and Egypt with relentless fury. Then he went on to the temple of Jupiter Ammon, so that by a lie contrived for the occasion he might wipe out the disgrace of an uncertain father and the infamy of an adulterous mother.

For, as their own historians say, he summoned the priest of that shrine to him and secretly instructed him what answer he wanted to be given to himself when he consulted the oracle. Thus Alexander was certain, and has revealed to us, that since the gods themselves are dumb and deaf, it lies either in the power of the priest to invent what he wishes or in the will of the inquirer to hear what he prefers.
Returning from Ammon to the third Persian war, he founded Alexandria in Egypt.
Darius, having lost all hope of peace, set four hundred thousand infantry and a hundred thousand cavalry against Alexander near Tarsus as he returned from Egypt.

There was no delay in joining battle. Both sides rushed upon the sword in blind fury: the Macedonians emboldened against enemies they had beaten so many times, the Persians preferring to die unless they won.
Rarely has so much blood been shed in any battle. When Darius saw his men being beaten, he was ready to die in the fight, but his followers persuaded him and forced him to flee.

In this battle the strength and the kingdoms of Asia fell, and the whole East passed under the power of the Macedonian empire. All the confidence of the Persians was so crushed in this war that afterwards no one dared to rebel, and the Persians, after ruling for so many years, patiently accepted the yoke of slavery.

For thirty-four days on end Alexander went through the plunder of the camp. He then attacked Persepolis, the capital of the Persian kingdom, the most famous city in the whole world and the most packed with wealth.

When he learned that Darius was being held by his own kinsmen, bound in golden fetters, he decided to pursue him. So he ordered the army to follow and set out himself with six thousand horsemen. On the road he found Darius abandoned and alone, pierced with many wounds and breathing out the last of his life through them.

With empty pity he ordered the dead man to be carried back to the tombs of his ancestors and buried, though he was holding in cruel captivity not only, I need hardly say, his mother and wife, but even his little daughters.

Amid so great a multitude of evils the account is very hard to believe: in three battles and as many years one million five hundred thousand infantry and cavalry were destroyed, and that from the same kingdom and the same peoples from whom, it is reported, one million nine hundred thousand had already been lost not many years before.

And besides these disasters, in those same three years a great many cities of Asia were overwhelmed, all Syria was laid waste, Tyre was destroyed, Cilicia was emptied, Cappadocia was subdued, and Egypt was made subject. The island of Rhodes too, trembling with fear, submitted to slavery of its own accord, and many provinces lying below the Taurus, and even Mount Taurus itself, conquered and overcome, accepted the yoke it had long refused.

And lest anyone should suppose that at that time only the East was subdued by Alexander's forces, or only Italy worn down by Roman restlessness: at that very time there were also being waged the war of Agis, king of the Spartans, in Greece, the war of Alexander, king of Epirus, in Lucania, and the war of the governor Zopyrion in Scythia.
Of these, Agis the Lacedaemonian stirred up all Greece and brought it into revolt with him; he engaged the very strong forces of Antipater, and amid great slaughter on both sides he himself fell.

Alexander, meanwhile, aspiring in Italy to an empire of the West in rivalry with Alexander the Great, after waging many hard wars there, was defeated by the Bruttians and Lucanians, and his body was sold for burial.
Zopyrion, governor of Pontus, gathered an army of thirty thousand and dared to make war on the Scythians; he was cut down to the point of annihilation and utterly wiped out with all his forces.

So Alexander the Great, after the death of Darius, subdued the Hyrcanians and the Mardi. There, while he was still intent on war, Thalestris, also called Minithyia, a brazen Amazon, came to him with three hundred women, stirred by the wish to bear a child by him.
After this he attacked the Parthians, who resisted for a long time, and he had all but annihilated them before he conquered them.

From there he subdued the Drangae, the Euergetae, the Parimae, the Parapamenae, the Adaspii and the other peoples who lived at the foot of the Caucasus, and founded there the city of Alexandria on the river Tanais.

But his cruelty toward his own people was no less than his fury against the enemy. This is shown by the murder of his cousin Amyntas, the killing of his stepmother and her brothers, the slaughter of Parmenio and Philotas, the destruction of Attalus, Eurylochus, Pausanias and many leading men of Macedonia, and also the wicked murder of Clitus, a man weighed down with years and an old friend.

At a banquet, trusting in the king's friendship, Clitus defended the memory of the king's father against the king, who was ranking his own achievements above those of his father Philip. The king took offense, though without cause, and ran him through with a hunting spear, and dying he stained the shared banquet with his blood.
But Alexander, never sated with human blood, whether of enemies or even of allies, nevertheless always thirsted for fresh gore.

So, rushing into wars with relentless drive, he received the surrender of the Chorasmians and the Dahae, an untamed people. He put to death the philosopher Callisthenes, his fellow pupil under Aristotle, together with many other leading men, because Callisthenes had set aside the customary form of greeting and would not worship him as a god.

After this he made for India, so as to bound his empire with the Ocean and the farthest East. He reached the city of Nysa; he took by storm the Daedalian mountains and the kingdom of Queen Cleophis, who, after surrendering, bought back her kingdom by sleeping with him.

When Alexander had traversed and subdued India and came to a rock of remarkable ruggedness and height, where many peoples had taken refuge, he learned that Hercules had been prevented from storming this same rock by an earthquake. Moved by rivalry and wishing to surpass the deeds of Hercules, he took the rock with the greatest toil and danger and received the surrender of all the peoples of that place.

He waged a most bloody war with Porus, the bravest of the kings of the Indians. In it Alexander met Porus himself in single combat, and when his horse was killed and he was thrown, he escaped the presence of death only because his bodyguards rushed to his aid. Porus, pierced with many wounds, was captured.

Porus was restored to his kingdom as a tribute to his courage, and Alexander founded two cities there, Nicaea and Bucephala, which he ordered to be named after his horse. From there the Macedonians cut down the armies of the Adrestae, the Cathaei, the Praesidae and the Gangaridae and conquered them.

When they came to the Cofides, they fought a battle there against two hundred thousand enemy horsemen. Worn out by age, sick at heart and drained of strength, they won only with difficulty, and to commemorate it they built a camp more splendid than usual.

Next Alexander went on to the river Acesines, and down it he sailed to the Ocean. There he crushed the Gesonae and the Sibi, whom Hercules had founded. From there he sailed to the Adri and the Subagrae, peoples who met him with eighty thousand armed infantry and sixty thousand cavalry.

Battle was joined, and the fighting, long doubtful and bloody, at last gave the Macedonians a victory that was nearly a grief to them. For when the enemy forces had been routed, Alexander led the army to the city; and having been the first to climb the wall, he thought the city empty and leapt down inside alone.

When hostile enemies surrounded him on every side, it is incredible to tell how neither the multitude of the enemy, nor the great storm of missiles, nor the enormous shouting of his attackers frightened him, and how he alone cut down and put to flight so many thousands.

But when he realized that he was being overwhelmed by the crowd pouring around him, he protected his back with the barrier of the wall and so more easily held off those in front of him, until, in response to his danger and the shouting of the enemy, the whole army broke through the walls and burst in.
In that battle he was pierced by an arrow below the breast, and on bended knee he kept fighting until he had killed the man who had wounded him.

Then, having boarded ships and while sailing along the shores of the Ocean, he came to a certain city ruled by King Ambira. In the siege of the city he lost a large part of his army to the enemy's poisoned arrows; but afterwards, when a herb shown to him in a dream was given to the wounded in a drink and the rest were relieved, he stormed the city and took it.
After this, as though he had rounded the turning post, he entered the river Indus from the Ocean and quickly returned to Babylon.

There envoys from the terrified provinces of the whole world awaited him: from the Carthaginians and all the cities of Africa, and also from the Spaniards, the Gauls, Sicily and Sardinia, and from most of Italy besides.

So great a fear of a general stationed in the farthest East had seized the peoples of the farthest West that you could see an embassy traveling from there across the whole world, to a place you would hardly believe even rumor had reached.
Alexander, however, died at Babylon, still thirsting for blood, his greed ill-restrained, after he had drunk poison through the treachery of a servant.

O hard mind of men and heart forever inhuman! I myself, who am reviewing these things to demonstrate the alternating calamities of all ages, in recounting so great an evil, at which the whole world trembled, whether at the death itself or at the dread of death it received, did I shed a tear? Did I grieve in my heart? As I turned these things over, did I, because of the condition of life we all share, make the miseries of our forefathers my own?

And yet, whenever I speak of my own experiences, how I first saw barbarians unknown to me, how I avoided those who were hostile, how I flattered those who held power, how I guarded against unbelievers, how I slipped away from those lying in wait for me,

and finally how I escaped, wrapped in a sudden mist, from those who pursued me at sea and attacked me with stones and spears and were all but laying hands on me, I would wish all who hear me to be moved to tears, and I silently grieve over those who do not grieve, reflecting on the hardness of those who do not believe what they themselves have not endured.

The Spaniard and the Morinian went to Babylon to plead with Alexander, and, so as not to receive him as an enemy, they of their own accord sought out a bloody master through Assyria and India, traveling to the ends of the earth and becoming unhappily acquainted with both Oceans. And yet the memory of so violent a necessity has either faded into oblivion or grown cheap with age.

And do we think it will cling to everlasting memory that a fugitive robber violated a single corner while most of the world remained secure? As though, I will not say an Indian or an Assyrian in reverse, but even the Spaniard himself, who suffers the enemy, has had to beg the Goths and the Suebi for peace!

But if those times of Alexander are judged to deserve praise for the valor by which the whole world was won, rather than condemnation for the ruin by which the whole world was overthrown, then there will be found even now very many who judge the present events praiseworthy, because the invaders have conquered much, and who count the miseries of others as their own good fortune.

But someone may say: these men are enemies of the Roman world. The answer will be: the whole East thought the same of Alexander at that time, and the Romans too seemed the same to others when they attacked peoples unknown and at peace. But those sought to win kingdoms, while these seek to overthrow them. The destruction wrought by an enemy is one thing, the judgments of a conqueror another.

For those too first afflicted with wars the peoples whom they later set in order with their own laws; and these men now are disturbing as enemies the lands which, if they held them subdued—which God forbid—they would strive to organize according to their own customs, and they would be called great kings by posterity, who are now judged by us to be the most savage of enemies.

By whatever name these deeds are reckoned, that is, whether they are called miseries or acts of valor, both are smaller in our time when compared with former times, and so both tell in our favor in the comparison with Alexander and the Persians: if it is to be called valor now, the enemy's is less; if misery, that of the Romans is less.

In the 450th year from the founding of the City, when Fabius Maximus was consul for the fifth time and Decius Mus for the fourth, four of the bravest and most flourishing peoples of Italy came together in a single army and alliance. For the Etruscans, Umbrians, Samnites and Gauls, conspiring in one column, attempted to destroy the Romans.

The spirits of the Romans were shaken by this war and their confidence undermined, and they did not dare to rest all their hopes on their strength. They divided the enemy by a stratagem, thinking it safer to entangle themselves in many wars than in heavy ones.

So, by sending some of their men ahead into Umbria and Etruria to lay waste the enemy's fields, they forced the army of the Umbrians and Etruscans to return to defend their own lands, and then they hastened to open the war with the Samnites and Gauls.
In this war, when the Romans were hard pressed by the onslaught of the Gauls, the consul Decius was killed. Fabius, however, after great slaughter in Decius' part of the army, at last won.
In that battle forty thousand Samnites and Gauls were killed, while seven thousand Romans are reported to have perished, from Decius' part alone, the part of the one who was killed.

Livy reports that, not counting the Etruscans and Umbrians, whom the Romans drew away from the war by cunning, there were one hundred forty thousand three hundred thirty Gallic and Samnite infantry and forty-seven thousand cavalry, and that a thousand chariot-fighters stood in arms against the Roman battle line.

But—as has often been said, the domestic peace of the Romans was always interrupted by foreign wars, or their successes abroad were weighed down by internal ills, so that their great spirit was pressed hard on every side in every way—plague in the city burdened this bloody and grievous victory, and funeral processions of the dead coming the other way defiled the triumphal parades. Nor was there anyone who could be persuaded to rejoice at the triumph, since the whole city was sighing either over its sick or over its dead.
There followed a year in which the Samnites renewed the war and the Romans were defeated and fled to their camp.
Later, however, the Samnites, taking on a new dress and a new spirit—that is, with silvered arms and garments, and minds resolved to die unless they won—offered themselves to battle.

The consul Papirius was sent against them with an army, and when the augurs who kept the sacred chickens, making empty conjectures, forbade him to engage, he laughed at them and brought the war to as fortunate a conclusion as he had resolutely taken it up.

For in this battle [?] thousand of the enemy are reported killed and three thousand captured. But this victory too, truly worthy of praise, which the empty soothsayers could not hinder, was spoiled by diseases that suddenly broke out.

For so great and so unbearable a plague then seized the city that, in order to allay it by any means whatever, they thought the Sibylline Books should be consulted, and they brought in that horrible serpent of Epidaurus together with the very stone of Aesculapius—as though plague had never been allayed before or had never arisen afterwards!
Moreover, in the second year after this, the consul Fabius Gurges fought badly against the Samnites; for he lost his army, was defeated and fled back to the City.

So when the senate was deliberating about removing him, his father Fabius Maximus, pleading against his son's disgrace, of his own accord offered to go as his son's lieutenant, if his son were given the opportunity to wipe away the disgrace and to wage war again.

This was granted and battle was joined. When he suddenly saw his son the consul, in the thick of the fight, hemmed in by the pressure of Pontius, the Samnite general, and by the hostile missiles of the enemy, the devoted old man rode on horseback into the middle of the battle line.
Stirred by this deed, the Romans threw their whole battle line into the attack there, until they had destroyed the enemy army and captured Pontius the general himself, defeated and overpowered.

In that battle twenty thousand Samnites were killed and four thousand captured along with their king. And at last the Samnite war, which had dragged on for forty-nine years with great loss to the Romans, was ended by the loss of their captured leader.

In the following year war was waged with the Sabines under the consul Curius, and how many thousands of men were killed and how many captured, the consul himself made plain: when he wished to report in the senate the size of the Sabine land acquired and the multitude of people captured, he could not express the number.

In the 463rd year from the founding of the City, when Dolabella and Domitius were consuls, the Lucanians, the Bruttians and also the Samnites formed an alliance with the Etruscans and the Senonian Gauls and were preparing to revive the war against the Romans, so the Romans sent envoys to win over the Gauls by entreaty.

When the Gauls killed them, the praetor Caecilius was sent with an army to avenge the murder of the envoys and to put down the uprising of the enemy, but he was overwhelmed by the Etruscans and Gauls and perished.
In that battle seven military tribunes were also killed, many nobles were slaughtered, and thirteen thousand Roman soldiers were laid low in that war.
Thus every time the Gauls flared up, Rome was worn down with all its resources, so that now, under the present raids of the Goths, it ought rather to remember the Gauls.

But now I am called back to review, for this same period in which the Romans suffered these things, the wars that the Macedonian generals waged among themselves. After Alexander's death they received different provinces by lot and wore one another out in wars.

When I look at that most turbulent time, I seem to myself like someone gazing at night from a mountain lookout over some vast camp, who sees nothing across the wide expanse of the plain but countless fires.
In the same way, throughout the whole Macedonian kingdom, that is, throughout all Asia, most of Europe and the greater part of Libya, dreadful masses of war suddenly blazed up together.
They laid waste above all the places where they broke out, and threw everything else into confusion with the terror of rumour, as if with a pall of smoke.
But I shall not set out the wars and destruction of so many kings and kingdoms until I have first set out the kingdoms themselves together with their kings.

For twelve years, then, Alexander held down with the sword a world that trembled beneath him, but his chief men tore it apart for fourteen years. Like greedy cubs ripping up rich prey brought down by a great lion, they were roused against one another into strife by rivalry over the spoil, and broke one another.
So Egypt and part of Africa and Arabia fell by lot first to Ptolemy. Laomedon of Mytilene received Syria, which borders that province; Philotas received Cilicia, and Philo the Illyrians.
Atropates was set over Greater Media, and Perdiccas' father-in-law over Lesser Media. The people of Susiana were assigned to Scynus, and Greater Phrygia to Antigonus son of Philip.
Nearchus received Lycia and Pamphylia by lot, Cassander Caria, Menander Lydia. Leonnatus received Lesser Phrygia.

Thrace and the regions of the Pontic Sea were given to Lysimachus, Cappadocia together with Paphlagonia to Eumenes. The supreme command of the camp fell to Seleucus son of Antiochus; Cassander son of Antipater was put in charge of the king's bodyguards and attendants.
In further Bactria and the regions of India the former governors, who had taken office under Alexander, remained. Taxiles held the Seres, who live between the two rivers Hydaspes and Indus.
Python son of Agenor was sent to the colonies founded among the Indians. Oxyartes received the Parapamenae on the border of the Caucasus mountains.

The Arachosians and Gedrosians were assigned to Sibyrtius. Stasanor received the Drangians and Arians by lot, Amyntas the Bactrians, Scythaeus the Sogdians; Stasanor obtained the Parthians, Philip the Hyrcanians, Phrataphernes the Armenians, Tlepolemus the Persians, Peucestes the Babylonians, Archon the Pelasgians, and Archelaus Mesopotamia.

The cause and origin of the wars, then, was a letter of King Alexander ordering that all exiles be restored to their country and their freedom. The powerful men of the Greek cities, fearing that the exiles, once their freedom was restored, would plot revenge, revolted from the Macedonian kingdom.

The Athenians were the first. They gathered an army of thirty thousand men and two hundred ships and made war on Antipater, to whom Greece had fallen by lot. Through the orator Demosthenes they also won over Sicyon, Argos, Corinth and the other cities as allies, and they put Antipater under siege.

There their commander Leosthenes was pierced by a missile thrown from the walls and killed. The Athenians went to meet Leonnatus, who was bringing help to Antipater, crushed his forces and killed him.

Perdiccas, for his part, made war on Ariarathes, king of the Cappadocians, and defeated him. From that victory he gained nothing but wounds and dangers, for before he broke into their city all the inhabitants set fire to their own houses and burned themselves and all their possessions.
After this war arose between Antigonus and Perdiccas. Many provinces and islands were most grievously torn apart for having refused help

or given it, and it was long debated whether the war should be carried into Macedonia or fought in Asia. At last Perdiccas himself made for Egypt with a huge army. So Macedonia, with its generals running off in two directions, took up arms against its own vitals.
Ptolemy, equipped with the strength of Egypt and the forces of Cyrene, prepared to meet Perdiccas in war. Meanwhile Neoptolemus and Eumenes fought it out with each other in a most bloody battle.
Neoptolemus, defeated, fled to Antipater and pressed him hard to crush Eumenes by a surprise attack. Eumenes, foreseeing this, caught the ambushers in an ambush of his own.
In that war Polyperchon was killed. Neoptolemus and Eumenes ran each other through with wounds, but Neoptolemus died, while Eumenes came away the victor.

Perdiccas clashed with Ptolemy in a most bitter war, lost his forces and was himself killed as well. Eumenes, Python, Illyrius and Alcetas, Perdiccas' brother, were declared public enemies by the Macedonians, and the war against them was entrusted to Antigonus.

So Eumenes and Antigonus gathered very large forces against each other and fought. Eumenes was defeated and fled to a strongly fortified stronghold, from which he sent envoys to ask for help from Antipater, who was then very powerful. Alarmed by this news, Antigonus abandoned the siege.

But even so Eumenes had no firm hope and no certain safety. As a last resort, therefore, he asked for help from the Argyraspides, so called from their silver-plated arms, that is, the soldiers who had served under Alexander.

They listened to their commander with disdain when he was planning the campaign, and were defeated by Antigonus and stripped of their camp, losing their wives and children and everything they had acquired under Alexander.
Afterwards they shamefully sent envoys to beg the victor to give back what they had lost. Antigonus promised to return it if they would bring Eumenes to him in chains.

Lured by the hope of recovering their goods, they committed a most disgraceful betrayal: captives themselves, they led away captive and in chains the commander whose standards they had followed a little before. Soon afterwards they were broken up and scattered through Antigonus' army in the foulest disgrace.

Meanwhile Eurydice, wife of Arrhidaeus, king of the Macedonians, committed many crimes in her husband's name through Cassander. She had known him in a shameful liaison and had raised him through every grade of office to the highest rank, and to gratify the woman's lust he afflicted many cities of Greece.

Then Olympias, the mother of King Alexander, at Polyperchon's urging, came from Epirus into Macedonia, escorted by Aeacides, king of the Molossians. When Eurydice tried to keep her out of the country, she had King Arrhidaeus and Eurydice put to death with the support of the Macedonians.

Yet Olympias herself soon paid the penalty her cruelty deserved. With a woman's boldness she carried out many murders of leading men, and on hearing that Cassander was approaching, and not trusting the Macedonians, she withdrew with her daughter-in-law Roxane and her grandson Hercules into the city of Pydna.
There Cassander soon captured her and put her to death. The son of Alexander the Great was sent with his mother to be held under guard in the citadel of Amphipolis.
With Perdiccas, Alcetas, Polyperchon and the other generals of the opposing side, whom it would take too long to list, now dead, the wars among Alexander's successors seemed to be over,
when Antigonus, burning with lust for power, pretended that Hercules, the king's son, must be freed from confinement by war.

On learning this, Ptolemy and Cassander formed an alliance with Lysimachus and Seleucus and energetically prepared for war by land and sea. In that war Antigonus was defeated together with his son Demetrius.

Cassander, who had shared the victory with Ptolemy, was returning to Apollonia when he came upon the Autariatae. Because of an unbearable multitude of frogs and mice, they had left their native land and ancient dwellings and were migrating in search of new homes, professing peace for the time being.

But Cassander, recognizing both the courage and the numbers of this people, and fearing that necessity might drive them to shake Macedonia with war and invade it, received them as allies and settled them in the farthest borders of Macedonia.
Then, when Hercules, the son of Alexander, was fourteen years old, Cassander, fearing that everyone would prefer him as the lawful king, secretly had him killed together with his mother.
Ptolemy fought Demetrius again, in a naval battle, and after losing almost his entire fleet and army fled defeated to Egypt.
Elated by this victory, Antigonus ordered that he and his son Demetrius be called kings. All the others followed this example and took for themselves the name and dignity of king.

Ptolemy, Cassander and the other leaders of the opposing faction, then, seeing that Antigonus was outwitting them one by one, encouraged one another by letter, agreed on a time and place to unite, and prepared war against Antigonus with their combined strength.
Cassander, caught up in wars with his neighbours, sent Lysimachus, the most famous general of them all, with a huge force to help the allies in his place.
Seleucus too came down from Greater Asia and joined as a new enemy of Antigonus. This Seleucus had waged a great many wars in the East among the partners in the Macedonian kingdom.
First he attacked Babylon and took it. He subdued the Bactrians, who were rising in new revolts.

Then he crossed into India. After Alexander's death India had, so to speak, shaken off the yoke from its neck and killed his governors, under the leadership of one Androcottus, who took up the cause of its freedom. Afterwards he treated his countrymen cruelly and himself oppressed with slavery those he had defended from foreign rule.
Though Seleucus fought many heavy wars with this Androcottus, in the end he settled the terms of their kingdoms, made peace and withdrew.

So when the forces of Ptolemy and his allies had been united, battle was joined. The mightier the preparations, the heavier the ruin, for in it the strength of almost the whole Macedonian kingdom then collapsed.

Antigonus was killed in this very war. But the end of this war was the beginning of another, for when the victors could not agree about the spoils, they split again into two factions: Seleucus joined Demetrius, and Ptolemy Lysimachus.
On Cassander's death his son Philip succeeded him. Thus new wars arose in Macedonia as if from the start.
Antipater ran through with his own hand his mother Thessalonice, Cassander's wife, though she pitifully begged for her life.
His brother Alexander, while preparing war against his brother to avenge their mother, was trapped and killed by Demetrius, whose help he had sought.
Lysimachus, hard pressed in a most bitter war by Dorus, king of the Thracians, was unable to fight against Demetrius.
Demetrius, elated at gaining Greece and all Macedonia, planned to cross into Asia.

But Ptolemy, Seleucus and Lysimachus, having learned in the earlier contest how great is the strength of concord, again formed an alliance, united their armies and carried the war into Europe against Demetrius.

Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, joined them as companion and ally in the war, hoping that Demetrius could be driven out of Macedonia. Nor was his hope in vain: Demetrius' army was won over, he himself was put to flight, and Pyrrhus seized the kingdom of Macedonia.
Then Lysimachus killed his son-in-law Antipater, who was plotting against him, and, hating his own son Agathocles beyond all human measure, put him to death.
In those very days the city of Lysimachia was overthrown by a most terrifying earthquake and became a cruel tomb for its crushed people.

As for Lysimachus, who was staining himself with repeated murders of his own kin, all his allies abandoned him and went over to Seleucus. They urged him, a king already inclined to it out of rivalry for power, to make war on Lysimachus.
It was a most disgraceful spectacle: two kings, Lysimachus seventy-four years old and Seleucus seventy-seven, clashing to snatch each other's kingdoms, standing in the battle line, bearing arms.
This was indeed the last war of Alexander's comrades in arms, but one that seems to have been kept back as an example of human wretchedness.

For when thirty-four of Alexander's generals were already dead and these two alone possessed the world, they did not look at the very narrow bounds of their old age and their lives, but thought the bounds of the whole world too narrow for their rule.
In that war Lysimachus, who before this battle had either lost or put to death fifteen children, was killed, the last of them. Thus Lysimachus was the end of the Macedonian struggle.

But not even Seleucus rejoiced in so great a victory with impunity. Even after seventy-seven years he did not find the rest of a natural death, but ended a life wretchedly wrenched from him by what was, as it were, an untimely death.
For at the instigation of Ptolemy, whose sister Lysimachus had had as his wife, he was trapped in an ambush and killed.
Such were the dealings of kinship and alliance among parents, children, brothers and allies. So little did they value the obligations of divine and human law.

Let those blush indeed at the memory of the past who now know that, through the intervention of the Christian faith alone and merely by the pledge of an oath, they live with enemies and do not suffer hostilities.

By them it is proved beyond all doubt that it is not, as with those men of old, that “they joined their treaties over a slaughtered sow,” but that now, between barbarians and Romans, the Gospels, brought in for the oath as they call their Creator and Lord to witness, preserve a faithfulness so great as nature could not then preserve even between parents and children.
Now, however, let the end of the Macedonian war be the end of the book as well, especially since from here the wars of Pyrrhus begin, and the Punic wars soon follow.
THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS OF PAULUS OROSIUS

Virgil relates that Aeneas, when after his own dangers and the shipwrecks of his men he was struggling to console his remaining companions, said: “Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.”

This saying, once aptly framed, always carries a threefold force with very different effects. Past things are held to be all the more pleasant in the telling the more grievous they are reported to have been in the doing; and future things, since they become desirable through weariness with the present, are always believed to be better.

But no fair comparison of miseries can be applied to present things at all, because the things that are, however slight they may be, trouble us far more than those which, whether past or to come, however great they are said to be, meanwhile simply do not exist at that moment.

It is as if someone, bitten by fleas at night and kept anxiously awake by them, should happen to remember other sleepless nights he once endured for a long time from the most burning fevers: beyond doubt he will bear the restlessness of the present nights less patiently than the memory of the former.

But although it may seem so to everyone's feelings according to the circumstances of the moment, will there nevertheless be anyone who, even in the midst of his distress, would declare that fleas are worse than fevers? Or who would think it harder to lie awake in health than to be unable to sleep when about to die?

This being so, I grant to these pampered and querulous contemporaries of ours, after a fashion, that they may feel the things by which we are now and then admonished, because it is good for us, to be heavy; but I do not turn a blind eye when they go on to assert that, by comparison, they are heavier.

Suppose someone coming out in the morning from very soft bedding and a most comfortable bedroom saw that the surface of the pools had frozen stiff with the night's frost and the grass had turned white, and, struck by the unexpected sight, said, “It is cold today”: I should by no means think him to blame, since he would have spoken either from common usage or from his own sensation.

But suppose he ran back in alarm to his bedroom and, covering himself, or rather burying himself, in his bedclothes, cried out that it was altogether as cold as it had never been even in the Apennines when Hannibal, trapped and overwhelmed by the snows, lost his elephants, his horses and the greater part of his army.

Such a man, squeamish from childish indulgence, I would not only refuse to tolerate when he said such things; I would even drag him from the very bedclothes that witness to his idleness out among the people and into public, and having brought him outdoors I would show him children playing in that frost and with it, enjoying themselves and sweating,

so that his wordy triviality, spoiled by pampered upbringing, might be taught that the severity lay not in the season but the sloth in himself, and that, when matters are judged by comparison, it might be proved not that his elders had endured small things but that he is not equal to enduring even small ones.
This I shall demonstrate more clearly by recalling the actual disasters of the past, setting out first, as the order requires, the war with Pyrrhus. Its cause and origin were as follows.

In the 464th year from the founding of the City, the Tarentines, seeing from their theatre a Roman fleet that happened to be passing by, attacked it as enemies. Only five ships barely escaped by flight; the rest of the fleet was dragged into the harbour and destroyed. The ships' commanders were slaughtered, all men fit for war were killed, and the rest were sold for a price.
The Romans at once sent envoys to Tarentum to complain of the wrongs inflicted, but they were beaten by the same people and brought back still greater wrongs. From these causes a great war arose.

The Romans, measuring what enemies were raging around them and how great they were, were driven by the utmost necessity to force even the proletarii to take up arms, that is, to enrol in the army those who always remained free in the City for the purpose of producing offspring; for it is vain to care about offspring unless present affairs are looked after.

So the Roman army under the consul Aemilius burst into all the territory of the Tarentines, laid everything waste with fire and sword, stormed a great many towns, and cruelly avenged the insult it had received.

At once the Tarentines, already propped up by many garrisons from their neighbours, were supported [?] above all by Pyrrhus, who because of the greatness of his strength and judgment took over to himself the chief command and the name of the war.

For to defend Tarentum, a city founded by the Lacedaemonians and so kin to Greece, he brought the entire forces of Epirus, Thessaly and Macedonia, and he was the first to bring into Italy elephants, twenty of them, until then never seen by the Romans. He was formidable by land and sea, in men and horses, in arms and beasts, and finally in his own strength and cunning,
except that, deceived by the ambiguous reply of that most empty Delphic spirit and most lying rogue, whom they themselves call a great prophet, he met the end of one who had never consulted it.

So the first battle between King Pyrrhus and the consul Laevinus was fought near Heraclea, a city of Campania, and the river Liris. The day was spent in a most fierce struggle, with everyone on both sides intent on dying and not knowing how to flee.

But when the Romans saw the elephants brought in among the clashing columns, savage in appearance, foul in smell and terrifying in bulk, they were overwhelmed and terrified by this new kind of fighting, and, with the horses especially panicking, they scattered in flight.

But then Minucius, first hastatus of the Fourth Legion, cut off with his sword the trunk a beast had stretched out at him, and drove the animal, maddened by the pain of the wound, to turn from the battle and rage against its own side. The elephants began to throw their own men into confusion and disorder by their wild running about, and an end was put to the battle, helped also by the coming of night.

That the Romans had been defeated was betrayed by their shameful flight. Of them, it is reported, 14,880 infantry fell then and 1,310 were captured; of the cavalry 246 were killed and 802 captured; and 22 standards were lost.

How large a number of Pyrrhus' allies was killed on the other side has not been handed down to memory, chiefly because it is the custom of the ancient writers not to record the number of the slain on the side that won, so that the victor's losses may not stain the glory

of the victory, unless perhaps so few fall that the very smallness of the losses heightens admiration for their valour and the terror it inspires, as happened with Alexander the Great in the first engagement of the Persian war: of the nearly 400,000 enemies killed, only nine foot soldiers are said to have been missing from his army.

But Pyrrhus bore witness before his gods and men to the dreadfulness of the slaughter he had suffered in this war, by fixing an inscription in the temple of Jupiter at Tarentum, in which he wrote: “Men who before were unconquered, best father of Olympus, these I conquered in battle, and by them I was conquered.”

And when his allies reproached him for calling himself conquered when he had conquered, he is said to have replied: “Truly, if I conquer again in the same way, I shall return to Epirus without a single soldier.”
Meanwhile the Roman army, after its defeat and its secret flight from the camp, found the wretched disaster of the war increased and heaped higher by still graver portents.
For some foragers who happened to have gone out were caught by a storm that arose like an enemy, with a terrible crash from the sky, and were burned up by fearful thunderbolts.

The same whirlwind struck down thirty-four of them; twenty-two were left half dead, and a great many pack animals were killed or carried off, so that it may rightly be said to have happened not as a sign of devastation to come but as devastation itself.

The second battle between Pyrrhus and the Roman consuls took place in the territory of Apulia. There the losses of war fell on both sides, but above all on Pyrrhus, and the victory went to the Romans.

For when everyone had long been rushing stubbornly into mutual slaughter and the outcome of the battle hung in the balance, Pyrrhus, wounded by a spear through his arm, was the first to withdraw from the fight. But the legate Fabricius was also wounded then.

The elephants, once it was discovered in the first battle that they could be wounded and put to flight, were then driven wild by fires thrust under their hindquarters and soft parts, and carrying the burning towers on their backs about in their frenzied panic, they brought ruin on their own side.
In that battle 5,000 Romans were killed, while 20,000 of Pyrrhus' army were laid low. Fifty-three of the king's standards were taken; the Romans lost eleven.
Pyrrhus, broken by the war, was summoned to rule over Sicily after the death of Agathocles, king of Syracuse, and withdrew to Syracuse.
But Rome's misery knows no truce. The pauses between wars were taken up by the evils of disease, and when fighting stopped abroad, anger was at work at home.

From heaven [?]. In the second consulship of Fabius Gurges, with Gaius Genucius Clepsina as his colleague, a severe plague swept through the City and its territory. It struck everyone, but above all women and livestock: it killed the young in the womb and so robbed the future of its offspring. Premature births were forced out and cast away, at risk to the mothers' lives, so that people believed the succession of generations would fail and the race of living creatures would die out, since the natural course of birth had been taken away.
Meanwhile the consul Curius met Pyrrhus on his return from Sicily, and this third war against the Epirotes was fought in Lucania, on the Arusinian Plains.

At the first clash Pyrrhus' soldiers wavered under the Roman onslaught, looked about for a way to flee and were preparing to give up the fight, so Pyrrhus ordered the elephants to be brought up from the reserves.

But the Romans were by now used to fighting beasts. They had prepared fire-darts wrapped in tow and smeared with pitch, with hooked barbs on top so that they would stick, and they hurled them, blazing, at the backs of the beasts and at their towers. Maddened and burning, the beasts were easily turned back to destroy the very men whose support they had been.
They say the king had eighty thousand infantry in that battle and six thousand cavalry. Of these, thirty-three thousand are reported to have been killed and thirteen hundred captured.

At last, in the fifth year after his arrival, Pyrrhus fled from Italy in defeat. After the many very heavy wars he fought in Greece, he was lured by his desire for the kingdom of Sparta and was killed by a blow from a stone at Argos, a most flourishing city of Achaea.
At that time too, at Rome, Sextilia, a Vestal virgin, was convicted and condemned for unchastity and buried alive by the Colline Gate.

In the 475th year from the founding of the City, the Tarentines, learning of Pyrrhus' death, once again stirred up war against the Romans. Through envoys they asked the Carthaginians for help and received it.
Battle was joined and the Romans won. Even then the Carthaginians, though not yet declared enemies, realized that they could be beaten by the Romans.
The following year Roman severity cut away a great part of its own flesh [?].

Some time before, when Pyrrhus was approaching, the Eighth Legion lost faith in Rome's prospects and dared a new crime: it killed all the people of Rhegium, whom it had been stationed there to protect, and seized all the plunder and the town itself for itself.

The consul Genucius was ordered to punish this crime by such wicked rebels. He besieged the city of Rhegium and captured them all. He himself inflicted fitting punishment on the rest, the deserters and brigands, but he sent the Roman soldiers of the legion to Rome intact. There, by order of the people, they were beaten with rods in the middle of the Forum and beheaded with the axe.
Rome thought she had won a victory when she put to death an entire legion of her own; yet had she lost it in battle with an enemy, she would without doubt have been defeated.

In the 478th year from the founding of the City, ill-omened and dreadful portents were either seen at Rome or reported there. The temple of Salus was wrecked by a thunderbolt, and part of the wall in the same place was, as they say, struck from heaven.
Three wolves entered the City before dawn and brought in a half-eaten corpse; frightened off by the noise of people, they left it scattered limb by limb in the Forum.
At Formiae the walls were struck by many thunderbolts and scorched and shattered all round.

In the territory of Cales a flame suddenly burst out from a chasm that split open in the earth. For three days and three nights it raged terribly, and it burned five iugera of land to ash, drying up all the richness of the soil, so that it is said to have consumed not only the crops but even the trees down to their deepest roots.

The next year the consul Sempronius led an army against the Picentes. When the two battle lines had been drawn up within a spear's throw of each other, the earth suddenly shook with such a terrifying roar that both armies were stunned and paralyzed with fear at the wonder.
For a long time both peoples stood dumbfounded and hesitated, conscious that the undertaking had been judged in advance. At last they rushed forward and joined battle.

That war was so grim that it may rightly be said the earth trembled then with a dreadful groan because it was about to receive so much human blood. The Romans, very few of whom came out of that battle alive, won.

In the 480th year from the founding of the City, among many portents, blood was seen to flow from the earth and milk from the sky. In very many places blood gushed out of springs and flowed, and milk fell drop by drop from the clouds like rain, so that dreadful showers, as it seemed to the people, drenched the earth.

At that time the Carthaginians had given help to the Tarentines against the Romans. When the senate charged them with this through envoys, they piled shameless perjury on top of the disgraceful stain of a broken treaty.
Then too the Volsinians, the most flourishing of the Etruscans, almost perished through luxury.
For their licence had grown into habit: they freed their slaves indiscriminately, invited them to their banquets and honored them with marriages.

The freedmen, once admitted to a share of power, began to plot to seize the whole of it by crime. Freed from the yoke of slavery, they burned with ambition for domination; and the masters whom they had loved contentedly as subjects, they now, as free men, cursed, because they remembered that these had been their masters.

So the freedmen conspired in crime. Their band was so large that they carried out their venture without opposition. They seized the city and claimed it for their own class alone, criminally took over their masters' estates and wives, and drove the masters far away into exile. These wretched men, exiled and destitute, made their way to Rome. There they displayed their misery and tearfully pressed their complaint, and through Roman severity they were both avenged and restored.
In the 481st year from the founding of the City, a huge plague blazed up at Rome. I am content to indicate its savagery, since I cannot describe it fully in words.

If one asks how long it lasted, it went on ravaging for more than two years. If one asks how great a toll it took, a census was ordered to find out not how many people had died but how many were left. If one asks how violently it struck, the Sibylline Books are witnesses: they answered that it had been imposed by heavenly wrath.

But lest anyone take offense, as if at an attempt at quibbling, because when the Sibyl spoke of angry gods we seem to have spoken of heavenly wrath, let him hear and understand that, although these things are usually brought about through the powers of the air, they never happen at all without the decision of almighty God.
At the same time Caparronia, a Vestal virgin, was charged with unchastity and died by hanging; her seducer and the slaves who were his accomplices were put to death.

See how many and how great are the things we have recounted, one after another, as happening in individual years—very many of them—and among those years there were surely few or almost none in which nothing grim took place. And this even though those same writers, who had set themselves the business of praise instead, took care to avoid recounting the full number of miseries,
so as not to offend the very people for whom and about whom these things were written, and not to seem to frighten their readers with examples from the past rather than to instruct them.
Moreover, we who live at the end of the ages can know the misfortunes of the Romans only through those who praised the Romans.
From this we may understand how great were the things deliberately suppressed because of their horror, when we find such great ones that managed to seep out thinly among the praises.

And since from this point the Punic Wars follow, the subject itself demands that something at least be said, following Pompeius Trogus and Justin, about Carthage—which, we find, was founded by Elissa seventy-two years before the city of Rome—and about its disasters and domestic troubles.
The Carthaginians always had a native and internal evil among themselves, namely discord. Unhappily stirred up by it, they never spent any period either prosperous abroad or peaceful at home.

When, among their other evils, they were also suffering from plague, they used murder as a remedy: they sacrificed human beings as victims and brought to the altars children not yet grown, an age that would have moved even enemies to pity.

I cannot find what most needs to be said about this kind of sacred rite, or rather sacrilege. If certain demons dared to prescribe rites of this sort, so that the deaths of men would be atoned for by the slaughter of men, they ought to have realized that they were being hired as laborers and helpers of the plague, to kill with their own hands those whom it had not seized.
For it is the custom to offer healthy and unblemished victims, so that these people were not checking the disease but getting ahead of it.

So the Carthaginians—the gods having turned away from them because of such rites, as Pompeius Trogus and Justin admit, but, as is plain to us, because God was angered by their presumption and impiety—

after fighting long and unsuccessfully in Sicily, shifted the war to Sardinia and were defeated there again, even more disastrously. For this they ordered their general Mazeus and the few soldiers who had survived into exile. The exiles sent envoys asking for pardon, and when they were rebuffed they surrounded their homeland with war and siege.

Then Mazeus, the leader of the exiles, when his son Carthalo, a priest of Hercules, came to meet him dressed in purple as if to taunt him, hanged him on a cross in sight of his homeland, just as he was, in his purple and his priestly fillets.
A few days later he took the city itself. After killing very many of the senators, he ruled cruelly until he was himself killed. These things took place in the time of Cyrus, king of the Persians.
After this Himilco, king of the Carthaginians, while waging war in Sicily, suddenly lost his army to a horrible plague. There was no delay:

the people fell in droves to the disease; each man was quickly seized, soon dead, and no longer even buried. When news of this disaster filled Carthage with stunned and sudden grief, the city was thrown into turmoil just as if it had been captured.

Everything rang with wailing; doors were shut everywhere; all public and private business was abandoned. Everyone ran down to the harbor and questioned the few survivors of the disaster, as they disembarked, about their own people.

When the wretched people, from the silence or groans of the survivors, understood the fate of their own, then the cries of mourners were heard along the whole shore, then the wailing and tearful laments of unhappy mothers.

Amid all this the commander himself stepped off his ship, ungirt, in a dirty slave's tunic. At the sight of him the mourning crowds closed in; and he too, stretching his hands to heaven, now blamed and bewailed his own misfortune, now the misfortune of the state.

Finally, crying aloud through the city, he at last went into his house. He dismissed all who had followed him in tears with a last address; then he barred the doors, shutting out even his sons, and ended his grief and his life with a sword. These things took place in the time of Darius.

After this Hanno, a Carthaginian whose private wealth exceeded the resources of the state, conceived the desire to seize absolute power. He thought it a useful plan to pretend to celebrate his only daughter's wedding and, over the wine, to poison all the senators whose standing he judged would obstruct his designs.

The plot was betrayed by servants and averted without any punishment, lest, in the case of so powerful a man, the deed once exposed should cause more trouble than it had when only planned. Foiled in this scheme, Hanno prepared to attempt the crime by another device: he stirred up the slaves, intending to overwhelm the unsuspecting city with them suddenly.
But when he realized, before the day set for the massacre, that he had been betrayed and forestalled, he seized a fortress with twenty thousand armed slaves.

While he was there stirring up the Africans and the king of the Moors, he was captured. First he was beaten with rods; then his eyes were gouged out and his hands and legs broken, as though punishment were being exacted from each limb in turn; and he was put to death in sight of the people.

His body, torn by the lashes, was fixed to a cross, and his sons and all his kin were handed over for execution, so that no one of the same family should ever think of imitating or avenging him. These things took place in the time of Philip.

After this, when the Carthaginians learned that the city of Tyre, the founder of their own race, had been captured and destroyed by Alexander the Great, they feared he would cross into Africa next. So they sent a certain Hamilcar, surnamed Rhodanus, a man outstanding for his eloquence and shrewdness, to investigate Alexander's activities.

He was received through Parmenion as though he were a deserter and then admitted into the king's service, and he reported everything to his fellow citizens on tablets that he wrote and afterwards covered over with wax. When he returned to Carthage after Alexander's death, they put him to death, as if he had tried to sell the city to the king—not only out of ingratitude but out of cruel envy.

Later, while they were waging constant and never quite successful wars against the Sicilians, and had besieged Syracuse, then the most flourishing city of Sicily, they were outwitted by the remarkable cunning of Agathocles, king of Sicily, and brought to the brink of despair.

For Agathocles, besieged at Syracuse by the Carthaginians, saw that he was neither a match for them in war in the equipment of his forces nor able to endure a siege with sufficient supplies. So, with a plan well laid and even better concealed, he crossed over with his army into Africa. There he revealed to his men what he was undertaking, and then explained what needed to be done.
