At once, with one accord, they first burned the ships in which they had come, so that there would be no hope of retreat. Then, as he was laying waste everything in his path and burning farms and forts, he was met by a certain Hanno with thirty thousand Carthaginians. He killed Hanno along with two thousand of his men, while he himself lost only two in that battle.

This battle broke the spirit of the Africans to an incredible degree and raised that of his own men immensely. He stormed cities and forts, carried off huge amounts of plunder and slaughtered many thousands of the enemy.

Then he pitched camp at the fifth milestone from Carthage, so that the people could watch from the walls of their own city the loss of their richest possessions, the devastation of their fields and the burning of their farmhouses.

To these present evils was added still grimmer news: it was reported that in Sicily too the African army had been destroyed together with its commander. In fact Andro, Agathocles' brother, had caught it off guard and almost idle and crushed it.

When this rumor spread through all Africa, not only the tributary cities but even allied kings deserted the Carthaginians. Among them Ophellas, king of Cyrene, made a pact with Agathocles to share in the war, since he was eagerly aiming at the kingship of Africa.
But after they had joined their armies and camps into one, he was ensnared by Agathocles with flattery and treachery and killed.

The Carthaginians gathered forces from every side and blazed up into war. Agathocles, with Ophellas' troops alongside his own, engaged them and defeated them in a hard battle with heavy bloodshed on both sides.

The outcome of this contest brought such despair to the Carthaginians that, had a mutiny not broken out in Agathocles' army, Hamilcar, the Carthaginian general, would have gone over to him with his army. For this offense he was fastened to a gibbet in the middle of the forum by order of the Carthaginians and made a cruel spectacle for his people.

Then, after the death of Agathocles, when the Carthaginians fitted out a fleet and were ravaging Sicily, they were often defeated on land and sea by Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, who had been summoned from Italy, and finally they turned to wars with Rome.
Alas! Do those who complain about recent times read these things about the past? Yes, they read them, but they weigh them not with fairness but with rivalry.

For they are pricked by that very great and unspeakable goad [?], which they themselves cannot discern, not because the times are bad but because the times are Christian. It is the discharge of an envious sore, so that whatever is done under what they detest seems more atrocious.

So too among us, it often happens that in the eyes of enemies the people they detest do nothing in word or deed that is not perverse, nothing that is not underhanded, nothing that is not aimed at wounding them—and they see it this way in all sincerity, for envy so warps a captive heart that it cannot see what is naturally straight.

These people are of that number, but far more wretched, because they are enemies of God and therefore enemies of the truth. We say these things about them with tears, and we rebuke them with compassion, if they will allow it, so that we may

heal them. They see these things with a diseased eye, and so what they see appears double to them; confused by the darkness of their wickedness, they reach the point where they see more by seeing less, while still being unable to see what is as it is.
They consider a father's scourges heavier than an enemy's fires; they call God, who coaxes, warns and redeems, harsher than the devil, who persecutes, dominates and slaughters.

Yet if they understood that it was a father, they would rejoice in the chastisement; if the fruit of the instruction were foreseen, the discipline would be bearable; and because of the hope that has now been given to the nations, but did not exist before, they would count their sufferings lighter, even if they suffered more heavily.

And yet they could learn contempt for miseries even from their own people, among whom the greatest evils were valued as the greatest goods, if only they could thereby win celebrated and illustrious fame.
From them we may gather how much we, to whom a blessed eternity is promised, ought to endure for the sake of life, when they could endure so much for the sake of fame.

In the 483rd year from the founding of the City, that is, in the consulship of Appius Claudius and Quintus Fabius, the Romans sent the consul Appius Claudius with an army to help the Mamertines, whose city was Messana, a famous city of Sicily, against Hiero, king of Syracuse, and the Carthaginian forces that had joined Hiero.
He defeated the Syracusans and Carthaginians so quickly that the king himself, terrified by the magnitude of events, declared that he had been beaten before he had even engaged.
After that, with his strength broken and his confidence lost, he humbly begged for peace and received it, being fined two hundred talents of silver by order of the consuls.
The consuls surrounded Agrigentum, a city of Sicily, and the Carthaginian garrison in it with siege works and a rampart.

When Hannibal the Elder, the Carthaginian general shut up by that siege, had been reduced to extreme want, Hanno, the new general of the Carthaginians, intervened unexpectedly with fifteen hundred cavalry, thirty thousand infantry and thirty elephants as well, and delayed the storming of the city for a short while.

But the city was soon taken. The Carthaginians were defeated and routed in a very great battle, eleven elephants were captured, and all the people of Agrigentum were sold into slavery. Hannibal the Elder made a sortie with a few men and escaped.

In the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Asina and Gaius Duilius, when Hannibal the Elder was ravaging the coast of Italy with a fleet of seventy ships he had fitted out, the Romans too ordered a fleet to be built and equipped.
The consul Duilius carried this out swiftly: within sixty days after the trees had been felled, a fleet of a hundred and thirty ships was launched and lay at anchor.

Cornelius Asina, the other consul, made for the island of Lipara with sixteen ships. There Hannibal summoned him as if to a conference about peace; he was captured by Punic treachery and put to death in chains.

When Duilius, the other consul, heard of this, he set out against Hannibal with thirty ships. In the naval battle that followed, Hannibal lost the ship he was sailing in, slipped away in a small boat and escaped. Thirty-one of his ships are reported to have been captured and thirteen sunk, three thousand men killed and seven thousand taken prisoner.

Later, in the consulship of Gaius Aquilius Florus and Lucius Cornelius Scipio, the Carthaginians appointed Hanno, who had replaced Hannibal, to command in a naval battle for the defense of the Sardinians and Corsicans. He was defeated by the consul Scipio and lost his army; then he threw himself into the thickest of the enemy and was killed there.

In the same year three thousand slaves and four thousand naval allies conspired to destroy the city of Rome, and had the plot not been betrayed in time to forestall it, the city, left without a garrison, would have perished at the hands of slaves.
In the following year the consul Calatinus, marching on Camarina, a city of Sicily, rashly led his army into a narrow pass that the Carthaginian forces had blocked long before.

He had no means at all of either resisting or escaping, but he was rescued by the courage and effort of Calpurnius Flamma. With a picked band of three hundred men, Calpurnius seized a hill held by the enemy and, by fighting, drew all the Carthaginians against himself, until the Roman army, no longer pressed by the enemy, got through the blocked pass.
All three hundred were killed in that fight. Calpurnius alone escaped, though he was pierced with many wounds and buried under corpses.

Hannibal the elder, again put in command of the fleet by the Carthaginians, met the Romans in an unsuccessful naval battle and was defeated. A mutiny broke out in his own army, and he died buried under stones.
The consul Atilius ranged over Lipara and Melita, famous islands near Sicily, and laid them waste.

The consuls, ordered to carry the war into Africa, made for Sicily with three hundred and thirty ships. Hamilcar, the Carthaginian general, and Hanno, commander of the fleet, came out to meet them. A naval battle was fought, and the Carthaginians were put to flight with the loss of sixty-four ships.
The victorious consuls crossed into Africa, and the first city of all that they received in surrender was Clupea.
From there they marched on Carthage, plundered three hundred or more fortified places, and carried their hostile standards all around Carthage.
The consul Manlius, leaving Africa with the victorious fleet, brought back to Rome twenty-seven thousand captives along with enormous spoils.

Regulus, to whom the Carthaginian war had fallen by lot, was on the march with his army and pitched camp not far from the river Bagradas. There a serpent of astonishing size was devouring a great many of the soldiers who had to go down to the river for water, and Regulus set out with his army to destroy the beast.

But javelins made no impression on its back, and every blow of their weapons was wasted: they slid off the dreadful lattice of its scales as if off a slanting testudo of shields, and in some marvellous way were thrust back by the body itself so that they could not wound it. When, moreover, he saw a great number of men crushed by its bite, trampled by its charge, and even struck dead by its pestilential breath, he ordered ballistas to be brought up. With these a millstone was hurled, struck its spine, and broke apart the frame of its whole body.

For such is the nature of a serpent that, though it seems to lack feet, it is so equipped with ribs and scales, arranged evenly from the top of the throat down to the bottom of the belly, that it supports itself on its scales as on claws and on its ribs as on legs.

It does not move like a worm, which has no rigid spine and makes its way in a straight line by stretching out the contracted parts of its little body one after another and drawing in the stretched ones. Instead, straining with alternating efforts, it swings its winding sides around, so that along the outer curve of its spine it extends the stiff row of its ribs, and on the ribs, which nature has set upright to their tips, it plants the claws of its scales. By doing this alternately and rapidly it not only glides over level ground but even climbs slopes, furnished with as many footholds as it has ribs.

This, then, is why, if it is struck a blow anywhere on its body from the belly to the head, it is crippled and cannot move: wherever the blow falls, it breaks the spine through which the feet of the ribs and the movements of the body were driven. And so this serpent too, which had held out so long, invulnerable to so many javelins, was crippled by the blow of a single stone, gave way, and was soon surrounded by weapons and easily overpowered.
Its skin was carried to Rome. It is said to have been a hundred and twenty feet long, and for some time it was a marvel to everyone.

Regulus waged a most savage war against three generals, namely the two Hasdrubals and Hamilcar, who had been summoned from Sicily. In it seventeen thousand Carthaginians were killed and five thousand captured, eighteen elephants were led away, and eighty-two towns surrendered to the Romans.

The Carthaginians, broken by wars and drained by defeats, asked Regulus for peace. But when they heard the harsh and intolerable terms of peace, they judged it safer to die under arms than to live in misery, and decided to hire auxiliaries, not only from Spain and Gaul, of whom they had long had a great many, but also from Greece.

So they summoned Xanthippus, king of the Lacedaemonians, with auxiliary forces and put him in command of the war. Xanthippus inspected the Carthaginian forces, led them out onto the plain, and, having changed their equipment greatly for the better, joined battle with the Romans.

The Roman forces suffered a tremendous disaster there, for thirty thousand Roman soldiers were laid low in that engagement. Regulus, that famous general, was captured with five hundred men and thrown into chains, and so in the tenth year of the Punic War he at last provided the Carthaginians with a famous triumph.
Xanthippus, aware of how bold his deed had been and fearing a change in so unstable a state of affairs, left Africa at once for Greece.

So the consuls Aemilius Paullus and Fulvius Nobilior, on hearing of Regulus' capture and the destruction of the Roman army, were ordered to cross into Africa with a fleet of three hundred ships, and they made for Clupea. The Carthaginians came there at once with an equal fleet, and the naval battle could not be put off.

A hundred and four Carthaginian ships were sunk and thirty captured with their fighting men aboard, and in addition thirty-five thousand of their soldiers were killed. The Romans had nine ships sunk and lost eleven hundred soldiers. The consuls pitched camp near Clupea.
The two Hannos, generals of the Carthaginians, again gathered there with a large army, joined battle, and lost nine thousand soldiers.

But in those days the Romans never had lasting good fortune, and whatever successes they had were straightway buried under great masses of evils. As the Roman fleet was returning to Italy laden with plunder, it was overwhelmed in an appalling shipwreck: of three hundred ships, two hundred and twenty were lost, and eighty barely saved themselves by throwing their cargo overboard.

Hamilcar, the Carthaginian general, was sent with an army into Numidia and Mauretania. After dealing with all the people there as enemies and with bloodshed, because they were said to have welcomed Regulus gladly, he fined the survivors a thousand talents of silver and twenty thousand oxen, and nailed the leading men of all the peoples to the gibbet.

Two years later, since unbridled madness always quickly forgets its dangers, the consuls Servilius Caepio and Sempronius Blaesus crossed into Africa with two hundred and sixty ships. They ravaged the whole coastline lying around the Syrtes, advanced inland, captured and destroyed a great many cities, and carried enormous plunder back to the fleet.

Then, as they were returning to Italy, near the promontory of Palinurus, which juts out from the Lucanian mountains into the sea, they were dashed against the rocks and lost a hundred and fifty transport ships, and with them, unluckily, the famous plunder they had so cruelly acquired.

At last the sheer scale of their miseries overcame the shameless greed of the Romans. The senators, now thoroughly sick of seafaring, decreed that no fleet of more than sixty ships should be kept for the defence of Italy. But they broke this very decree straightway, driven on by their unconquerable greed.

Besides this, the consul Cotta crossed into Sicily and fought a great many battles on land and sea against the Carthaginians and the Sicilians, and all over Sicily he left heaps of unburied dead, partly of enemies and partly of allies too.

In the consulship of Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Gaius Furius Placidus, Hasdrubal, the new Carthaginian general, came from Africa to Lilybaeum with a hundred and thirty elephants and more than thirty thousand cavalry and infantry, and at once joined battle with the consul Metellus near Panormus.

But Metellus, fearing the great strength of the beasts, by a very shrewd plan first put them to flight or to death, and so easily overcame the enemy's forces, large as they were. Twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed in that battle. Twenty-six elephants were also killed and a hundred and four captured; these were led through Italy and gave the Italian peoples a magnificent spectacle. Hasdrubal fled with a few men to Lilybaeum and was condemned to death in his absence by the Carthaginians.

After this the Carthaginians, worn out by so many misfortunes, decided that they must ask the Romans for peace. For this purpose they thought that Atilius Regulus, formerly a Roman general, whom they had now held captive for five years, should above all be sent among the other envoys. When he returned from Italy without obtaining peace, they cut off his eyelids, bound him in a machine, and killed him by keeping him awake.

Next another Atilius Regulus and Manlius Vulso, both consuls for the second time, set out for Lilybaeum with a fleet of two hundred ships and four legions. The Romans tried to besiege this town, which stands on a promontory, but Hannibal, the son of Hamilcar, came upon them and they were defeated. They lost the greater part of their army and themselves barely escaped.

After them the consul Claudius set out against the enemy with a fleet of a hundred and twenty ships to the harbour of Drepana, where he was soon met by the Carthaginian fleet and defeated. He himself fled with thirty ships to the camp at Lilybaeum; all the rest, that is, ninety, were either captured or sunk. Eight thousand soldiers are reported killed and twenty thousand captured. Gaius Junius, Claudius' colleague, also lost his entire fleet in a shipwreck.
In the following year, moreover, the Carthaginian fleet crossed to Italy and laid waste a great many parts of it far and wide.

Meanwhile Lutatius crossed into Sicily with a fleet of three hundred ships. While he was rousing the fight among the foremost ranks near the city of Drepana, he was pierced through the thigh and, when he was already being overwhelmed, was rescued with the greatest difficulty.

Then the Carthaginians, led by Hanno, converged on Sicily with four hundred ships and large forces. Nor was Lutatius slow; on the contrary, he forestalled the Carthaginians' plans with astonishing speed. The two fleets lay close to each other near the Aegates Islands all night long, their anchors almost intertwined, and at daybreak Lutatius was the first to give the signal for battle.

As the fighting grew fierce, Hanno was beaten, turned his ship about, and was the first to lead the flight. A considerable part of his army made for Africa with him; others fled to Lilybaeum. Sixty-three Carthaginian ships were captured and a hundred and twenty-five sunk; thirty-two thousand men were captured and fourteen thousand killed. The Romans had twelve ships sunk.
Lutatius then came to the city of Eryx, which the Carthaginians held, joined battle there, and killed two thousand Carthaginians.
Then the Carthaginians in headlong haste sent envoys to the consul Lutatius and afterwards to Rome. They begged for peace, and obtained it at once on the terms offered earlier.
The terms were that they should withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia and, to cover the costs of the war, pay three thousand Euboic talents of pure silver in equal instalments over twenty years.
This peace was concluded in the twenty-third year after the First Punic War had begun.

Who, I ask, could set out in words this one war between two cities, waged for twenty-three years: how many Carthaginian kings, how many Roman consuls, how many columns of armies, how great a number of ships it drew together, ruined and crushed? Only then, once these things have been fully weighed, let judgment be passed on the present.

In the 507th year from the founding of the City, a sudden catastrophe in Rome itself forestalled the Romans' triumph. Indeed I would not lightly name a time when some sudden and most grievous sorrow did not come upon Rome and crush even a modest rejoicing. For in the consulship of Quintus

Lutatius Catulus and Aulus Manlius, disasters of fire and of water, one after the other, almost destroyed the City. The Tiber, swollen by unusual rains and overflowing beyond all expectation in both duration and extent, destroyed every building in Rome that stood on low ground.
Different kinds of ground came to the same ruin: the buildings that the slower flood held fast it soaked and dissolved, and those that the torrent found in its course it struck and threw down.

This most grievous disaster of water was followed by a still more grievous devastation by fire. The fire, whose origin is unknown, swept through a great many parts of the city, causing a pitiful destruction of people and houses, and also consumed in a single blaze more wealth than many victories over foreign peoples could have brought in.

Then, as it laid waste everything around the Forum, it seized the temple of Vesta, and, since the gods could not even help themselves, a temporary fire overwhelmed that fire which was believed to be eternal. Metellus, too, while rescuing the gods from burning, barely escaped with his arm half-burnt.
In the consulship of Titus Sempronius Gracchus and Gaius Valerius Falto, the Romans made war on the Faliscans, and in that battle fifteen thousand Faliscans were killed.

In the same year the Cisalpine Gauls rose up as new enemies. The war against them was fought with varying fortune: in the first clash, under the consul Valerius, three thousand five hundred Romans fell; in the second, fourteen thousand Gauls were killed and two thousand captured. But because of the earlier defeat the consul was refused a triumph.

In the consulship of Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gaius Atilius Bulbus, the island of Sardinia rebelled at the instigation of the Carthaginians. The Sardinians were soon subdued and crushed, and it was decreed that war be made on the Carthaginians for violating the peace they themselves had begged for.

The Carthaginians, for their part, humbly begged for peace. Envoys were sent twice and accomplished nothing; then ten of their leading men pleaded twice in the same way and still did not obtain it. Finally they won it through a speech by Hanno, the least distinguished man among the envoys.
In this year the gate of Janus Geminus was closed, because there was no war anywhere that year, something that had happened only under King Numa Pompilius.

Here at last I ought to be silent, and it is best to pass over in silence times with which our own can in no way be compared, lest by this clamour I stir up those who disparage the days of their own lifetime to taunt us all the more.
See: the gates of Janus were closed, Rome had no war abroad, and Rome held all her offspring resting in her lap and did not sigh.

And when was this? After the First Punic War. After how long? After 440 years. For how long? For one year. And what followed in the next? To say nothing of the rest, the Gallic War, and Hannibal with the Second Punic War.

Alas, how ashamed I am even to have learned these things and laid them bare! Was that peace of a single year, or rather that shadow of peace, a soothing of miseries or a spur to evils? Did that drop of oil falling into the midst of a great blaze put out the tinder of so great a fire, or feed it? Did a sip of cold water swallowed in the most burning fever cure the sick man, or rather inflame him?

For nearly seven hundred years, that is, from Tullus Hostilius to Caesar Augustus, only for a single summer did the bowels of Rome not sweat blood; and through the many ages of long centuries that wretched city, truly a wretched mother, scarcely once had rest from the fear of grief, not to say from grief itself.

If any man had had so little rest in his life, would he even be said to have lived? Or if someone were racked by pains and torments for a whole year, and in the middle of that year spent just one day in peace and free of struggle, would he gain from that any relief from his ills, and not count the whole year
as one of misery? "But," someone says, "they set this year up as a glorious emblem of tireless valour." Would that they had passed it over, so that their unbroken calamity might be forgotten!

For just as in the human body leprosy is recognized only when a different colour shows here and there among healthy patches of skin, whereas if it spreads everywhere so as to make the whole body one colour, however unnatural, the distinction disappears, so too, if their continual toil had flowed on with even endurance and no longing for a breathing space, it would have been called a settled purpose of the will and a chosen way of life.

But since the rejoicing of the ancestors and the eager praise of their descendants rest so heavily on this tiny scrap of leisure, the contrast is plain: how much delight that brevity held and how much bitterness that long stretch; that is, how welcome that rest would have been had it lasted, and how much this unceasing misery ought to have been avoided, had there been any way to avoid it.
In the 517th year from the founding of the City, Hamilcar, the Carthaginian general, was killed by the Spaniards in battle while he was secretly preparing another war against the Romans.
The following year Roman envoys were killed by the Illyrians.
Afterwards a most savage war was waged against these same Illyrians, in which many towns and peoples were wiped out, and the rest surrendered to the consuls Fulvius and Postumius.

Two years later, priests powerful only for evil defiled the wretched city with sacrilegious sacrifices. The decemvirs, going beyond even the custom of their ancient superstition, buried alive in the Forum Boarium a Gallic man and a Gallic woman together with a Greek woman.
But this magical binding at once turned against them, for they atoned for those dreadful deaths they had inflicted on foreigners by most hideous slaughters of their own people.

For in the consulship of Lucius Aemilius Catulus and Gaius Atilius Regulus the senate was thrown into great alarm by the revolt of Cisalpine Gaul, while news also came that a huge army was approaching from Further Gaul, chiefly of the Gaesatae, a name that denotes not a people but Gallic mercenaries.

The consuls, therefore, deeply alarmed, gathered the forces of all Italy to defend the empire. When this was done, the armies of the two consuls are reported to have numbered eight hundred thousand armed men, as the historian Fabius, who took part in that very war, has written.
Of these, the Romans and Campanians made up [?] thousand two hundred infantry and twenty-six thousand six hundred cavalry; the rest of the host were allies.

Battle was joined near Arretium and the consul Atilius was killed. Eight hundred thousand Romans fled after losing a part of their number not even as large as ought to have frightened them; for historians record that three thousand of them were killed at that time.

It is all the more shameful and disgraceful that such huge columns ran away after losing so few, because it betrayed that in their other victories they had prevailed not by strength of spirit but by the chances of war. For who, I ask, would believe that such a number was ever even in a Roman army, let alone that it fled?
After this a second battle was fought with the Gauls, in which fully forty thousand Gauls were slaughtered.

The following year the consuls Manlius Torquatus and Fulvius Flaccus were the first to lead Roman legions across the Po. There they fought the Insubrian Gauls, of whom twenty-three thousand were killed and five thousand captured.

Then in the year after that, dreadful portents terrified the wretched City, wretched indeed, since it was terrified on one side by the roar of enemies and on the other by the wickedness of demons. In Picenum a river flowed with blood; among the Etruscans the sky was seen to be on fire; and at Ariminum, deep in the night, a bright light was said to have shone out, and three moons to have appeared, rising in separate regions of the sky.
At that time, too, Caria and the island of Rhodes were so shaken by a great earthquake that, as houses everywhere collapsed, even the huge Colossus fell.
In the same year the consul Flaminius, scorning the auspices which forbade him to fight, engaged the Gauls and won. In that war nine thousand Gauls were killed and seventeen thousand captured.

After this the consul Claudius destroyed thirty thousand of the Gaesatae; there he himself advanced into the front line and killed their king Viridomarus. And among the many towns of the Insubres that he forced to surrender, he also took Mediolanum, a most flourishing city.
Next the Istrians were roused as new enemies, and the consuls Cornelius and Minucius subdued them, though at the cost of much Roman blood.
Here that old Roman craving for wicked glory, won even by murdering their own kin, surfaces for a moment.

For Fabius Censorinus killed his son Fabius Buteo, who had been accused of theft: a fitting crime, no doubt, for a father to think it should be punished even by killing his own son, when even the laws prescribed for any man nothing more than a fine or, at most, exile.

In the 534th year from the founding of the City, Hannibal, commander of the Carthaginians, destroyed Saguntum, the most flourishing city of Spain and a friend of the Roman people. He first attacked it in war, then surrounded it with a siege and tormented it with hunger. Out of regard for the loyalty they had pledged to the Romans, the people bravely endured everything, whether fit to be suffered or not, and the city fell only in the eighth month.
When Roman envoys were sent to him, he insulted them grossly and would not even admit them to his presence.

After that, driven by hatred of the Roman name, he set out in the consulship of Publius Cornelius Scipio and Publius Sempronius Longus. At the age of nine he had sworn this hatred before the altars to his father Hamilcar, and he kept that oath most faithfully, though in all else he was utterly faithless. He crossed the Pyrenees, cut a path with the sword through the fiercest tribes of the Gauls, and on the ninth day reached the Alps from the Pyrenees.

There he overcame in battle the mountain Gauls, who were struggling to drive him back from the ascent, and broke through trackless crags with fire and iron. After a delay of four days, he finally reached the plains on the fifth, with the greatest toil.
His army at that time is reckoned at one hundred thousand infantry and twenty thousand cavalry.

The consul Scipio was the first to meet Hannibal. In the battle fought at the Ticinus he was himself gravely wounded, and he escaped from the very jaws of death only through his son Scipio, then still a boy in the toga of youth, who was later given the surname Africanus. Almost the entire Roman army was cut down there.

Next, under the same consul, a battle was fought at the river Trebia, and again the Romans were defeated with equal slaughter. When the consul Sempronius learned of his colleague's misfortune, he returned from Sicily with his army. He too engaged at the same river, lost his army, and escaped almost alone. In that battle, however, Hannibal was also wounded.

Afterwards, as Hannibal was crossing into Etruria at the beginning of spring, he was caught by a storm on the heights of the Apennines. For two days on end he and his army were shut in by snow, unable to move, weighed down and frozen stiff. A great number of men, a great many pack animals, and almost all the elephants perished there from the bitterness of the cold.
Meanwhile the other Scipio, brother of the consul Scipio, waged a great many wars in Spain; he also defeated and captured Mago, a Carthaginian general.

At that time the Romans were also terrified by dreadful portents. The sun's disc seemed to shrink; at Arpi shields were seen in the sky, and the sun was seen fighting with the moon; at Capena two moons rose in the daytime; in Sardinia two shields sweated blood; among the Falisci the sky seemed to split open as if with a great gash; and at Antium bloody ears of grain fell into the baskets of the reapers.

Hannibal, then, knowing that the consul Flaminius was alone in his camp, advanced at the beginning of spring so as to crush him all the more quickly while he was unprepared. He took the shorter but marshy route, at a time when the Sarnus happened to have overflowed far and wide and left the plains sodden and loose; it is of these that it was said: "and the plains which the Sarnus waters."

As Hannibal advanced into them with his army, the mists rising from the marsh in particular took away all view ahead, and he lost a large part of his allies and pack animals. He himself, riding the one elephant that alone [?] remained, barely got through the difficulties of the march; but from the violence of the cold, sleeplessness and toil he lost an eye, which had long been ailing.
When he came near the camp of the consul Flaminius, he provoked Flaminius to battle by laying waste the surrounding country.

This battle was fought at Lake Trasimene. There the Roman army, trapped by Hannibal's cunning, was most disastrously surrounded and slaughtered to a man; the consul himself was killed as well. Twenty-five thousand Romans are reported to have been slain in that battle and six thousand taken prisoner. Of Hannibal's army two thousand fell.

This battle at Lake Trasimene became famous for the scale of the Roman disaster, and above all because the fighters' passion was so intense that they did not feel at all a very severe earthquake which happened to occur at that time. It is said to have been so violent that it threw down cities, moved mountains, split rocks and forced rivers to flow backwards.
The disaster at Trasimene was followed by the battle of Cannae, although in between came the time of the dictator Fabius Maximus, who checked Hannibal's onslaught by delaying.

In the 540th year from the founding of the City, the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paulus and Publius Terentius Varro were sent against Hannibal. Through the impatience of the consul Varro they met with utter disaster at Cannae, a village in Apulia, and lost almost all the strength on which Rome's hopes rested.
In that battle forty-four thousand Romans were killed, though a large part of Hannibal's army was also cut down. Yet in no other Punic war were the Romans brought so close to utter annihilation.

For the consul Aemilius Paulus perished in it; twenty men of consular or praetorian rank were killed; thirty senators were captured or killed, as were three hundred men of noble birth, forty thousand foot soldiers and three thousand five hundred cavalry. The consul Varro fled to Venusia with fifty horsemen.
Nor is there any doubt that this would have been the last day of the Roman state, if Hannibal had pressed on to storm the City immediately after his victory.
As proof of his victory Hannibal sent to Carthage three measures of gold rings, which he had pulled from the hands of the Roman knights and senators who had been killed.

Among the surviving Romans despair for the commonwealth went so deep that the senators thought they should take counsel about abandoning Italy and seeking new homes. This would have been decided, at the urging of Caecilius Metellus, had not Cornelius Scipio, then a military tribune, the same who was later Africanus, deterred them with drawn sword and instead compelled them to swear, in words he dictated, to defend their country.

The Romans, daring to breathe again in hope of life as if returned from the underworld, appointed Decimus Junius dictator. He held a levy of everyone from the age of seventeen up and scraped together from every quarter four legions of raw and undisciplined troops.

He then also enrolled under the military oath slaves of proven strength and willingness, holding out the promise of freedom; some were offered by their owners, others, where necessary, were bought at public expense. Weapons that were lacking were taken down from the temples, and private wealth was poured into the empty treasury. So the equestrian order and the frightened common people alike forgot their own interests and looked to the common good.

The dictator Junius also recalled an ancient expedient from Rome's distress. To fill up the army, he opened something like an asylum by edict: whoever was liable for crimes or debts was promised impunity and pressed into military service. Their number came to six thousand men.
Campania, or rather all Italy, utterly despairing of any recovery of the Roman state, went over to Hannibal. After this Lucius
Postumius, a praetor sent to fight against the Gauls, was cut down together with his army.

Then, in the consulship of Sempronius Gracchus and Quintus Fabius Maximus, Claudius Marcellus, a former praetor appointed proconsul, routed Hannibal's army in battle. He was the first, after such ruin of the commonwealth, to raise the hope that Hannibal could be overcome.

In Spain, meanwhile, the Scipios crushed in a very heavy battle Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian commander, who was preparing an army for Italy; they reduced his army by thirty-five thousand soldiers, either killed or captured.

They also enticed Celtiberian soldiers with pay away from their alliance with the enemy and brought them into their own camp. These were the first foreign troops that the Romans began to keep in their camp.
The proconsul Sempronius Gracchus was led into an ambush by his host, a certain Lucanian, and killed.
Centenius Penula, a centurion, asked of his own accord to be given command of the war against Hannibal; he was cut down by Hannibal together with the eight thousand soldiers he had led into battle.
After him the praetor Gnaeus Fulvius was defeated by Hannibal, lost his army, and barely escaped.
It is shameful to recall. Should I speak of the Romans' wickedness or rather of their misery? More truly, of a wicked misery or a miserable wickedness.

Who would believe it? At a time when the treasury of the Roman people was begging a pittance by private collection; when the soldiers in camp were nothing but boys, slaves, criminals or debtors, and even so were not enough in number; when the senate in the curia seemed almost entirely made up of new men; when, finally, everything was so diminished and broken that men despaired and a plan to abandon Italy was being considered:

at that very time, when, as we have said, the single war at home could in no way be borne, three further wars were taken up overseas! One in Macedonia against Philip, the most powerful king of Macedonia; a second in Spain against Hasdrubal, Hannibal's brother; a third in Sardinia against the Sardinians and another Hasdrubal, a Carthaginian general; and besides these, a fourth, that of Hannibal, by which they were hard pressed in Italy.

And yet a courageous despair, facing either outcome, turned things for the better: in all these wars they fought out of despair, and by fighting they won. This shows clearly that those times were not more peaceful and full of leisure, but that the men were stronger in their miseries.

In the 543rd year from the founding of the City, Claudius Marcellus took Syracuse, the wealthiest city of Sicily, with difficulty at the second assault. He had besieged it long before but could not capture it, since he was driven back by the machines of Archimedes, a citizen of Syracuse endowed with marvelous genius.

In the tenth year after Hannibal had come into Italy, in the consulship of Gnaeus Fulvius and Publius Sulpicius, Hannibal moved his army out of Campania. Wreaking enormous havoc on everyone, he marched by the Latin Way through the territory of Sidicinum and Suessa to the river Anio, and encamped three miles from the City, to the incredible

terror of the whole city. While the senate and people were in alarm over their various concerns, even the matrons, out of their minds with fear, ran along the battlements, eager to carry stones onto the walls and to be the first to fight in their defense.

Hannibal himself advanced menacingly with light cavalry right up to the Colline Gate, and then drew up all his forces in battle line. But the consuls and the proconsul Fulvius did not refuse battle either.

But when the battle lines had been drawn up on both sides and stood facing each other, in full view of Rome, which was to be the victor's prize, such a downpour mixed with hail suddenly burst from the clouds that the ranks were thrown into confusion and, barely keeping hold of their weapons, withdrew to their own camps.

Then, when fair weather returned and the forces had gone back onto the field and into battle line, a still more violent storm broke out once more. With greater terror it checked the daring of mortals and forced the frightened armies to flee back into their tents.
Then Hannibal, turning to religious awe, is said to have remarked that at one time he was not given the will, at another not the power, to take Rome.

Let the detractors of the true God answer me here: was it Roman courage or divine mercy that kept Hannibal from seizing and overthrowing Rome? Or perhaps these men, who were themselves preserved, disdain to admit what Hannibal feared even as victor and acknowledged as he withdrew. And

if it is evident that this divine protection came from heaven by means of rain, and that rain itself is not supplied at fitting and needed times except through Christ, who is the true God, then I think even people of this sort know this with sufficient certainty and cannot deny it,

above all now. For, as proof of his power, whenever drought distresses us and it happens that rain is constantly sought, and by turns now the pagans, now the Christians pray for it, it has never happened, even by their own testimony, that the longed-for rains came except on the day when Christ was prayed to and the Christians were allowed to pray.

So it is beyond doubt that the city of Rome, through this same true God, who is Christ Jesus, ordering all things according to the good pleasure of his ineffable judgment, was preserved then for the belief of the faith that was to come, and is now chastised in part for its unbelief.

In Spain, meanwhile, both Scipios were killed by Hasdrubal's brother. In Campania, Capua was taken by the proconsul Quintus Fulvius; the leading men of the Campanians took their own lives by poison, and Fulvius put the whole senate of Capua to death by execution, even though the Roman senate forbade it.
After the Scipios had been killed in Spain, and while everyone hesitated, struck with fear, Scipio, still a very young man, volunteered himself. And since the treasury was in a shameful

state of want, on the proposal of Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Laevinus, who were then consuls, all the senators publicly brought their coined gold and silver to the quaestors for the public use. They kept nothing back except a single ring and a bulla each for themselves and their sons, and for each of their daughters and wives only an ounce of gold and no more than a pound of silver apiece.

Scipio, at the age of twenty-four, received by lot proconsular command in Spain. Bent above all on avenging his father and uncle, he crossed the Pyrenees and at the first assault captured New Carthage, where the Carthaginians kept their largest war funds, strong garrisons, and great stores of gold and silver. There he also captured Mago, Hannibal's brother, and sent him to Rome with the other prisoners.
The consul Laevinus, returning from Macedonia, stormed Agrigentum, a city of Sicily, and captured there Hanno, the African general. He received forty towns in surrender and took twenty-six by storm.
In Italy Hannibal killed the proconsul Gnaeus Fulvius, together with eleven tribunes and seventeen thousand soldiers.

The consul Marcellus fought Hannibal for three days on end. On the first day they parted with the battle even; on the next the consul was defeated; on the third he was victorious, killed eight thousand of the enemy, and forced Hannibal himself to flee to his camp with the rest.

The consul Fabius Maximus stormed and recaptured Tarentum, which had revolted from the Romans. There he destroyed large forces of Hannibal's together with their commander Carthalo, sold thirty thousand captives, and paid the proceeds into the treasury.
The following year in Italy the consul Claudius Marcellus was killed by Hannibal together with his army.

In Spain Scipio defeated the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal and stripped him of his camp. He also brought eighty towns under his power, by surrender or by war. He sold the Africans into slavery but released the Spaniards without ransom.
Hannibal trapped both consuls, Marcellus and Crispinus, in an ambush and killed them.

In the consulship of Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator, Hasdrubal, Hannibal's brother, was coming from Spain through Gaul to Italy, under orders from the Carthaginians to join his brother with his forces, and was bringing large auxiliary forces of Spaniards and Gauls with him. But although he had hastened his coming, the consuls were informed that he had already come down from the Alps. Before Hannibal knew of it, he was intercepted by the Roman army and killed with his whole army.
For a long time the outcome of the battle was uncertain, chiefly because the elephants were wreaking havoc on the Roman line. They were dealt with by the Roman soldiers whom

they call velites, from their darting about. This kind of soldier had been devised a little earlier: young men chosen for their agility sat with their weapons behind the horsemen, and when they came up to the enemy they leapt down from the horses and at once fought as foot soldiers themselves, driving the enemy back, while on the other side the horsemen who had carried them there fought as well.

So when the elephants had been driven back by these velites and could no longer be controlled by their own riders, they were killed by a carpenter's chisel driven in between the ears. This method of killing the beast when necessary had first been devised by this same general Hasdrubal.

In this battle the river Metaurus, where Hasdrubal was defeated, was to the Carthaginians what Lake Trasimene had been to the Romans, and Cesena, a town of Picenum, what that village of Cannae had been;

for fifty-eight thousand of Hasdrubal's army were killed there and five thousand four hundred captured. Among them four thousand Roman citizens were found and recovered, which was a consolation to the victorious consuls, for eight thousand of their own army had also fallen.

The head of his brother Hasdrubal was thrown down in front of Hannibal's camp. When he saw it and at the same time learned of the Carthaginian disaster, he withdrew into the land of the Bruttii, in the thirteenth year after he had come into Italy.

After this, for a whole year, there seemed to be a pause from the turmoil of war between Hannibal and the Romans, because sickness was raging in the camps and both armies were afflicted by a very severe plague.

Meanwhile Scipio, having made all Spain from the Pyrenees to the Ocean into a province, came to Rome. Elected consul with Licinius Crassus, he crossed into Africa, killed Hanno son of Hamilcar, the Carthaginian general, and destroyed his army, partly by slaughter and partly by capture; for he killed eleven thousand Carthaginians in that battle.

The consul Sempronius engaged Hannibal, was defeated, and fled back to Rome. In Africa Scipio attacked the winter quarters of the Carthaginians and those of the Numidians, both of which were not far from Utica, and had them set on fire in the dead of night.

The Carthaginians, panic-stricken and thinking the fire had started by accident, ran unarmed to put it out, and so were easily overwhelmed by armed men. In the two camps forty thousand men were consumed by fire and sword, and five thousand were captured; the generals themselves, wretchedly burned, barely escaped.
The commander Hasdrubal came to Carthage as a fugitive. Syphax and Hasdrubal soon raised a very large army again and once more engaged Scipio, but they were routed and fled.

As Syphax fled, Laelius and Masinissa captured him. The rest of the multitude took refuge in Cirta, which Masinissa besieged and received in surrender. He brought Syphax in chains to Scipio, who handed him over to Laelius to be taken to Rome together with immense spoils and a great many captives.

Hannibal was ordered to return to Africa to help the exhausted Carthaginians. He left Italy in tears, after killing all the soldiers of Italian stock who were unwilling to follow him. As he drew near the African coast, one of the sailors was ordered to climb the ship's mast and look out from there to see what region they were approaching. He answered that he could see a ruined tomb. Hannibal, taking the words as an evil omen, changed course and landed his forces at the town of Leptis.

After at once restoring his troops, he came to Carthage and then asked for a conference with Scipio. There the two most famous generals gazed long at each other, struck with mutual admiration; but when no peace was achieved, battle was joined.

It had long been prepared by the great skill of the generals, was carried on by great masses of troops, was decided by the great strength of the soldiers, and gave the victory to the Romans. Eighty elephants were captured or killed there, and twenty thousand five hundred Carthaginians were slain. Hannibal, who had tried everything both before the battle and during it, slipped away in the confusion with a few men, that is, scarcely four horsemen, and took refuge at Hadrumetum.

Afterwards he came to Carthage, thirty-six years after he had left it as a small boy with his father, and persuaded the senate, which was deliberating, that no hope remained except in suing for peace.

In the consulship of Gaius Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Aelius Paetus, peace was granted to the Carthaginians through Scipio, by the will of the senate and people. Nevertheless more than five hundred ships were taken out to sea and burned in sight of the city.

Scipio, who already bore the surname Africanus, entered the City in triumph. Terence, later the comic poet, one of the noble Carthaginian captives, followed behind the triumphal chariot wearing the freedman's cap, the sign of the freedom granted him.

In the 546th year after the founding of the City, the Second Punic War came to an end; it had been waged for seventeen years. It was followed at once by the Macedonian War. The consul Quintius Flamininus received this command by lot, and after many very heavy battles in which the Macedonians were defeated, he granted Philip peace.
Then he fought the Lacedaemonians. After defeating their leader Nabis, he led before his chariot two hostages of the highest rank: Demetrius, son of Philip, and Armenes, son of Nabis.

All the Roman captives who had been sold throughout Greece under Hannibal were recovered. With their heads shaved as a sign that their slavery had been wiped away, they followed the chariot of the man celebrating the triumph.

At the same time the Insubres, the Boii and the Cenomani joined their forces under the leadership of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian who had stayed behind in Italy. They laid waste Cremona and Placentia, but after a very hard war they were overcome by the praetor Lucius Fulvius.
Later Flamininus, as proconsul, subdued in war King Philip, and with him the Thracians, Macedonians and Illyrians, as well as many other peoples who had come to his aid.

The defeated Macedonians lost their camp. Polybius writes that eight thousand of the enemy were slain that day and five thousand captured; Valerius says forty thousand were massacred; Claudius, however, records thirty-two thousand killed.

But this disagreement among the writers is certainly a sign of falsehood, and the cause of the falsehood is surely flattery, since they are eager to heap up the praises of the victor and to exalt the valor of their country, whether for their contemporaries or for posterity. Otherwise, if the number had not been carefully ascertained, no figure of any sort would have been given.

Yet if it is glorious for a general and his country to have slain a great many of the enemy, how much more joyful for the country, and how much more fortunate for the general, it must seem to have lost none of their own men, or very few!

So it is perfectly clear that with the same shamelessness in lying by which the number of enemy slain is inflated, the losses of their own side are also played down, or even passed over in complete silence.
Thus Sempronius Tuditanus was overwhelmed in war in Nearer Spain and killed together with his whole Roman army.

The consul Marcellus was overwhelmed by the Boii in Etruria and lost a large part of his army. Afterward Furius, the other consul, came to his aid, and together they laid waste the whole nation of the Boii with fire and sword and destroyed it almost to nothing.
In the consulship of Lucius Valerius Flaccus and Marcus Porcius Cato, Antiochus, king of Syria, who was preparing war against the Roman people, crossed from Asia into Europe.

At that time Hannibal too was ordered by the senate to be produced at Rome, because of rumors circulating among the Romans that he was stirring up war. He left Africa secretly and went over to Antiochus, and finding him hesitating at Ephesus, he soon drove him into war.

At that time also the law that had been passed by Oppius, tribune of the plebs, forbidding any woman to own more than half an ounce of gold, to wear multicolored clothing, or to ride in a carriage through the City, was repealed after twenty years.

In the consulship of Publius Scipio Africanus, for the second time, and Titus Sempronius Longus, ten thousand Gauls were slain near Mediolanum; in a following battle eleven thousand Gauls were killed, but also five thousand Romans.
The praetor Publius Digitius lost almost his entire army in Nearer Spain. The praetor Marcus Fulvius defeated the Celtiberians together with the neighboring peoples and captured their king.
Minucius was brought into the utmost danger by the Ligurians and was surrounded by an enemy ambush; he was barely rescued through the efforts of the Numidian cavalry.
Scipio Africanus, sent with other envoys to Antiochus, even had a friendly conversation with Hannibal. But he left Antiochus without having concluded a peace.
In both Spains wars that were extremely savage and bloody for both peoples were waged by the praetors Flaminius and Fulvius.

In the consulship of Publius Cornelius Scipio and Manius Acilius Glabrio, Antiochus, although he had occupied Thermopylae so that its defenses might make him safer against the uncertain outcome of the war, was nevertheless defeated by the consul Glabrio when battle was joined. He barely escaped from the fight with a few men and reached Ephesus.

He is said to have had sixty thousand armed men, of whom forty thousand are reported to have been slain and more than five thousand captured. The other consul, Scipio, fought against the nation of the Boii, and in that battle he killed twenty thousand of the enemy.

The following year Scipio Africanus, with the help of Eumenes, son of Attalus, fought a naval war against Hannibal, who was then in command of Antiochus' fleet. When Hannibal had been defeated and put to flight and his whole army lost as well, Antiochus asked for peace and of his own accord sent back Africanus' son; whether he had captured him while scouting or in battle is uncertain.
In Further Spain the proconsul Lucius Aemilius was cut down by the Lusitanians and perished with his whole army.

Lucius Baebius, setting out for Spain, was surrounded by the Ligurians and killed with his whole army. It is well established that not even a messenger survived, so that it was the people of Massilia who took care to report the massacre at Rome.

The consul Fulvius crossed from Greece into Gallograecia, which is now Galatia, and came to Mount Olympus, where all the Gallograeci had taken refuge with their wives and children. There he waged a very bitter war. For the Romans were badly battered by arrows, sling-bullets, stones and other missiles hurled from the higher ground, but at last they broke through to close quarters with the enemy. Forty [?] thousand Gallograeci are reported to have been killed in that battle.

The consul Marcius set out against the Ligurians and was defeated, losing four thousand soldiers. Had he not fled quickly back to his camp after his defeat, he would have suffered the same annihilation that Baebius had suffered not long before at the hands of the same enemy.

In the consulship of Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Quintus Fabius Labeo, King Philip, who had killed envoys of the Roman people, obtained pardon through the most modest entreaties of his son Demetrius, whom he had sent as an envoy.

Soon afterward he poisoned this same son as a friend of the Romans and a traitor to himself, with the young man's own brother acting as his father's agent in the murder, while the poor youth suspected no evil from either of them.

In the same year Scipio Africanus, long an exile from the City that had been ungrateful to him, died of illness at the town of Amiternum. In those same days Hannibal, staying with Prusias, king of Bithynia, poisoned himself when the Romans demanded his surrender; and Philopoemen, leader of the Achaeans, was captured and killed by the Messenians.
In Sicily at that time the island of Vulcan, which had not existed before, suddenly rose out of the sea, to everyone's amazement, and remains to this day.
The praetor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, in a very great battle in Nearer Spain, routed twenty-three thousand men and captured four thousand.
Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, in Further Spain, forced one hundred and five towns, emptied and shattered by the wars, to surrender.
That same summer Lucius Postumius also killed forty thousand of the enemy in battle in Nearer Spain. The praetor Gracchus, in the same region, again stormed and captured two hundred towns.

In the consulship of Lepidus and Mucius, the extremely fierce nation of the Bastarnae, incited by Perseus, son of Philip, with the hope of plunder and the opportunity of crossing the river Hister, was destroyed without any battle or any enemy. For at that time the Danube, which is also called the Hister, happened to be covered with thick ice and easily allowed a crossing on foot.

So when a countless multitude of men and horses was recklessly crossing all at once in one huge column, the frozen surface cracked under the enormous weight and the pounding of their steps, and the crust of ice burst apart. Overcome at last and shattered, it gave way in midstream beneath the whole column it had long supported, and then, closing over them again, it drowned them, its fragments hindering their escape. Out of that whole people only a few barely escaped to either bank, their bodies badly cut.

In the consulship of Publius Licinius Crassus and Gaius Cassius Longinus, the Macedonian War was waged, which deserves to be counted among the greatest of wars. For on the side of the Romans were first the whole of Italy, then Ptolemy, king of Egypt, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, Eumenes of Asia, and Masinissa of Numidia. Perseus and the Macedonians were joined by the Thracians with their king Cotys and by all the Illyrians with their king Gentius.

So when the consul Crassus arrived, Perseus met him, and when battle was joined the Romans were miserably defeated and fled. In the following battle the losses on both sides were nearly equal, and they withdrew into winter quarters.

Then Perseus, having crushed the Roman army in many battles, crossed into Illyricum and took by assault the town of Sulcamum, which was defended by Roman garrisons. There he killed part of the great number of Roman troops in the garrison, sold part into slavery, and led part away with him into Macedonia.

Later the consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus fought against him and defeated him, killing twenty thousand infantry in that war. The king slipped away with his cavalry, but he was soon captured and driven before the chariot in the triumph together with his sons, and afterward he died in custody at Alba.

His younger son learned the trade of a coppersmith at Rome to make a living in his poverty, and ended his days there. Besides these, a great many other wars, with very different outcomes, were waged by many peoples everywhere, which I have passed over for the sake of brevity.

In the 600th year after the founding of the City, in the consulship of Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Aulus Postumius Albinus, an enormous fear of the Celtiberians had seized all the Romans, and there was no one among them all who dared go to Spain either as a soldier or as a legate. Then Publius Scipio, who would later be called Africanus, volunteered of his own accord to serve in Spain, although he had already been assigned to Macedonia by lot.

So he set out for Spain and inflicted great slaughter on its peoples, often performing the duties of a soldier rather than those of a general; indeed, he even met a barbarian who challenged him to single combat and killed him.
The praetor Sergius Galba, however, was defeated by the Lusitanians in a great battle; he lost his entire army and barely got away himself with a few men.

At the same time the censors decided that a stone theater should be built in the City. Scipio Nasica prevented this from happening then by a very weighty speech, saying that this device for fostering idleness and wantonness would be most hostile to a warlike people. He so moved the senate that it not only ordered everything that had been prepared for the theater to be sold, but even forbade benches to be set up at the games.

Let our people, then, understand this—those who are offended by anything that falls outside the pleasures of their lust: the reason they themselves feel and admit that they are weaker than their enemies is to be blamed on the theaters, not on the times;

and it is not the true God, who to this day forbids such things, who should be blasphemed, but their own gods, or demons, who should be abhorred, for it was they who demanded these shows. By requiring such a sacrifice they gave ample proof of the depth of their malice, since they fed no less on the ruin of human virtue than on the shed blood of cattle.

For certainly at that time there was no lack of enemies, or famine, or disease, or portents; on the contrary, there were a great many of them. But there were no theaters, in which—incredible to say—the virtues are slaughtered as victims on the altar of luxury.
The Carthaginians once saw fit to sacrifice human beings, but that wrongly adopted belief was soon abandoned. The Romans, however, demanded that men

devote themselves to their own destruction. It was done, it is done, it is loved, and there are loud cries for it to be done. People who would perhaps be offended at the slaughter of a beast from their own flock rejoice at the killing of the virtue of their own hearts. Let those who think the Christians should be reproached rather blush before Nasica, and let them complain, not to us about the enemies they have always had, but to him about the theater he had forbidden them to have.

So in Spain the praetor Sergius Galba, after receiving the surrender of the Lusitanians living on this side of the river Tagus, who had given themselves up voluntarily, killed them through a crime. Pretending that he was going to deal with their interests, he surrounded them with soldiers and cut them all down while they were unarmed and off their guard. This deed later became the cause of the greatest uprising throughout all Spain on account of the Romans' treachery.

In the 602nd year after the founding of the City, in the consulship of Lucius Censorinus and Marcus Manilius, the Third Punic War broke out. When the senate had decreed that Carthage must be destroyed, the consuls set out for Africa together with Scipio, then a military tribune, and occupied the old camp of the elder Africanus near Utica.

There they summoned the Carthaginians and ordered them to hand over their arms and ships. The Carthaginians did so without delay, and so great a quantity of arms was handed over at once that the whole of Africa could easily have been armed with them.

But after the Carthaginians had handed over their arms and were ordered to abandon their city and withdraw ten miles from the sea, their grief turned to desperation, and they resolved either to defend their city or to be buried with it and by it. They appointed two Hasdrubals as their leaders.
They set about making arms first, and made up for the shortage of bronze and iron with gold and silver. The consuls decided to besiege Carthage, whose site is said to have been as follows:

It was enclosed by a wall twenty-two miles long and was surrounded almost entirely by the sea, except for an isthmus three miles wide. At that point it had a wall thirty feet thick, built of squared stone to a height of forty cubits.

The citadel, which was called Byrsa, measured a little more than two miles. On one side the wall shared by the city and the Byrsa overhung the sea, which they call the Lagoon, because it is made calm by a long tongue of land lying across it.

Although the consuls had battered with siege engines and knocked down a considerable part of the wall, they were nevertheless defeated and driven back by the Carthaginians. Scipio protected them as they fled, driving the enemy back within the walls. Censorinus returned to the City. Manilius left Carthage and turned his arms against Hasdrubal.

After Masinissa's death Scipio divided the kingdom of Numidia among Masinissa's three sons. When he had returned to the area around Carthage, Manilius stormed and plundered the city of Tezaga; twelve thousand Africans were slain there and six thousand captured. Hasdrubal, the commander of the Carthaginians and grandson of Masinissa, was killed in the senate house by his own people with pieces of broken benches, on suspicion of treachery.
The praetor Juventius engaged the Pseudo-Philip in Macedonia and was killed, with very great slaughter of the whole Roman army.

In the 606th year after the founding of the City, that is, in the fiftieth year after the Second Punic War, in the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius, Publius Scipio, consul of the previous year, striving to destroy Carthage with a final stroke, entered the Cothon.

There the fighting went on for six days and nights without a break, until utter desperation drove the Carthaginians to surrender, asking that those whom the disasters of war had left alive might at least be allowed to live as slaves.

First a pitiful column of women came down, then a column of men, more wretched still. It is recorded that there were twenty-five thousand women and thirty thousand men. King Hasdrubal surrendered of his own accord.

The deserters who had seized the temple of Aesculapius threw themselves down of their own will and were consumed by fire. Hasdrubal's wife, with a man's grief and a woman's fury, threw herself and her two sons with her into the middle of the blaze. Thus the last queen of Carthage met the same death that the first had once met.
The city itself burned for seventeen days on end and offered its conquerors a wretched spectacle of how changeable the human condition is.
Carthage was razed, and all the stone of its walls was ground to dust, in the seven hundredth year after it was founded.
The whole mass of captives, except for a few leading men, was sold. Thus the Third Punic War was ended in the fourth year after it had begun.

But however diligently I search—being, after all, a man of rather slow wit—I have nowhere been able to discover the cause of the Third Punic War: what Carthage had done to provoke such anger that its overthrow was justly decreed. And what troubles me most of all is this: if, as in the earlier wars, a clear cause and a sense of grievance had kindled the Romans against a rising enemy, there would have been no need for debate.

But in fact some Romans judged that Carthage must be destroyed for the lasting security of Rome, while others held that Carthage should be left unharmed in its present state for the lasting preservation of Roman valor, which they would always have to maintain out of their wariness of a rival city, so that Roman vigor, always kept in practice by wars, would not dissolve into sluggish idleness through security and leisure. So I find that the cause arose not from any wrongs done by provoking Carthaginians but from the fickleness of Romans who were growing sluggish.

Since this is so, why do they blame Christian times for their own dullness and rust, which has made them coarse on the outside and eaten away within? For nearly six hundred years ago, just as their own wise and fearful men had foretold, they destroyed Carthage, that great whetstone of their brilliance and sharpness.

So I will bring this volume to an end, lest by grinding too hard I scrape off the rust only for a while and, when I cannot draw out the needed edge, find only useless roughness. And yet I would by no means fear the roughness that confronts me if I could find the hope of an edge within.
THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS BY PAULUS OROSIUS.

I know that from here on some people may be troubled by the fact that Roman victories multiply with the slaughter of many nations and cities. Yet if they weigh the matter carefully, they will find that more harm was done than good. For we should not think lightly of so many wars: servile, social, civil and the wars against runaway slaves. They brought no profit of any kind and yet great misery.

But I will look the other way and let things seem to have been just as they wish. So I suppose they will say: "What could be happier than those times, with their unbroken triumphs, famous victories, rich spoils and splendid processions, when great kings and conquered nations in long columns were driven before the chariot?"

To them the brief answer will be that they themselves are in the habit of complaining about the times, and that we have taken up this discussion on behalf of those same times. And clearly those times did not belong to one city alone but were common to the whole world. See: Rome's victories were as fortunate as the defeats of everything outside Rome were unfortunate.

How much, then, should we value this drop of toilsome good fortune, to which the happiness of a single city is credited, amid so vast a mass of misfortune that brought about the overthrow of the whole world? Or if those times are thought happy because the wealth of one city increased, why should they not rather be judged most unhappy, since in them the mightiest kingdoms of many well-ordered nations fell in pitiful devastation?

Or did Carthage perhaps see it differently then? For a hundred and twenty years she dreaded now the disasters of war, now the terms of peace, and with intentions now rebellious, now suppliant, she traded peace for war and war for peace. At the last her wretched citizens threw themselves into the fire everywhere in final despair, and the whole city became a single funeral pyre. Even now, small in size and stripped of her walls, she counts it among her miseries to hear what she once was.

Let Spain give her verdict. For two hundred years she watered her fields everywhere with her own blood. She could neither drive off nor endure a relentless enemy who harassed her door to door of his own accord. Her people, broken by the slaughter of wars and drained by the hunger of sieges, killed their wives and children and then, to end their misery, cut one another's throats in wretched encounters and mutual slaughter in their various cities and places. What did she think of her times then?

Finally, let Italy herself speak. Why for four hundred years did she oppose, resist and fight against the Romans, who were after all her own people, if their good fortune was not her misfortune, and if the Romans' becoming masters of the world did not stand in the way of the common good?

I do not ask about the countless peoples of various nations, long free before, who were then conquered in war, carried off from their homelands, sold for a price and scattered into slavery: what they would have preferred for themselves then, what they thought of the Romans, what they judged of the times.

I pass over the kings, men of great wealth, great strength and great glory, long most powerful, who were at last captured, chained like slaves, sent under the yoke, driven before the chariot and slaughtered in prison. To ask their opinion would be as foolish as it would be hard-hearted not to grieve at their misery.

Let us consult ourselves, I say, ourselves and the way of life we have chosen and accepted. Our ancestors waged wars, and when they were worn out by wars they sought peace and offered tribute. Tribute is the price of peace.

We pay tribute so as not to suffer wars, and so we stand and remain in the harbor where they at last took refuge to escape the storms of their troubles. So I will leave it to others to say whether our times are happy; at any rate we consider them happier than theirs, since what they chose only at the last we possess continually.
For the turmoil of wars that wore them down is unknown to us. We are born and grow old in the peace that they only barely tasted after the rule of Caesar and the birth of Christ.

What for them was a tax owed as the price of servitude is for us a free contribution for defense. And the difference between past and present times is so great that what Rome once wrung by the sword from our people to spend on her own luxury she now contributes together with us for the use of the common state. Or if anyone says that the Romans were more tolerable enemies to our forefathers than the Goths are to us, let him hear and understand how different things seem to him from how they are where he himself is concerned.

Once, when wars raged throughout the world, each province lived under its own kings, its own laws and its own customs, and there was no fellow feeling where different powers were at odds. And then, what could ever bring together in fellowship lawless, barbarous peoples who were divided even by religion, since each was trained in different sacred rites?

So if in those days someone, overcome by the bitterness of his troubles, abandoned his homeland along with the enemy, to what unknown place could he go as a stranger? What nation, which was an enemy as a rule, would he as an enemy entreat? To whom could he entrust himself at their first meeting, when he was not drawn by a shared name, not brought by a common law, not made secure by a single religion?

Or are there too few examples? Busiris in Egypt, the most impious sacrificer of strangers who had the misfortune to fall into his hands; the shores of Diana of Tauris, most cruel to foreigners, but her rites still more cruel; Thrace with her Polymestor, wicked even toward guests who were his kin. And lest I seem to dwell on ancient tales, Rome is witness to the murder of Pompey, and Egypt to Ptolemy his murderer.
But for me, when I flee at the first stir of any disturbance, I am secure in having a place of refuge: everywhere is my homeland, everywhere my law and my religion.

Now Africa has welcomed me as gladly as I came to her confidently. Now, I say, this Africa has received me with simple peace, into her own embrace, under a common law, this Africa of which it was once said, and truly said: "We are denied the shelter of the sand; they stir up wars and forbid us to set foot on the shore." Now of her own accord she opens her kindly bosom wide to receive those who share her religion and her peace, and of her own accord invites the weary to come and be cared for.

The breadth of the East, the abundance of the North, the wide expanse of the South, and the most spacious and secure homes of the great islands are mine by right and name, because as a Roman and a Christian I come to Christians and Romans.

I do not fear the gods of my host; I do not fear that his religion will be my death. I have no such place to dread, where the owner may do whatever he likes and the stranger may not do what is proper, where my host's law would not be mine.

One God, who in the times when he chose to make himself known established this unity of empire, is loved and feared by all. The same laws, which are subject to the one God, prevail everywhere. Wherever I go as a stranger, I do not dread sudden violence as one left without protection.

Among Romans, as I have said, I am a Roman; among Christians a Christian; among men a man. I appeal to the state through its laws, to conscience through religion, to nature through our common humanity. For the time being I make use of every land as my homeland, because the true homeland, the one I love, is not on earth at all.

I have lost nothing where I loved nothing, and I have everything when the one I love is with me, especially because he is the same among all. He makes me not only known to all but a neighbor to all, and he does not desert me in need, because the earth and its fullness are his, and from it he has commanded that all things be common to all.

These are the blessings of our times, which our ancestors never had in full, whether in the tranquility of the present, the hope of the future, or a common refuge. Because of this they waged ceaseless wars: since they were not free to move their homes in common, they stayed in their own lands and were either killed miserably or enslaved shamefully. This will be shown more clearly and plainly when the deeds of the ancients themselves are set out in order.

In the 606th year from the founding of the City, that is, in the same year in which Carthage was destroyed, in the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius, the overthrow of Corinth followed the ruin of Carthage. Within a brief space of a single season, the pitiful fires of two most powerful cities blazed together in different parts of the world.
For the praetor Metellus had defeated the Achaeans and Boeotians, who were allied, in two battles, first at Thermopylae

and again in Phocis. The historian Claudius reports that twenty thousand were killed in the first battle and seven thousand slain in the second. Valerius and Antias state that the battle was fought in Achaea and that twenty thousand Achaeans fell together with their leader Diaeus. Polybius the Achaean, although he was then in Africa with Scipio, could not have been ignorant of a disaster at home; he asserts that there was a single battle in Achaea, with Critolaus as leader, and tells how Diaeus, bringing up troops from Arcadia, was crushed with his army by the same praetor Metellus.

But I have already said a good deal about the disagreements among conflicting historians. Let it suffice to have exposed this mark of their falsehoods, already notorious, for those who differ even about what they saw themselves clearly show that they deserve little trust in other matters.

So when all the defenses of Achaea had been destroyed and the praetor Metellus was planning to overthrow the defenseless cities, the consul Mummius arrived suddenly in the camp with a few men. He at once dismissed Metellus and without delay stormed Corinth, then by far the wealthiest city in the whole world, for it had been for many centuries a kind of workshop of all craftsmen and crafts and the common market of Asia and Europe.

License to plunder was cruelly granted even to the captives, and everything was so filled with slaughter and fire that the blaze poured out from within the circuit of the walls as from a furnace, narrowing to a single peak. Most of the people were consumed by sword and flame, and the rest were sold at auction.
