The city was burned and the walls razed to their foundations; the stone of the walls was ground to dust, and enormous plunder was carried off.

Indeed, because of the great number and variety of statues and images, in that burning of the city gold, silver and bronze and all the metals together melted and ran into one mass, and a new kind of metal was formed. From this, as tradition has handed down, comes the name, still used today, of Corinthian bronze and Corinthian vessels, whether made from that metal itself or in imitation of it.

In the same consulship Viriathus, a Lusitanian by birth, a herdsman and a bandit, became the greatest terror to all the Romans: first by infesting the roads, then by laying waste the provinces, and finally by defeating, routing and subduing the armies of Roman praetors and consuls.

For as he ranged far and wide across the Ebro and the Tagus, very great rivers in widely separated regions, the praetor Gaius Vecilius met him. Vecilius's army was at once cut down almost to the last man, and the praetor himself barely slipped away in flight with a few men.

Next the same Viriathus broke the praetor Gaius Plautius in many battles and put him to flight. After that Claudius Unimanus was sent against Viriathus with great preparations for war, as if to wipe out the earlier stain, but he himself brought on a more shameful disgrace.

For when he engaged Viriathus he lost all the forces he had brought with him, and the Roman army lost its greatest strength. Viriathus set up the robes of office, the fasces and the other Roman insignia as trophies in his mountains.
At the same time three hundred Lusitanians joined battle with a thousand Romans in a mountain pass. Claudius reports that seventy Lusitanians fell in it, but three hundred and twenty Romans.

The victorious Lusitanians were going off scattered and unconcerned, and one of them, far separated from the rest, was caught on foot and surrounded by cavalry. He ran one rider's horse through with his lance and cut off the rider's head with a single stroke of his sword. He struck them all with such fear that, while they all looked on, he walked off contemptuously and at his leisure.

In the consulship of Appius Claudius and Quintus Caecilius Metellus, Appius Claudius engaged the Salassi, a Gallic people, was defeated, and lost five thousand soldiers. When battle was renewed he killed five thousand of the enemy. Under the law, it had been laid down that anyone who killed five thousand of the enemy had the right to a triumph, and he too sought a triumph. But because of his earlier losses he did not obtain it, and with notorious shamelessness and ambition he held a triumph at his own expense.

In the consulship of Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus, among other prodigies a hermaphrodite was seen at Rome and was drowned in the sea at the command of the soothsayers. But the performance of this impious expiation did no good, for suddenly so great a plague broke out that those who served at funerals were first too few and then gone altogether. Even great houses were left empty of the living and full of the dead: very rich inheritances inside, and no heirs at all.

In the end, people were denied the chance not only to live in the City but even to come near it, so fierce was the stench that rose throughout the whole City from the bodies rotting in their homes and in their beds.

That cruel expiation, which paved the way for the deaths of men by the death of a man, was at last recognized as wretched and futile by the Romans, who blushed for it amid their miseries. For it had been carried out beforehand as a means of forestalling disaster, and the plague followed all the same. Yet the plague subsided without any atoning sacrifices, simply when the chastisement had run its course according to the measure of a hidden judgment.

If those artful deceivers, the soothsayers, had happened to perform their rite just as the disease was waning, as they usually do, they would no doubt have claimed for themselves, their gods and their rites the glory of restoring health. So that wretched city, devout to the point of sacrilege, was made a fool of by lies from which it could not free itself.

Then the consul Fabius, fighting against the Lusitanians and Viriathus, drove off the enemy and relieved the town of Buccia, which Viriathus was besieging, and accepted its surrender along with that of very many other strongholds. He also committed a crime that would be abhorrent even to the remotest barbarians of Scythia, to say nothing of Roman good faith and restraint. For he cut off the hands of five hundred of their leaders, whom he had invited into alliance and received under the terms of surrender.

Pompey, consul the following year, entered the territory of the Numantines and withdrew after suffering a very great defeat. Not only was almost his whole army routed, but very many of the nobles serving in that campaign were killed.

Viriathus, after crushing Roman generals and armies for fourteen years, was killed through the treachery of his own men. In this alone did the Romans act honorably regarding him: they judged his assassins unworthy of reward.

Now, and often before, I could have woven into my account those tangled wars of the East, which seldom begin or end except in crimes. But the deeds of the Romans, with whom we are concerned, are so many that foreign affairs are rightly passed over with distaste.

At that time Mithridates, king of the Parthians and sixth in line from Arsaces, defeated a general of Demetrius and as victor invaded the city of Babylon and all its territory. He also subdued all the nations that lie between the river Hydaspes and the Indus, and extended his bloody rule as far as India.

When Demetrius himself met him in a second war, he defeated and captured him. After Demetrius was captured, a certain Diodotus, together with his son Alexander, seized his kingdom and the royal title.
Later he killed that very son Alexander, whom he had had as a partner in danger while seizing the kingdom, so as not to have him as a partner in holding it.

In the consulship of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Gaius Hostilius Mancinus various prodigies appeared and, as far as was in their power, were dealt with according to custom. But favorable chances do not always come to the aid of the soothsayers, those hunters after outcomes and builders of deceptions.

For after the consul Mancinus took over the army from Popilius at Numantia, he fought every battle so unsuccessfully and was brought to such utter despair that he was forced to make a most shameful treaty with the Numantines.

Although Pompey too had made another equally shameful treaty with the same Numantines a little before, the senate ordered that the treaty be annulled and that Mancinus be handed over to the Numantines. He was set out before the gates of Numantia with his body stripped and his hands tied behind his back, and he stayed there until nightfall, abandoned by his own people and not accepted by the enemy, a pitiful spectacle to both sides.

At this point grief compels me to cry out. Why, Romans, do you falsely claim for yourselves those great names of justice, good faith, courage and mercy? Learn these more truly from the Numantines. Was courage needed?
They conquered by fighting. Was good faith required? Trusting that others would act as they did, they made a treaty and let go those they could have killed. Did justice need to be proved?

Even the senate proved it by its silence when the same Numantines, through their envoys, demanded either that the peace be kept inviolate or that all those whom they had released alive on the pledge of peace be returned.
Did mercy need to be tested? They gave proof enough, both by letting an enemy army go free with their lives and by refusing to take Mancinus for punishment.

Should Mancinus, I ask, have been handed over, he who warded off the slaughter hanging over a defeated army by holding up the shield of a treaty, who preserved his country's endangered strength for better times?

Or if the treaty that was made displeased you, why was the army ransomed by this pledge received back when it returned, or not given up when it was demanded back? Or if you were pleased with whatever provision was made for saving the army, why was Mancinus, who agreed to it, the only one handed over?

Not long before, Varro, to bring on a battle too hastily, overrode his colleague Paulus, who resisted him, and drove his frightened army headlong. At Cannae, notorious for Roman disasters, he did not deploy his ill-fated forces for battle but exposed them to death. Through his impatience alone, on which Hannibal had long been counting for victory, he lost more than forty thousand Roman soldiers there. He also lost his colleague Paulus—and what a man he was!
—and at last he had the effrontery to return to the City almost alone, and he received the reward of his effrontery.
For thanks were publicly given him in the senate because he had not despaired of the republic, which he himself had reduced to desperation.
Mancinus, on the other hand, who labored not to lose an army trapped by the fortunes of war, was condemned by the same senate to be handed over to the enemy.

I know, Romans, that the one thing displeased you in Varro too, but you made allowance for the moment; and the other pleased you in Mancinus, but you took liberties because of the moment. And so from the beginning you have brought it about that no citizen should look after the interests of an ungrateful people, and no enemy should place faithful trust in the faithless.

Meanwhile Brutus in Further Spain crushed sixty thousand Gallaecians who had come to help the Lusitanians, in a very harsh and difficult war, even though he had caught them off guard and surrounded them. Fifty thousand of them are reported killed in that battle and six thousand captured; few escaped by flight. In Nearer Spain the proconsul Lepidus stubbornly tried to conquer the Vaccaei,

a harmless people who were begging for peace, even though the senate forbade it. But he soon suffered a very heavy defeat and paid the penalty for his wicked stubbornness. Six thousand Romans were most justly slain in this unjust war; the rest escaped, stripped of their camp and having lost even their weapons.

This defeat under Lepidus was no less shameful than the one under Mancinus. So let people now count these times as happy—I will not say the Spaniards, battered and exhausted by so many wars, but at least the Romans themselves, beaten down by such continual defeats and conquered so many times.

Not to reproach them with how many of their praetors, legates, consuls and legions, and how many great armies were destroyed, I recall only this: how dull and senseless with fear the Roman soldier had become, so that he could no longer even stand his ground or steady his courage to try a battle, but as soon as he caught sight of an enemy, especially a Spaniard, he fled, believing himself beaten almost before he was seen.

This makes it plain that both sides judged those times wretched. The Spaniards, even though they could win, were unwilling to leave their pleasant peace and endure foreign wars; and the Romans, the more shamelessly they thrust themselves upon the peace of others, the more shamefully they were defeated.

In the consulship of Servius Fulvius Flaccus and Quintus Calpurnius Piso, a boy was born at Rome to a slave woman with four feet, four hands, four eyes, as many ears, and double male organs. In Sicily

Mount Etna belched out and poured forth vast fires, which rushed headlong down the slopes like torrents and burned up everything nearby with devouring flames, while farther off they scorched the land with hot ashes flying far and wide in heavy vapor. This kind of portent, always native to Sicily, does not usually foretell evil but inflicts it. In the territory of Bononia crops grew on trees.
Then a slave war broke out in Sicily, so grave and savage in the number of slaves, the equipment of their forces and the greatness of their strength that

it terrified—I will not say the Roman praetors, whom it utterly routed, but even the consuls. For seventy thousand slaves are reported to have conspired and taken up arms at that time, except in the city of Messana, which kept its slaves at peace by treating them generously.

Sicily was all the more wretched in this too: as an island, never with a constitution suited to her condition, she was subject now to tyrants, now to slaves. The former exacted servitude by wicked domination; the latter, with perverse presumption, seized liberty in exchange for it. Above all, being shut in on every side by the sea, she cannot easily cast her internal evil out.

For she nourished a viper's brood to her own ruin, swollen by her own lust and destined to live by her own death. And a slave uprising is all the more savage for being rarer than others, because a free multitude is stirred with the aim of enlarging its homeland, a servile one with the aim of destroying it.

In the 620th year from the founding of the City, the treaty made at Numantia was weighing on the honour of Rome with a disgrace almost greater than that of the old treaty at the Caudine Forks. Scipio Africanus was elected consul by the vote of every tribe and sent with an army to take Numantia.
Numantia lay in Nearer Spain, not far from the Vaccaei and the Cantabri, at the edge of Gallaecia, and was the farthest city of the Celtiberians.
For fourteen years, with only four thousand of its own men, it had not only held out against forty thousand Romans but defeated them and forced shameful treaties on them.

So when Scipio Africanus entered Spain, he did not throw himself on the enemy at once in the hope of catching them off guard. He knew that this kind of people never grew so slack in body and mind through idleness that their very habits of life did not make them superior to other people's preparations. Instead, for some time he drilled his soldiers in camp as if in a school.
He spent part of the summer and the whole winter without even attempting a battle, and even so he gained almost nothing by these efforts.

For when the chance to fight came, the Roman army was overwhelmed by the Numantine charge and turned its back. But the consul threw himself in their way, scolding and threatening them and holding them back with his own hands, until at last they grew angry with themselves, turned back on the enemy, and forced those they had been fleeing to flee. The story is hard to believe as told: the Romans put the Numantines to flight and saw them running away.
Although Scipio was glad of this and boasted of it, since it had happened beyond all hope, he declared that no further risk should be taken in battle against them.
So Scipio decided to follow up this unexpected success. He shut the city in with a siege and surrounded it with a ditch ten feet wide and twenty deep.

Then he strengthened the rampart itself with a palisade of stakes and many towers, so that if the enemy broke out and tried to attack it, he would no longer be fighting as a besieger against the besieged, but the other way round, as one besieged against a besieger.
Numantia stood on a hill not far from the river Douro, and its wall had a circuit of three miles. Some writers, however, claim that it was small in extent and had no wall.

So it is believable that, when they were hard pressed by war, they enclosed this space for the purpose of feeding and guarding their livestock, or even to farm the land conveniently, while they themselves held a small citadel fortified by nature. Otherwise, so large a city circuit would seem to betray rather than protect so small a number of men.

So the Numantines, long shut in and wasting away from hunger, offered to surrender if tolerable terms were imposed. They also often begged for the chance of a fair battle, so that they might be allowed to die like men.

At last they all suddenly burst out of two gates, having first drunk deeply, not of wine, which that region does not produce in abundance, but of a liquor skilfully made from wheat. They call this liquor caelia, from the word for heating.

For the vital force of the sprouting grain is first moistened and roused by fire, then dried, then ground into flour and mixed with a mild liquid; this fermentation gives it a sharp taste and the heat of intoxication. Warmed again by this drink after their long hunger, they offered themselves to battle.

The fighting was fierce and long, and went so far as to endanger the Romans. Once again the Romans would have proved by running away that it was Numantines they were fighting, had they not been fighting under Scipio. The Numantines, after their bravest men had been killed, gave up the fight, but they returned to the city in good order and not like men in flight. When the bodies of their dead were offered to them for burial, they refused to accept them.
Then, with the last hope of despair, all of them resolved to die. They shut their city and set fire to it themselves from within, and all alike perished by sword, poison and fire.

The Romans gained absolutely nothing from these conquered people except their own safety. Even with Numantia overthrown, they did not consider that they had conquered the Numantines so much as escaped them.

The victor's chains did not hold a single Numantine; Rome saw nothing from which a triumph could be granted; there was no gold or silver that could have survived the fire, for they were poor; and the fire consumed their weapons and clothing.

At the very time when these things were happening at Numantia, the seditions of the Gracchi were stirring at Rome. When Scipio, after Numantia was destroyed, was settling the other peoples of Spain in peace, he asked a certain Thyresus, a Celtic chieftain, by what means Numantia had first remained unconquered and then been overthrown. Thyresus answered: "Concord kept it unconquered; discord was its ruin."

The Romans took this as a warning, as though it had been said to them and about them, since news was already reaching them of seditions dividing the whole City. With Carthage and Numantia destroyed, the useful practice of taking counsel together for the future died among the Romans, and shameful strife born of ambition arose.

Gracchus, a tribune of the plebs, was angry with the nobility because he had been censured as one of the authors of the Numantine treaty. He decreed that land hitherto held by private persons should be divided among the people. When Octavius, a tribune of the plebs, opposed him, he stripped him of his office and gave him Minucius as a successor. For these reasons anger took hold of the senate, and arrogance of the people.

It happened that at this time Attalus, son of Eumenes, had died and in his will had made the Roman people heir to the rule of Asia. Gracchus, seeking to buy the people's favour, carried a law that the money that had belonged to Attalus be distributed to the people. Nasica opposed him, and Pompeius also pledged that he would prosecute Gracchus as soon as he left office.

Gracchus strove to remain tribune of the plebs himself for the following year, and on the day of the elections he was inflaming the people to sedition. Then the nobility, roused by Nasica, drove off the plebs with pieces of broken benches.

Gracchus, his cloak torn off, fled down the steps above the Calpurnian Arch. He was struck by a piece of a bench and fell; as he was getting up again, he was killed by another blow, a club smashed into his skull.
Two hundred others were also killed in that sedition, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. The corpse of Gracchus himself was left unburied to rot. Moreover, the contagion of the slave war
that arose in Sicily infected many provinces far and wide. At Minturnae 450 slaves were crucified, and at Sinuessa about four thousand slaves were crushed by Quintus Metellus and Gnaeus

Servilius Caepio. In the Athenian mines, too, a similar slave rising was broken up by the praetor Heraclitus, and on Delos slaves swelling with a new revolt were put down by the townspeople, who acted first. All this was besides that first source of the Sicilian trouble, from which these sparks, as it were, flew out and kindled these fires in different places.
For in Sicily, after the consul Fulvius, the consul Piso stormed the town of the Mamertines, where he killed eight thousand runaway slaves and crucified those he was able to capture.

When the consul Rutilius succeeded him, he too took Tauromenium and Henna, the strongest refuges of the runaways, by force of arms. More than twenty thousand slaves are said to have been slaughtered then.

Wretched indeed, and hopelessly tangled, was the cause of such a war. The masters would certainly have perished unless the insolence of the slaves had been met with the sword. And yet, in the most unhappy losses of battle and the even unhappier gains of victory, the victors lost as much as the number of the vanquished who perished.

In the 622nd year from the founding of the City, Publius Licinius Crassus, consul and chief pontiff, was sent against Aristonicus, the brother of Attalus, who had seized Asia after it had been bequeathed to the Romans by will. He was sent with

a very well-equipped army, and was also helped by great kings, namely Nicomedes of Bithynia, Mithridates of Pontus and Armenia, Ariarathes of Cappadocia and Pylaemenes of Paphlagonia, with their very large forces. Yet when battle was joined he was defeated.

His army was put to flight after a great slaughter, and he himself was surrounded by the enemy and nearly captured. He then thrust the switch he used on his horse into the eye of a Thracian; the barbarian, burning with anger and pain, ran Crassus through the side with his sword. So by this deliberately contrived way of dying he escaped both disgrace and slavery.

The consul Perpenna, who had succeeded Crassus, on hearing of Crassus' death and the defeat of the Roman army, hurried swiftly to Asia. He attacked Aristonicus with an unexpected assault while he was taking his ease after his recent victory, stripped him of all his forces and put him to flight.

He besieged the city of Stratonicea, where Aristonicus had taken refuge, and forced him by starvation to surrender. The consul Perpenna was seized by illness at Pergamum and died; Aristonicus was strangled in prison at Rome by order of the senate.

In the same year Ptolemy, king of the Alexandrians, ended his wretched life in a still more wretched way. He had debauched his own sister, then taken her in marriage, and finally cast her off more shamefully than he had married her.

He took as his wife his stepdaughter, that is, the daughter of his sister and wife, and he killed both the son he had had by his sister and his brother's son. For these great incests and murders of kin he was loathed by the Alexandrians and driven from his kingdom.

At the same time Antiochus, not content with Babylon, Ecbatana and the whole empire of Media, engaged Phraates, king of the Parthians, and was defeated. Although he appeared to have a hundred thousand armed men in his army, he was dragging along more than two hundred thousand camp servants and sutlers, mixed with prostitutes and actors. So he was easily overwhelmed by the Parthian forces and perished with his whole army.

In the consulship of Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus and Manius Acilius, Publius Scipio Africanus declared publicly before an assembly that he had learned that his life was being threatened by wicked and ungrateful men because of his labours for his country; the next morning he was found dead in his bedroom. I would not be wrong to count this among the greatest misfortunes of the Romans, especially since the vigour and moderation of Africanus carried such weight in that city that it was believed that, while he lived, neither a war with the allies nor a civil war could easily have arisen.

Some say he was murdered by the treachery of his wife Sempronia, the sister of the Gracchi. Thus, I believe, that wicked family, born for the ruin of its country, was made more monstrous not only by the impious seditions of its men but also by the crimes of its women.

In the consulship of Marcus Aemilius and Lucius Orestes, Etna was shaken by a huge tremor and poured out balls of fire. And again on another day the island of Lipara and the sea around it boiled so violently that it even split the scorched rocks, melted the wax on ships and parched their planking, cooked the dead fish floating on the surface, and suffocated people too, except those who were able to flee far enough, for as they breathed in the hot air their insides were burned.
In the consulship of Marcus Plautius Hypsaeus and Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, Africa had scarcely found rest from the devastation of wars when a horrible and unheard-of destruction followed.

Immense swarms of locusts had gathered all over Africa. They had not only scraped away every hope of crops and devoured all the grass with part of its roots, and the leaves of the trees with their tender shoots, but were even gnawing the bitter bark and the dry wood. Then they were suddenly carried off by a wind, driven together into masses, borne for a long time through the air, and plunged into the African sea.

When the waves, pressed on by the sea, had driven huge heaps of them far along the wide stretches of shore, the rotting, decaying mass gave off a foul stench, pestilential beyond belief. From it followed so great a plague among all living creatures alike that the corpses of birds, cattle and wild beasts, killed by the corrupted air, lay rotting everywhere and made the contamination still worse.

But as for how great the pestilence among human beings was, I shudder in my whole body even as I tell it. In Numidia, where Micipsa was then king, eight hundred thousand people are reported to have died, and along the seacoast, especially the shores near Carthage and Utica, more than two hundred thousand. At the city of Utica itself, thirty thousand soldiers who had been stationed there to defend all Africa were wiped out and destroyed.
This disaster struck so suddenly and so violently that at Utica, it is said, more than fifteen hundred bodies of those young men were carried out through a single gate in a single day.

Yet by the peace and grace of almighty God, in whose mercy and in reliance on whom I speak, let me say this: although even in our own times locusts sometimes appear in various places, and often do damage, though bearable damage, never in Christian times has so great an inescapable evil occurred that a plague of locusts, which could in no way be endured while alive, did more harm when dead, and that, whereas while it lived everything was going to perish, once it had perished everyone, perishing, would rather have wished that it had not perished.

In the 627th year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Lucius Caecilius Metellus and Quintus Titius Flamininus, Carthage in Africa was ordered to be rebuilt. In the twenty-second year after its destruction it was rebuilt and repopulated, families of Roman citizens being settled there to live in it. A great portent came before this.

For when the surveyors sent to mark out the boundaries of Carthaginian territory found that the stakes they had set up as boundary markers had been pulled up in the night by wolves and gnawed to pieces, there was some hesitation over whether it was in the interest of Roman peace for Carthage to be restored.
In the same year Gaius Gracchus, brother of the Gracchus who had already been killed in the sedition, was elected tribune of the plebs amid uproar and became a great bane to the commonwealth.

For he often stirred the Roman people to the most bitter seditions with handouts and extravagant promises, above all over the agrarian law for which his brother Gracchus had also been killed. At last he left the tribunate, Minucius succeeding him.

When Minucius, tribune of the plebs, had overturned most of the measures of his predecessor Gracchus and repealed his laws, Gaius Gracchus, with Fulvius Flaccus and surrounded by a huge throng, went up to the Capitol, where an assembly was being held. There a great uproar broke out, and a herald was killed by the Gracchans, which served as a signal for war.

Flaccus, flanked by his two armed sons and accompanied also by Gracchus, who wore his toga and hid a short sword under his left arm, seized the Dianium as if it were a citadel, although he had sent a herald ahead in vain to call the slaves to freedom.

Against them Decimus Brutus, a man of consular rank, charged down from the Publician slope with a great struggle. There Flaccus fought long and most stubbornly. Gracchus, after he had withdrawn into the temple of Minerva, wanted to fall on his sword but was held back by the intervention of Laetorius. The fighting went on for a long time with the outcome in doubt, until at last archers sent by Opimius broke up the packed crowd.

The two Flacci, father and son, leapt through the temple of Luna into a private house and barred the doors, but the wattle wall was torn open and they were stabbed to death. Gracchus, while his friends fought and died for him for a long time, reached the Sublician Bridge with difficulty, and there, so as not to be taken alive, offered his neck to his own slave.

Gracchus' head was cut off and brought to the consul; his body was taken to his mother Cornelia at the town of Misenum. This Cornelia, the daughter of the elder Africanus, had withdrawn to Misenum, as I have said, after the death of her first son. Gracchus' property was confiscated. The young Flaccus was put to death in the dungeon. Two hundred and fifty of Gracchus' faction are said to have been killed on the Aventine.

The consul Opimius, brave as he was in war, was just as cruel in his inquiry. He put more than three thousand people to death, most of them innocent, killed without even being allowed to plead their case.
At the same time Metellus overran and subdued the Balearic Islands in war, and with great slaughter of the inhabitants suppressed the piracy that was then springing up from there.

Gnaeus Domitius, as proconsul, also defeated the Allobroges, a Gallic people, near the town of Vindalium in a very hard-fought war, chiefly because the enemy's horses, and the enemy themselves, were terrified by the strange shape of the elephants and fled. Twenty thousand of the Allobroges are said to have been killed there and three thousand captured.

At the same time Mount Etna erupted more violently than usual. Torrents of fire poured down and spread far and wide, overwhelming the city of Catina and its territory, so that the roofs of the houses, scorched and weighed down by hot ashes, collapsed. To relieve this disaster the senate remitted the Catinians' taxes for ten years.

In the 628th year from the founding of the City, the consul Fabius went to meet Bituitus, king of the Arverni, a Gallic people, who was preparing for war on a vast scale. Fabius came against him with so small an army that Bituitus boasted that the handful of Romans would hardly be enough to feed the dogs he had with his column.
Realizing that one bridge over the river Rhône was not enough to bring his forces across, he built another out of boats bound together with chains, with planks laid over them and fastened down.

Battle was joined and fought hard for a long time. The Gauls were beaten and turned to flight, and as each man feared for himself, they crowded together recklessly and in their headlong rush across the bridge broke its fastenings, and soon sank together with the boats themselves.
There are said to have been a hundred and eighty thousand armed men in Bituitus' army, of whom a hundred and fifty thousand were either killed or drowned.

The consul Quintus Marcius made war on a Gallic people living at the foot of the Alps. When they saw themselves surrounded by Roman forces and understood that they would be no match for them in war, they killed their wives and children and threw themselves into the flames.

Those who had been prevented by the Romans from carrying out their own deaths at the time and had been captured did away with themselves, some by the sword, some by hanging, some by refusing food. Not a single one survived, not even a small child, who would accept the condition of slavery out of love of life.

In the 635th year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Publius Scipio Nasica and Lucius Calpurnius Bestia, the senate, with the consent of the Roman people, declared war on Jugurtha, king of the Numidians.

But I will touch on Jugurtha only briefly, to keep the order of events and so that he is not passed over. Thanks to the rich brilliance of the historians, everyone already knows quite enough about his changeable and intolerable character and about his deeds, carried out with as much cunning as energy.

Jugurtha, then, was the adopted son of Micipsa, king of the Numidians, and was made his heir alongside his natural sons. First he turned on his co-heirs: he killed Hiempsal, and he defeated Adherbal in war and drove him out of Africa.
Next he bribed the consul Calpurnius, who had been sent against him, and brought him to accept the most shameful terms of peace.

Moreover, when he came to Rome himself, he either bribed or tried to bribe everyone, and stirred up riots and quarrels. As he was leaving the city, he branded it with a notorious saying: "O city for sale, and doomed to perish soon, if it finds a buyer!"

In the following year Aulus Postumius, brother of the consul Postumius, had been placed by the consul in command of an army of forty thousand men. Near the city of Calama, where Postumius was greedily eyeing the royal treasures stored there, Jugurtha crushed him in battle and, having defeated him, forced on him a most disgraceful treaty. He then joined to his kingdom almost the whole of Africa, which was falling away from the Romans.

Afterwards, however, he was held in check by the integrity and discipline of the consul Metellus. He was also defeated in two battles, and saw with his own eyes his Numidia being laid waste without any means of defending it. Forced by Metellus to surrender, he handed over three hundred hostages, promised to supply grain and other provisions, and returned more than three thousand deserters.

Then, since he was unreliable in peace and did not restrain his wicked raids, he was broken by Roman strength and by the consul Gaius Marius, whose cunning was almost the equal of his own. This was especially so after Marius took by a stratagem the city of Capsa, said to have been founded by the Phoenician Hercules, which at that time was crammed with royal treasure.

Losing confidence in his own resources and strength, Jugurtha then made an alliance with Bocchus, king of the Moors. Hugely strengthened by Bocchus' cavalry, he wore down Marius' army with constant raids.
Finally, near Cirta, an ancient city that had been Masinissa's royal seat, he confronted the Romans, who were preparing to storm it, with a force of sixty thousand cavalry.

Never did the Roman soldier face a more chaotic or terrifying battle. The horsemen dashed about, charged and roared, and the dust they raised veiled the sky, took away the daylight and drew a night over everything. So great a cloud of missiles rained down that no part of the body was safe from a blow, for the darkness kept the men from seeing ahead, and

the crush of the crowd left them no room to move and take cover. Nor did the Moorish and Numidian horsemen trouble to pick out an enemy in a good position with a well-timed throw. They simply hurled their javelins at random, sure that the wounds would not be random. So the Roman infantry were forced to pack together into a single mass. Nightfall brought a pause in this great danger.

The next day the face of the war and of the danger was the same. The soldier could not break out against the enemy, though his sword was drawn, because javelins drove him back from a distance; nor could the men flee, since the cavalry, quicker in pursuit, had shut them in on every side.

The third day came, with no help from any quarter, and the dreadful face of death confronted them everywhere. At last the consul Marius, through brave despair, opened a path for hope: he burst out of the rampart with the whole column at once and threw himself onto the open plain and into battle.

The enemy poured around them again, not only tearing at the ends of the column but even cutting down its center with javelins hurled from far off. The Romans were in confusion, and the heat of the sun, unbearable thirst and death on every side were wearing them down to the very edge of despair. Then suddenly the Romans' well-known help against the Africans, storms and rain, was sent from heaven and brought them a deliverance they had not hoped for.

For the sudden rain gave the thirsty, sweltering Romans relief and drink. It also made the shafts of the Numidians' javelins, which they usually hurl by hand without throwing-thongs, slippery and therefore useless.

Their shields, too, made of stretched and hardened elephant hide, were light to carry and safe. But it is the nature of that hide to soak up rain like a sponge and so become unmanageable from the sudden weight. Since the shields could no longer be swung about, they gave no protection. So the Moors and Numidians were unexpectedly thrown into confusion and left helpless, and Bocchus and Jugurtha fled.

After this the same kings threw ninety thousand armed men against the Romans in a final battle. These too are reported to have been cut down to the last man by the victorious Romans. After that Bocchus gave up hope of war and sued for peace. As the price of peace, he had Jugurtha captured by treachery, loaded him with chains, and sent him to Marius through his legate Sulla.
Jugurtha was led in the triumph before Marius' chariot together with his two sons, and shortly afterwards he was strangled in prison.

In those same days an obscene and grim portent was seen. Lucius Helvius, a Roman knight, was returning from Rome to Apulia with his wife and daughter when he was caught in a storm. Seeing that his daughter was terrified, and wanting to reach the nearest shelter more quickly, he left the carriages behind and took to horseback. He placed his young unmarried daughter, mounted on a horse, in the middle of the party.

The girl was killed at once by a stroke of lightning. All her clothes were stripped off without being torn, the bands around her breast and feet were undone, and even her necklaces and rings were shaken off. Her body itself was unharmed, except that she lay naked in an obscene manner, with her tongue sticking out a little. The horse she had been riding also lay dead some distance away, its saddle-cloths, bridle and girths undone and scattered all around.

A short time after this, Lucius Veturius, a Roman knight, secretly seduced and defiled the Vestal Virgin Aemilia. This same Aemilia also enticed two other Vestal Virgins to share in her unchastity, and exposed them and handed them over to the companions of her seducer. When a slave informed on them, all of them were punished.
Also during the time of the Jugurthine War, the consul Lucius Cassius pursued the Tigurini through Gaul as far as the Ocean, but was then caught by them in an ambush and killed.

Lucius Piso, a former consul and legate of the consul Cassius, was also killed. Gaius Publius, the other legate, wanted to keep the rest of the army, which had fled into the camp, from being wiped out, so he gave the Tigurini hostages and half of everything the Romans had, under a most shameful treaty. When he returned to Rome, Caelius, tribune of the plebs, brought him to trial for having given hostages to the Tigurini, and he fled into exile.

The proconsul Caepio captured a city of the Gauls called Tolosa and took from the temple of Apollo one hundred thousand pounds of gold and one hundred and ten thousand pounds of silver. He sent it under guard to Massilia, a city friendly to the Roman people. But the men to whom he had entrusted its safekeeping and transport were secretly killed, as some testify, and he is said to have stolen the whole of it by this crime. For this reason a great inquiry was later held at Rome.

In the 64[?]th year from the founding of the City, the consul Gaius Manlius and the proconsul Quintus Caepio were sent against the Cimbri, Teutones, Tigurini and Ambrones, Gallic and German peoples who had then conspired to destroy the Roman Empire. The two commanders divided the provinces between themselves, with the river Rhône as the boundary.

There, while they quarreled with each other in the bitterest jealousy and rivalry, they were defeated, to the great disgrace and peril of the Roman name. In that battle the former consul Marcus Aemilius was captured and killed, and two sons of the consul were slain.
Antias writes that eighty thousand Romans and allies were slaughtered on that occasion, and forty thousand camp servants and sutlers killed.
So, it is reported, out of the entire army only ten men survived, to bring back the wretched news and add to the misery.
The enemy took both camps and an enormous amount of plunder, and then destroyed everything they had captured in a strange, unheard-of ritual of execration.

Clothing was torn up and thrown away, gold and silver were cast into the river, the men's breastplates were hacked to pieces, the horses' trappings were destroyed, the horses themselves were drowned in the river's whirlpools, and men were hanged from trees with nooses around their necks. Thus the victor took no plunder, and the vanquished found no mercy.
At Rome there was then not only the deepest grief but also the deepest fear that the Cimbri would cross the Alps at once and destroy Italy.

At the same time Quintus Fabius Maximus banished his young son to the countryside and killed him, using two slaves as accomplices in the murder. He then immediately freed those very slaves as payment for the crime. He was brought to trial on the accusation of Gnaeus Pompeius and condemned.

Marius, then consul for the fourth time, had pitched camp near the place where the rivers Isère and Rhône flow together. For three days on end the Teutones, Cimbri, Tigurini and Ambrones fought around the Roman camp, trying somehow to dislodge the Romans from the rampart and draw them out onto the level ground. After that they decided to make for Italy in three columns.

After the enemy had left, Marius moved camp and seized a hill overlooking the plain and the river where the enemy had spread out. When his army ran short of drinking water and everyone reproached him with complaints, he answered that there was indeed water in sight, but it would have to be won with the sword. So the camp servants rushed into the fight first with a shout, and the army followed them. Soon the ranks were properly formed, a regular battle was fought, and the Romans won.

On the fourth day both sides again led their battle lines out onto the plain, and they fought on almost equal terms until nearly midday. Then, as the sun grew hot, the soft bodies of the Gauls melted away like snow, and until nightfall it was a slaughter rather than a battle that
was drawn out. Two hundred thousand armed men were killed in that war and eighty thousand captured, and scarcely three thousand are said to have escaped. Their leader Teutobodus was also killed.

Their women, with greater resolve than if they had won, asked the consul to spare their lives on condition that their chastity be kept inviolate and they be allowed to serve the sacred virgins and the gods. When their request was refused, they dashed their little children against the rocks and all killed themselves with the sword or by hanging. Such were the events concerning the Tigurini and the Ambrones.

The Teutones and Cimbri, however, with their forces intact, crossed the snows of the Alps and overran the plains of Italy. There that hardy race was softened over a long time by milder air, drink, food and baths. Marius, consul for the fifth time, and Catulus were sent against them. When a day and a field had been fixed for the battle, they followed Hannibal's cunning: they drew up their line of battle in the fog, and fought in the sun.

The first thing that threw the Gauls into confusion was that they ran into the Roman line, already drawn up, before they realized it was there. Their horsemen were wounded at once and forced back onto their own men, throwing into disorder the whole multitude, which was still arriving in no formation. Then the sun, rising with the wind, blazed out in their faces: the dust filled their eyes and the glare dulled their sight.

So it came about that this huge and terrifying multitude was cut down, at very small cost to the Romans and with their own utter destruction. One hundred and forty thousand of them are said to have been killed in that battle, and sixty thousand captured.

The women put up an almost fiercer fight. They arranged the wagons around themselves like a camp and fought from on top of them, holding off the Romans for a long time. But the Romans terrified them with a new kind of slaughter: the crowns of their heads were sliced off together with the hair, and they were left disfigured by a truly shameful wound. Then they turned the steel they had taken up against the enemy on themselves and their own.

Some ran at one another and cut each other's throats; some seized each other by the throat and strangled one another. Some tied ropes around the legs of horses, put the same ropes around their own necks, and then at once goaded the horses on, and so were dragged along and killed. Others hanged themselves with nooses from the raised poles of the wagons.

One woman was even found who had tied nooses around the necks of her two sons and bound them to her own feet, so that when she let herself drop to die by hanging, she dragged them with her to their deaths.
Amid these many pitiful kinds of death, two chieftains are also said to have run upon each other with drawn swords. The kings Lugius and Boiorix fell in battle; Claodicus and Caesorix were captured.

Thus in these two battles three hundred and forty thousand Gauls were killed and one hundred and forty thousand captured, not counting the countless multitude of women who killed themselves and their little ones in a woman's frenzy but with a man's strength.
Then an unbelievable crime, never before known to the Romans, was suddenly committed at Rome. It cast a shadow over Marius' great triumph and the Roman victory, as the whole City was turned
to horror and grief. For Publicius Malleolus, with the help of slaves, killed his own mother. He was condemned for parricide, sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea.

So the Romans brought to completion both the crime and its penalty, on which even Solon of Athens had not dared to legislate, since he did not believe such a thing could happen. But the Romans, knowing that they were descended from Romulus, understood that even this could happen, and established a special punishment for it.

In the 645th year from the founding of the City came the Cimbric and Teutonic war and Marius' fifth consulship, through which the Roman Empire is rightly judged to have been preserved. But in the sixth consulship of this same Gaius Marius it was so badly shaken that it very nearly collapsed altogether in civil disaster.
To unravel and go through the twists of these quarrels and the tangled causes of the riots seems to me both unprofitable and lengthy.

It will be enough to touch on them briefly. The first instigator of the uproar was Lucius Apuleius Saturninus, the bitterest enemy of Quintus Metellus Numidicus, a truly eminent man. When Metellus was elected censor, Saturninus dragged him from his house, and when Metellus took refuge on the Capitol, Saturninus besieged him with an armed mob. The anger of the Roman knights drove Saturninus down from there, after a great slaughter in front of the Capitol. Next, Saturninus and Glaucia, through the treachery of the consul Gaius Marius, killed Aulus Nunius, Saturninus' rival for office.

In the following year Marius, consul for the sixth time, Glaucia as praetor and Saturninus as tribune of the plebs conspired to drive Metellus Numidicus into exile by any means at all. He was brought to trial, and the innocent Metellus was criminally condemned by judges planted by that same faction. He went into exile, to the grief of the whole City.

This same Saturninus feared that Memmius, a vigorous man of integrity, would be made consul. He suddenly stirred up a riot, and as Memmius fled, Saturninus had him beaten to death with a rough club by his henchman Publius Mettius.

The senate and the Roman people were in an uproar over such great evils befalling the state. The consul Marius, adapting himself to the moment, joined the united front of the good citizens and calmed the agitated plebs with a mild speech. Saturninus, in his infamous audacity, held an assembly at his own house, and there some hailed him as king and others as commander.

Marius organized the plebs into companies, posted the other consul with troops on the hill, and fortified the gates himself. Battle was joined in the Forum. Driven out of the Forum by Marius' men, Saturninus took refuge on the Capitol, and Marius cut the pipes that carried water up to it.

Then a truly dreadful fight took place at the approach to the Capitol, and many of those around Saufeius and Saturninus were killed. Saturninus shouted openly, declaring that Marius was behind all his schemes.

But when Saturninus himself, Saufeius and Labienus, under pressure from Marius, took refuge in the senate house, the Roman knights broke down the doors and killed them. Gaius Glaucia was dragged out of the house of Claudius and slaughtered.

Furius, tribune of the plebs, decreed that the property of all of them be confiscated. Gnaeus Dolabella, Saturninus' brother, was killed together with Lucius Giganius as he fled through the vegetable market. So, once the leaders of this great riot had been killed, the people had peace.
Then Cato and Pompeius proposed a bill to recall Metellus Numidicus, to the joy of the whole City. Its passage was blocked by the factions of the consul Marius and of Furius, tribune of the plebs.

Rutilius, too, a man of the highest integrity, kept so steadfastly to his honor and innocence that when his accusers brought him to trial, he did not let his hair or beard grow before the hearing. He did not try to win supporters with mourning clothes or a humble bearing, he did not try to soothe his enemies or soften his judges, and even the speech that the praetor allowed him was no more submissive than his spirit.

Although he was the victim of obvious false accusation, and in the opinion of all good men deserved to be acquitted, he was condemned by the perjury of the judges. He moved to Smyrna and grew old there, devoted to literary studies.
In the 659th year after the founding of the City, in the consulship of Sextus Julius Caesar and Lucius Marcius Philippus, the Social War, arising from internal causes, shook the whole of Italy.
For Livius Drusus, a tribune of the people, had lured all the Latins with the hope of freedom, and when he could not make good on his promise, he stirred them up to take arms.
On top of this, dreadful portents terrified the grieving City. At sunrise a globe of fire flashed out from the northern quarter with a tremendous crash in the sky.
Among the people of Arretium, when loaves were being broken at banquets, blood flowed from the middle of the bread as if from wounds in a body.

Besides this, for seven days on end a hail of stones, mixed with fragments of pottery, battered the earth over a very wide area. Among the Samnites flame burst out of a vast chasm in the earth and seemed to stretch up to the very sky.

Moreover, a number of Romans on a journey saw a golden-colored globe roll down from the sky to the earth, then, grown larger, rise again from the earth up into the heights toward the rising sun, and by its size blot out the sun itself.
Drusus, troubled by such great evils, was killed in his own house, though by whose hand is uncertain.

So the Picentes, Vestini, Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Samnites and Lucanians, while they were still secretly plotting revolt, killed the praetor Gaius Servius, who had been sent to them as an envoy, at Asculum; then at once they shut the city and, proclaiming a massacre, butchered all the Roman citizens there.

This most atrocious slaughter was immediately preceded by the most ill-omened portents. Animals of every kind that had been used to bearing the touch of human hands gently and to living among people left their stalls and pastures and fled to the woods and mountains, bleating, neighing and lowing piteously. Even dogs, whose nature it is that they cannot live apart from humans, roamed about like wolves, howling mournfully. And so Gnaeus

Pompeius, the praetor, waged war against the Picentes by order of the senate and was defeated, after the Samnites had put Papius Mutilus in command over them, and the Marsi had chosen Agamemnon, a pirate chief, as their leader.

Julius Caesar, beaten in battle by the Samnites, fled with his army cut to pieces. The consul Rutilius chose his kinsman Marius as his legate. Marius kept advising him that delay would serve the war well and that the raw recruits ought to be trained in camp for a while,

but Rutilius, thinking he was doing this out of guile, ignored him and recklessly threw himself and his whole column into an ambush of the Marsi. There the consul himself was killed, many nobles were slain, and eight thousand Roman soldiers were cut down.

The river Tolenus carried the arms and bodies of the slain into the sight of Marius the legate and brought them out as evidence of the disaster. Marius at once gathered his forces, fell upon the victors when they least expected it, and himself killed eight thousand of the Marsi.

Caepio, however, was led into an ambush by the Vestini and Marsi and slaughtered with his army. But Lucius Julius Caesar, after being defeated at Aesernia and fleeing, gathered forces from every side, fought against the Samnites and Lucanians, and killed many thousands of the enemy.

When he had been hailed as imperator by the army and had sent messengers to Rome with news of the victory, the senate, cheered by this hope, laid aside the military cloak, that is, the garment of mourning which it had put on when the Social War broke out, and took back the ancient dignity of the toga. Marius then cut down six thousand of the Marsi and stripped seven thousand of their arms.

Sulla was sent with twenty-four cohorts to Aesernia, where Roman citizens and soldiers were hard pressed by a very close siege; through heavy fighting and great slaughter of the enemy he saved the city and the allies.

Gnaeus Pompeius routed the Picentes in a fierce battle, and on account of this victory the senate took back the broad-striped tunics and the other insignia of rank, having resumed only the toga when Caesar's victory first gave it breathing space. The praetor Porcius Cato conquered the Etruscans, and the legate Plotius the Umbrians, at the cost of much blood and with the greatest difficulty.

In the consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius and Lucius Porcius Cato, Pompeius besieged the city of Asculum for a long time, and he would not have taken it had he not crushed the populace with tremendous slaughter when they burst out onto the plain. In that battle eighteen thousand Marsi were cut down together with their commander Francus, and three thousand were captured.
But four thousand Italian men who had fled from that slaughter happened to climb a mountain ridge in a single packed column, where, overwhelmed and stifled by the snow, they froze to death miserably.

For just as they had stood, stunned with fear of the enemy, some leaning against tree stumps or rocks, others propped on their weapons, all with eyes open and teeth bared, they looked as if they were alive; and to those viewing them from a distance there was no sign of death except their long stillness, which the vigor of human life can by no means endure for long.

On the same day the Picentes joined battle and were defeated. Their leader Vidacilius called his chief men together, and after a lavish banquet and generous drinking, urged them all to follow his example, drank poison and died. All praised his deed, but no one followed him.

In the 661st year after the founding of the City, when the Roman army had gone to besiege Pompeii, Postumius Albinus, a man of consular rank who was then Lucius Sulla's legate, had roused the hatred of all the soldiers against himself by his intolerable arrogance, and he was stoned to death.

Sulla, the consul, declared that the blood of citizens could be atoned for only with the blood of the enemy. Stirred by awareness of this, the army attacked so fiercely that each man felt he must die unless he won. Eighteen thousand Samnites were cut down in that battle; Sulla also pursued and killed Juventius, the Italian general, and a great many of his people.

The consul Porcius Cato, who commanded Marius' troops, after achieving a number of things vigorously, boasted that Gaius Marius had done nothing greater. For this reason, while he was waging war against the Marsi at Lake Fucinus, he was struck down by the son of Gaius Marius in the confusion of battle, as though by an unknown hand.

The legate Gaius Gabinius was killed while storming an enemy camp. The Marrucini and Vestini were laid waste by Sulpicius, Pompeius' legate, who pursued them. Popaedius and Obsidius, the Italian commanders, were crushed and killed by the same Sulpicius in a horrific battle at the river Teanus.

Pompeius entered Asculum and had the prefects, centurions and all the leading men flogged and beheaded; he sold the slaves and all the plunder at auction, and ordered the rest to depart, free indeed but stripped and destitute. And although the senate hoped that some help toward the public payroll would come from this plunder, Pompeius contributed nothing from it to the needy treasury.

For at that same time, when the treasury was completely exhausted and funds were lacking even for the grain allowance, the public properties around the Capitol, which had been handed over for the use of the pontiffs, augurs, decemvirs and flamens, were sold under the pressure of need, and a sum of money was raised that sufficed to relieve the shortage for the time being.

Indeed, at the very time when the wealth scraped from every side out of all the overthrown cities and stripped lands was being heaped into the lap of that very city, Rome herself, driven by shameful poverty, was auctioning off her principal parts.

Let Rome, then, consider those times of hers, when, like an insatiable belly that devours everything and is always hungry, she was more wretched than all the cities she made wretched, leaving them nothing and having nothing herself, and was driven by the goad of hunger at home to keep up the restlessness of war without end.

At this same time King Sothimus entered Greece with large Thracian auxiliaries and ravaged all the territory of Macedonia; at last he was defeated by the praetor Gaius Sentius and forced to return to his kingdom.

In the 662nd year after the founding of the City, before the Social War was over, the first civil war broke out at Rome; and in the same year the Mithridatic War began, which, though less notorious, was no less serious.

Indeed, accounts of the length of the Mithridatic War differ: whether it first began at this point or only then flared up most fiercely, especially since some say it was waged for thirty years and others for forty. But although these events, taking place at the same time, blazed up together in a tangle of evils, I will nevertheless set them out one by one, though briefly.

When Sulla, as consul, was about to set out with an army for Asia against Mithridates, but was still delayed in Campania by the remnants of the Social War, Marius grasped at a seventh consulship and at the command of the Mithridatic War.

When Sulla learned of this, being truly an impatient young man and driven by unrestrained anger, he first encamped before the City with four legions, where he killed Gratidius, Marius' legate, as the first victim, so to speak, of the civil war. Soon afterward he burst into the City with his army and called for torches to set the City on fire. With everyone hiding in fear, he advanced at a quick march along the Sacred Way into the Forum.

Marius had tried in vain to stir up the nobility, inflame the common people, and finally arm the equestrian order against Sulla; at last he called the slaves to arms with the hope of freedom and plunder, and after daring to resist to no purpose, he finally withdrew to the Capitol. But when Sulla's cohorts burst in there, he fled with great slaughter of his followers.

It was then that Sulpicius, Marius' colleague, was struck down after being betrayed by his own slave. The consuls decreed that the slave himself should be freed for having informed on an enemy, but thrown from the Tarpeian Rock for having betrayed his master.

Marius, fleeing, was hemmed in by his relentless pursuers and hid in the marshes of Minturnae. He was dragged out of them, to his misfortune smeared with mud and in disgrace, and was led into Minturnae in a shameful spectacle and thrust into prison; there, by his look alone, he terrified the executioner sent to kill him.

Then he slipped out of his chains and escaped to Africa, and after summoning his son from Utica, where he was being held in custody, he immediately returned to Rome and joined the consul Cinna in a partnership of crimes.

So, in order to destroy the whole commonwealth, they divided their army into four parts. Three legions were given to Marius; Gnaeus Carbo was put in charge of part of the forces; Sertorius received another part—that same Sertorius who was already at this point an instigator of and partner in the civil war, and who, even after it was over, stirred up another war later in Spain, which he dragged out for many years with very great losses to the Romans. The remaining part of the army followed Cinna. Gnaeus

Pompeius, moreover, who had been summoned by the senate with his army to help the commonwealth, and had long held himself in suspense, angling for advantage from the upheaval, was scorned by Marius and Cinna; he went over to Octavius, the other consul, and soon clashed with Sertorius.
Nightfall broke off the ill-fated battle; six hundred soldiers were killed on each side.

The next day, as the bodies, lying all mixed together, were being sorted for burial, a soldier of Pompeius recognized the body of his own brother, whom he himself had killed: in the clash the helmet had kept them from recognizing each other's faces, and rage from looking closely. Yet ignorance does little to lessen the guilt, for though he may seem not to have known it was his brother, there is no doubt that he knew it was a fellow citizen.

And so the victor, more unhappy than the vanquished, when he recognized both his brother's body and his own crime of kin-murder, cursed civil wars, at once ran his sword through his own breast, and, pouring out tears and blood together, threw himself on his brother's corpse.

And what good did it do toward shaming that cruel undertaking that, at the very outset of the civil wars, this terrible story spread far and wide: that brothers had clashed, unaware indeed that they were brothers, but well aware that they were fellow citizens; that the brother who had won by a crime had gone for the spoils of the brother he had slain; and that soon afterward, guilty of such monstrous savagery, he had avenged by his own death, with the same sword and the same hand, the murder of kin that he had committed?

Did so sad an example move the passions of the factions bent on war? Did the horror of such an error drive anyone back from the danger of crime? Did that natural affection and reverence, which we share even with the beasts, make anyone tremble that what one man had committed by killing and by dying could be done to himself, and, overcome by conscience, draw back from such an undertaking?

On the contrary, for nearly forty years after this the civil wars went on so continuously that the greatness of one's glory was thought to be measured by the greatness of one's crime. For after such a lesson, everyone would have shrunk from the danger of killing their own kin in such warfare, had they not actually wanted to kill their own kin.
So Marius forced his way into the colony of Ostia and practiced every kind of lust, greed and cruelty there.

Pompeius died struck by lightning, and his army, seized by a plague, was almost entirely wiped out. For eleven thousand men died in Pompeius' camp, and six thousand on the side of the consul Octavius were struck down.

Marius burst into the cities of Antium and Aricia as an enemy, killed everyone in them except those who had betrayed them, and let his men plunder their property. Afterward Cinna the consul, with his legions, and Marius, with his runaway slaves, entered the City and killed all the noblest members of the senate and a great many men of consular rank.
But how small a part is this of the misery on display? [?] to sum up in a single word the slaughter of good men, which was so vast in number, so long-lasting, so cruel and so varied?
Yet it is fairer that I should have withheld something useful from my case than force so much horror upon my readers' knowledge, whether these things are put before the learned or the unlearned.

For we are speaking of our country, of our fellow citizens and of our ancestors, who, driven by these evils, did such abominable things that even their descendants shudder to hear of them—descendants who surely do not want these things exaggerated too much, either because, if they already know them, a moderate account is knowledge enough, or because, if they do not, they look on them with pity and reverence.

So Marius, after heaping up the heads of murdered citizens—brought into banquets, displayed on the Capitol, gathered on the Rostra for show and decoration—and after seizing a seventh consulship with Cinna, who was consul for the third time, was at last carried off at the very beginning of his consular term by a death that came late.

Cinna followed up the killings of good men with the slaughter of bad ones. For the band of runaway slaves brought in by Marius was insatiable for plunder and gave no share of the spoils to the consuls who had made the plunder possible; so it was lured into the Forum as if to receive pay, surrounded by soldiers, and wiped out while unarmed. On that day eight thousand runaway slaves were cut down in the Forum of the City. And this same Cinna, consul for the fourth time, was killed by his own army.

Meanwhile the remaining senators, who had escaped by flight the power of Cinna, the cruelty of Marius, the madness of Fimbria and the recklessness of Sertorius, crossed over to Greece and with their pleas prevailed on Sulla to bring help to his country, which was in danger, indeed already almost lost.

So as soon as Sulla reached the coast of Campania, he crushed the consul Norbanus in battle. On that occasion Romans killed seven thousand Romans, and six thousand of the same were captured by the same; one hundred twenty-four fell on Sulla's side.

Fabius Hadrianus, who held command as propraetor, aimed at making himself king of Africa with a band of slaves; at Utica he was burned alive with his whole household by the slaves' masters, who piled brushwood around him.

The praetor Damasippus, at the instigation of the consul Marius, summoned Quintus Scaevola, Gaius Carbo, Lucius Domitius and Publius Antistius to the senate house as if for consultation and murdered them most cruelly. The bodies of the slain were dragged by executioners with a hook and thrown into the Tiber.

At the same time Sulla's generals fought a great many battles against the Marian party with most unhappy success. For Quintus Metellus cut down the forces of Carrinas and seized his camp, and Gnaeus Pompey slaughtered Carbo's cavalry heavily.
There was also at that time a very great battle between Sulla and the young Marius at Sacriportus, in which twenty-five thousand of Marius' army were cut down, as Claudius writes.

Pompey also drove Carbo from his camp, and pursuing him as he fled, now by slaughter, now by forcing surrender, deprived him of the greater part of his army. Metellus crushed Norbanus' column, and nine thousand of the Marian party were killed there.
Lucullus, when he was being besieged by Quintius, broke out and in a sudden battle destroyed the besieging army. More than ten thousand are reported to have been cut down there.

Then Sulla engaged Camponius, the leader of the Samnites, and the remaining forces of Carrinas before the very City at the Colline Gate, at the ninth hour of the day, and after a very hard battle at last won. Eighty thousand men are said to have been routed there; twelve thousand surrendered, and the rest of the multitude, turned to flight, were consumed by the insatiable anger of the victorious citizens.

As soon as Sulla entered the City as victor, he killed three thousand men who had surrendered through envoys, unarmed and feeling safe, against all right and against the pledge he had given. A great many others were also killed then—not merely innocent men, I would say, but even men of Sulla's own party—and they are said to have numbered more than nine thousand. Thus killings went on freely throughout the City, with assassins roaming everywhere as anger or plunder tempted each of them.

So when everyone was now openly muttering what each privately feared, Quintus Catulus said to Sulla publicly: "With whom, then, are we to live as victors, if we kill men armed in war and unarmed in peace?"

Then Sulla, at the suggestion of Lucius Fursidius, a senior centurion, was the first to introduce that infamous list of proscription. The first proscription was of eighty men, among whom were four men of consular rank—Carbo, Marius, Norbanus and Scipio—and among them Sertorius, who was then the most to be feared.

Another list was likewise posted with five hundred names. While Lollius was reading it, quite at ease since he had nothing on his conscience, he suddenly came upon his own name, and as he was slipping out of the Forum in alarm with his head covered, he was killed.
But not even in the lists themselves was there any reliability or end to the evils. For some whom they had proscribed they butchered, while others they proscribed after butchering them.

Nor was there a single way or one manner of death, such that in killing citizens at least the law that holds for enemies might be kept—enemies who demand nothing more from the vanquished than their lives. Marcus

Marius, for instance, was dragged out of a goat shed, and Sulla ordered him bound, led across the Tiber to the tomb of the Lutatii, and there, with his eyes gouged out and his limbs cut off or even broken bit by bit, put to death. After him Publius

Laetorius, a senator, and Venuleius, a triumvir, were killed. The head of Marcus Marius was sent to Praeneste; on seeing it, Gaius Marius, seized by utter despair while he was being besieged there by Lucretius, rushed with Telesinus into a mutual death, so as not to fall into the hands of his enemies.

But while he himself was striking at his opponent more violently, he blunted the blow of the man striking him, so that the wound he received was slight. So, having killed Telesinus and being himself only lightly wounded, he offered his neck to his own slave.
Sulla had the praetor Carrinas butchered. Then he set out for Praeneste and ordered all the leading officers of the Marian army—that is, the legates, quaestors, prefects and tribunes—to be killed.
Pompey had Carbo, who was trying to flee from the island of Cossyra to Egypt, brought back to him in Sicily, and killed him along with a number of his associates.
Sulla was made dictator, so that his lust for domination and cruelty might be both armed and veiled by the respect due to an honorable and preeminent title.
Pompey crossed over to Africa and, in a sortie made near Utica, killed eighteen thousand men. In that war Domitius, the Marian general, was killed while fighting in the front ranks.

Pompey also pursued Hiarbas, king of Numidia, and as he fled had him stripped of all his forces by Bogud, son of Bocchus, king of the Moors. When Hiarbas soon returned to Bulla, the town was handed over to Pompey and he killed him.
So, when Publius Servilius and Appius Claudius had been elected consuls, Sulla was at last seen as a private citizen.
With this end two most deadly wars were concluded: the Italian Social War and Sulla's civil war. Drawn out over ten years, they consumed more than one hundred and fifty thousand Romans;

and in this civil war Rome lost as many of her finest men and home-born soldiers as the census had found in her at an earlier time, counting the age-groups separately [?], when she was already looking around to defend herself against Alexander the Great;

besides this, twenty-four men of consular rank, six of praetorian rank, sixty of aedilician rank and nearly two hundred senators, not counting the countless peoples of all Italy who were wiped out everywhere without discrimination. Who in his right mind would deny that Rome won her victory at the same cost to herself as Italy suffered in losing?

For shame! Do our times need any doubtful comparison here too? Indeed they do, most of all, they say: for what can be compared so fittingly as civil wars with civil wars? Or will it perhaps be said that there have been no civil wars in these times as well?

To them we shall answer that these would more justly be called social wars, but that it serves our case if they are called civil. For when everything is shown to be equal in causes, names and passions, then the reverence of the Christian religion can claim all the more credit in them, the less the angry power of the victor has presumed.

For very often wicked tyrants, rashly seizing the state and usurping royal status, have torn the body of the Roman Empire apart, and from it have either brought on wars that were unjust in themselves or provoked just wars against themselves, having been both created and equipped by Britons and Gauls:

these wars, which are as close to foreign wars as they are remote from civil ones—what should they rightly be called but social wars, since the Romans themselves never anywhere called even the wars of Sertorius or Perperna or Crixus or Spartacus civil wars?
In such a defection or rebellion of allies, then, our times would certainly now bear less reproach, even if perhaps a heavy battle or a bloody victory had taken place.

Nevertheless, since in these times everything—that is, the cause, the battle and the victory—carries more of necessity and less of shame, whether it be to stamp out the insolence of tyrants, or to check the defection of allies, or to brand an example of vengeance:
who, pray, can doubt how much more mildly and how much more mercifully the civil wars, as they call them, are now waged when they are stirred up—or rather, how they are suppressed rather than waged?

For who has heard of a single civil war carried on for ten years in these times? Who remembers one hundred and fifty thousand men slaughtered in one war, even enemies by enemies, let alone citizens by citizens?

Who has known that multitude of excellent and illustrious men, which it would take long to list, to be butchered in peacetime? Finally, who has feared, read or felt those infamous lists of men marked for death?

Is it not rather known to all that everyone, settled in one peace and secure in the same safety, vanquished and victors alike, rejoiced together in common gladness, and moreover that in all the many provinces, cities and peoples of the whole Roman Empire scarcely a few have ever been found whom just vengeance condemned, even against the will of the victor?

And, not to heap words on words, I would not be speaking rashly if I said that in recent times, even in war, the band of common soldiers destroyed was no larger than the number of nobles slaughtered then in peace.

So when Sulla was dead, Lepidus, champion of the Marian party, rising against Catulus, the Sullan leader, stirred the revived ashes of the civil wars. Twice at that time battle was joined in the field; very many Romans were slain, when the wretched were already few and still raving with that madness.

The city of Alba, attacked by siege and tormented by extreme hunger, was saved by the surrender of its pitiable remnant; there Scipio, the son of Lepidus, was then captured and killed. Brutus, fleeing into Cisalpine Gaul with Pompey in pursuit, was killed at Regium.
So this civil war, not so much through the clemency [?] of Catulus as through weariness of Sulla's cruelty, died out as quickly as it had flared up, like fire in stubble.

In the six hundred and seventy-third year from the founding of the City, with the crash of wars sounding on every side—one in Spain, another in Pamphylia, a third in Macedonia, a fourth in Dalmatia—the Roman state, still drained of blood and exhausted by internal ruin as if by fevers, was forced to drive back with arms the bravest nations of the West and the North.
Sertorius, a man powerful in guile and daring, who had belonged to the Marian party, fled from Sulla, slipped away from Africa into the Spanish provinces, and roused the most warlike nations to arms.
Against this war, to put it briefly, two generals were sent, Metellus and Domitius; of these Domitius was crushed with his army by Hirtuleius, Sertorius's general.

Manlius, proconsul of Gaul, crossed into Spain with three legions and fifteen hundred horsemen and joined an unequal battle with Hirtuleius; stripped by him of his camp and forces, he fled almost alone into the town of Ilerda.
Metellus, worn out by many battles, wandered through out-of-the-way places and wearied the enemy by delay until he could join Pompey's camp.
Pompey, having gathered an army at Palantia, tried in vain to defend the city of Lauro, which Sertorius was then besieging, and fled in defeat.
Sertorius, having beaten and routed Pompey, took Lauro and ravaged it most bloodily; the rest of the people of Lauro who had survived the slaughter he led off into Lusitania in wretched captivity.
And he boasted that he had defeated Pompey—that is, the famous general of the Romans—whom Rome, full of great confidence, had sent to this war not as proconsul but in place of the consuls.
Galba writes that Pompey then had thirty thousand infantry and a thousand cavalry, and records that Sertorius had sixty thousand infantry and eight thousand cavalry.
Later, however, Hirtuleius engaged Metellus near Italica, a city of Baetica, lost twenty thousand soldiers, and in defeat fled into Lusitania with a few men.

Pompey took Belgida, a famous city of Celtiberia. Then Sertorius engaged Pompey and killed ten thousand of his soldiers; but as Pompey was victorious on the other wing, he himself lost almost as many.

Many other battles were fought between them besides. Memmius, Pompey's quaestor and also his sister's husband, was killed. The brothers of Hirtuleius were slain. Perperna, who had joined Sertorius, was crushed.
