Finally Sertorius himself, at last in the tenth year after the war began, was killed by the treachery of his own men, just as Viriathus had been, and so put an end to the war and gave the Romans a victory without glory; although part of his army afterwards followed Perperna, who was defeated by Pompey and killed together with his whole army.

All the cities were received in surrender willingly and without delay; only two held out, namely Uxama and Calagurris. Of these Pompey overthrew Uxama, while Afranius wore Calagurris down by continuous siege, and after it had been driven by pitiable want to unspeakable food, destroyed it with a final slaughter and fire.
The assassins of Sertorius did not think they should even ask the Romans for a reward, since they remembered that it had earlier been refused to the assassins of Viriathus.

And although they secured Rome's safety at that time for no reward, yet Spain, ever strong in loyalty and in strength, while she has given the state its best and most invincible emperors, has never, from the beginning down to the present day, either sent forth any tyrant born of herself or let any who invaded her from outside go away alive or still in power.
Meanwhile Claudius, having received the Macedonian war by lot, [faced] various nations that live around the Rhodope mountains and were then ravaging Macedonia most cruelly—

for among other things, horrible to tell and to hear, which they did to their captives, whenever they needed a cup they would seize human skulls, still bloody and covered with hair and smeared inside their hollows with badly scooped-out brains, and use them greedily and without horror as if they were real cups; of these nations the bloodiest and most savage were the Scordisci—

these nations, then, as I said, Claudius tried to drive by war from the borders of Macedonia, and he threw himself against a great mass of troubles; whereupon, sick at heart and beset by cares, and seized by illness besides, he died.
His successor Scribonius, avoiding the strength of the peoples attacked in the previous war, turned his arms against Dardania and conquered it.

Publius Servilius, the former consul, attacked Cilicia and Pamphylia most cruelly and, while striving to subdue them, almost destroyed them. He besieged, overwhelmed and captured Lycia and its cities.

Moreover, ranging over Mount Olympus, he overthrew Phaselis and demolished Corycus; and, searching out also the slopes of the Taurus range that face Cilicia, he broke the Isaurians in war and brought them under subjection. He was the first Roman to lead an army through the Taurus, and he opened a route across it. When the three years in which the war was waged had passed, the name of Isauricus
he took for himself. Cosconius, having been allotted Illyricum as proconsul, crushed and subdued Dalmatia, and after two years at last stormed and captured Salonae, a most flourishing city.

In the six hundred and seventy-ninth year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Lucullus and Cassius, seventy-four gladiators escaped from the training school of Gnaeus Lentulus at Capua. Led by the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus and the Thracian Spartacus, they at once seized Mount Vesuvius; breaking out from there, they stormed the camp of the praetor Clodius, who had surrounded them with a siege, put him to flight, and carried off everything as plunder.

From there they made their way around through Consentia and Metapontum and in a short time gathered huge bands. Crixus is said to have had a host of ten thousand, and Spartacus three times that number; for Oenomaus had already been killed in an earlier battle.

So, while they were throwing everything into confusion with slaughter, burning, plunder and rape, at the funeral of a captive matron who had killed herself in grief at her violated chastity, they put on a gladiatorial show of four hundred captives—men, that is, who had been meant to be spectators were now to be the spectacle—acting more like trainers of gladiators than commanders of soldiers.

Then the consuls Gellius and Lentulus were sent against them with an army. Gellius crushed Crixus in battle, though he fought most fiercely; Lentulus was beaten by Spartacus and fled. Later both consuls joined their forces, but in vain: they suffered a heavy defeat and fled. After this the same Spartacus defeated the proconsul Gaius Cassius in battle and killed him.
The City was therefore terrified, trembling with fear hardly less than when Hannibal had raged around its gates, and the senate sent Crassus with the consuls' legions and a fresh levy of soldiers.

As soon as he engaged the runaways in battle, he killed six thousand of them and captured nine hundred. Then, before attacking Spartacus himself, who was encamped at the source of the river Silarus, he defeated his Gallic and German auxiliaries, killing thirty thousand of them together with their leaders.

Last of all he met Spartacus himself in a set battle and struck him down, and with him very great forces of runaways. Sixty thousand of them are reported to have been slain and six thousand captured, and three thousand Roman citizens were recovered.
The rest, who had slipped away from this war and were wandering about, were worn down by several commanders through repeated hunting.

But I repeat it again and again: do our times need any comparison here too? Who, I ask, would not shudder to hear—I do not say of such wars—but even of so many names of wars: foreign, servile, social, civil, wars of runaways?

These do not even follow one another as the waves of a stormy sea follow, however huge their mass; rather, stirred up on every side by different causes, names, forms and evils, they rush together in a heap.

To begin again from the most recent, and to pass over that infamous servile war: the Jugurthine war had not yet finished thundering from the south-west when the Cimbric war was already flashing its lightning from the north-west.

Foul and vast torrents of shed blood were still pouring from those Cimbric clouds when wretched Italy was already breathing out the mists of the Social War, which would soon gather into great clouds of evils.

Even after the endless and repeated storm of the Italian war, no one could by any means travel safely through Italy; so everyone, quite apart from those most dangerous whirlpools of hostile cities, was tottering in a loose and slippery peace;

already Rome was in labour with her own destruction by Marius and Cinna, and from the other side the East and the North threatened another, the Mithridatic war, which, begun in the earlier period, stretches on into the later one.

From the Marian torch the pyre of the Sullan disaster was kindled; from that most deadly pyre the burning brands of Sulla's civil war were scattered through very many parts of the earth, and from one tinder they spread many fires.

For Lepidus and Scipio in Italy, Brutus in Gaul, Domitius, Cinna's son-in-law, in Africa, Carbo in Cossura and Sicily, Perperna in Liguria and afterwards with Sertorius in Spain, and, most savage of all, Sertorius in that same Spain, stirring up these civil wars—or by whatever other name they should be called—made many wars out of one, and great ones out of a great one;

not counting those three vast wars which were then called foreign, namely the Pamphylian, the Macedonian and the Dalmatian, and leaving aside even that great Mithridatic war, by far the longest, most dangerous and most fearsome of them all;

then, while Sertorius's war in Spain was not yet finished—indeed while Sertorius himself was still alive—this war of runaways, or to speak more truly, of gladiators, broke out in all its horror, no longer a show for a few to watch but a thing to be feared everywhere.

Because it is called the war of runaways, let no one think it of little account because of its name: in it the consuls were often defeated one at a time, and once both together, after joining their forces in vain, and very many nobles were slaughtered; and the runaways themselves who were slain numbered more than a hundred thousand.

We recall this so that Italy may console herself for the harassment she suffers from foreigners in the present by remembering how her own sons in the past, sprung from her and fighting within her, tore her apart incomparably more cruelly.

For this reason I shall now bring this fifth book to an end, so that the civil wars mixed everywhere with foreign ones, both those already told and those that follow, may at least be separated by the boundary of a book, since they clung so closely together in the sequence of time and in the evils that followed one upon another.
PAULUS OROSIUS
THE SIXTH BOOK OF THE HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS

All people, whatever their sect, way of life or country, are always lifted by a natural good toward the outlook of wisdom. So even if they do not put the reason of the mind ahead of the pleasure of the body in practice, they still know in their judgment that it ought to be put first. The mind, lit up under the guidance of reason, rises with genuine favour into the company of the virtues, even though vice pulls it down, and it looks out from there on the knowledge of God as if from a citadel. For anyone can despise God

for a time, but no one can be wholly ignorant of him. That is why some people, believing that God was present in many things, invented many gods out of a fear that made no distinctions. But people have now largely turned away from this, both through the working of the authority of truth and through the examination of reason itself.

Their own philosophers, to say nothing of our saints, searched and examined everything with intense mental effort and found one God, the author of all things, to whom alone all things should be referred. So even now the pagans, whom the truth, now made plain, convicts of stubbornness rather than ignorance, admit when we question them that they do not follow many gods but venerate many ministers under one great god.

What remains, then, is a confused disagreement about how the true God is to be understood, arising from many conjectures, since nearly everyone holds a single opinion about there being one God. Human inquiry has been able to reach this far, though with toil. But where reasoning fails, faith comes to help.

For unless we believe, we shall not understand. Whatever you want to know truly about God, hear it from God himself and believe God himself. This same one true God, then, toward whom every sect converges, as we have said, even if from different opinions, changes kingdoms, orders the times, and also punishes sins. He chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and he founded the Roman Empire by raising up a shepherd of the poorest condition.
This empire was advanced for a long time under kings and consuls. After it had won mastery over Asia, Africa and Europe, God by his own ordering gathered all of it

under one emperor, who was at once very brave and very merciful. Under this emperor, whom nearly all nations rightly honoured with a mixture of love and fear, the true God, who had been worshipped with anxious superstition by people who did not know him, opened that great fountain of knowledge of himself. To teach human beings more readily through a human being, he sent his Son, who worked miracles beyond human power and exposed the demons whom some had taken for gods. In this way those who had not believed in him as a man might believe his works as the works of God.

He also did this so that, in deep quiet and a peace that stretched far and wide, the glory of the new name and the news of the salvation now announced might spread quickly and without hindrance. Or it was so that his disciples, travelling among different nations and freely offering the gifts of salvation to all, might have a safe freedom to go about and preach, being Roman citizens among Roman citizens.
I have thought this worth mentioning because this sixth book extends up to Caesar Augustus, of whom these things are said.

Some may think this very clear argument worthless and give the credit instead to their own gods. They say that they first chose these gods wisely and then won them over with special worship, so that through them this vast and splendid empire might be founded for them.

This is what they boast: by the finest kind of rites they earned the gods' special favour, and when those rites were taken away or neglected, "all the gods departed, leaving their shrines and altars, the gods by whom this empire had stood."
On this matter Your Holiness, whom I revere, has already argued a great deal, very forcefully and very truly, yet the subject requires me too to add a few things.

If the Romans earned the favour of the gods by worshipping them and lost it by ceasing to worship them, then whose worship earned it that Romulus himself, the father of Rome, should survive so many evils that pressed on him from his very birth?

Was it his grandfather Amulius, who exposed him to die? His father, who was not even known for certain? His mother Rhea, who was charged with unchastity? His Alban kinsmen, who also persecuted the very seeds of the Roman name from the beginning? Or the whole of Italy, which for four hundred years, as long as it dared, longed for Rome's destruction?
No, they say: the gods themselves, knowing that they would be worshipped, guarded their future worshippers. In that case they have foreknowledge.

If they have foreknowledge, why, out of all the ages of so many years, did they bring this empire to the highest pinnacle of power at exactly the time when he chose to be born among men and to be recognised as a man? After his name appeared, they themselves were despised as nothing, and even those whom they had raised up ran to him along with the whole world.

But, they say, he crept in humbly and entered in secret. If he was hidden and humble, where did such widespread fame come from, such unshaken faith, such evident power? By certain signs and miracles, they say, he captured and held minds made anxious by superstition. But if a man could do these things, the gods ought to have been able to do more.

Or was it because he proclaimed that this power had been handed to him by the Father that people at last came to understand that God who is both known and unknown, whom, as I have said, no one can grasp except through him? And no one can do so unless he has examined himself thoroughly and come to despise himself, has turned to the wisdom of God, and has handed over all the reasoning of inquiry to the faith of belief.

All the same, I will discuss it briefly. These gods, whom they call so great that they seem to have advanced the Roman state when they were favourable and afflicted it when they were hostile, were certainly being worshipped with the greatest devotion and attention at the time when Christ chose to be born and began to be proclaimed to the nations. This is openly agreed.

Were they, then, though they were looking after both themselves and their worshippers, unable either to suppress or to drive back his "superstition," which they saw would cause them to be despised and their worshippers to abandon them? Yet if those worshippers abandoned them unwillingly, they should have been pardoned and not deserted. If they did so willingly, the gods should have used their foreknowledge and never helped them in the first place.

That was done, they say: "We stirred up nations, inflamed kings, made laws, appointed judges, and prepared punishments with tortures and crosses. We searched the whole world in case the Christian name and worship could somehow be scraped off the face of the earth."

That was done only for as long as a cruelty that proved fruitful kept advancing, amid torments and through torments, until the faith took hold of the very summit of royal power, which alone could have stopped it.

And what followed after that? The Christian emperors, they say, ordered the rites to stop and the temples to be closed, and so "all the gods departed, leaving their shrines and altars, the gods by whom this empire had stood."

How great is the light of truth, and how freely it shines, if only weak eyes did not shut themselves so unhappily against it as it offers itself! For many past ages the Christian faith could in no way be suppressed, though nations, kings, laws, slaughters, crosses and deaths raged against it on every side. Indeed, as I have said, it grew amid these things and through them. The worship of idols, on the other hand, already failing somehow of its own accord and ashamed of itself, came to an end at a single, very merciful command, without any threat of punishment. Who can doubt, then,

that through the demonstration of this knowledge the creature has at last come to know about its Creator what it had been seeking until then through various reasonings of the mind, however earnest, while other things clouded its view? And who can doubt that for this reason it at once clung to the love of him whom it had loved even without knowing him?

It is no wonder, then, if in a great household some slaves are found who have grown used to the habits and wantonness of those who lead them astray, and who abuse their master's patience until they hold him in contempt. For this reason God rightly rebukes the ungrateful, the unbelieving and even the defiant with various chastisements.

This must always be acknowledged, but above all for the time when there was as yet no church anywhere in the world that, through the intercession of faithful prayers, could entreat God's clemency and so soften the punishments the world deserved and the just judgement of God. So these things that seem evil to people, whatever they may be, were all without doubt heavier then, as will be proved by the very order in which they began.
The Mithridatic War, or rather, to speak more truly, the disaster of the Mithridatic War, engulfed many provinces at once and dragged on for forty years.

As I have said, it broke out in the 665th year from the founding of the City, the same year in which the first civil war had begun, and it was finally ended in the consulship of Cicero and Antonius, "scarcely by barbarian poison," to use the words of the best of poets. Within this period, however, only thirty years of actual fighting are found.
Why most writers have spoken of forty years is not easy to work out.

Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia, tried to deprive Nicomedes, king of Bithynia and a friend of the Roman people, of his kingdom. The senate warned him that if he attempted it, the Roman people would make war on him. In his anger he at once invaded Cappadocia, drove out its king Ariobarzanes, and laid waste the whole province with fire and sword.

Next he struck Bithynia with the same devastation, and he ruined Paphlagonia in the same way, driving out its kings Pylaemenes and Nicomedes. Then, when he had come to Ephesus, he issued a cruel edict ordering that every Roman citizen found anywhere in Asia should be killed on a single day.

And it was done. No words can in any way express or capture how great a multitude of Roman citizens was slaughtered then, what grief filled very many provinces, and what groaning came alike from those about to be killed and from those who were killing, since each person was forced either to betray innocent guests and friends or to face danger himself and share his guests' punishment.
Archelaus, Mithridates' general, was also sent ahead into Achaea with 120,000 infantry and cavalry, and he took Athens and all Greece, partly by force and partly by surrender.

Sulla, to whom the Mithridatic War had fallen after his consulship, besieged Archelaus for a long time at the Piraeus, the port of the Athenians, which was fortified with a sevenfold wall, and he took the city of Athens itself by storm. Afterwards he fought Archelaus in a pitched battle. It is reported that 110,000 of Archelaus' army were killed and that barely 10,000 survived.

When Mithridates learned of the disaster, he sent Archelaus 70,000 picked soldiers from Asia as reinforcements. In a second battle 50,000 of these were killed, and there Diogenes, the son of Archelaus, was slain.

In a third battle all the forces Archelaus had were wiped out. Twenty thousand of his soldiers were driven into a marsh, and when they begged for Sulla's mercy, they were killed by the victor's insatiable anger. As many more were forced into a river and drowned, and the rest of the wretched men were slaughtered wherever they were.

Meanwhile in Asia, Mithridates had set his mind on killing the leading men of the most famous cities and confiscating their property. He had already killed sixteen hundred in this way when the Ephesians, fearing the same fate, drove out his garrison and shut their gates against him. The people of Smyrna, Sardis, Colophon and Tralles did the same.

Thrown into confusion, Mithridates made peace with Sulla through his general Archelaus. Meanwhile Fimbria, an accomplice in the crimes of Marius' party and the most reckless of all men, killed the consul Flaccus, under whom he had served as legate, at Nicomedia.

Soon afterwards he seized the army, drove Mithridates' son out of Asia to Miletopolis, attacked the king's headquarters, and expelled the king himself from Pergamum. He pursued him as he fled and besieged him at Pitane. He would certainly have captured him if Lucius Lucullus had put the interests of the state ahead of civil quarrels and been willing to hem him in from the sea by bringing up his fleet.

Next Fimbria, angry with the people of Ilium because they appeared to have shut their gates against him out of support for Sulla's party, utterly destroyed the city of Ilium itself, that ancient mother of Rome, by slaughter and fire. But Sulla immediately rebuilt it. When this same Fimbria was besieged at Thyatira by Sulla's army, he was driven to despair and killed himself with his own hand in the temple of Aesculapius.

Fannius and Magius, deserters from Fimbria's army, joined Mithridates. At their urging, Mithridates made a treaty with Sertorius through envoys sent to Spain. Sertorius sent Marcus Marius to him to confirm the treaty. The king kept Marius with him and soon made him a general in place of Archelaus, who had gone over to Sulla with his wife and children.
Marius and Eumachus, generals sent by Mithridates against Lucullus, quickly gathered a large army and engaged Publius Rutilius near Chalcedon. They killed him along with the greater part of his army.

While Mithridates was besieging the people of Cyzicus, Lucullus surrounded him with a trench and made him suffer what he was inflicting on others. He sent a message to the people of Cyzicus to keep up their courage, carried by one of his soldiers who was a skilled swimmer. Held up by two inflated skins, gripping a crossbar between them and paddling with his feet, the man crossed seven miles of water.

Struggling with shortage of supplies, Mithridates ordered part of his forces, fully armed, to go home. Lucullus intercepted it and destroyed it entirely; he is said to have killed more than 15,000 men on that occasion.

At that time too, Fannius, who had joined Mithridates, and Metrophanes, the king's praetor, were defeated by Mamercus and fled with 2,000 horsemen into Moesia. From there they moved on into Maeonia and came upon the Inarimian hills and plains.

There not only can one see scorched mountains and rocks darkened as if by soot, but the plains too lie barren and crumbling over fifty miles, their soil burnt, without any sign of fire or furnace, with ash hanging down into the depths. In three places scorching chasms are also shown, which the Greeks call physae.
After wandering among these for a long time, they at last escaped unforeseen dangers and secretly reached the king's camp. Deiotarus, king of Gallograecia, killed the king's prefects in battle.

Meanwhile at Cyzicus, Mithridates was himself besieged for as long as he was besieging, and he reduced his army to severe hunger and plague. He is said to have lost more than 300,000 men to famine and disease in that one siege. He himself seized a ship and slipped secretly out of the camp with a few companions.

Lucullus, without shedding his soldiers' blood, watched the enemy's disaster and so won a new kind of victory. Soon afterwards he attacked Marius, defeated him and put him to flight. More than 11,000 of Marius' soldiers are reported to have been killed in that battle.

Later Lucullus engaged the same Marius in a naval battle and either sank or captured thirty-two of the king's ships and a number of transports. Many of those whom Sulla had proscribed were killed there.
The next day Marius was dragged out of the cave where he was hiding and paid the penalty he deserved for his hostility.
In the same campaign Lucullus laid waste Apamea, and at the foot of Mount Olympus he captured and stormed Prusa, a heavily fortified city, and plundered it.

Mithridates sailed against Byzantium with a fleet ready for battle, but he was caught in a storm and lost eighty warships. When his own ship was already shattered and sinking, he leapt across into the light galley of the pirate Seleucus, with the pirate's own help. From there he made his way with great difficulty to Sinope and afterwards to Amisus.
In the same year at Rome, Catiline was accused of incest on the charge that he had committed it with the Vestal Virgin Fabia, but he escaped, supported by the influence of Catulus.
Lucullus had laid siege to Sinope in order to storm it. The arch-pirate Seleucus and the eunuch Cleochares, who were in command of the garrison, plundered it, set it on fire and abandoned it.

Lucullus was moved by the internal ruin of his wretched enemies, hurried there, and put out the fire they had set. So that unhappy city saw the roles of enemy and ally reversed: it was destroyed by those who should have defended it and saved by those who should have destroyed it.
Marcus Lucullus, who had succeeded Curio in Macedonia, attacked the whole nation of the Bessi and received their surrender.

At the same time Metellus, praetor of Sicily, found the island ruined by that utterly disgraceful praetorship of Gaius Verres, and above all being torn apart by the wicked plundering and murders of the arch-pirate Pyrganio, who had routed the Roman fleet and seized the harbour of Syracuse. Metellus soon crushed him in battles by sea and land and forced him to leave Sicily.

Lucullus, moreover, crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris and engaged Mithridates and Tigranes near the city of Tigranocerta. With a very small force of his own he killed a great number of the enemy; 30,000 men are reported to have been slain in that battle.

Tigranes barely escaped with 150 horsemen, having thrown away his diadem and tiara so as not to be recognised. Then envoys from almost the whole East came to Lucullus as suppliants. With winter approaching, he withdrew through Armenia into Mesopotamia, where he stormed and captured Nisibis, a famous city in those parts at that time.

In those same days pirates scattered over every sea. No longer content with seizing ships' cargoes, they were also ravaging islands and provinces. Since many people were joining them, drawn by the impunity of their crimes and their greed for plunder, they grew to an enormous number. They had long been causing great devastation by land and sea, but Gnaeus Pompey crushed them with remarkable speed.
At the same time Metellus devastated the island of Crete over two years, subdued it in a long war, brought it under Roman control, and replaced the laws of Minos with Roman laws.

Afterwards Pompey, Lucullus' successor, shut the king's camp in under siege in Lesser Armenia near Mount Dastracus. The king broke out with all his forces during the night, and he also resolved to drive back his pursuer in battle. Pompey set out to pursue the fleeing army.

So the battle was fought at night. The moon had then risen behind the Romans. The king's men took the length of the shadows to mean that the enemy was close, and they hurled all their weapons in vain. The Romans then attacked them as if they were unarmed and defeated them without effort.
Forty thousand of the king's army were killed or captured, while a thousand Romans were wounded and barely forty killed.

In the turmoil of the battle the king slipped away in flight and escaped, helped also by the dimness of the night. Abandoned by all his friends, philosophers, writers of history and poetry, and physicians, he went alone along remote paths, leading his horse by hand and trembling at every noise in the night. He turned aside to a certain fortress and from there went on into Armenia.

Pompey, meaning to pursue the king, founded the city of Nicopolis between two rivers that rise from one mountain in different caves, the Euphrates and the Araxes. He settled it with old men, camp followers and the sick who were willing to stay.

He pardoned Tigranes when he begged for mercy. He defeated the army of Horodes, king of the Albanians, and his prefects in three battles. Afterwards he gladly accepted letters and gifts from Horodes to restore peace with the Albanians. He routed Artaces, king of Iberia, in battle and received the surrender of all Iberia.
Then, after settling affairs in Armenia, Colchis, Cappadocia and Syria, he advanced from Pontus into Parthia and on the fiftieth day reached Ecbatana, the capital of the Parthian kingdom.
In the Bosporus, while Mithridates was celebrating the rites of Ceres, an earthquake suddenly broke out so violent that it is said to have brought great destruction on cities and countryside alike.
At the same time Castor, Mithridates' governor in command of Phanagoria, killed the king's friends, seized the citadel, and sent four of Mithridates' sons over to the Roman garrisons.

Mithridates, inflamed with anger, burst out into crimes. He then killed a number of his friends and his son Exipodras, having already slaughtered Machares in an earlier act of murder against his own child.
Pharnaces, another of his sons, frightened by what had happened to his brothers, won over the army sent to pursue him and soon led it against his father.

Mithridates long pleaded in vain with his son from the top of a very high wall, and when he saw that he could not be moved, he is said to have cried out as he prepared to die: "Since Pharnaces orders me to die, I pray to you, gods of my fathers, if you exist, that someday he too may hear these words from his own children." At once he went down to his wives, concubines and daughters and gave poison to them all.

He drank it last of all himself. But because of the antidotes with which he had often fortified his vital organs against harmful drugs, the poison could not finish him off. He walked about in vain, hoping that by some means the activity of his body might at last drive the poison he had taken through his veins. Finally he called over a Gallic soldier who was running about now that the wall had been breached, and offered him his throat.

Such was the end of Mithridates' life. He was, so they say, the most superstitious of all men, seventy-two years old, and always kept philosophers and experts in every art around him; yet he left us the strongest proof of what he really believed.

"Gods of my fathers, if you exist," he said. Thus, through long worship and long inquiry, he had come to perceive that those who were thought to be gods were not certain gods. A king of great experience and burdened with years, he did not understand the true God, to whose knowledge one comes only through hearing, by faith. But by the light of reason itself he had seen clearly that these gods were false, giving one thing to custom and another to his own mind.

"If you are gods," he said; that is to say: "Sensing that above mankind there is a power mightier than man himself, and moved by the need to pray, I commend my diligence and excuse my ignorance; I call upon Him who is, while I address those who are not."

We must therefore consider with grief and fear what punishment or what judgment will be deserved by those who, against the prohibition of a truth now revealed and made public, follow and worship gods whom even those men could already doubt in those days, though they could as yet know nothing besides them.

Nevertheless, I briefly ask: what did the times look like then throughout the whole East, when for forty years wretched nations were ground down by the alternating devastations of such great commanders; when every city, caught in the middle of such clashes, was inevitably in danger, bound to inflame one side by the very means with which it had pacified the other, and soon to find punishment in what had served for a time as its remedy;

when anxious embassies from various provinces were shuttled back and forth between the successive Roman generals and Mithridates, the more savage of whom they had experience, now to one, now to the other, as the fortune of war raised each up, with uncertain offers of submission, thereby increasing the very dangers they were trying to cure?
For I will set out in a few words what Pompey, and Pompey at that, the most moderate of the Romans, did straight afterward throughout many parts of the East once the Mithridatic War was over.

In the 689th year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Marcus Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius, Pompey, on receiving the news that Mithridates had been killed, attacked Coele-Syria and Phoenicia in war. He first subdued the Ituraeans and the Arabs and took their city, which they call Petra.

From there he sent Gabinius with an army against the Jews, who were ruled by Aristobulus, the first of their priests to become king, after he had driven out his brother Hyrcanus, and against their city Jerusalem. He himself followed immediately; he was received into the city by the elders but was driven back from the wall of the Temple by the common people, and he set about storming it.

The Temple was fortified not only by the nature of the site but also by a huge wall and a very great ditch. He forced legion after legion to relieve one another day and night without rest, and barely took it in the third month. Thirteen thousand Jews are said to have been slaughtered there; the rest of the multitude surrendered.

Pompey ordered the city walls to be torn down and leveled to the ground. After beheading a number of the leading Jews, he restored Hyrcanus to the priesthood and led Aristobulus captive to Rome. Pompey himself declared before a public assembly that he had waged this war in the East against twenty-two kings.

Meanwhile, in those same days, the conspiracy of Catiline against his country was hatched and betrayed in the City, and was stamped out in a civil war in Etruria; at Rome the accomplices in the conspiracy were put to death.
But since this history, through Cicero's prosecution and Sallust's account, is well enough known to everyone, it is enough for us now to have touched on it briefly.

An uprising among the Paeligni, too, started by the Marcelli, father and son, was betrayed by Lucius Vettius; once Catiline's conspiracy was exposed, it was crushed as though its root had been cut away. Punishment was exacted on both, by Bibulus among the Paeligni and by Cicero among the Bruttii.

In the 693rd year from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Gaius Caesar and Lucius Bibulus, three provinces with seven legions were given to Caesar for five years by the Vatinian law: Transalpine Gaul, Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum. The senate later added Long-haired Gaul.
This history Suetonius Tranquillus has set out in full; we have picked out from it the small portions that suit our purpose.

A certain Orgetorix, a chief of the Helvetii, had stirred the spirits of that people, the bravest of all the Gauls, to take up arms in the hope of invading the whole of Gaul. Their bravery came chiefly from the fact that they were almost constantly at war with the Germans, from whom they are separated only by the river Rhine.

The other nobles arrested him and drove him to his death, but they could not restrain the common people, once roused by the hope of plunder. These formed a conspiracy, fixed a day, burned their villages and houses so that they would have no longing to return, and set out.

Caesar met them at the river Rhône, defeated them twice in a great and difficult war, and forced them in defeat to surrender. When they first set out, the whole multitude of the Helvetii, Tulingi, Latobrigi, Rauraci and Boii, of both sexes, came to about one hundred and fifty-seven thousand people. Of these forty-seven thousand fell in the war; the rest were sent back to their own lands.

Afterward Caesar defeated King Ariovistus in the territory of the Sequani. Ariovistus had stirred up and brought with him incredible forces of Germans, with which he boasted he had recently subdued all the peoples of Gaul. Caesar's army, terrified by the numbers and courage of the Germans, had long shrunk from battle.

Ariovistus at once seized a small boat, crossed the Rhine and fled into Germany; his two wives and as many daughters were captured. In Ariovistus' army were the Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Sedusii and Suebi.

The fighting was especially heavy because of the German phalanx. They had packed themselves into a single column with their shields interlocked over their heads, so that, protected on every side, they could break through the Roman line.

But some of the Roman soldiers, outstanding for their agility and daring, leapt onto the shield-roof covering them, tore away the shields one by one as if they were scales, and from above stabbed down into the bare shoulders of the trapped and exposed men. The enemy, terrified by this new danger of death, broke up their fearsome formation.

Then they were put to flight and cut down without mercy over fifty miles, and no one could estimate the number of the Germans, either how many had taken part in the battle or how many had been killed.
After this the nation of the Belgae, who make up a third of Gaul, flared up against Caesar.

Their forces, people by people, were as follows. The Bellovaci, who were thought to surpass the rest in numbers and courage, had sixty thousand picked men under arms; the Suessiones, from twelve towns, fifty thousand;

the Nervii, whose untamed ferocity was so widely spoken of that up to that time they had never let merchants come to them bringing wine and other wares, whose pleasures might bring on a softening of their courage, likewise had fifty thousand;

the Atrebates and Ambiani ten thousand; the Morini twenty-five thousand; the Menapii nine thousand; the Caleti ten thousand; the Velocasses and Viromandui likewise ten thousand; the Aduatuci eighteen thousand; and the Condrusi, Eburones, Caeroesi and Paemani, who are called by the single name of Germans, forty thousand.
Thus there are said to have been two hundred and seventy-two thousand picked men under arms.

When these suddenly burst out of a forest, Caesar's army was thrown into confusion and put to flight with heavy losses. At last, urged on by their general, they made a stand, attacked the victors, and destroyed them almost to the last man.
So Caesar, having achieved great things in Gaul, decided to set out for Italy, and sent Galba with the twelfth legion against the Veragri and Seduni.

Galba had settled for the winter in a village of the Veragri named Octodurus and had given the inhabitants half of the town, which was divided by a torrent. One day he saw that they had left during the night and occupied the nearest hill.

For they despised the small numbers of what was barely half a legion, thought it a prize that had fallen into their hands and would cost them no trouble, and had summoned their neighbors to join them in this partnership of slaughter and plunder.

So while Galba, hemmed in by such immediate dangers, was anxious and, amid futile consultations, unsure of any firm plan, the Gauls suddenly poured down the mountain, surrounded the unfinished camp, and showered stones and javelins on the few defenders along the rampart.

When the camp was already being broken into, on the advice of Pacuvius, the senior centurion, and Volusenus, a tribune, all the Romans burst out of the gates, attacked the unsuspecting enemy suddenly, first threw them into confusion, and then put them to flight and routed them with pitiful slaughter. More than thirty thousand barbarians are reported to have been killed then.
So when Caesar thought that all the peoples of Gaul were now pacified, he was drawn back into a new and very great war.

For while the young Publius Crassus was wintering with the seventh legion among the Andes, out by the Ocean, the Veneti and their neighbors suddenly conspired to take up arms. They put the Roman envoys in chains and informed the Romans that they would give them back only if they received their own hostages in return.
For this war they enlisted as allies the Osismi, Lexovii, Namnetes, Ambiliati, Morini, Diablintes and Menapii; they also sent for reinforcements from Britain.

Caesar learned from Crassus of the revolt of the peoples who had surrendered. Although he understood how difficult it would be to undertake the war, he nevertheless judged that so serious a matter must not be neglected, lest the others be given a precedent and

license to dare the same. So, after trying in vain to pursue the enemy in a land battle, since the enemy were protected by the estuaries that flowed in from the Ocean and by inaccessible hiding places in safe inlets of the coast, he ordered warships to be built on the river Loire.

These were brought down it into the Ocean, and as soon as the enemy saw them, two hundred and twenty of their ships, ready and thoroughly equipped with every kind of weapon, immediately came out of harbor and took up position facing them.

Brutus saw that the naval contest was very unequal, since the barbarians' ships were built of solid oak and hardened with immensely strong hulls, so that, like rocks, they blunted the blows of the beaked ships driven against them.

The first help in this was that he had prepared very sharp sickles, not fixed firmly onto poles but tied to them with ropes. With these, when needed, they could catch hold of the rigging at a distance, then withdraw the poles and cut the rigging by pulling the sickle back with the rope.

Once these were quickly made ready, he ordered the tackle of the enemy's yardarms to be cut through. As the yards came crashing down, he at once rendered a number of ships immobile, as good as captured.

Others, terrified by this danger, hoisted their sails and tried to flee wherever the wind carried them, but when the wind soon dropped they were left stranded and became a laughingstock to the Romans.
So all the ships were burned and the Gauls who had fought were killed, and all the rest surrendered.

But Caesar, chiefly because of the wrong done to the envoys, and to brand a people ready to change at every turn with the mark of a terrible example, had all the leading men tortured to death and sold the rest into slavery.

In those same days Titurius Sabinus made a sally and with incredible slaughter destroyed the Aulerci Eburovices and the Lexovii, who had killed their own leading men because they refused to be instigators of renewing the war.

Publius Crassus, on reaching Aquitania, was met with war. For the Sontiates attacked the Romans with a large cavalry force and very strong infantry, and for a long time threw them into serious difficulty.
Afterward they were defeated, driven into the town of the Sontiates and besieged. When they saw that the town was being taken, they handed over their arms and were accepted in surrender.

The Aquitanians, alarmed by this defeat, gathered an army from every side. They also sent for reinforcements from Hither Spain, and put in command of the war chiefly men who had served under Sertorius.

While they were all preparing to besiege Crassus, Crassus overwhelmed them and destroyed them in their own camp. Of the Aquitanians and the Cantabrians, fifty thousand of whom had then come as reinforcements, thirty-eight thousand are said to have been killed.

Caesar attacked the Germans, who had crossed the Rhine with immense forces and were also preparing to subject the whole of Gaul to themselves, and slaughtered them almost to the last man. Their number is said to have been about four hundred and forty thousand.

Then Caesar built a bridge and crossed into Germany. He freed the Sugambri and the Ubii from siege, and by his arrival struck terror into the Suebi, a very large and very fierce nation, said by many to comprise a hundred cantons and peoples, and into all of Germany. Soon he cut down the bridge and withdrew into Gaul.

From there he came to the Morini, from whose land the crossing to Britain is nearest and shortest. Having prepared about eighty transports and fast ships, he crossed over into Britain. There he was first worn down by a bitter battle, then caught by a storm, and lost the greater part of his fleet and no small number of soldiers, and almost all his cavalry.
Returning to Gaul, he sent the legions into winter quarters and ordered six hundred ships to be built, suited to both purposes.

With these he crossed again into Britain at the beginning of spring. While he himself was marching against the enemy with the army, the ships riding at anchor were caught by a storm and either dashed against one another or driven onto the sands and broken up. Forty of them were lost; the rest were repaired with great difficulty.

Caesar's cavalry was defeated by the Britons in the first engagement, and there the tribune Labienus was killed. In a second battle, at great risk to his own men, he defeated the Britons and put them to flight.

From there he set out for the river Thames, which they say can be forded at only one place. On its far bank an immense host of the enemy had taken up position under the command of Cassivellaunus, and had lined the riverbank and almost the whole ford beneath the water with very sharp stakes.

When the Romans discovered and avoided these, the barbarians, unable to withstand the charge of the legions, hid themselves in the forests, from which they often inflicted heavy losses on the Romans with frequent sallies.
Meanwhile the very strong city of the Trinovantes, with its leader Mandubracius, gave forty hostages and surrendered to Caesar.

Following this example, several other towns entered into treaty with the Romans, and with them showing the way, Caesar at last, after a hard battle, took the stronghold of Cassivellaunus, which lay between two marshes, was further protected by a screen of forests, and was very well stocked with everything.

Then Caesar returned from Britain to Gaul, and after he had sent the legions into winter quarters he was suddenly surrounded and beset on every side by sudden outbreaks of war. For Ambiorix, conspiring with the Eburones and the Aduatuci and encouraged by the counsel of the Treveri, ambushed the legates Cotta and Sabinus among the Eburones and killed them together with their entire legion.

Elated by this victory, Ambiorix hastily called the Aduatuci, the Nervii and many others to arms and marched against the legate Cicero, who was likewise then in command of a legion in winter quarters.

The size of the enemy's host can be gauged from this: when, in besieging the camp, they were taught by Roman prisoners that they must surround it with a rampart, and they had no farming tools, they cut the earth with their swords and carried it away in their cloaks, and in barely three hours completed a rampart ten feet high and a ditch fifteen feet wide running fifteen miles around. Besides this they built a hundred and twenty towers of remarkable height.

When wave after wave of the enemy had been fighting for seven days and nights, and a very strong wind had suddenly risen, they slung red-hot clay pellets and hurled into the camp missiles set alight in their fires, which soon caught and glowed red.

Upon this the wind, sweeping swiftly over the thatched roofs, fanned the scattered flames into a blaze. But even so the Romans, though beset on every side, did not give way to wounds, toil, sleeplessness, hunger or fire.
At last word reached Caesar that one legion had been destroyed and a second was now almost finished.

As Caesar approached with two legions, the enemy abandoned the siege, gathered their forces and all rushed against him. Caesar deliberately shut himself up in a very small camp and sent his cavalry ahead with orders to feign flight, so as to lure the enemy, contemptuous of him, into crossing the valley that lay between them, which seemed dangerous to him.

As they approached, he gave orders that the gates should even be blocked up. Seeing this, the Gauls, as if they had already won, turned to building a rampart around the camp from outside. Suddenly Caesar poured his army, ready for action, out of every gate, put the Gauls to flight and destroyed them with enormous slaughter.
For there are said to have been sixty thousand of them at the time, of whom only a few escaped through the trackless marshes.

Indutiomarus, chief of the Treveri, who had great forces under arms, on learning that all Gaul was united, resolved to destroy Labienus' camp and the legion he commanded, which he thought would be easy to do, and then to join with the Eburones and Nervii and go on to crush Caesar.

Labienus feigned fear by every means he could, and so, when Indutiomarus grew careless and was riding about in front of the rampart with his forces jeering, Labienus made a sudden sally and struck him down.
By this victory of Labienus the remaining efforts of the Gauls were checked, and Caesar was somewhat less troubled for the rest of the winter.

But he understood that greater tasks of war still lay ahead of him, above all because, having lost the greater part of his army and with others badly wounded, he did not seem strong enough even to withstand the onslaught of the Gauls, let alone to crush it. So he asked the proconsul Gnaeus Pompey to enroll legions and send them to his aid, and before the winter was over three legions arrived at his camp.

So Caesar prepared, before the enemy's forces could unite, to attack them at the start of spring while they were still alarmed, and to crush them while they were scattered in their own territories. First, therefore, he plundered the lands of the Nervii and gave the booty, which was very plentiful, to his army.

Next he invaded the Menapii with three columns. They believed themselves very well protected by vast marshes and almost impassable forests. After a massive slaughter carried out far and wide, he accepted the survivors' surrender as they begged for mercy.
In a following battle Labienus, having cunningly provoked them into fighting before they could join the approaching Germans, killed all the forces of the Treveri, and at once took their city itself.
Caesar wished to avenge the death of the legates Sabinus and Cotta. Ambiorix and the Eburones, the authors of the legion's destruction,

had, he discovered, fled back into the Ardennes Forest, the largest forest in all Gaul, which stretches from the banks of the Rhine and the territory of the Treveri all the way to the Nervii and extends in length more

than fifty miles. Reckoning that it would be extremely dangerous for his men if, as strangers to the area, they were split up among the dense and far-reaching woods while searching for an enemy who knew the ground intimately, he sent messengers inviting all Gaul to come, each as he pleased, to search out and seize the plunder hidden in the Ardennes Forest.
In this way, with Gauls dying on both sides, he avenged the very great wrongs done to the Romans without risk to a single Roman.
So, having won by this safest kind of victory, he returned to Italy free from care.

So when Caesar had gone back to Italy, Gaul conspired to take up arms again, and many peoples joined together at once. Their leader was Vercingetorix, on whose advice all the Gauls at once set fire to their own towns of their own accord. The first town burned by its own people was that of the Bituriges.
From there they launched an attack on Caesar, who had hurried back in secret, by forced marches through the province of Narbonensis, to rejoin his army.

At that time Caesar had laid siege to a town called Cenabum. It held out against assault for a long time, but at last, after the Romans had suffered many losses, it was taken and destroyed on a rainy day, when the enemy's engines and their cords had gone slack, by bringing up siege towers against it.
Forty thousand people are said to have been there, of whom barely eighty escaped by flight and reached the nearest camp of the Gauls.
Besides this, the Arverni and their other neighbors, who had also drawn the Aedui to their side, fought many battles against Caesar.

When, worn out by the fighting, they had withdrawn into a certain fortress, the soldiers, greedy for plunder, set their minds on storming the town, though Caesar protested in vain that the ground was unfavorable. And so Caesar was overwhelmed there by the enemy as they burst out on him from above; he lost a large part of his army and fled in defeat.

While this was happening at Alesia, Vercingetorix, whom all had with one accord chosen as their king, urged that everyone in all Gaul who could bear arms should come and serve in this war. For this, he said, was the one war that would bring either lasting freedom, or everlasting slavery, or death for all.
And so, besides the countless host he had already gathered, about eight thousand cavalry and two hundred and fifty thousand infantry were assembled.

Then the Romans and the Gauls occupied two hills facing each other. Fighting from there with many sorties and with varying success, at last the Romans won [?], chiefly through the valor of the German cavalry, long their friends, whom they had now summoned to their aid.

The next day Vercingetorix gathered all who had escaped by flight and told them that he had in good faith been the author of the defense of their freedom and of the breaking of the treaty, and that now he would be ready in spirit, whether they all offered themselves to the Romans to die, or surrendered him alone on behalf of all.

So the Gauls, as though they were adopting the king's own advice, embraced the wish that shame had for some time made them conceal: at once they begged for pardon and handed him over alone, as the author of a great crime.

The Bellovaci were reckoned, in their own opinion, braver than all the nations of the Gauls. Under their leader Correus they renewed the war, and they joined to themselves in alliance for the war they had undertaken the Ambiani, the Aulerci, the Caleti, the Velocasses and the Atrebates. They seized a place enclosed and hemmed in on every side by marshes, and when battle was joined they slaughtered a large force of the Remi who were serving as auxiliaries to the Romans.

Then they occupied a place they had chosen as suitable for an ambush. When the Romans learned of this, they came to the site of the ambush drawn up in battle order. Battle was joined, and the Romans shut the fleeing Gauls in by the very defenses of the place in which they had themselves been enclosed, and cut them all down to the last man.
There Correus, refusing either to flee or to surrender, killed the Romans who pressed on him to take him alive, and so forced them to kill him.

So when Caesar judged that all Gaul was at peace and would not dare to attempt any further uprisings, he sent the legions into winter quarters. He himself, however, laid waste with a horrifying slaughter of people the territory of Ambiorix, who had stirred up so many wars.
But the legate Gaius Caninius found war among the Pictones. There a great multitude of the enemy surrounded his legion while it was hampered on the march and brought it into the gravest danger.

Then the legate Fabius, on receiving a letter from Caninius, set out for the Pictones. There, informed by prisoners about the lie of the land, he fell upon the enemy unawares, inflicted great slaughter and carried off a vast amount of plunder.

Then, when he had signaled his arrival to Caninius, Caninius suddenly burst out with his whole camp and threw himself on the enemy. So, with Fabius pressing from one side and Caninius from the other, countless forces of the Gauls were slaughtered in a very great and long battle.

From there Fabius set out against the Carnutes, for he knew that Dumnacus, a leader of long standing and the instigator of the whole rebellion, had escaped from this battle, and that if he joined forces with the Armorican peoples he would again stir up great disturbances in Gaul. But with remarkable courage and speed Fabius subdued those peoples while they were still alarmed by the very suddenness of events. Meanwhile,
when Drappes, and Lucterius with him, saw that Caninius and his legions were in their territory, they gathered forces from every side and occupied the town of Uxellodunum.

This town hung on the loftiest summit of a mountain. On two sides it was girded by a sizable river along steep cliffs; halfway down the slope it was secured by a very abundant spring, and inside it was protected by a great store of grain, so that it could look down from afar on the futile maneuvers of its enemies.

Caninius, doing the only thing that Roman foresight could do, lured both leaders out onto the plain with the greater part of their forces and defeated them in a very great battle. For one of the leaders was killed and the other fled with very few men; none returned to the town. But to besiege the town itself Caesar was needed.

So Caesar, informed by messengers, hurried there, and after surveying everything he saw that if he tried to take the town by force, his army would be destroyed as a game and a spectacle for the enemy; the only resource left was if the enemy could somehow be cut off from water.

But even this no one but Caesar could have done, since the spring from which they drew their drinking water poured out halfway down the side of the sloping mountain. Caesar ordered mantlets to be moved up as close as possible to the spring and a tower to be built. At once a great sally was made from the town. The townspeople fought without danger to themselves, and though the Romans resisted stubbornly and kept moving up in close succession, many of them were nevertheless killed.

So a siege mound was built and a tower sixty feet high, whose top could be level with the site of the spring, so that missiles could be thrown at it on equal terms and there would be no need to fear rolling rocks hurled down from above.

But when the townspeople saw not only their cattle but also the weaker among their people dying of thirst, they filled barrels with pitch, tallow and wooden shingles, set them on fire and rolled them down the slope, and then they themselves poured out of the whole town after them.

As the engines burned, Caesar saw that the battle was going hard and dangerously for his men, so he ordered cohorts to go quickly and secretly around the town and suddenly to raise a great shout on every side. When this was done, the townspeople were thrown into panic, and in their eagerness to run back and defend the town, they abandoned their attack on the tower and their demolition of the mound.

Meanwhile those who were digging tunnels in safety under cover of the mound to cut off the veins of the spring found the hidden channels of the water and, by dividing them into many branches, made them dwindle and dry up of themselves. With the spring dried up, the townspeople were seized by utter despair and surrendered.
Caesar, however, cut off the hands of all who had borne arms and left them their lives, so that the punishment of the wicked might bear stronger witness even to future generations.

For a visible example of punishment is very effective in restraining boldness, since the very sight of a wretched man still living both reminds those who know of the deed and compels those who do not know to ask about it.

With the Gauls drained and subdued, Caesar returned to Italy with his legions free from care, fearing no uprisings of the Gauls behind him, for he knew for certain that he had left almost no one who would either dare to rise or be worth fearing if they did.

I should like now to set before our eyes Gaul, bloodless and exhausted: how she fares after those burning fevers and the inner heat that scorched the best of her vital organs, how wasted and how pale she is, how dejected and limp she lies, how she dreads even the movements of necessary activity, lest they bring back the same onslaught of misfortunes.
For the Roman army fell upon her in a sudden attack, like a stronger plague upon a very strong body, a plague that burns all the more fiercely the less patiently it is endured.

The wretched land was thirsty, when at the point of the sword she was forced to pledge herself to everlasting slavery and her hostages were torn away besides. She thirsted, as I have said, for that familiar sweetness of freedom, the sweetest of all things to everyone, like cool water; and the more she understood it was being taken from her, the more eagerly she longed for it.

Hence those frequent bold attempts against what was forbidden: to defend freedom, they seized an ill-timed freedom, and the license to grasp insatiably at what had been snatched away seemed to quench the destruction that had wrongly been brought on, but instead increased it.

Hence the Roman was a craftier plotter before battle, hence a fiercer enemy in battle, hence a harsher victor after battle; hence everything grew more cruel in order to tame their impatience of the yoke; hence no trust was placed even in remedies any longer.

And so, if I could ask this nation of which we are speaking what she thought of those times when she was suffering these very things, she would answer, I believe, saying: 'That fever left me so bloodless and cold at the time that even this present one, which has touched almost everyone, could not heat or stir me; and the Romans bent me so low that I will not rise even against the Goths.'

But not even Rome herself escaped the disasters she inflicted. Over long exercise, throughout all the corners of the world, the power of her generals and the strength of her legions grew, so that, clashing with one another, they would win their victories to the loss of the very city by whose peril they would be conquered. For civil wars accompanied Caesar on his victorious return from Gaul, as did other very grievous evils, and they were preceded by the killing of Crassus among the Parthians and the slaughter of his army..... [?]

In the 697th year from the founding of the City, Crassus, the colleague of Pompey in the consulship, received by lot the province of the Parthians. A man of insatiable greed, he heard of the wealth of the temple in Jerusalem, which Pompey had left untouched, and turned aside into Palestine; he came to Jerusalem, broke into the temple and plundered its riches.

From there, as he made his way through Mesopotamia toward Parthia, he demanded auxiliary troops from the allied cities wherever he passed and exacted payments. As soon as he crossed the Euphrates, he was met at once by Vagises, an envoy sent to him by Orodes, king of the Parthians, who sharply rebuked him for having crossed the Euphrates, led on by greed, contrary to the treaty of Lucullus and Pompey. For this reason, he said, it would not be long before he was loaded with Seric iron instead of Parthian gold.

And so, when they had come near Carrhae, the Parthians suddenly fell upon the Romans with their commanders Surena and Silaces and overwhelmed them with arrows. A great many senators fell there, as well as several men of consular and praetorian rank. Crassus too, the son of Crassus, a most excellent young man, was killed in the battle line. Besides this, four cohorts with the legate Vargunteius were caught in the middle of the plains and killed.

Surena quickly gathered his cavalry and set out in pursuit of Crassus; he surrounded him, and when Crassus vainly sought a parley, he killed him, although he would have preferred to carry him off alive. A few, saved by the cover of night, took refuge in Carrhae.

When the Roman defeat became known, many provinces of the East would have abandoned their alliance with and loyalty to the Roman people, had not Cassius, gathering a few soldiers from the rout, held down Syria, which was swelling with unrest, by his outstanding courage and moderation. He also defeated in battle and killed Antiochus with his huge forces, and he drove out by war the Parthians sent into Syria by Orodes, who had already entered Antioch, and killed their leader Osaces.

So the condition of Rome is always driven by alternating change, like the pattern of the Ocean, which differs every day: now for seven days it rises with successive increases, now for the same number of days following it is drawn back by a natural loss and inner ebbing.

To begin with the most recent events: when the Roman army perished at the river Rhône as the Cimbri and Tigurini prevailed, Rome felt the tightest straits; but as soon as the disaster was paid back upon the Cimbri, she was carried away by great successes and forgot her earlier losses.

Then the Italian War and the havoc of Sulla chastised this boasting over her very recent prosperity. Again, after this domestic and internal ruin, by which she had been almost disemboweled and eaten away to the marrow, within almost equal spans of time she was not only restored but even extended, when Lucullus subdued Asia, Pompey Spain and Caesar Gaul, and the Roman Empire was spread almost to the furthest bounds of the earth.

Now this most ample expansion is followed by a most devastating collapse. For among the Parthians a Roman consul is killed and his army destroyed; that most dreadful civil war of Pompey and Caesar is begun; and in the midst of all this Rome itself is seized by a sudden fire and burned.

For in the 700th year from the founding of the City a fire, arising from no one knows where, swept through the greater part of the City, and they say the City had never before been seized and ravaged by so great a fire. Indeed it is recorded that fourteen districts were destroyed, together with the Vicus Iugarius. Next the civil war broke out, which had long been in preparation through great quarrels and schemes.

Returning victorious from Gaul, Caesar demanded that a second consulship be voted to him in his absence. This was opposed by the consul Marcellus with Pompey's support. The senate then decreed that Caesar should not come into the City unless he had first disbanded his army, and on the authority of the consul Marcellus, Pompey was sent with full command to the legions stationed at Luceria.

Caesar withdrew to Ravenna. Mark Antony and Publius Cassius, tribunes of the people, interposed their veto on Caesar's behalf; but the consul Lentulus forbade them, and they were barred from the senate house and the forum. They set out to join Caesar, accompanied by Curio and Caelius.

Caesar crossed the river Rubicon, and as soon as he reached Ariminum he explained what needed to be done to the five cohorts that were all he then had, the force with which, as Livy says, he attacked the whole world. Lamenting the wrongs done to him, he declared that the cause of the civil war was the restoration of the tribunes to their country.

Then, through Antony, he took over from Lucretius seven cohorts that were stationed at Sulmo, and he brought over to his side three legions that were stationed with Domitius at Corfinium. Pompey and the whole senate, alarmed at Caesar's growing strength, crossed into Greece as though driven out of Italy, and chose Dyrrachium as their base for waging the war.

Caesar came to Rome, and when money from the treasury was refused him, he broke open the doors, forced his way in, and carried off four thousand one hundred and thirty-five pounds of gold and nearly nine hundred thousand pounds of silver.

Leaving the City, he went to his legions at Ariminum, then crossed the Alps and came to Massilia. Because it had not admitted him, he left Trebonius with three legions to besiege it and hurried on to the Spains, which the Pompeian generals Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius and Marcus Varro held with their legions. There he defeated Petreius and Afranius in many battles, came to terms with them, and let them go. In Further Spain, moreover, he took over two legions from Marcus

Varro. His generals had similar success: Curio drove Cato out of Sicily, Valerius drove Cotta out of Sardinia, and Varus drove Tubero out of Africa. Caesar, returning to Massilia, subdued it by siege; he granted its people only their lives and liberty and stripped them of everything else.

Meanwhile Dolabella, of Caesar's party, was defeated in Illyricum by Octavius and Libo, lost his forces, and fled to Antony. Basilus and Sallust, each with the single legion he commanded, and Antony as well, and Hortensius too, hurrying up from the Lower Sea with a fleet, all set out together against Octavius and Libo, and all were defeated.

When Antony had surrendered to Octavius with fifteen cohorts, Libo led them all off to Pompey. Curio crossed from Sicily into Africa with an army, but King Juba at once intercepted him and slaughtered him with all his forces. Octavius tried to storm Salonae and lost almost all the forces he had brought.

Caelius deserted Caesar and joined the exile Milo; and when the two of them attempted to attack Capua with a band of slaves, they were killed. Bibulus, at Corcyra, overcome with shame because the enemy had slipped past the guard he had posted over sea and town, wore himself out with fasting and sleeplessness until he died.

Appius Claudius Censorinus, who was guarding Greece on Pompey's orders, wished to test the credibility of the Pythian oracle, which had already lapsed. The prophetess, forced by him to go down into the cave, is said to have answered him when he asked about the war: "This war does not concern you, Roman; you will hold the Coela of Euboea." Now they call the Euboean gulf "Coela." So Appius went away perplexed and uncertain at the oracle.

This consulter of the oracle prompts us to put a question of our own to our detractors. They complain, of course, that because of the Christian faith their sacred rites have been forbidden and their ceremonies abolished, and above all that, now that the reading of entrails and prophecies has ceased, future disasters cannot be known and so are not avoided.

Why then, long before Caesar's rule and the birth of Christ, as their own authors testify, had the credibility of the Pythian oracle lapsed? It lapsed because it was despised. And why was it despised, unless because it was false, or empty, or ambiguous? Hence the poet wisely gave warning: "They go away unanswered and hate the Sibyl's seat."

And lest they should perhaps think it of little account that what lapsed and fell out of use through contempt was either a deity or a shrine: this was that Pythian Apollo who, they say, after killing the great serpent Python, the author and chief of all prophecy, became heir to its seat, its divination and its divinity, and chose to give his answers in the very place where divination itself seemed to have arisen along with its author;

the god, moreover, whom in other parts of the world too all the madness of frenzied devotees belches forth, with foaming mouths and raving dashing about; to whom very many kings of the earth hastened as to the living voice of a deity they were consulting; to whom the Romans themselves very often sent the richest gifts.

But if this Pythian Apollo was gradually despised, abandoned and abolished as experience showed him for what he was, what life can be hoped for from a dead beast, what truth from a crazed little woman? And finally, "when the fat Tyrrhenian has blown his ivory pipe at the altars," and the entrails of the fattened victim are laid out, what will a hungry man not invent, if, as they themselves admit, Apollo himself leads people astray by speaking either obscurely or falsely?

Let them therefore bear it calmly, even if for the present they will not follow our example, that we, by the judgement of truth, actually forbid what their ancestors were able to despise merely from experience.

Meanwhile many kings of the East gathered with auxiliary forces to Pompey at Dyrrachium. When Caesar arrived there, he besieged Pompey to no purpose, fortifying fifteen miles of land with a trench while the seas lay open to the other side.

Pompey overthrew a fort near the sea which Marcellinus was guarding, and killed the garrison of Caesar's men stationed there. Caesar attacked Torquatus and a single legion, intending to overwhelm them.

When Pompey learned of the danger to his allies, he concentrated all his forces at that spot, and Caesar at once abandoned the siege and turned against him. Torquatus, however, immediately burst out and pursued him from behind.

So Caesar's soldiers, terrified at being caught between two dangers, took to flight, though Caesar himself tried in vain to stop them. Pompey, the victor even by Caesar's own testimony, called back his army from the pursuit. Four thousand of Caesar's soldiers, twenty-two centurions and a number of Roman knights were killed in that battle.
From there Caesar marched rapidly through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompey followed with very large forces, and battle was joined.

So the lines were drawn up on both sides. Pompey placed eighty-eight cohorts in three lines. There were forty thousand infantry, six hundred cavalry on the left wing and five hundred on the right, besides many kings, a great many senators and Roman knights, and a large body of light-armed troops in addition.
Caesar likewise drew up eighty cohorts in three lines; he had fewer than thirty thousand infantry and a thousand cavalry.

There one could see, and groan to see, the gathered strength of the Romans standing on the plains of Pharsalus for mutual slaughter—forces which, had concord guided them, no peoples and no kings could have withstood.

At the first encounter Pompey's cavalry was driven back and left the left flank exposed. Then, while for a long time men were cut down on both sides with the outcome in doubt, and while on the one side Pompey, in the course of encouraging his men, kept saying, "Spare your fellow citizens," yet did not do so himself, and on the other Caesar did what he urged, saying, "Soldier, strike at the face," at last Pompey's whole army fled and his camp was plundered.

In that battle fifteen thousand Pompeians and thirty-three centurions were killed. This was the outcome of the battle at Old Pharsalus. Pompey fled, found a merchant ship at the mouth of the river Peneus, and crossed over to Asia.

From there he came by way of Cyprus to Egypt, and as soon as he reached the shore he was killed on the orders of the young Ptolemy, to win the favour of the victorious Caesar. Pompey's wife and sons fled. The rest of the Pompeian fleet was plundered and all aboard were butchered most cruelly; there too Pompeius Bithynicus was killed. Lentulus, a man of consular rank, was put to death at Pelusium.

Having settled affairs in Thessaly, Caesar came to Alexandria. When Pompey's head and ring were brought to him and he saw them, he wept. After he had taken up residence in the palace, the king's guardians tricked him so that he should not obtain money: they cunningly stripped their own temples, both to show that the royal treasury was empty and to stir the people up to hatred of Caesar.

Besides this, Achillas, the king's general, having once steeped himself in Pompey's blood, was now plotting Caesar's death too. For when he was ordered to disband the army he commanded, twenty thousand armed men, he not only scorned the order but actually drew up his troops for battle.

During the battle itself the royal fleet, which happened to have been drawn up on shore, was ordered to be set on fire. When the flames spread to part of the city as well, they burned four hundred thousand books that happened to be stored in the buildings nearby—truly a unique monument to the learning and diligence of earlier generations, who had gathered together so many great works of brilliant minds.

So although bookcases still stand in the temples today, which we ourselves have seen, and people report that these were plundered and emptied by men of our own day in our own times—which is indeed true—it is nevertheless more honourable to believe that other books were acquired afterward to emulate the earlier zeal for learning, than that there was at that time some other library, standing apart from the four hundred thousand books, that might be believed to have escaped for that reason.

Caesar afterward captured the island on which the Pharos stands. Achillas came there with the Gabinian soldiers. A great battle was fought: a large number of Caesar's soldiers fell there, and all the murderers of Pompey were also killed.

Caesar, hard pressed by the force of the enemy bearing down on him, climbed into a small boat. When it was soon weighed down and swamped by the men who followed him, he swam two hundred paces to a ship, holding up one hand in which he carried papers. Soon after, attacked in a naval engagement, he with great good fortune either sank or captured the royal fleet.

At the request of the Alexandrians he gave them back their king, warning him to seek the experience of Roman friendship rather than of Roman arms. Yet as soon as he was free, the king made war; but he was promptly destroyed, himself along with his whole army. Twenty thousand men are reported killed in that war, and twelve thousand surrendered along with seventy warships; five hundred of the victors are said to have fallen.

The young king himself was taken aboard a small boat to escape, but when many men leaped into it, it sank and he drowned. His body, washed up on the shore, was identified by his golden breastplate. Caesar sent this ahead to Alexandria and so drove all the Alexandrians to surrender in despair, and he gave the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra.

After this he travelled through Syria and defeated Pharnaces in Pontus. Then, after he came to Rome and was made dictator and consul, he crossed into Africa and fought at Thapsus against Juba and Scipio, killing a very great number of men there. The camps of both were plundered, and sixty elephants were captured.

Cato killed himself at Utica. Juba paid a man to strike him and offered him his throat; Petreius ran himself through with the same sword. Scipio, who had been trying to flee to Spain by ship and had been forced back to Africa by the wind, cut his own throat aboard that ship.

Titus Torquatus was also killed on the same ship. Caesar ordered the death of the grandsons of Pompey the Great and of his daughter Pompeia, and along with them Faustus Sulla, Afranius, and the daughter [?] of Petreius.

Then, after entering the City in four triumphs and setting in order the state of the recovered commonwealth, he at once set out for the Spains against the Pompeys, Pompey's sons. He reached Saguntum on the seventeenth day after leaving the City, and immediately fought many battles, with varying fortune, against the two Pompeys, Labienus and Attius Varus.

The last battle was fought near the river Munda.
