There the fighting was so fierce and the slaughter so great that even Caesar, seeing his line being cut down and driven back, while even his veterans were not ashamed to give ground, thought of forestalling by death the disgrace of defeat that awaited him—when suddenly the Pompeian army turned and fled.

Indeed, this battle was fought on the very day on which Pompey the father had fled from the City to wage the war, and for four years this civil war had thundered without pause throughout the whole world. Titus Labienus and Attius Varus were killed in the battle. Gnaeus Pompey escaped with a hundred horsemen.

His brother [?] Pompey quickly gathered no small band of Lusitanians, but he engaged Caesonius, was defeated, and was killed as he fled. The city of Munda, besieged by Caesar, was taken only with difficulty and with immense slaughter.

Caesar returned to Rome. There, while he was restoring the condition of the commonwealth with a clemency contrary to the precedents of his ancestors, he was stabbed with twenty-three wounds in the senate house and died, at the instigation of Brutus and Cassius and with the knowledge of a large part of the senate.

They say that more than sixty were privy to that conspiracy. The two Bruti, Gaius Cassius and their other associates withdrew to the Capitol with drawn daggers. There was long debate over whether the Capitol should be set on fire along with the authors of the murder.
The people, roused by grief, seized his body and burned it in the forum on the broken pieces of the tribunals and benches.

Rome measured the breadth of her empire by her own disasters, and, turning to slaughter herself, she avenged every single nation on the very spot where she had subdued it. In Asia, Europe and Africa—I do not say in the three parts of the world, but in every corner of those three parts—she put on her own gladiators and forced upon her enemies, given a holiday, the spectacle of a wretched vengeance.

Yet it was not enough that the causes themselves had been destroyed along with their authors. The seeds sprang up again in the same field, ready to yield at once to the reapers a great increase of evils, at the cost of great sweat. Caesar, the victor in the civil war, is killed by his fellow citizens; whole crowds of conspirators are drawn into the murder of one man.

For it was certain that Caesar, slain so unworthily, could have many avengers; and a great part of the nobility was bound together in a single chain of crime, so that such an abundance of material for evil might not be thinned out by a swift punishment, but filled out to the full scale of a war.
Legends tell that Medea once sowed the teeth of a slain serpent, from which, as a crop fit for such seed, armed men sprang up out of the earth and soon struck one another down in battle.

This, of course, was an invention of the poets. But our Rome, once Caesar was killed, gave birth to what armed hosts from his ashes! What wars she stirred up as witness to her wretched fertility—wars not for schoolboys to read about but for whole peoples to watch!

And yet the beginning of all these evils is pride. From it the civil wars blazed up; from it they sprouted again. It is not, then, an unjust slaughter of those who unjustly pursue it, if the rivalry of ambition is both carried on and punished by them and among them, until those who refused a colleague learn to bear a master, and, the whole of supreme power being gathered into one man's hands, all people take up an entirely different way of life, so that all strive to please humbly rather than to give offence insolently.

But for so wholesome a teaching of humility a teacher is needed. And so, at the fitting moment, when the affairs of Augustus Caesar had been settled, the Lord Christ was born, who, though he was in the form of God, humbly took on the form of a servant, so that the teaching of humility might be most fitting at the very time when the punishment of pride, throughout the whole world, stood as an example to all.

In the 710th year from the founding of the City, after Julius Caesar had been killed, Octavian, who under the will of his great-uncle Julius Caesar had taken both his inheritance and his name, and who later, when he gained supreme power, was called Augustus, devoted his talents to civil wars as soon as he came to Rome, while still a very young man.

To set out this heap of evils briefly: he waged five civil wars, at Mutina, Philippi and Perusia, in Sicily and at Actium. Of these, he fought two, the first and the last, against Mark Antony; the second against Brutus and Cassius; the third against Lucius Antonius; and the fourth against Sextus Pompey, the son of Gnaeus Pompey.

Antony had been declared a public enemy by the senate, and he had shut Decimus Brutus up under siege at Mutina. The consuls Hirtius and Pansa, and Caesar with them, were sent to free Brutus and to crush Antony.

Pansa, arriving first, was caught in an ambush. Amid the slaughter of his men he too was badly wounded by a javelin, and he died of that wound a few days later. Hirtius came to his colleague's aid and destroyed Antony's large forces with enormous slaughter. Caesar for his part only [?] guarded the camp.

In the second battle against Antony there was great slaughter on both sides. It was there that the consul Hirtius was killed. Antony was defeated and fled, and Caesar won the victory. Decimus Brutus confessed to him his part in the conspiracy to kill Julius Caesar and poured out prayers of repentance.
Dolabella killed Trebonius, one of Caesar's assassins, at Smyrna. The senate declared Dolabella a public enemy. The armies of both slain consuls came under Caesar's command.
Later Decimus Brutus was captured and killed by the Sequani in Gaul. Basilus, another of the assassins, was put to death by his own slaves.
Through Lepidus' efforts Caesar took Antony back into favour, and as a pledge of their reconciliation he took Antony's stepdaughter in marriage.

Then, when they had approached the City and a rumour arose of a coming proscription, Gaius Thoranius, a former praetor who feared nothing of the kind, was killed in his own house when soldiers burst in, and several others were butchered.

So, to keep the slaughter from spreading more widely and more wildly without limit, the names of 132 senators were posted on a list, first by Lepidus' order and in his name, then in Antony's, and third in Caesar's.

On that list Antony had proscribed his enemy Tullius Cicero, and his own uncle Lucius Caesar, and, to make the crime worse, he did so while his mother was still alive. On it Lepidus had thrown his own brother Lucius Paullus into the same herd of the proscribed.
Later thirty Roman knights were added to the number of the proscribed. Many killings of every kind went on for a long time, and the houses of the proscribed were stripped of everything and torn down.

Meanwhile Dolabella fought many battles with Cassius in Syria; defeated by him, he killed himself. Brutus and Cassius gathered great armies, met at Athens, and plundered all Greece. Cassius attacked the Rhodians by land and sea, forced them to surrender, and left them nothing but their lives.

So Caesar and Antony pursued them into Macedonia with vast preparations for war and drove them to their deaths, although that battle was quite plainly decided not by the valour of Antony's side but by Caesar's good fortune.

For Caesar was ill at the time and had decided to stay in camp to rest. But at the urging and pleading of his physician, who declared that he had been warned in a dream to lead Caesar out of the camp that day for the sake of his life, he went out with difficulty onto the field among his troops, and soon afterwards his camp was captured by the enemy. But Caesar's soldiers in turn captured Cassius' camp.
Driven to despair by this, Brutus and Cassius brought on themselves an untimely death before the war was over: they summoned men to strike them, and Cassius offered his head, Brutus his side.

At Rome, meanwhile, Fulvia, Antony's wife and Caesar's mother-in-law, wielded power as a woman might. In this transition of consular and royal eminence it is uncertain whether she should be counted as the last of a failing power or the first of a rising one; certainly she was overbearing even toward those through whom she had the means to be overbearing.
When Caesar returned to Brundisium she assailed him with insults, factions and plots. Driven off by him, she went over to Antony in Greece.

When Sextus Pompey learned that he had been placed among the proscribed, he turned to piracy and laid waste the whole coast of Italy with murder and plunder. He seized Sicily, cut off the supplies, and brought famine on Rome.

Soon the triumvirs, not to call them tyrants, that is, Lepidus, Caesar and Antony, made peace with him. But when Pompey at once broke the agreement by enlisting runaway slaves, he was treated as an enemy.

Menas, Pompey's freedman, deserted to Caesar with a fleet of sixty ships, and by Caesar's order he himself was put in command of that fleet. He then promptly fought a naval war, together with Statilius Taurus, against Menecrates, Pompey's commander.
Next Caesar himself fought a most bloody naval war against the same Pompeians, but soon afterwards he lost almost his whole victorious fleet in a shipwreck off Scylaceum.

Ventidius routed the Persians and Parthians, who were invading Syria, in three very great battles, and killed their king Pacorus in battle, on the very day on which Crassus had been killed by the Parthians. Antony, having barely taken a single fortress, made peace with Antiochus, so that he might appear to have brought so great an affair to completion himself.

He put Ventidius in charge of Syria and ordered him to make war on Antigonus, who had happened at that time to subdue the Jews, had captured Jerusalem and plundered the Temple, and had given the kingdom to Herod. Ventidius quickly defeated him and accepted his surrender.

The freedman Menas went back to Pompey with six ships. Pompey received him mercifully, and he burned Caesar's fleet, although Caesar had recently lost another fleet in a second shipwreck. Later the same Menas was surrounded by Agrippa in a naval battle and went over to Caesar with six triremes. But Caesar, since this was his third desertion, merely spared his life and left him without a command.

Then Agrippa fought a naval battle between Mylae and the Lipari Islands against Demochares and Pompey and won it, sinking or capturing thirty ships and badly damaging the rest. Pompey fled to Messana.

Caesar meanwhile had crossed to Tauromenium, and Pompey struck him with a sudden attack. Having lost many of his ships, which were sunk, and a great number of his soldiers, Caesar fled to Italy; but without delay he returned to Sicily.
There he met Lepidus, who had come from Africa and was claiming the chief share of power for himself with intimidation, threats and arrogance.

A few days later, at Caesar's order, while Caesar watched from the shore with his army drawn up, Agrippa fought a ferocious naval battle against Pompey and won it, sinking or capturing 163 ships. Pompey barely slipped away with seventeen ships.

Lepidus, swollen with great arrogance because of his twenty legions, had given Messana over to his soldiers to plunder. When Caesar himself came to him, he spurned him once and again, and even ordered that he be attacked with missiles.

Caesar avoided these by wrapping his cloak around his left arm and warding them off. Then, spurring his horse, he got back to his own men, drew up his army, advanced against Lepidus, and, with only a few men killed, compelled most of Lepidus' legions to come over to his side.

At last Lepidus understood where his folly was leading. He put off his general's cloak, put on mourning clothes, and as a suppliant to Caesar obtained his life and his property, though he was sent into permanent exile. Taurus, Caesar's lieutenant, brought almost the whole of Sicily, which had been tested and terrified by the sword, into allegiance.

At that time there were forty-four legions under Caesar's sole command. The soldiers, made bolder by their numbers, stirred up some riots over receiving land. But Caesar, great of spirit, discharged twenty thousand soldiers, returned thirty thousand slaves to their masters, and crucified six thousand whose masters could not be found.

He entered the City in an ovation, and the senate decreed that he should hold the tribunician power for life. In those days, across the Tiber, a spring of oil gushed up from the ground out of a public lodging-house and flowed in a very abundant stream for a whole day.

Antony, meanwhile, after crossing the Araxes, was beset on every side by every kind of misfortune and at last barely got back to Antioch with a few men. In all the many battles he attempted against the mass of cavalry and archers he was always defeated and fled; besides this, hampered by an uncertain and unfamiliar country, he was driven by the most severe hunger to eat unspeakable foods, and a great many of his soldiers surrendered to the enemy.

From there he crossed into Greece and ordered Pompey, who after his defeat by Caesar was rebuilding an army and renewing the war, to come to him with a few men. Pompey fled, but was repeatedly defeated by Antony's commanders Titius and Furnius in battles on land and sea, was captured, and shortly afterwards was killed.

Caesar subdued and tamed Illyricum, Pannonia and part of Italy by war. Antony captured Artabanes, king of Armenia, by treachery and deceit, bound him with a silver chain, and forced him to reveal the royal treasures. Then he stormed the town in which the king had revealed that they were hidden and carried off a great quantity of gold and silver.
Elated by this wealth, he ordered war to be declared on Caesar and divorce to be announced to his wife Octavia, Caesar's sister, and he commanded Cleopatra to come from Alexandria to meet him.

He himself set out for Actium, where he had stationed his fleet. When he found that nearly a third of his rowers had died of hunger, he was not at all disturbed. "Only let the oars be safe," he said, "for there will be no shortage of rowers as long as Greece has men."

Caesar set out from Brundisium for Epirus with 230 warships. Agrippa, sent ahead by Caesar, captured many cargo ships laden with grain and arms that were coming from Egypt, Syria and Asia to support Antony; and sailing round the Peloponnesian gulf he stormed the city of Methone, which was fortified with a very strong garrison of Antony's men.

Next he took Corcyra; he pursued and routed the fleeing enemy in a naval battle, and after many very bloody actions he joined Caesar. Antony, alarmed by the desertions and hunger among his soldiers, decided to hasten the war; he suddenly drew up his forces, advanced on Caesar's camp, and was defeated.

On the third day after the battle Antony moved his camp to Actium, ready to decide the issue in a naval battle. Caesar had 230 warships with rams and thirty without rams, triremes as fast as Liburnian galleys, and eight legions embarked on the fleet, besides five praetorian cohorts.
Antony's fleet consisted of 170 ships, which were as much superior in size as they were inferior in number, for they stood ten feet above the sea. This was the famous and great battle of Actium.

From the fifth hour to the seventh, while the hope of victory was uncertain, there was very heavy slaughter on both sides; the rest of the day and the following night turned toward victory for Caesar.

Queen Cleopatra was the first to flee, with sixty of the fastest ships. Antony too took down the ensign of his flagship and followed his fleeing wife. As day was dawning, Caesar completed his victory.
Of the defeated, twelve thousand are reported to have fallen and six thousand were wounded, of whom a thousand died while being treated.

Antony and Cleopatra decided to send their children ahead to the Red Sea with part of the royal treasure. They themselves stationed garrisons around the two horns of Egypt, Pelusium and Paraetonium, and prepared a fleet and forces to renew the war.

Caesar, hailed as imperator for the sixth time and himself consul for the fourth time with Marcus Licinius Crassus, came to Brundisium. There he distributed his legions and arranged garrisons for the whole world. From there he set out for Syria and soon reached Pelusium, where he was received by Antony's garrisons of their own accord.

Meanwhile Cornelius Gallus, sent ahead by Caesar, received into allegiance the four legions that Antony had stationed at Cyrene as a garrison. From there he defeated Antony and took Paraetonium, the first city of Egypt on the Libyan side, and soon afterwards defeated Antony himself at Pharos.

Antony [?] then joined a cavalry battle against Caesar; in this too he was wretchedly defeated and fled. At first light on the Kalends of August, when Antony went down to the harbour to draw up his fleet, all the ships suddenly went over to Caesar. Stripped of his only defence, he retreated in panic with a few men into the palace.

Then, as Caesar drew near and the city was in turmoil, Antony ran himself through with a sword and was carried, half-dead, to Cleopatra in the tomb in which she had shut herself up, determined to die.

When Cleopatra realized that she was being kept alive for a triumph, she sought a voluntary death and was found lifeless, bitten, it is thought, by a snake on her left arm. Caesar even brought in Psylli, who are accustomed to draw out and suck snake venom from people's wounds, but in vain.

Caesar, as victor, took possession of Alexandria, by far the richest and greatest of all cities. Rome was so enriched by its wealth that, because of the abundance of money, the prices of property and of other goods for sale were set at double what they had been until then.

By Caesar's order there were put to death Antony's elder son; Publius Canidius, who had always been most hostile to Caesar but was also unfaithful to Antony; Cassius of Parma, the last victim offered for the outrage done to Caesar's father; and Quintus Ovinius, chiefly for this disgrace, that he, a senator of the Roman people, had not blushed to take charge, most shamefully, of the queen's wool-working and weaving shops.
After this Caesar went with his land forces to Syria, then withdrew to winter quarters in Asia, and afterwards travelled through Greece to Brundisium.

In the 725th year from the founding of the City, when the emperor Caesar Augustus himself was consul for the fifth time, with Lucius Apuleius, Caesar returned victorious from the East and on the sixth of January entered the City in a triple triumph. Then for the first time he himself closed the gates of Janus, all civil wars having been laid to rest and ended.

On this day he was first hailed as Augustus. This name, untouched [?] by all before him and not dared by other rulers down to the present, declares that the summit of power over the world had been lawfully assumed. From that same day supreme authority and power began to rest, and remained, in the hands of one man, which the Greeks call monarchy.

Moreover, no one, whether a believer or even an opponent of the faith, is unaware that this is the very day, the sixth of January, on which we observe the Epiphany, that is, the appearance or manifestation of the Lord's mystery.

Neither reason nor the occasion requires me to speak more fully now about the mystery of this most faithful observance of ours, so that we may be seen both to have kept it in reserve for those who seek and not to have forced it on those who do not care. But it was right to mention it faithfully, so that it may be proved that Caesar's rule was in every respect prepared for the grace of the coming Christ.

For when he first entered the City, returning from Apollonia after his great-uncle Gaius Caesar had been killed, at about the third hour, suddenly, in a clear and cloudless sky, a ring like a rainbow encircled the disk of the sun, as if to point him out as the one and most powerful man in this world and the most glorious in the whole earth, in whose time he would come who alone had made and who rules the sun itself and the whole world.

Then the second time, after he had received the legions from Pompey and Lepidus in Sicily, restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters, and alone distributed forty-four legions under his command for the protection of the world, and after he had entered the City in an ovation and decreed that all earlier debts owed to the Roman people should be remitted, the written records of them also being destroyed: in those very days, as I described above, a most abundant spring of oil flowed for a whole day from a public lodging-house. What sign could more clearly declare that the birth of Christ would take place in the days of Caesar, when he ruled the whole world? For in the language of the people in which and from which he was born, Christ means "the anointed one."

So, at the time when perpetual tribunician power was decreed for Caesar, a spring of oil flowed at Rome for a whole day. By this, the plainest signs in heaven and wonders on earth revealed, to those who would not listen to the voices of the prophets, these things: that under Caesar's rule and the Roman Empire, for a whole day, that is, for the entire span of the Roman Empire, Christ, and from him Christians, that is, the Anointed and from him the anointed, would come forth abundantly and unceasingly from the lodging-house, that is, from the hospitable and generous Church; that through Caesar all slaves who acknowledged their master would be restored, while the rest, who were found without a master, would be handed over to death and punishment; and that under Caesar the debts of sins would be remitted in the very city in which the oil had flowed of its own accord.

The third time, when he entered the City in triumph as consul for the fifth time, on the very day we named above, when he himself closed the temple of Janus for the first time in two hundred years and took the most glorious name of Augustus: what can be more faithfully and truly believed or recognized, since peace, name and day all came together in so great a manifestation, than that, by a hidden ordering of events, he was predestined to serve in preparing the way for Him? For on the very day on which Christ was shortly to be manifested to the world, Caesar both displayed the sign of peace and took the name of power.
But as for what happened at his fourth return, when, with the Cantabrian war ended
and all nations pacified, Caesar came back to the City, in witness to the faith we are setting out, that will be better presented in its proper order.

In the 726th year after the founding of the City, when the emperor Augustus Caesar was consul for the sixth time and Marcus Agrippa for the second, Caesar realized that little would have been accomplished in Spain over two hundred years if he allowed the Cantabrians and Asturians, the two bravest peoples of Spain, to live under their own laws. He therefore opened the gates of Janus and set out for the Spanish provinces himself with an army.
The Cantabrians and Asturians make up part of the province of Gallaecia, where the long ridge of the Pyrenees runs northward not far from the Ocean that lies alongside it.

These peoples were not only ready to defend their own freedom but even dared to rob their neighbours of theirs, and they ravaged the Vaccaei, the Turmogi and the Autrigones with constant raids. Caesar therefore pitched camp at Segisama and enclosed almost the whole of Cantabria with three columns.

For a long time his army was worn out to no purpose and often led into danger. At last he ordered a fleet to be brought up from the Gulf of Aquitaine across the Ocean while the enemy was off guard, and troops to be landed.

Only then did the Cantabrians join a great battle beneath the walls of Attica. Defeated, they fled to Mount Vinnius, which nature had made very secure, and there the famine of the siege wore them down almost to the last man. Next the town of Racilium, after resisting long and with great force, was finally taken and destroyed.
Besides this, the legates Antistius and Firmius subdued in great and hard-fought wars the farther parts of Gallaecia, which are thick with mountains and forests and are bounded by the Ocean.
For they surrounded Mount Medullius, which overhangs the river Minius and where a great multitude of people were defending themselves, with a ditch fifteen miles long and laid siege to it.

So when this people, savage and fierce by nature, understood that they could neither endure the siege nor match the Romans in war, they rushed to a voluntary death for fear of slavery. Almost all of them killed themselves, vying with one another, by fire, sword and poison.

The Asturians, for their part, pitched camp by the river Astura and, with great plans and great strength, would have crushed the Romans had they not been betrayed and forestalled. They had planned to overwhelm suddenly, with three columns of equal size, three legates with their legions, who were divided among three camps; but they were exposed by the treachery of their own people.

Afterward Carisius met them in battle and defeated them, though not without considerable loss to the Romans as well. Some of them escaped from the battle and fled to Lancia. When the soldiers, having surrounded the city, were preparing to attack it with fire, the general Carisius persuaded his own men to hold back from burning it and obtained from the barbarians their willingness to surrender. For he was eagerly striving to leave the city whole and unharmed as a witness to his victory.

Caesar paid this honour to the Cantabrian victory: he ordered that the gates of war be shut with a bar at that time as well. So Janus was then closed for the second time under Caesar and for the fourth time since the founding of the City.
After this Claudius Drusus, Caesar's stepson, who had been allotted Gaul and Raetia, subdued by arms the greatest and bravest peoples of Germany.

For at that time, as if they were hurrying toward a day appointed for peace, all the nations were stirred up in waves either to try war or to settle a treaty: ready either to accept terms of peace if they were defeated, or to enjoy their freedom in quiet if they were victorious.

The Noricans, Illyrians, Pannonians, Dalmatians, Moesians, Thracians, Dacians, Sarmatians and very many great peoples of Germany were, under various commanders, either conquered, or held in check, or else shut out behind the barrier of the greatest rivers, the Rhine and the Danube.
In Germany Drusus first subdued the Usipetes, then the Tencteri and the Chatti. He slaughtered the Marcomanni almost to the point of extermination.

Afterward he defeated, together and in a single war, the bravest nations, to whom nature had given strength and habit had given experience in using it: the Cherusci, the Suebi and the Sygambri. But it was a war harsh even for his own men.

Their courage and savagery can be judged from this: whenever their women were cut off by the Romans and shut in among their wagons, and they ran out of weapons or of anything their fury could use as a weapon, they would dash their little sons against the ground and hurl them into the faces of the enemy, so that in the killing of each son they became murderers of their kin twice over.

At that time too, in Africa, Cossus, Caesar's general, restrained the Musolani and Gaetuli, who roamed far and wide, by confining their territory, and through fear compelled them to keep away from the Roman frontiers.

Meanwhile envoys of the Indians and the Scythians, having crossed the whole world, at last found Caesar at Tarraco, a city of Nearer Spain, beyond which they could seek no farther, and they bestowed upon Caesar the glory that had once belonged to Alexander the Great.

For just as an embassy of Spaniards and Gauls had come to Alexander at Babylon, in the middle of the East, seeking peace, so now the Indian from the east and the Scythian from the north came as suppliants with gifts of their peoples and entreated Caesar in Spain, at the farthest edge of the West.

After the Cantabrian war had been waged for five years, and the whole of Spain had been settled and laid to rest in lasting peace, with a kind of sigh of relief from its weariness, Caesar returned to Rome.

In those days too he waged many wars, some himself and many through his generals and legates. Among others, Piso was sent against the Vindelici; when he had subdued them, he came victorious to Caesar at Lugdunum.
Tiberius, Caesar's stepson, destroyed the Pannonians, who were swelling with a fresh revolt, in a most bloody slaughter.
He at once attacked the Germans in war as well, and as victor carried off forty thousand captives from among them.
This was in truth a very great and most fearsome war, waged with fifteen legions for three years, and, as Suetonius attests, there was scarcely any greater war after the Punic war.
At the same time Quintilius Varus, who treated the subject peoples with astonishing arrogance and greed, was utterly destroyed with three legions by the Germans when they rebelled.
Caesar Augustus took this disaster to the state so hard that often, in the violence of his grief, he would beat his head against the wall and cry out, "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!"
Agrippa defeated the people of the Bosporus; having recovered in war the Roman standards they had once carried off under Mithridates, he forced the defeated to surrender.

The Parthians felt as if, now that the whole world had been either subdued or pacified, they were singled out before the eyes of all, and the whole strength of the Roman empire was bound to be turned against them alone, since the old guilt for the slaughter of Crassus gnawed at them. Of their own accord they sent back to Caesar the standards they had taken when Crassus was killed, handed over royal hostages, and by faithful supplication earned a firm treaty.

And so in the 752nd year after the founding of the City, when all nations from east to west, from north to south and around the whole circle of the Ocean had been settled in a single peace, Caesar Augustus himself then closed the gates of Janus for the third time.

From then on they stayed barred in the deepest quiet for nearly twelve years, so that even rust itself set its mark on them, and they were never opened until the very end of Augustus's old age, when they were struck open by a revolt of the Athenians and an uprising of the Dacians.

So, with the gates of Janus closed, he set about nurturing and enlarging in peace the commonwealth he had won by war, and he established a great many laws through which the human race might conform to good order out of free reverence.

Being a man, he refused the title of "lord." Once, when he was watching the games and the line "O just and good lord!" was spoken in a mime, the whole audience leapt up and applauded as if it had been said of him. He at once checked these unseemly flatteries with a gesture of his hand and a look on his face, and on the following day he rebuked them in a very stern edict. After that he would not allow himself to be called "lord" even by his own children or grandchildren, whether in earnest or in jest.

It was at that time, then, in the very year in which Caesar, by God's ordering, established the firmest and truest peace, that Christ was born. That peace served his coming; at his birth angels sang with joy while men listened: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." And at that same time this man, to whom supreme power over all things had passed, would not allow himself to be called lord of men—or rather did not dare to—at the time when the true Lord of the whole human race was born among men.

In that same year, too, this same Caesar, whom God had foreordained for these great mysteries, for the first time ordered a census to be taken of every province everywhere and all people to be registered, at the very time when God also deigned to be seen as a man and to be one. So it was then that Christ was born, and as soon as he was born he was enrolled in the Roman census.

This is that first and most famous enrollment, which, by publishing a register of all people one by one, marked out Caesar as the first among all and the Romans as masters of the world. In it he who made all people willed himself to be found a man and to be enrolled among men. Never at all, since the founding of the world and the beginning of the human race, had such a thing been granted in this way even to the Babylonian or the Macedonian kingdom, not to mention any lesser kingdom.

Nor is there any doubt—it lies open to everyone's knowledge, faith and examination—that our Lord Jesus Christ by his will enlarged and defended this city and raised it to this summit of power, since it was this city, above all, whose citizen he chose to be when he came; he must surely be called a Roman citizen, by the declaration of the Roman census.

Therefore, since we have come to that point in time at which the Lord Christ first lit up this world with his coming and gave Caesar a most peaceful reign, I will bring this sixth book too to a close here,

so that in a seventh book, if with the Lord's help I am equal to the task, I may cover the Christian era—sprouting, and growing all the more amid the hands of those who would repress it, and still, as it advances, gnawed at by the attacks of those very people to whom we are compelled to make this reply;

so that, since from the beginning I have not kept silent about how men sin and are punished for their sins, I may now also set out what persecutions of the Christians were carried out and what punishments followed—leaving aside the fact that all people are generally prone to sin and are therefore chastised individually.
HISTORIES AGAINST THE PAGANS
BOOK SEVEN

Sufficient proofs have now been gathered, I think, by which it can be shown openly, without recourse to any hidden teaching reserved for the few faithful, that the one true God whom the Christian faith proclaims both created the world and its creatures when he willed, and ordered it through many powers while he was unknown through the many, and established it under one when he was revealed through the One; and at the same time that his power and his patience have shone forth by many kinds of evidence.

I understand that narrow and abject minds are somewhat offended at this, because so great a patience is mixed with so great a power. "If he was powerful enough," they say, "to create the world, to establish peace in the world, and to instil in the world the worship and knowledge of himself, what need was there for such patience—or, as they see it, such ruinous patience—so that what could have begun in that way from the very beginning by the power of this God you preach came about only at the end, through the errors, disasters and toils of mankind?"

To them I could truthfully answer that the human race was created and established from the beginning for this purpose: that, living in religion, with peace and without toil, it might earn eternity as the fruit of obedience; but that, having abused the goodness of its Creator, it turned the freedom granted by his indulgence into defiant license, and slid from contempt into forgetfulness;

and that God's patience is now just, and just in both directions: so that, though scorned, he does not utterly destroy one on whom he wishes to have mercy, and, though scorned yet powerful, he allows that one to be afflicted with toils for as long as he wishes; and consequently that it is right for him always to exercise just governance even over one who does not know it, to whom, when he repents, he will one day mercifully restore the possibility of the ancient grace.

But although these things are said with perfect truth and force, they require a listener who is faithful and obedient; whereas I—whether they will one day believe, I shall see—am certainly now arguing with unbelievers. So I will more readily bring forward things which, even if they refuse to accept them, they cannot refute.

So, as far as the consciousness of human minds is concerned, both sides live in reverence for religion and in confession and worship of a higher power, differing only in faith. For our position is to confess that all things exist from one God and through one God; theirs, to think that there are as many gods as there are things.

"If it lay within the power of the God you preach," they say, "that the Roman empire should become so vast and so exalted, why did his patience stand in the way, so that it did not come about earlier?" To them we shall answer in the very same words: "If it lay within the power of the gods you preach that the Roman empire should become so vast and so exalted, why did their patience stand in the way, so that it did not come about earlier?"
Did the gods themselves not yet exist? Or did Rome itself not yet exist?

Were the gods not being worshipped? Or did Rome not yet seem fit for empire? If the gods did not yet exist, the charge falls; for why should I go into their delay, when I cannot even find their existence? But if the gods did exist, then either their power, which they themselves proclaim, or their patience is to blame: their patience, if they had it, or their power, if they lacked it.

Or, if it seems more convincing that the gods did exist then and could have advanced Rome, but that the Romans did not yet exist to be properly advanced, then I reply that we are looking for a power that is the author of things, not the skill of a craftsman. For the question concerns gods who are, as they suppose, great, not the meanest of workmen, whose craft stands idle unless they are supplied with material.

For if foreknowledge and will were always at their disposal—indeed with foreknowledge underlying the will, since for omnipotence, at least concerning its own works, to foreknow is the same as to will—then whatever was foreknown, and had their will in agreement with it, should not have been waited for but created; especially since they say that this Jupiter of theirs used to turn heaps of ants into nations of men for sport.

As for their careful observance of ceremonies, I do not think it even needs to be reviewed, since amid continual rites there was no end and no rest from incessant disasters until Christ, the Saviour of the world, shone forth. Although I think I have already shown sufficiently that the peace of the Roman empire was foreordained for his coming, I will nonetheless try to add a few more points.

At the beginning of the second book, when I was briefly treating in my narrative the period of Rome's founding, I set down many points of fitting correspondence between Babylon, the city of the Assyrians, then the chief of nations, and Rome, which now likewise rules the nations:

that the one was the first empire and the other the last; that the one gave way little by little, while the other gradually gained strength; that the one lost its last king at the very time when the other had its first; that the one, invaded by Cyrus, was then captured and collapsed as if into death, at the very time when the other, rising with confidence after the expulsion of its kings, began to enjoy the freedom to govern itself;

and especially that, just when Rome was asserting its freedom, the people of the Jews, who had been in servitude under kings at Babylon, also recovered their freedom, returned to holy Jerusalem, and rebuilt the temple of the Lord, as had been foretold by the prophets.

I had said, moreover, that between the Babylonian kingdom, which belonged to the east, and the Roman, which arose in the west and was nourished on the inheritance of the east, came the Macedonian and African kingdoms, which, as if from the north and the south, held for short periods the roles of guardian and trustee.

I know that no one has ever doubted that the Babylonian and Roman kingdoms are rightly called the kingdoms of the east and the west. That the Macedonian kingdom lay to the north is shown both by its very region of the sky and by the altars of Alexander the Great, which stand to this day beneath the Riphaean mountains;

and that Carthage was preeminent over all Africa, and extended the boundaries of its rule not only to Sicily, Sardinia and the other neighbouring islands but even into Spain, is declared both by the records of history and by the monuments of cities.
It has also been said that between the devastation of Babylon by the Medes and the breaking into Rome by the Goths, almost exactly the same number of years elapsed.
Now to these points I add the following, so that it may be all the clearer that there is one God who is judge of all ages, kingdoms and places.

The kingdom of Carthage lasted from its founding to its overthrow a little more than seven hundred years; likewise the kingdom of Macedonia lasted from Caranus to Perseus a little less than seven hundred. Yet both were brought to an end by that number seven, by which all things are judged.
Rome herself, too, although she was being carried forward to perfect dominion in readiness for the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ, nonetheless stumbled a little when she too encountered this number.

For in the seven hundredth year after her founding, a fire that broke out from no one knows where consumed fourteen of her districts, and, as Livy says, she was never devastated by a greater fire; so much so that some years later Caesar Augustus granted a large sum of money from the public treasury to restore what had then been burned.
I could also show that the same number, doubled, held for Babylon, which was finally captured by King Cyrus after some fourteen hundred years and more, were I not called back to consider the present.

This, however, I gladly add: in the reign of Ninus, the first of all kings—though his father Belus is obscurely reported to have reigned first—in the forty-third year, then, after this Ninus began to reign, the holy Abraham was born, to whom the promises were made, and from whose seed Christ was promised;

and now, in the reign of Augustus Caesar, the first of all emperors—though his father Caesar was rather the surveyor who marked out the empire than its emperor—when nearly forty-two full years had passed since this Caesar began to rule, Christ was born, who had been promised to Abraham under Ninus, the first king.

He was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, just when all the growth of the coming year begins. So it came about that, whereas Abraham was born in the forty-third year, the birth of Christ fell at the end of the forty-second, so that he was not born within part of the third year; rather, the third year began with him.

How rich that year was in blessings, how new and how unprecedented, is well enough known, I think, even without my setting it out: across the whole world there was one peace for all, through the abolition, not merely the suspension, of wars; the twin gates of Janus were closed, with the roots of war torn out rather than held down; and there was that first and greatest census, when the whole creation of great nations swore by this one name of Caesar and at the same time, by sharing in the census, was made into one society.

So it was in the 752nd year from the founding of the City that Christ was born, bringing the world the faith that saves. He is truly the rock set in the middle of all things, on which whoever stumbles is broken and whoever believes is saved. He is truly the burning fire: whoever follows him is enlightened, and whoever puts him to the test is consumed.

He is Christ, the head of Christians, the savior of the good, the punisher of the wicked, the judge of all. By word and deed he set a pattern for those who would follow him, and to teach them all the better that they must be patient in the persecutions they would endure for the sake of eternal life, he began his sufferings as soon as he was born of a virgin and appeared in the world. For as soon as Herod, king of Judea, learned of his birth, he resolved to kill him, and in hunting for one child he slaughtered a great many infants.

From this comes the just punishment of the wicked who shamelessly attack him. From this it follows that whatever peace the world enjoys is owed to the grace given to believers, and whatever ruinous disturbance it suffers is the punishment of blasphemers. Faithful Christians, meanwhile, are secure in every circumstance, for they have either the rest of eternal life safely in store or gain even in this present life. I will demonstrate this from the events themselves, so that it is all the clearer as I relate them in order.

After the Redeemer of the world, the Lord Jesus Christ, came to earth and was enrolled as a Roman citizen in Caesar's census, the gates of war, as I have said, stayed shut for twelve years in the most blessed calm of peace. During this time Caesar Augustus sent his grandson Gaius to organize the provinces of Egypt and Syria.

As Suetonius Tranquillus reports, when Gaius passed from Egypt along the borders of Palestine he disdained to worship at Jerusalem in the temple of God, which was then holy and much frequented. When Augustus learned of this from him, his judgment went astray and he praised Gaius for having acted wisely.

So it was that in the forty-eighth year of Caesar's reign so terrible a famine fell upon the Romans that Caesar ordered the troupes of gladiators and all foreigners, and also very large numbers of slaves, to be driven out of the City, with the exception of physicians and teachers. Thus, when the emperor sinned against the holy place of God and the people were chastised by famine, the kind of punishment showed how great the offense had been.

Then, to use the words of Cornelius Tacitus, 'the gate of Janus was opened when Augustus was an old man, and while new peoples were sought out at the farthest ends of the earth, often with profit and sometimes with loss, it remained open until the reign of Vespasian.' So far Cornelius.

But it was then, when the city of Jerusalem had been taken and destroyed, as the prophets had foretold, and the Jews had been wiped out, that Titus, who had been appointed by the judgment of God to avenge the blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, triumphed as victor together with his father Vespasian and closed the gate of Janus.
So, although the gate of Janus was opened in the last years of Caesar, for a long time afterward no wars resounded, even though the army stood ready for battle.

This is why the Lord Jesus Christ himself, at a time when the whole world was living in the deepest calm and a single peace covered all nations, said among other things in the Gospels, when his disciples asked him about the end of the times to come:

"You will hear of battles and rumors of battles. See that you are not alarmed, for these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be plagues and famines and earthquakes in various places. All these things are the beginning of the birth pangs. Then they will hand you over to persecution and will kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name."
In teaching this by divine foresight, he strengthened believers by forewarning them and confounded unbelievers by foretelling it.
In the 767th year from the founding of the City, after the death of Augustus Caesar, Tiberius Caesar obtained the imperial power and held it for twenty-three years.
He waged no wars in person, and not even any serious ones through his generals; only in a few places were uprisings of peoples detected in advance and quickly put down.
In the fourth year of his reign, indeed, Germanicus, the son of Drusus and father of Caligula, celebrated a triumph over the Germans, against whom Augustus had sent him in his old age.

For the greater part of his reign Tiberius himself governed the state with great and serious restraint, so much so that when certain governors urged him to raise the tribute of the provinces, he wrote back that a good shepherd shears his flock but does not flay it.

But after the Lord Christ had suffered and risen from the dead and sent out his disciples to preach, Pilate, the governor of the province of Palestine, reported to the emperor Tiberius and to the senate on the passion and resurrection of Christ and the miracles that followed, those done openly by Christ himself and those being done by his disciples in his name, and on how he was believed to be God by a great many people whose faith was growing rapidly.

Tiberius, strongly in favor, proposed to the senate that Christ be held a god. The senate, angered that the matter had not first been referred to it according to custom, so that it might itself decide first whether to accept a new cult, refused to consecrate Christ and decreed by edict that Christians were to be banished from the City. This was all the more so because Sejanus, Tiberius's prefect, most obstinately opposed the adoption of the religion.

Tiberius, however, by an edict threatened the accusers of Christians with death. And so, little by little, that much-praised restraint of Tiberius Caesar was turned into the punishment of the senate that had opposed him; for whatever the ruler did by his own will became his pleasure, and the gentlest of princes blazed out into the most savage of beasts.

He proscribed a great many senators and drove them to their deaths. He had chosen twenty patricians to serve as his council; of these he left scarcely two unharmed and put the rest to death on various pretexts. He killed his prefect Sejanus when he was plotting revolution.
He destroyed his sons Drusus and Germanicus, Drusus his son by birth and Germanicus by adoption, with clear signs of poison, and he killed the sons of his son Germanicus.

To relate his deeds one by one fills me with horror and shame. He seethed with such frenzied lust and cruelty that those who had scorned to be saved under Christ as king were punished under Caesar as king.

In the twelfth year of his reign, however, a new and incredible disaster occurred at the town of Fidenae: while the people were watching a gladiatorial show, the seating of the amphitheater collapsed and killed more than twenty thousand people.

This was surely an example of chastisement worth recording for posterity: that men eager to watch the deaths of men had gathered together at the very time when God had willed to become man in order to provide for the salvation of men.

Then, in the seventeenth year of the same reign, when the Lord Jesus Christ willingly gave himself up to his passion, but was wickedly seized by the Jews and fastened to the cross, a tremendous earthquake shook the world, rocks were split in the mountains, and large parts of many of the greatest cities collapsed under a shock more violent than usual.
On the same day, at the sixth hour, the sun was completely darkened, and a black night suddenly covered the earth, so that, as it has been said, "An impious age feared everlasting night."

It is quite clear that neither the moon nor clouds blocked the light of the sun, for it is reported that on that day the moon was in its fourteenth day, with the whole expanse of the sky between it and the sun, very far from the sun's path, and that the stars then shone across the whole sky during the daytime hours, or rather during that dreadful night. This is attested not only by the trustworthy holy Gospels but also by a number of Greek books.

From then on, after the passion of the Lord, whom the Jews persecuted as far as lay in their power, disasters have continually and ceaselessly resounded upon the Jews, until they should be emptied out, scattered, and brought to an end.

For Tiberius, under the pretext of military service, banished their young men to provinces with harsher climates, and removed from the City the rest of that nation, as well as those who followed similar practices, under penalty of perpetual slavery if they did not obey.
Indeed, he remitted the tribute of the cities of Asia that had been destroyed by that earthquake and gave them gifts from his own generosity as well. He died with ambiguous signs of poison.

In the 790th year from the founding of the City, Gaius Caligula, the third after Augustus, began to reign and held power for less than four full years. He was the most depraved of all men before him, and seemed truly a fitting punisher sent against the blaspheming Romans and the persecuting Jews.

To convey briefly the magnitude of his cruelty, he is said to have cried out, "Would that the Roman people had a single neck!" He also often complained about the state of his times, that they were not marked by any public calamities.

O blessed seeds of the Christian age, how greatly you have prevailed in human affairs, so that even the cruelty of a man could more easily long for disasters than find them! See how hungry savagery complains of the universal calm! Unholy Fury sits within, "savage upon his weapons, bound with a hundred knots of bronze behind his back, and roars, horrible, with bloody mouth."

Rebellious slaves and runaway gladiators once terrified Rome, overthrew Italy, and laid Sicily waste, so that they were feared by almost the whole human race throughout the world. But in the days of salvation, that is, in Christian times, not even a hostile Caesar can shatter the peace.

For he set out with great and incredible preparations to look for an enemy for his idle forces, and after hurrying through Germany and Gaul he halted on the shore of the Ocean within sight of Britain. There he received the surrender of Minocynobelinus, the son of the king of the Britons, who had been driven out by his father and was wandering about with a few followers; and then, for lack of anything to make war on, he returned to Rome.

In those same days the Jews, who were even then being harassed everywhere by disasters they had deserved because of the passion of Christ, stirred up a riot at Alexandria, were crushed with slaughter, and were driven out of the city. To lay their grievances before Caesar they sent as their envoy one Philo, a man of the very highest learning.

But Caligula, who was hostile to all men and especially to the Jews, scorned Philo's embassy and ordered all the holy places of the Jews, and above all that ancient sanctuary in Jerusalem, to be profaned with pagan sacrifices and filled with statues and images, and commanded that he himself be worshiped there as a god.

Meanwhile the governor Pilate, who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Christ, after he had suffered and provoked many riots in Jerusalem, was so hard pressed by the troubles that Gaius brought upon him that he ran himself through with his own hand, seeking a quick death as a short way out of his miseries.

To his lusts Gaius Caligula added this crime as well: he first defiled his sisters by incest and then condemned them to exile. Later he ordered all the exiles to be killed together. He himself, however, was killed by his own guards.

Two notebooks were found among his secret papers. On one was written "The Dagger" and on the other "The Sword" as a title. Both contained the names and marks of the most distinguished men of both the senatorial and the equestrian orders, who had been marked out for death. A huge chest of various poisons was also found. It is reported that when these were soon afterward sunk in the sea at the command of Claudius Caesar, they infected the waters, with great destruction of fish, which the tide cast up dead here and there along the nearby shores.

This was indeed a great sign of the mercy of God, both because of the support of his grace for a people who would soon in part come to believe, and because of the restraint of his anger toward a people then stubbornly unbelieving. From the multitude of dead fish one could learn how great a multitude of men had escaped the death prepared for them, and it became known to all what so vast a mass of poison, made more potent by skill, could have done in the wretched City, since even when carelessly poured out it polluted the very sea.
In the 795th year from the founding of the City, Tiberius Claudius, the fourth after Augustus, obtained the throne and held it for fourteen years.

At the beginning of his reign Peter, the apostle of the Lord Jesus Christ, came to Rome. He taught by faithful word the faith that saves all who believe and confirmed it by the most powerful miracles; and from then on there began to be Christians at Rome.

Rome felt the benefit conferred on it by its faith. For when Caligula had been killed, the senate and consuls had passed many decrees for abolishing the imperial power, restoring the republic to its ancient order, and completely wiping out the whole family of the Caesars.

But as soon as Claudius had secured his power, he showed a great clemency until then unknown at Rome: so that vengeance, once begun, should not rage against so great a number of nobles, he struck from memory those two days in which the state of the republic had been so unhappily debated and acted upon, and decreed pardon and oblivion forever for everything done or said during them.

This was that famous and celebrated amnesty of the Athenians, which the senate, on Cicero's advice, had indeed tried to introduce at Rome after the murder of Julius Caesar, but which had come to nothing when Antony and Octavian burst in to avenge the slain Caesar. Claudius, although he had far stronger provocation to slaughter the conspirators, confirmed this amnesty out of voluntary clemency, without anyone asking for it.

At the same time there also occurred a great miracle of the present grace of God. Furius Camillus Scribonianus, the legate of Dalmatia, plotting civil war, had enticed many of the strongest legions to change their oath of allegiance.

So on the day appointed for them all to assemble from every side to the new emperor, the eagles could not be decorated, and the standards could not in any way be pulled up or moved. The army, moved by the certainty of so great and so extraordinary a miracle, turned to repentance, at once abandoned Scribonianus and killed him on the fifth day, and held to the oath of its former service.

It is well enough known that nothing was ever sadder or more ruinous for the city of Rome than civil wars. So let anyone deny, if he will, that this tyranny as it was rising and this civil war as it was breaking out were suppressed by God because of the coming of the apostle Peter and the tender seeds of Christians, still few and only just bursting forth into the profession of the holy faith; but let him then prove a similar example from past times of civil wars being suppressed.

In the fourth year of his reign Claudius, wishing to show himself a ruler useful to the state, sought war everywhere and victory from any quarter. So he launched an expedition against Britain, which appeared to have been stirred into turmoil because deserters had not been returned. He crossed over to the island, which no one either before Julius Caesar or after him had dared to approach,

and there, to use the words of Suetonius Tranquillus, "within a very few days, without any battle or bloodshed, he received the surrender of the greater part of the island." He also added to the Roman Empire the Orkney islands, which lie in the Ocean beyond Britain, and returned to Rome in the sixth month after he had set out.

Now let anyone who wishes compare, with regard to this single island, one time with another, one war with another, one Caesar with another. I make no comparison of the outcome, since this one was a most fortunate victory and that one a most bitter disaster. And so at last let Rome recognize that, through the hidden providence of him whom it has now come to acknowledge, it had a share of good fortune in its affairs even before, and that now, having acknowledged him, it enjoys the fullest good fortune, so far as it is not corrupted by the stumbling blocks of blasphemy.

In the same year of his reign a very severe famine struck throughout Syria, which the prophets had also foretold. But Helena, queen of Adiabene, who had been converted to the faith of Christ, had grain brought from Egypt and most generously relieved the needs of the Christians at Jerusalem.
In the fifth year of his reign an island thirty stades in extent sprang up from the depths between Thera and Therasia.

In the seventh year of his reign, under Cumanus, procurator of Judea, so great a riot broke out in Jerusalem during the days of Unleavened Bread that, as the people were crowded together at the exits of the gates, thirty thousand Jews are said to have been killed by the sword or crushed to death in the crush.

Josephus reports that in the ninth year of the same reign the Jews were expelled from the City by Claudius. But I am more impressed by Suetonius, who speaks as follows: "Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews, who were constantly rioting at the instigation of Christ."

It cannot be determined at all whether he ordered the Jews who were rioting against Christ to be restrained and suppressed, or whether he also wished the Christians to be expelled along with them as people of a related religion.

Nevertheless, in the following year there was so great a famine at Rome that the emperor was seized by the people in the middle of the forum, most shamefully assailed with insults and pieces of bread, and barely escaped the fury of the aroused mob by fleeing through a back door into the Palace.
A short time later he put to death thirty-five senators and three hundred Roman knights on the most trivial grounds. He himself died with clear signs of poison.

In the 808th year from the founding of the City, Nero Caesar, the fifth after Augustus, obtained the principate and held it for less than fourteen full years. He was a follower, or rather a surpasser, of his uncle Gaius Caligula in every vice and crime, and there was no crime by which he did not indulge his wantonness, lust, extravagance, greed, and cruelty. Driven by wantonness, he toured almost all the theaters of Italy and Greece, even taking on the disgrace of costumes of every kind, and often fancied that he had outdone heralds, lyre players, tragic actors, and charioteers.

He was so driven by lust that he is said not to have kept his hands even from his mother or his sister or to have respected any tie of blood; he married a man as his wife, and was himself taken by a man as a wife.

His extravagance was so unbridled that he fished with golden nets drawn in by purple cords, and bathed in perfumes both cold and warm. It is also said that he never made a journey with fewer than a thousand carriages.
Finally, he made the burning of the city of Rome a spectacle for his own pleasure. For six days and seven nights the burning city fed the emperor's gaze.

Warehouses built of squared stone, and those great tenement blocks of earlier times, which the spreading flames could not reach, were battered down and set on fire with great siege engines once prepared for foreign wars, while the unhappy populace was driven to take shelter among tombs and burial places.
He watched this from that very high tower of Maecenas and, delighted, as he said, by the beauty of the flames, sang the Iliad in tragic costume.

His greed was so headlong that after this fire in the City, which Augustus had boasted he had turned from brick into marble, he allowed no one to go near the remains of their property; he himself carried off everything that had somehow survived the flames.

He ordered the senate to grant him ten million sesterces a year for his expenses. He stripped a great many senators of their property without any cause at all. On a single day, using torture as well, he wiped out the entire wealth of all the merchants.

He was so savage in his frenzied cruelty that he killed most of the senate and nearly emptied the equestrian order. He did not even refrain from murdering his own family: he struck down without hesitation his mother, his brother, his sister, his wife, and all his other kinsmen and relatives.

To this mountain of crimes he added the recklessness of impiety against God. For he was the first at Rome to inflict tortures and death on Christians, and he ordered them to be tormented by a similar persecution throughout all the provinces. Trying to root out the very name, he killed the most blessed apostles of Christ, Peter by the cross and Paul by the sword.

Soon disasters arose on every side and overwhelmed the wretched city in heaps. For the following autumn so great a plague fell upon the City that thirty thousand funerals were entered in the register of Libitina. Then, close on its heels, came the disaster in Britain, in which two chief towns were sacked with great slaughter and loss of citizens and allies.

In addition, in the East, after great provinces of Armenia had been lost, Roman legions were sent under the Parthian yoke, and Syria was retained only with difficulty. In Asia three cities, namely Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae, collapsed in an earthquake.

But when Nero learned that Galba had been made emperor by the army in Spain, he lost all courage and hope. While he was plotting incredible evils to throw the state into confusion, or rather to overthrow it, he was declared a public enemy by the senate, and fleeing in the most shameful manner, he killed himself at the fourth milestone from the City. With him the whole family of the Caesars came to an end.

In the 824th year from the founding of the City, Galba seized the imperial power in Spain. As soon as he learned of Nero's death he came to Rome. Since his greed, cruelty and sloth offended everyone, he adopted Piso, a noble and energetic young man, as his son and as heir to the throne. In the seventh month of his reign he was murdered by Otho, together with Piso.

Through the slaughter of its emperors and the civil wars that broke out, Rome paid for the wrongs it had recently done to the Christian religion. When the apostle Peter came to the City, the standards of the legions had been held fast by divine power and could not by any means be pulled up to start the civil war that Scribonianus was preparing. Now that Peter had been put to death in the City and the Christians torn apart by every kind of punishment, those same standards broke loose all over the world.
Galba had at once risen up in Spain; and as soon as he was crushed, Otho at Rome, Vitellius in Germany and Vespasian in Syria all seized power and took up arms at the same time.

Those who take offence at Christian times may well acknowledge, however unwillingly, both the power and the mercy of God. See how quickly the fires of such great wars were both kindled and put out! In earlier times great and lasting disasters were stirred up by the slightest causes, but now the mighty crash of great evils, resounding on every side, was quieted with very little trouble. For by now there was at Rome
a Church, though harassed by persecution, which would pray to Christ, the judge of all, even for its enemies and persecutors.

Otho, then, after Galba and Piso had been killed at Rome, seized power amid riots and bloodshed. He soon learned that Vitellius had been made emperor in Gaul by the German legions, and he began a civil war. At first he met Vitellius' generals in three minor battles, one near the Alps, another around Placentia, and a third near the place called Castores, and came out the victor. In a fourth battle, at Bedriacum, he saw that his men were being defeated, and he killed himself in the third month after he had begun to reign.

Vitellius came to Rome as victor. There he did many cruel and wicked things and also disgraced human life with his unbelievable appetite and gluttony. When he learned about Vespasian, he first tried to lay down his power. Then, urged on by certain men, he drove Vespasian's brother Sabinus, who suspected no harm at the time, into the Capitol together with the other Flavians. He set the temple on fire, and the flames and the collapse together brought them all to a single death and a single tomb.

Later his army went over to Vespasian's side and he was left deserted. As the enemy drew near he hid in terror in a small room next to the palace. He was dragged out of it in the most shameful way and led naked along the Sacred Way, while people on all sides threw dung in his face. He was brought into the Forum, and in the eighth month after he had seized the throne he was tortured to death at the Gemonian Steps with many tiny stabs. Then he was dragged off with a hook and thrown into the Tiber, and was denied even an ordinary burial.
For many days, moreover, Vespasian's soldiers raged against the senate and people of Rome in many wicked ways, killing without distinction.
In the 825th year from the founding of the City, when that brief but turbulent storm of tyrants had been driven off, peaceful [?] returned under the leadership of Vespasian.

To go back a little further: after the passion of Christ the Jews were wholly deprived of the grace of God and beset on all sides by every kind of evil. Some of them on Mount Carmel were led astray by oracles which foretold that leaders who arose from Judea would become masters of the world. Applying the prophecy to themselves, they broke out in rebellion. They wiped out the Roman garrisons, and when the governor of Syria came to help, they captured his eagle, cut his forces to pieces and put him to flight.

Vespasian was sent against them by Nero, and among his lieutenants was his elder son Titus; for he took many strong legions with him into Syria. He captured many of their towns and shut the Jews up under siege in the city of Jerusalem, where they had gathered in especially large numbers for a festival. When he learned of Nero's death, he was urged by a great many kings and generals to take the imperial power. He was swayed above all by the words of Josephus, a leader of the Jews, who, when he was captured and being thrown into chains, had declared with complete confidence, as Suetonius reports, that he would soon be freed by the same man, but by him as emperor. So Vespasian assumed the imperial power. He left his son Titus in the camp to carry on the siege of Jerusalem and set out for Rome by way of Alexandria; but when he learned that Vitellius had been killed, he stayed for a while in Alexandria.

Titus pressed the Jews hard in a long, heavy siege, and with siege engines and every kind of war machine, and not without much bloodshed among his own men, he at last broke through the city walls. But to storm the inner fortifications of the temple, which a crowd of priests and leaders who had shut themselves in were defending, required greater force and more time.

When it had been brought under his control, he admired it for its workmanship and its antiquity, and he long debated whether to burn it, since it spurred the enemy on, or to preserve it as a witness to his victory. But since the Church of God was now flourishing richly throughout the world, by God's decision this temple, worn out and empty and of no good use, had to be removed.

So Titus, who had been proclaimed emperor by the army, burned and destroyed the temple at Jerusalem, which had stood for 1,102 years from the day it was first founded to the day of its final overthrow. He levelled all the walls of the city to the ground.

Cornelius Tacitus and Suetonius report that 600,000 Jews were killed in that war. But Josephus the Jew, who commanded in that war at the time and had won pardon and favour with Vespasian for foretelling his rule, writes that 1,100,000 perished by the sword and by famine, and that the remnant of the Jews were driven off under various conditions and scattered over the whole world. Their number is said to have been about 90,000 people.

The emperors Vespasian and Titus entered the City celebrating a magnificent triumph over the Jews. Among the 320 triumphs that had been held from the founding of the City up to that time, this was a fair sight and one never before seen by any mortal: a father and son riding in one triumphal chariot, bringing home a most glorious victory over those who had offended the Father and the Son.

They at once put down all wars and disturbances at home and abroad and proclaimed peace throughout the world, and they themselves decreed that the double Janus be shut fast with its bars, only the sixth time this had been done since the founding of the City. It was right that the same honour should be given to avenging the Lord's passion as had been given to his birth.

From then on, without any tumult of war, the Roman state grew beyond measure. Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, Cilicia and Commagene were then for the first time made into provinces and became subject to Roman judges and laws.
In the ninth year of his reign three cities of Cyprus collapsed in an earthquake, and there was a great plague at Rome.
Vespasian died of dysentery on his own estate in the Sabine country in the ninth year of his reign.

In the 828th year from the founding of the City, Titus, the eighth emperor after Augustus if Otho and Vitellius are left out of the count, reigned for two years after Vespasian. His reign was so peaceful that he is said never to have shed anyone's blood in governing the state.

Yet at that time a fire suddenly broke out at Rome and a great many public buildings were burned down. They say too that the summit of Mount Vesuvius then burst open and poured out great fires, and that torrents of flame destroyed the surrounding region together with its cities and people.
Titus died of illness, amid the deep grief of all, on the same estate as his father.

In the 830th year from the founding of the City, Domitian, the brother of Titus and the ninth emperor after Augustus, succeeded his brother on the throne. Over fifteen years he climbed step by step through every degree of crime, until he dared to try to tear up the Church of Christ, now firmly established throughout the world, by issuing edicts of the cruellest persecution everywhere.

He sank into such arrogance that he ordered himself to be called, addressed in writing and worshipped as lord and god. Out of envy and for plunder he put to death some of the noblest members of the senate openly; others he drove into exile and had them murdered there. He committed every unbridled lust that can be imagined. He put up a great many buildings in the City, ruining the fortunes of the Roman people to do so.

He waged war against the Germans and the Dacians through his generals, with equal ruin to the state: in the City he himself tore the senate and people to pieces, while abroad his badly led army was being worn down by constant slaughter at the hands of the enemy.

I would set out at length how great were the battles of Diurpaneus, king of the Dacians, with the general Fuscus, and how great the losses of the Romans, had not Cornelius Tacitus, who wrote this history with the greatest care, said that Sallust and a great many other authors had made it a rule to keep silent about the number of the slain, and that he himself had chosen to do the same above all. Domitian, however, puffed up with the most perverse boastfulness, celebrated a triumph for his destroyed legions under the name of conquered enemies.

Wild with the same pride that made him want to be worshipped as a god, he ordered a persecution of the Christians, the second after Nero's. At this time the most blessed apostle John was also banished to the island of Patmos.

Among the Jews, too, orders were given to hunt out the line of David through harsh tortures and the bloodiest interrogation, and to put it to death. For he both feared and believed the holy prophets, as though someone were still to come from the seed of David who could gain the kingdom.
Soon after, however, Domitian was cruelly murdered in the palace by his own people. His corpse was carried out on a common bier by the undertakers of the poor and buried in the most shameful way.

In the 846th year from the founding of the City (though Eutropius wrote that it was the 850th), Nerva, a very old man, was made the tenth emperor after Augustus by Petronius, the praetorian prefect, and by Parthenius the eunuch, Domitian's murderer. He adopted Trajan as heir to the throne, and through him divine providence truly came to the aid of the afflicted state.

By his first edict he recalled all the exiles; and so the apostle John too was freed by this general pardon and returned to Ephesus. After completing one year of his reign, Nerva was overcome by illness and died.
In the year [?] from the founding of the City, Trajan, a Spaniard by birth and the eleventh emperor after Augustus, took over the helm of the state from Nerva and held it for nineteen years.

He assumed the insignia of imperial power at Agrippina, a city of Gaul. He soon restored Germany beyond the Rhine to its former state; beyond the Danube he subdued many nations; and he made provinces of the regions lying beyond the Euphrates and the Tigris.

He occupied Seleucia, Ctesiphon and Babylon. In persecuting the Christians, however, he was led astray by error, being the third to do so after Nero. He had ordered that Christians found anywhere should be forced to sacrifice to idols and those who refused should be killed, and very many were being killed. Then he was informed by a report from Pliny the Younger, who had been appointed persecutor along with other judges, that these people did nothing against Roman law apart from confessing Christ and holding decent gatherings, and that, trusting in their innocent confession, none of them thought death grievous or frightening. At once he softened the edict with milder rescripts.

Even so, soon afterwards the Golden House at Rome, which Nero had built at the cost of all private and public wealth, was suddenly consumed by fire. This was so that it might be understood that the persecution, though launched by another, was being punished above all in the monuments of the man with whom it had first begun, and in its very author.

Four cities of Asia, Elea, Myrina, Pitane and Cyme, were overthrown by an earthquake, as were two cities of Greece, those of the Opuntians and the Oritae; three cities of Galatia were destroyed in the same earthquake. The Pantheon at Rome was burned by lightning. An earthquake at Antioch brought down almost the entire city.

Then, in an incredible uprising, the Jews broke out all at once in different parts of the world, as though driven wild with frenzy. Throughout all Libya they waged the most savage wars against the inhabitants, and the land was so laid waste by the killing of those who farmed it that it would have remained completely empty, stripped of its people, had not the emperor Hadrian later gathered colonists from elsewhere and settled them there.

They threw all Egypt, Cyrene and the Thebaid into turmoil with bloody revolts. At Alexandria, however, they were defeated and crushed in battle. In Mesopotamia too, war was made on them by the emperor's order when they rebelled; and so many thousands of them were wiped out in a vast slaughter.
They also destroyed Salamis, a city of Cyprus, killing all its inhabitants. Trajan, as some report, died of dysentery at Seleucia, a city of Isauria.
In the 867th year from the founding of the City, Hadrian, the son of Trajan's cousin, became the twelfth emperor after Augustus and reigned for twenty-one years.
