He was taught and instructed through books written about the Christian religion by Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, by Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom, and by Serenus Granius, a legate. He gave orders in a letter sent to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that no one should be allowed to condemn Christians without a charge being brought or proved.

Soon afterwards he was given the title Father of his Country in the senate, contrary to ancestral custom, and his wife was named Augusta. Hadrian ordered the state with the most just laws. He waged war against the Sarmatians and conquered them.

The Jews, driven wild by the turmoil of their own crimes, were ravaging the province of Palestine, once their own. He subdued them with a final slaughter and avenged the Christians, whom the Jews under their leader Cochebas were torturing because they would not side with them against the Romans.

He ordered that no Jew should be allowed to enter Jerusalem, and the city was opened to Christians only. He restored it to an excellent condition by building walls, and ordered it to be called Aelia after his own first name.

In the 888th year from the founding of the City, Antoninus, surnamed Pius, was made the thirteenth emperor after Augustus. With his children Aurelius and Lucius he governed the state for not quite twenty-three years, so peacefully and righteously that he was rightly named Pius and Father of his Country.

In his time, however, the arch-heretic Valentinus and Cerdo, the teacher of Marcion, came to Rome. But Justin the philosopher presented to Antoninus a book he had written in defence of the Christian religion, and made him kindly disposed toward Christians. Antoninus fell ill at the twelfth milestone from the City and died.

In the 911th year from the founding of the City, Marcus Antoninus Verus, the fourteenth emperor after Augustus, took the throne together with his brother Aurelius Commodus and held it for nineteen years. They were the first to govern the state with equal rights.

They then waged war against the Parthians with remarkable courage and success. Annius Antoninus Verus set out for that war; for Vologeses, king of the Parthians, had made a fierce invasion and was ravaging Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria.

But Antoninus, after great exploits carried out by his very energetic generals, captured Seleucia, a city of Assyria on the river Hydaspes, with 400,000 people, and celebrated a triumph over the Parthians with his brother. Not long afterwards, while sitting in a carriage with his brother, he was struck by the illness the Greeks call apoplexy and choked to death.

After his death Marcus Antoninus ruled the state alone. But during the Parthian war, by his command, severe persecutions of the Christians took place in Asia and Gaul, the fourth since Nero, and many of the saints were crowned with martyrdom.

There followed a plague that spread through a great many provinces, and so great a pestilence ravaged all Italy that everywhere estates, fields and towns were left without farmers or inhabitants and fell into ruins and forest.

They say that the Roman army and all the legions stationed far and wide in distant winter quarters were so wasted away that the Marcomannic War, which broke out immediately afterwards, could only be fought with a new levy of soldiers, which Marcus Antoninus carried on continuously for three years at Carnuntum.
That this war was directed by the providence of God has been shown quite plainly by many proofs, and above all by a letter of that most dignified and moderate emperor.

Peoples of barbarous savagery and countless numbers had risen up: the Marcomanni, Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Suebi and almost all Germany. The army had advanced into the territory of the Quadi and was surrounded by the enemy, and because of the lack of water it faced a more pressing danger from thirst than from the enemy.

Then some soldiers, with great steadfastness of faith, suddenly poured themselves out in prayer and openly called on the name of Christ. At this such a downpour of rain fell that it refreshed the Romans abundantly and without harm, while the barbarians, terrified by repeated strokes of lightning, especially as very many of them were being killed, were driven to flight.

The Romans cut them down from behind until they were wiped out, and with a small number of raw soldiers but with the mighty help of Christ they won a most glorious victory, one to be ranked above almost all the honours of the ancients.

It is said that letters of the emperor Antoninus still exist in many people's hands, in which he admits that both that thirst was driven off and the victory was granted through the calling on of the name of Christ by Christian soldiers.

This same Antoninus took his son Commodus as co-ruler. He also remitted the taxes owed from past years in all the provinces, ordered all the vexatious records of fiscal business to be gathered together in the Forum and burned, and softened the harsher laws with new enactments. Finally, while staying in Pannonia, he died of a sudden illness.
In the 930th year from the founding of the City, Lucius Antoninus Commodus, the fifteenth emperor after Augustus, succeeded his father on the throne and held it for thirteen years.

He waged war successfully against the Germans. But in everything else he was corrupted by the disgrace of luxury and obscenity. He very often fought with gladiator's weapons in the training school and frequently exposed himself to wild beasts in the amphitheatre. He also put to death a great many senators, especially those he noticed excelled in nobility and ability.

The punishment of the City followed the crimes of its ruler. The Capitol was struck by lightning, and the fire that started from it, in a devouring whirlwind, burned that library which had been assembled through the care and zeal of their ancestors, along with other buildings nearby. Later another fire broke out at Rome and levelled the temple of Vesta, the Palace and a great part of the City to the ground.
Commodus, a nuisance to everyone, is said to have died by strangulation in the house of Vestilianus, having been judged an enemy of the human race, even of one [?].

After him the old man Helvius Pertinax was made emperor by the senate, the sixteenth after Augustus. In the sixth month after he had begun to reign he was murdered in the palace through the crime of Julianus, a jurist.

After Pertinax was killed, Julianus seized power, but he was soon defeated in civil war by Severus at the Milvian Bridge and killed, in the seventh month after he had begun to reign. So one year was taken up between Pertinax and Julianus.

In the 944th year from the founding of the City, Severus, an African from Tripolitania, from the town of Leptis, became the seventeenth emperor after Augustus. He wished to be called Pertinax after the emperor whose murder he had avenged. He gained the empire when it had been left without a ruler and held it for eighteen years.

Cruel by nature and constantly harassed by many wars, he ruled the state very vigorously, but with very great toil. At Cyzicus he defeated and killed Pescennius Niger, who had aimed at tyranny in Egypt and Syria. He put down the Jews and Samaritans with the sword when they tried to rebel.
He overcame the Parthians, the Arabs and the Adiabeni. He tortured the Christians in the fifth persecution since Nero, and a great many of the saints in various provinces were crowned with martyrdom.

This impious presumption of Severus against the Christians and the Church of God was followed at once by heavenly vengeance. For straightaway Severus was hurried, or rather dragged back, from Syria to Gaul for a third civil war.

He had already fought one at Rome against Julianus and another in Syria against Pescennius. The third was stirred up by Clodius Albinus, Julianus' partner in the murder of Pertinax, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul. In this war much Roman blood was shed on both sides. Albinus, however, was crushed and killed at Lugdunum.

Severus, the victor, was drawn into Britain by the defection of almost all the allies. There, after often fighting great and hard battles, he decided that the part of the island he had recovered should be separated from the other, unconquered peoples by a rampart. So he built a great ditch and a very strong rampart, reinforced as well with many towers, for 132 miles from sea to sea.
There he died of illness at the town of Eboracum. He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Geta was declared a public enemy and died; Bassianus took the surname Antoninus and gained the throne.
In the 962nd year from the founding of the City, Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, also called Caracalla, became emperor, the eighteenth from Augustus, and he held the office for not quite seven years.

He lived more harshly than his father, and more unrestrained in lust than any man, for he even married his stepmother Julia. While preparing a war against the Parthians, he was surrounded by the enemy between Edessa and Carrhae and killed.

After him Opilius Macrinus, who was praetorian prefect, seized power as the nineteenth from Augustus, together with his son Diadumenus; but as soon as a year had passed he was killed in a military uprising at Archelais.
In the 970th year from the founding of the City, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus became emperor, the twentieth from Augustus, and held power for four years.

He was a priest of the temple of Heliogabalus, and left behind no memory of himself except an infamous one of debauchery, outrages and every kind of obscenity. When a military uprising broke out, he was killed at Rome together with his mother.

In the 974th year from the founding of the City, Aurelius Alexander was made emperor, the twenty-first from Augustus, by the will of the senate and the soldiers, and for thirteen years he earned well-deserved praise for his justice.

His mother Mamaea, a Christian, took care to hear the presbyter Origen. And indeed, as soon as he had launched an expedition against the Persians, he crushed their king Xerxes and was victorious in a very great war.
With Ulpian as his assessor he showed the greatest moderation in governing the state; but he was killed in a military uprising near Mainz.

In the 987th year from the founding of the City, Maximinus, the twenty-second from Augustus, was made emperor by the army without any consent of the senate, after he had waged a successful war in Germany, and he carried out a persecution against the Christians, the sixth since Nero.

But at once, that is, in the third year of his reign, he was killed by Pupienus at Aquileia, and so came to the end of both his persecution and his life. He had launched the persecution against the priests and clergy, that is, the teachers, chiefly because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of Alexander's mother Mamaea, and above all because of the presbyter Origen.

In the 991st year from the founding of the City, Gordian was made emperor, the twenty-third from Augustus, and remained in office for six years. For Pupienus, the killer of Maximinus, and his brother Balbinus, who had usurped power, were soon killed in the Palace.

Gordian, still quite a boy, when about to set out for the East to the Parthian war, opened the gates of Janus, as Eutropius writes. Whether anyone closed them after Vespasian and Titus I do not recall anyone having written, although Cornelius Tacitus reports that they were opened by Vespasian himself a year later.
So Gordian, after fighting great battles successfully against the Parthians, was killed through the treachery of his own men not far from Circesium on the Euphrates.
In the 997th year from the founding of the City, Philip was made emperor, the twenty-fourth from Augustus; he made his son Philip his partner in rule, and remained in power for seven years.

He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian, and after the third year of his reign the thousandth year from the founding of Rome was completed. Thus this birthday year, the most august of all that had passed, was celebrated with magnificent games by a Christian emperor.

Nor is there any doubt that Philip gave the thanks and honor for this great devotion to Christ and the Church, since no author reports that there was any procession up to the Capitol or that victims were sacrificed according to custom.
Both of them, however, though in different places, were killed in a military uprising and through the treachery of Decius.

In the 1004th year from the founding of the City, Decius, who had both stirred up and put down the civil war, seized power after the Philips were killed, the twenty-fifth from Augustus, and held it for three years.

At once, thereby showing that he had killed the Philips for this very reason, he sent out deadly edicts, the seventh after Nero, for the persecution and killing of Christians, and sent very many of the saints from their crosses to the crowns of Christ.
He also chose his son as Caesar, and together with him was soon killed in the midst of the barbarians' territory.
In the 1007th year from the founding of the City, Gallus Hostilianus gained the throne, the twenty-sixth from Augustus, and held it with his son Volusianus for barely two years.

Vengeance for the violated Christian name now came forth, and as far as the edicts of Decius had run for the destruction of the churches, so far did a plague of incredible diseases spread. There was scarcely a Roman province, scarcely a city, scarcely a house, that was not seized and emptied by that universal pestilence.

Gallus and Volusianus, notable only for this calamity, were killed while preparing a civil war against Aemilianus, who was plotting revolution. Aemilianus, however, perished in the third month of the tyranny he had seized.

In the 1010th year from the founding of the City, two emperors were made in the twenty-seventh place after Augustus: Valerian was hailed as Augustus by the army in Raetia, while at Rome Gallienus was made Caesar by the senate. Gallienus remained on the throne unhappily for fifteen years, while the human race had a brief respite from that pestilence, which had been more continuous and severe than usual. But forgetful wickedness provokes its own punishment. For impiety does indeed feel the scourges when it is tormented, but, hardened, it does not perceive by whom it is scourged.

To say nothing of earlier times: after Decius had carried out his persecution of the Christians, a great pestilence afflicted the whole Roman Empire. Iniquity lied to itself, ensnared to its own ruin by perverse judgment, claiming that the pestilence was a common chance and that death from disease was nature's end, not a punishment.

So once again, and quickly, it provokes the wrath of God by wicked deeds, only to receive a blow that it would be forced to remember for some time. For as soon as Valerian had seized power, he, the eighth after Nero, ordered Christians to be driven to idolatry by torture and those who refused to be killed, and the blood of the saints was shed throughout the whole breadth of the Roman realm.

Immediately Valerian, the author of that wicked edict, was captured by Shapur, king of the Persians, and he, emperor of the Roman people, grew old among the Persians in the most shameful servitude. For as long as he lived he was condemned without respite to this degrading duty: bending down to the ground, he would always lift up the king when he was about to mount his horse, not with his hand but with his back.

Gallienus, terrified by so clear a judgment of God and shaken by the wretched example of his colleague, restored peace to the churches with anxious amends. But the captivity of one impious man, however lasting and however exceedingly abominable, does not make up the measure of injury and vengeance for so many thousands of tortured saints; and the blood of the righteous, crying out to God, asks to be avenged in the very land where it was shed.

For just judgment demanded punishment not only of the man who issued the decree but also of those who carried it out, the informers, the accusers, the spectators and the judges, and finally of all who assented to that most unjust cruelty even by silent consent—since God knows what is hidden. And since these made up the greater part of the people in every province, it was just that they should be struck by the same blow of vengeance. Suddenly, by God's permission, the nations placed and left all around for this very purpose were let loose on every side, and with the reins slackened they burst into every territory of the Romans.

The Germans broke through the Alps, Raetia and all Italy and reached as far as Ravenna; the Alamanni roamed through the provinces of Gaul and even crossed into Italy; Greece, Macedonia, Pontus and Asia were laid waste by a flood of Goths; Dacia beyond the Danube was lost forever; the Quadi and Sarmatians ravaged the Pannonias; Germans from farther away stripped Spain bare and took possession of it; the Parthians took Mesopotamia and scraped Syria clean.

Even now, throughout various provinces, there remain small and poor dwellings amid the ruins of great cities, which preserve the marks of those miseries and the traces of their names. Among them we too in Spain can point to our own Tarragona, as a consolation for our recent misery.

And lest any part of the Roman body should escape this tearing apart, tyrants conspired within, civil wars arose, and everywhere a great deal of Roman blood was shed, with Romans and barbarians alike raging. But the wrath of God was soon turned to mercy, and the vengeance that had begun was counted as full measure more for the shape it took than for the punishment it actually inflicted.

So first Ingenuus, who had assumed the imperial purple, was killed at Mursa. Postumus seized power as a usurper in Gaul, though greatly to the benefit of the state, for over ten years, acting with great courage and moderation, he drove out the enemies who were lording it there and restored the lost provinces to their former condition; yet he was killed in a mutiny of the soldiers.

Aemilianus was crushed near Mainz while plotting revolution. After the death of Postumus, Marius seized power in the same place but was killed at once. Then Victorinus was made emperor by the Gauls of their own accord, and was killed shortly afterward.

He was succeeded by Tetricus, who at the time was serving as governor of Aquitania. He endured many mutinies of the soldiers. In the East, however, a certain Odenathus gathered a band of country folk, by which the Persians were defeated and driven back, Syria was defended and Mesopotamia recovered; and the peasants of Syria, with their Odenathus, went on conquering as far as Ctesiphon.
Gallienus, meanwhile, having abandoned the state and giving himself over to his lusts at Milan, was killed.

In the 1025th year from the founding of the City, Claudius, the twenty-eighth, took power by the will of the senate. He at once attacked the Goths, who had already been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years, and destroyed them with incredible slaughter. For this the senate decreed him a golden shield in the senate house and a statue, likewise of gold, on the Capitol. But soon afterward, before he had completed two years in power, he was seized by disease at Sirmium and died.

After Claudius died, his brother Quintillus was chosen emperor by the army. He was a man of singular moderation, the only one fit to be preferred even to his brother, but he was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign.
In the 1027th year from the founding of the City, Aurelian, the twenty-ninth, gained power and held it for five years and six months, a man most outstanding in military skill.

Undertaking an expedition to the Danube, he routed the Goths in great battles and restored Roman rule to its ancient boundaries. Then, turning to the East, he brought under his power Zenobia, who after the killing of her husband Odenathus was claiming for herself the recovered Syria; and he did so more by the terror of battle than by battle itself.

Tetricus, who in Gaul was quite unable to withstand the mutinies of his own soldiers and even wrote to him, "Rescue me, unconquered one, from these evils," and so betrayed his own army, he overcame without effort. Thus, as the recoverer of East and North, he celebrated a triumph with great glory.

He surrounded the city of Rome with stronger walls. Finally, when he decreed that a persecution be carried out against the Christians, the ninth since Nero, a thunderbolt fell in front of him, to the great terror of those standing around, and not long afterward he was killed on a journey.

In the 1032nd year from the founding of the City, Tacitus, the thirtieth, gained power and was killed in Pontus in the sixth month. After him Florianus, meeting a like fate in his reign, was killed at Tarsus in only the third month.

In the 1033rd year from the founding of the City, Probus, the thirty-first, obtained the throne and held it for six years and four months. Through many hard battles he at last destroyed the enemy and completely freed the provinces of Gaul, which had long been occupied by barbarians.

After this he waged two civil wars, indeed with a great deal of bloodshed: one in the East, in which he crushed and captured Saturninus, who had relied on usurped power; the other in which he defeated Proculus and Bonosus at Cologne in great battles and killed them. He himself was killed in a military uprising at Sirmium, in an iron-clad tower.

In the 1039th year from the founding of the City, Carus of Narbo, the thirty-second, took up power and held it for two years. He made his sons Carinus and Numerian partners in rule, and in the Parthian war, after capturing two of the most renowned cities of the Parthians, Coche and Ctesiphon, he was struck by lightning in his camp on the Tigris and died. Numerian, who had been with his father, was killed on the return journey through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper.

In the 1041st year from the founding of the City, Diocletian, the thirty-third, was chosen emperor by the army and reigned for twenty years. As soon as he had the means of power, he killed Aper, the murderer of Numerian, with his own hand. Then, in a very hard war and with very great effort, he overcame Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Dalmatia and who was living a scandalous life.

Next, when in Gaul Amandus and Aelianus had gathered a band of peasants, whom they called Bagaudae, and stirred up dangerous disturbances, he made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, Caesar and sent him to Gaul. He easily subdued, by military

skill, the untrained and disorderly band of country folk. Then a certain Carausius, a man of the lowest birth but quick in counsel and action, had been stationed to guard the shores of the Ocean, which at that time the Franks and Saxons were harassing. But he acted more to the ruin than to the advantage of the state: he returned none of the plunder recovered from the raiders to its owners but kept it all for himself, and so aroused the suspicion that he was deliberately and cunningly neglectful, allowing the enemy themselves to raid the frontier. For this reason Maximian ordered him to be put to death, whereupon he assumed the purple and seized Britain.

So throughout all the territories of the Roman Empire the crash of sudden upheavals resounded: Carausius was in revolt in Britain, Achilleus in Egypt, while the Quinquegentiani were harassing Africa and Narses, king of the Persians, was pressing the East with war.

Alarmed by this danger, Diocletian promoted Maximian Herculius from Caesar to Augustus, and chose Constantius and Maximian Galerius as Caesars. Constantius took as his wife Theodora, the stepdaughter of Maximian Herculius, and by her had six sons, the brothers of Constantine.

Carausius, after claiming and holding Britain most vigorously for seven years, was at last killed through the treachery of his associate Allectus. Allectus then held the island he had taken from Carausius for three years; but Asclepiodotus, the praetorian prefect, crushed him and recovered Britain after ten years.

Constantius Caesar, in Gaul, saw his army routed by the Alamanni in the first battle and himself barely escaped; but in the second a quite favorable victory followed, for sixty thousand Alamanni are reported to have been slain within a few hours.

Maximian Augustus, for his part, subdued the Quinquegentiani in Africa. Diocletian, moreover, besieged Achilleus at Alexandria for eight months, captured him and put him to death. But he used his victory without restraint, gave Alexandria over to plunder, and defiled all Egypt with proscriptions and massacres.

Galerius Maximian, meanwhile, after having already fought two battles against Narses, engaged him a third time between Callinicum and Carrhae and was defeated; having lost his forces, he fled back to Diocletian. He was received by him with the utmost arrogance, so much so that he is reported to have run for several miles in front of Diocletian's carriage, dressed in his purple.

Yet he used this insult as a whetstone for his courage: by it the rust of royal pride was rubbed away and the edge of his mind was sharpened. So he soon gathered forces from all sides through Illyricum and Moesia, swiftly returned against the enemy, and overcame Narses by great strategy and strength.

Having destroyed the Persian forces and put Narses himself to flight, he seized his camp, captured his wives, sisters and children, plundered an immense quantity of the Persian treasure, and led away a great many Persian nobles as captives. On his return to Mesopotamia he was received by Diocletian with the greatest honor.

Afterwards, under the same commanders, vigorous campaigns were fought against the Carpi and the Bastarnae. Then they defeated the Sarmatians, and distributed a very large multitude of captives among the garrisons along the Roman frontiers.

Meanwhile Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered the churches to be laid waste and the Christians to be afflicted and killed, the tenth persecution after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those before it, for it was carried on without ceasing for ten years, with the burning of churches, the proscription of the innocent and the slaughter of martyrs.

There followed an earthquake in Syria, in which many thousands of people were crushed at Tyre and Sidon as buildings collapsed everywhere. In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian compelled the unwilling Maximian to lay down the purple and the imperial power together with him, so that, with younger men put in their place to run the state, they themselves might grow old in private leisure. So on a single day Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down both the power and the regalia of empire.

Galerius and Constantius, as Augusti, were the first to divide the Roman Empire into two parts: Galerius Maximian took Illyricum, Asia and the East, and Constantius Italy, Africa and the provinces of Gaul. But Constantius, a most peaceable man, was content with Gaul [and Spain] alone and yielded the other regions to Galerius.

Galerius chose two Caesars: Maximinus, whom he installed in the East, and Severus, to whom he entrusted Italy, while he himself was based in Illyricum. Constantius Augustus, a man of the greatest gentleness and courtesy, died in Britain. He left his son Constantine, born of his concubine Helena, as emperor of the Gauls.
In the 1061st year from the founding of the City, Constantine, the thirty-fourth, took over the helm of the empire from his father Constantius, and held it most successfully for thirty-one years.

Here I am suddenly confronted and mocked with a sort of victory dance. "Aha!" they say, "at last you have come into our pits, as we have long expected! Here we were waiting for you to run down; here we pounce on you as you slip; here we hold you in confusion. Until now we have put up with you as you fitted, artfully and cunningly in a way, the chance changes of the times to vengeance for the Christians.

And at times, it is true, moved by the appearance of plausibility, being men ignorant of divine secrets, we turned pale with fear. But now our Maximian has emptied the whole stage of your fable, and the antiquity of our religion has shone out as an impregnable pillar.

For ten years your churches were overthrown, as even you admit; the Christians throughout the world were torn apart by torture and wiped out by death. We hold your own clear testimony that no earlier persecution was so severe or so long.

And yet look: amid the most tranquil blessings of the times there was also an unprecedented good fortune for the very emperors who did these things—no famine at home, no pestilence, no war abroad except by choice, in which strength could be exercised rather than put at risk.

Besides, there was something hitherto unknown to the human race: a partnership of many rulers at once, who bore with one another, in great harmony, and a shared power which, never before but now, looked to the common good.

Then too—something never before known to mortals—those emperors, who were the greatest of rulers and also the persecutors, laid aside their honors and took up a life of rest as private citizens, which people judge the most blessed state and the highest good of a good life; and the authors of the persecution obtained this as a kind of reward at the very time when the persecution they had kindled was raging in mid-course throughout the world.
Or do you claim that even this happiness befell them in those times as a punishment, and are you trying to frighten us with this too?"

To them I would humbly reply that, girded with the deepest concern of devotion, I am warning them about what is true, not frightening them with what is false. The Church of Christ suffered ten persecutions from Nero to Maximian. Nine of them, as I have said, were followed close on their heels by acts of vengeance—or by calamities, as they themselves do not deny. Nor do I insist on the word: whether they are seen as deserved vengeance or as chance changes, they were nevertheless disasters, by my testimony and by theirs.

In the tenth, the wretched and blind think, the pattern faltered, not seeing that it was all the heavier for them the less it was understood. For the wicked man is scourged and does not feel it. When this has been set out, they will admit, however unwillingly, because of the very evidence of the facts, that from that greatest punishment for the persecution under Maximian came those wounds from which they still suffer even now—and suffer so much that they even cry out and provoke us to answer back, so that we must take care how they may be brought to silence.

In the first book we showed that Pompeius Trogus and Cornelius Tacitus mention, though not fully, what our own Moses, whose reliability even they attest, recorded faithfully and in sufficient detail: that the Egyptians and their king were afflicted with ten most bitter plagues. This happened because, when the people of God were intent on serving their God and ready to do so, the Egyptians, driven by a wish to hinder their devotion, called them back to the mud and the straw.

Then, broken by the violence of these afflictions, the Egyptians not only drove the people out in haste but even loaded them with their own vessels of silver and gold. Afterward, forgetting their punishment and greedy for plunder they had no right to, and envious too of another people's religion, they eagerly pursued the innocent, until at last the Red Sea swallowed them all and they perished utterly. I now recall and proclaim this, and even if it is not accepted on faith, it will be proved by the outcome, because these things were done as a figure of us.

Both peoples belong to the one God, and the cause of both peoples is one. The synagogue of the Israelites was subject to the Egyptians; the Church of the Christians is subject to the Romans. The Egyptians persecuted; the Romans persecuted too. There were ten refusals against Moses; here there were ten edicts against Christ. There, various plagues fell on the Egyptians; here, various calamities on the Romans.

To compare the plagues themselves with one another, so far as a figure can be compared with what it prefigures: there the first chastisement was that blood everywhere either oozed from the wells or ran in the rivers; here the first plague, under Nero, brought it about that everywhere there was the blood of the dying, whether corrupted by disease in the City or poured out in wars across the world.

There the next plague showed that frogs, croaking and leaping about in the innermost rooms of houses, all but drove the inhabitants to starvation and exile; here the next punishment, under Domitian, likewise showed that through the wicked and unbridled raids of his henchmen and soldiers, who carried out the orders of a most bloodthirsty emperor, nearly all Roman citizens were reduced to poverty and scattered into exile.

There the third affliction brought gnats, tiny but most savage flies, which often in the height of the summer heat gather in dense, quivering swarms over squalid places, glide in with a whining flight, and burrow into the hair of men and the bristles of cattle with a burning bite. Here likewise the third plague, under Trajan, stirred up the Jews. Though they had previously been scattered everywhere and lay so quiet that they were as if they did not exist, all of them were suddenly seized by a fever and raged throughout the world against the very people among whom they lived. And this is not to mention the great ruin of many cities that frequent earthquakes overthrew at that same time.

There in the fourth plague came dog-flies, truly the nurslings of putrefaction and the mothers of worms; here likewise the fourth plague, under Marcus Antoninus, was a pestilence poured over very many provinces, which struck down all Italy together with the city of Rome, and the Roman army scattered along distant frontiers and in various winter quarters, and gave them over in death to putrefaction and worms alike.

There the fifth chastisement was fulfilled in the sudden death of flocks and beasts of burden; here similarly, by the fifth vengeance, under the persecutor Severus, the very vitals and supports of the commonwealth, that is, the populations of the provinces and the legions of soldiers, were shattered by very frequent civil wars.

There the sixth affliction brought boils breaking out in blisters and running sores; here equally the sixth punishment came after the persecution of Maximinus, who had ordered that bishops and clergy in particular, the leaders of the churches, be slaughtered, while the common crowd was passed over. So the wrath and ill-will that kept swelling up was vented not through the slaughter of the common people but through the wounds and deaths of rulers and men of power.

There the seventh plague counted was hail poured down from the thickened air, which brought destruction to men, beasts and crops; here similarly the seventh plague arose under Gallus and Volusianus, who had succeeded the persecutor Decius after he was soon killed: a pestilence poured out from corrupted air, which through all the expanses of the Roman realm from East to West not only gave over to death almost every kind of man and beast but also "tainted the lakes and poisoned the pastures with its rot."

There the eighth crushing of Egypt was wrought by locusts roused from every side, seizing, grinding down and covering everything; here likewise peoples roused from every side brought the eighth plague to overthrow the Roman world, and they laid waste all the provinces with slaughter and fire.

There the ninth disturbance was a long-lasting, thick and almost palpable darkness, which threatened far more danger than it caused; here likewise there was a ninth chastisement, when Aurelian was decreeing a persecution and a terrible and grim thunderbolt, amid fearful whirlwinds, crashed down at his very feet, showing what so great an Avenger could do when such vengeance was called for, were he not both merciful and patient. Even so, within six months from then three successive emperors, namely Aurelian, Tacitus and Florian, were killed for various reasons.

There, finally, the tenth plague, which was also the last of all, was the slaying of the sons that each had begotten first; here no less the tenth, that is, the last punishment, is the destruction of all the idols, which they loved first of all because they had made them first.

There the king felt, acknowledged and feared the power of God, and therefore allowed the people of God to go away free; here the king felt, acknowledged and believed in the power of God, and therefore allowed the people of God to be free. There the people of God were never afterward dragged back into slavery; here the people of God were never afterward forced into idolatry. There the precious vessels of the Egyptians were handed over to the Hebrews; here the chief temples of the pagans passed to the churches of the Christians.

Yet, as I said, I think this must be proclaimed: just as eternal destruction fell upon the Egyptians through the sea brought over them when, after these ten plagues, they set out to pursue the Hebrews they had released, so a persecution by the Gentiles awaits us too, who are now journeying in freedom as pilgrims; it will come upon us at some time, until we cross the Red Sea, that is, the fire of judgment, with our Lord Jesus Christ himself as our leader and judge.

Those into whom the figure of the Egyptians passes will rage with power granted them for a time, and by God's permission they will persecute the Christians with the most grievous tortures. But all these same enemies of Christ, together with their king, Antichrist, will be received into the lake of eternal fire, which they enter without seeing it because a great darkness blocks their sight, and their lot will be perpetual destruction, to burn in undying torments.

So, when Constantius died in Britain, as I said, Constantine was made emperor. He was the first Christian among the emperors, except for Philip, who, it seems to me, was established as a Christian for only a very few years solely so that the thousandth year of Rome might be dedicated to Christ rather than to idols.

From Constantine onward, however, all the emperors created down to the present day have been Christians, except Julian, whose life, so they say, failed him in ruin while he was plotting impious deeds.

This is that slow but certain punishment of the pagans. Because of it the sane go mad, the unwounded feel the sting, the laughing groan, the living waste away; because of it those whom no one persecutes are tortured in secret; because of it very few now remain who have never been punished by any persecutor.
Nevertheless I will explain what end then awaited those persecutors, about whose escape from punishment the pagans try not only to boast but even to taunt us.

While Constantine was governing the commonwealth with great energy in Gaul, the praetorian soldiers at Rome proclaimed as Augustus Maxentius, the son of Herculius, who was living as a private citizen in Lucania.

Maximian Herculius, by now a private citizen instead of Augustus but still a public persecutor, was tempted by the opportunity his son's elevation offered and, though he had cast off imperial power, seized the tyranny.
Galerius Augustus sent Severus Caesar with an army against Maxentius at Rome.
While Severus was besieging the City, he was deserted and betrayed through the treachery of his own soldiers, fled, and was killed at Ravenna.

Herculius Maximian, a persecutor and, having once been Augustus, now a tyrant, tried to strip his son, already established in power, of his royal robes and authority. But he was openly frightened off by the abuse and uproar of the soldiers and set out for Gaul, intending by an equally treacherous alliance to take the empire from Constantine, his son-in-law.
But he was found out and betrayed by his daughter, and then, having taken to flight, he was caught and killed at Massilia.
Meanwhile Galerius, after Severus had been killed, made Licinius emperor.

Galerius had himself added even harsher edicts to the persecution launched by Diocletian and Maximian, and for ten years he drained the provinces of every kind of person. Then his chest rotted inwardly and his vital organs decayed; beyond the horror of ordinary human misery he even vomited worms, and his physicians, no longer able to bear the stench, were put to death one after another at his order.

Rebuked by one physician who took courage from despair, and told that his suffering was the wrath of God and therefore could not be cured by physicians, he sent edicts far and wide recalling the Christians from exile. He himself, however, unable to bear his torments, took his own life.
Thus the commonwealth was then under four new rulers: Constantine and Maxentius, sons of Augusti, and Licinius and Maximinus, new men.
Constantine granted peace to the churches after they had been harassed by the persecutors for ten years.
Then civil war broke out between Constantine and Maxentius. Maxentius, worn down in many battles, was finally defeated and killed at the Milvian Bridge.
Maximinus, the instigator and most hostile executor of the persecution of the Christians, died at Tarsus while preparing a civil war against Licinius.
Licinius, roused by a sudden fit of madness, ordered all Christians to be expelled from his palace. Soon war flared up between this same Licinius and Constantine.

Constantine first defeated Licinius, his sister's husband, in Pannonia, then crushed him at Cibalae, and, having gained possession of all Greece, at last forced him to surrender after Licinius had risen against him again and again in repeated wars on land and sea and been beaten back.

But, moved by the example of his father-in-law Herculius Maximian, and fearing that Licinius might again take up the purple he had laid down, to the ruin of the commonwealth, he ordered him to be killed as a private citizen,

although, since all the other agents of that wicked persecution had by then been destroyed, a fitting punishment was also demanding this man, who had been a persecutor so far as he had been able to show himself one.
Constantine's sons Crispus and Constantine, and the young Licinius, son of Licinius Augustus and Constantine's nephew through his sister, were made Caesars.
In these days Arius, a presbyter of the city of Alexandria, strayed from the truth of the catholic faith and set up a doctrine that proved deadly to very many.

As soon as he had become known, or rather notorious, at Alexandria, amid a crowd of followers and opponents all mixed together, he was driven out of the Church by Alexander, who was then bishop of that city.

And when he went on to stir up to sedition the people he had led into error, a council of three hundred and eighteen bishops was held at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia. Through them the Arian doctrine was most clearly shown to be deadly and wretched, and was publicly exposed and condemned.

But the reasons remain hidden why the emperor Constantine turned the avenging sword and the punishment intended for the impious even against his own kin. For he put to death his son Crispus and his sister's son Licinius.

Moreover, he subdued many peoples in various battles. He was either the first or the only one of the Roman rulers to found a city bearing his own name. This city alone was free of idols, and, founded by a Christian emperor, it advanced in a very short time to the point that it alone can rightly be compared in beauty and power with Rome, which had risen through so many centuries and miseries.
Then Constantine was the first to reverse the situation, in just and pious order: he issued an edict that the temples of the pagans should be closed without any killing of men.
He [?] destroyed the very strong and populous nations of the Goths in the very heart of barbarian territory, that is, in the region of the Sarmatians.
He crushed a certain Calocaerus who was plotting revolution in Cyprus. At his thirtieth-year jubilee he chose Dalmatius as Caesar.
While he was preparing war against the Persians, he died at a public villa near Nicomedia, handing over to his sons a commonwealth well ordered.

In the 1092nd year from the founding of the City, Constantius, the thirty-fifth emperor, obtained the empire together with his brothers Constantine and Constans, and held it for twenty-four years. Among Constantine's successors there was also Dalmatius Caesar, his brother's son, but he was at once cut off by a military faction.

Meanwhile the devil's malicious hostility, ever at war with the true God, which from the beginning of the world until now has spread the fogs of error and thrown the slippery hearts of men into confusion, leading them off the straight path of faith and religion, ceased to persecute Christ's Church through zeal for idolatry once Christian emperors began to turn the supreme royal power toward better ends. So it found another device by which to harass Christ's Church through these same Christian emperors.

Thus Arius, the author of a new error, and his disciples found ready access and an easy way to the friendship of the emperor Constantius. Constantius was persuaded to believe in certain grades within God; and he who had gone out through the door from the error of idolatry was led back into its bosom, as it were through a back door, while he sought gods within God.

So power, deceived, was armed with perverse zeal, and under the name of piety the violence of persecution was set in motion. A struggle arose over the choice of a new name, so that the churches should belong to the Arians rather than to the catholics.

There followed a terrible earthquake, which leveled very many cities of the East. Constantine, while attacking his brother Constans in war, exposed himself to danger with reckless insolence and was killed by Constans's generals.

Constans fought nine battles, with little success, against the Persians and Sapor, who had laid Mesopotamia waste. Finally, forced by the mutiny and lack of discipline of his soldiers to join battle at night, he not only lost a victory almost won but was himself defeated.

Afterward, when he had given himself over to intolerable vices and was buying the soldiers' favor at the expense of the provincials, he was killed through the treachery of Magnentius in a town called Helena, near Spain.
For Magnentius had seized imperial power at Augustodunum, and at once extended it through Gaul, Africa and Italy.
In Illyricum, meanwhile, the soldiers made Vetranio their emperor, a man of great age, simple by nature and pleasant to all, but one who had never learned even the first rudiments of letters.

So, while the old emperor was studying the first letters and syllables, now and then against his will, he was ordered to lay down his power by Constantius, who, burning to avenge his brother, was then preparing war against Magnentius. Casting aside his purple along with his letters, and content with the leisure of a private life, he gave up palace and school alike.

Next Nepotian, the son of Constantine's sister, relying on a band of gladiators, seized imperial power at Rome. Because he was wicked, and therefore hated by all, he was crushed by Magnentius's generals.
There followed that terrible war between Constantius and Magnentius fought at the city of Mursa, in which the great destruction of Roman strength did harm even for the future.

Magnentius, however, was defeated and fled, and not long after killed himself with his own hand at Lugdunum. His brother Decentius too, whom he had put in charge of Gaul as Caesar, ended his life with a noose at Senones.

Constantius at once chose as Caesar Gallus, his uncle's son; but since Gallus behaved cruelly and tyrannically, he put him to death shortly after appointing him. He also took care that Silvanus, who was eager for revolution in Gaul, should be promptly trapped and crushed.

So, after Silvanus had been killed, he made his cousin Julian, the brother of Gallus, Caesar and sent him to Gaul. Julian Caesar, with great energy, restored to wholeness the provinces of Gaul, which had been overturned and oppressed by the enemy; with small forces he routed a great multitude of Alamanni, and he confined the Germans behind the Rhine.

Puffed up by these successes, he usurped the rank of Augustus, and soon, overrunning Italy and Illyricum, he deprived Constantius, who was occupied with wars against the Parthians, of part of his realm.
When Constantius learned of Julian's crime, he abandoned the Parthian campaign, and while returning for civil war he died on the march between Cilicia and Cappadocia.

Thus he who, by tearing apart the peace and unity of the catholic faith and arming Christians against Christians, had rent the members of the Church in what I may call a civil war, spent, passed and exhausted the whole time of his restless reign and the most troubled span of his life in civil wars, stirred up even by his own relatives and kinsmen.

In the 1116th year from the founding of the City, Julian, formerly Caesar, and afterward, as the thirty-sixth from Augustus, master of the state, held supreme power alone for one year and eight months.

He attacked the Christian religion by cunning rather than by force, striving to induce people with honors rather than compel them with tortures to deny the faith of Christ and take up the worship of idols.

Yet he openly decreed by edict that no Christian should be a professor teaching the liberal arts. But, as we have learned from our elders, nearly everyone everywhere accepted the terms of the decree and preferred to give up their office rather than their faith.

Julian, however, while preparing war against the Parthians and drawing Roman forces gathered from every quarter along with him to their appointed destruction, vowed the blood of the Christians to his gods, intending to persecute the churches openly if he could win the victory.

For he even ordered an amphitheater to be built at Jerusalem, in which, on his return from the Parthians, he would throw the bishops, monks and all the saints of that place to beasts made even more savage by training, and watch them being torn apart.

So, after he had moved camp from Ctesiphon, he was led into the desert through the trickery of a certain deserter. As the army was perishing, worn out by thirst and the heat of the sun and, besides, by the toil of the sands, the emperor, anxious at so great a danger, wandered too carelessly through the wastes of the desert, was struck by the lance of an enemy horseman who met him, and died. Thus the merciful God brought impious plans to nothing by the death of the impious man.

In the 1117th year from the founding of the City, Jovian, the thirty-seventh emperor, was made emperor by the army at a moment of extreme crisis. Trapped by the unfavorable terrain and surrounded by enemies, he found no means of escape, and so he made a treaty with Sapor, king of the Persians, which, though considered hardly honorable, was nevertheless quite necessary:
for, in order to free the Roman army safe and unharmed not only from enemy attack but also from the dangers of the terrain, he ceded to the Persians the town of Nisibis and part of upper Mesopotamia.

Then, while traveling through Galatia on his way back to Illyricum, he retired to sleep in a newly built bedchamber, and was overcome and suffocated by the heat of the coals and the fumes from walls recently plastered with lime. So he ended his life in only the eighth month after he had begun to reign.
In the year 1118 from the founding of the City, Valentinian, the thirty-eighth emperor, was made emperor at Nicaea with the agreement of the soldiers, and he held the office for eleven years.

While he was serving under Julian Augustus as tribune of the Scutarii, a Christian keeping his military oath with his faith intact, he was ordered by that sacrilegious emperor either to sacrifice to idols or to leave the army. Knowing faithfully that God's judgments are weightier and his promises better, he left of his own accord.

So, after a short interval, when Julian had been killed and Jovian had soon died, the man who had lost his tribunate for the name of Christ received the empire in place of his persecutor, as Christ's reward.
He later made his brother Valens a partner in the empire, and killed the usurper Procopius and afterwards many of his followers.

An earthquake occurred throughout the whole world and stirred up the sea so violently that, as the sea poured back over the neighbouring lowland areas, a great many cities on islands are said to have been shaken, overthrown and destroyed.

Valens was both baptized and persuaded by Bishop Eudoxius, a champion of the Arian doctrine, and turned aside into that most savage heresy. But for a long time he concealed his malicious hostility and did not let his power serve his wishes, so long as he was held in check by the authority of his brother while he lived.
For he considered how much force could be exerted, as emperor, in avenging the faith by a man who had shown such constancy in holding on to it when he was once a soldier.
In the third year of their reign Gratian, the son of Valentinian, was made emperor. In the same year, at the town of the Atrebates, real wool fell from the clouds mixed with rain.

Moreover, Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted the Christians among his people with the greatest cruelty and raised a great many barbarians, killed for their faith, to the crown of martyrdom. Many of them, however, fled for their confession of Christ to Roman soil, not fearfully, as though going to enemies, but confidently, because they were going to brothers.

Valentinian crushed the Saxons, a people living on the shores of the Ocean and in impassable marshes, fearsome for their courage and swiftness, who were planning with a great force a dangerous invasion of Roman territory; he overwhelmed them on the very borders of the Franks.
There was also the Burgundians, a new name for new enemies, who, it is said, settled on the bank of the river Rhine with more than eighty thousand armed men.

They are said to have once been stationed in camps by Drusus and Tiberius, the adopted sons of Caesar, after the interior of Germany had been subdued, and to have grown together into a great people, and so also to have taken their name from their work, because dwellings set up at frequent intervals along the frontier are commonly called burgi. That their force is very powerful and destructive the Gallic provinces bear witness even today, where they live on the land they have seized.

However, by the providence of God they have all now become Christians of the Catholic faith and have received our clergy, whom they obey, and they live gently, mildly and harmlessly, not as though with subject Gauls but truly with Christian brothers.

In the eleventh year of his reign, when the Sarmatians had spread through the Pannonian provinces and were laying them waste, Valentinian, while preparing war against them at the town of Brigetio, was choked by a sudden effusion of blood, which in Greek is called apoplexy, and died.

After him his son Gratian held the empire of the West, while his uncle Valens was established in the regions of the East; he also made his brother Valentinian, who was still very young, his partner in the empire.

In the year 1128 from the founding of the City, Valens, the thirty-ninth emperor, held the empire for four years after the death of Valentinian, the only man before whom he could have felt shame for his impious conduct. At once, with the reckless boldness of unbridled freedom, he passed a law that monks—that is, Christians who give up the many-sided business of worldly affairs and devote themselves to the single work of faith—should be compelled to serve in the army.

At that time a great multitude of monks had filled and were living in those vast deserts of Egypt and the wide-spreading sands, which human society had never known because of the thirst, the barrenness and the most dangerous abundance of snakes.
Tribunes and soldiers were sent there to drag away the holy and true soldiers of God under another name for persecution. Many companies of saints were killed there.

As for what was done in the various provinces everywhere under these and similar orders against the Catholic churches and the peoples of the right faith, let it be enough that it has been sufficiently indicated by my very choice to keep silent.

Meanwhile, in the regions of Africa, Firmus stirred up the Moorish tribes, set himself up as king, and laid waste Africa and Mauretania. He took Caesarea, the most famous city of Mauretania, by treachery, then filled it with slaughter and fire and gave it to the barbarians as plunder.

So Count Theodosius, father of the Theodosius who later ruled the empire, was sent by Valentinian. He broke the widely scattered Moorish tribes in many battles and drove Firmus himself, beaten and crushed, to his death.

Afterwards, when with the most experienced foresight he had restored all Africa, together with Mauretania, to a better state than before, he was ordered to be put to death through the goading and creeping of envy. At Carthage he chose first to be baptized for the remission of sins, and after he had obtained the sacrament of Christ which he had sought, following a glorious life in this world and now secure also of eternal life, he willingly offered his throat to the executioner.

Meanwhile the emperor Gratian, still quite young, seeing a countless multitude of enemies pouring into Roman territory, relied on the power of Christ and, with a far inferior number of soldiers, threw himself against the enemy. At once, at Argentaria, a town of the Gallic provinces, he brought a most fearsome war to an end with incredible success. For it is said that more than thirty thousand Alamanni were killed in that battle with very slight loss to the Romans.

In the thirteenth year of Valens' reign, that is, a short time after Valens had carried out the tearing apart of churches and the slaughter of saints throughout the whole East, that root of our miseries sprouted at once a great abundance of shoots.

For the people of the Huns, long shut away behind inaccessible mountains, were seized by a sudden frenzy and blazed out against the Goths, threw them into confusion everywhere and drove them from their ancient homes. The Goths, fleeing across the Danube, were received by Valens without any treaty agreement, and did not even hand over their weapons to the Romans, which would have made it safer to trust the barbarians.

Then, driven by hunger and ill-treatment because of the intolerable greed of the general Maximus, they rose up in arms, defeated the army of Valens and poured out across Thrace, throwing everything into confusion with slaughter, burning and plunder.

Valens set out from Antioch, and as he was being drawn on by the final fate of that ill-starred war, he was spurred by a late repentance for his very great sin and ordered the bishops and other holy men to be recalled from exile.

So in the fifteenth year of his reign he fought that lamentable war in Thrace against the Goths, who by then were very well equipped through the exercise of their strength and the abundance of their resources. There, at the very first onset of the Goths, the squadrons of Roman cavalry were thrown into disorder and abandoned the infantry, leaving them unprotected.

Soon the legions of infantry, surrounded on all sides by the enemy cavalry, were first overwhelmed by clouds of arrows; then, as they were driven out of their minds with fear and scattered over trackless ground, they were utterly cut down and perished by the swords and lances of their pursuers.

The emperor himself, wounded by an arrow and put to flight, was carried with difficulty to the hut of a small farmstead and was hiding there when he was discovered by the pursuing enemy; fire was set beneath it and he was burned to death. And so that the testimony of his punishment and of God's indignation might be a more terrible example to later generations, he was even denied a common burial.

Let the obstinacy and wretchedness of the heathen console itself—but in this alone: that in Christian times and under Christian rulers such great disasters, heaped up together, weighed down the bowed neck of the state: provinces overthrown, an army destroyed, an emperor burned. This is truly a great cause of grief to us, and all the more wretched for being so new.

But what does this contribute to the consolation of the pagans, who plainly see that in these events too it was a persecutor of the churches who was punished? The one God has handed down one faith and has spread one Church throughout the whole world: this Church he looks upon, this he loves, this he defends. Under whatever name anyone may hide himself, if he is not joined to it he is a stranger; if he attacks it, he is an enemy.

Let the heathen console themselves as much as they like with the punishments of Jews and heretics, so long as they acknowledge—and above all from this proof, the death of Valens—that there is one God and that he shows no partiality.

The Goths had earlier asked as suppliants, through envoys, that bishops be sent to them from whom they might learn the rule of the Christian faith. The emperor Valens, with ruinous perversity, sent teachers of the Arian doctrine. The Goths held to what they had received as the first rudiments of the faith. And so, by the just judgment of God, they burned alive the very man because of whom they too, even after death, will burn for the fault of their error.

In the year 1132 from the founding of the City, Gratian, the fortieth emperor from Augustus, held the empire for six years after the death of Valens, although he had already been reigning for a long time before that with his uncle Valens and his brother Valentinian.

Seeing the state of the commonwealth [?] and almost collapsed, with the same foresight by which Nerva had once chosen the Spaniard Trajan, through whom the commonwealth was restored, he too chose Theodosius, likewise a Spaniard, and because of the need to restore the commonwealth clothed him in the purple at Sirmium and set him over the government of the East and of Thrace as well,

showing in this an even better judgment, because, while Theodosius was equal to Trajan in all the virtues of human life, in the sacrament of faith and the worship of religion he surpassed him beyond all comparison: for the one was a persecutor of the Church, the other a promoter of it.

So it was that to the one not even a single son of his own was granted, in whom he might rejoice as his successor; whereas the glorious offspring of the other rules both East and West through successive generations down to the present.

So Theodosius believed that the state, afflicted by the wrath of God, was to be restored by the mercy of God. Placing all his confidence in the help of Christ, he attacked without hesitation those very great Scythian peoples, feared by all our ancestors and avoided even by Alexander the Great himself, as Pompeius and Cornelius have testified, but who now, after the destruction of the Roman army, were very well equipped with Roman horses and arms—that is, the Alans, the Huns and the Goths—and defeated them in many great battles.
He entered the city of Constantinople as victor and, so as not to wear down by continual fighting the small band that remained of the Roman army, he made a treaty with Athanaric, king of the Goths.
Athanaric, however, died as soon as he came to Constantinople. When their king was dead, all the Gothic peoples, seeing the courage and kindness of Theodosius, surrendered themselves to Roman rule.

In those same days the Persians too, who, after Julian had been killed and other emperors often defeated, and now that Valens had also been put to flight, were belching out the surfeit of their very recent victory in crude insolence, of their own accord sent envoys to Theodosius at Constantinople and humbly begged for peace. A treaty was then concluded, which the whole East enjoys in the greatest tranquillity down to the present.

Meanwhile, when Theodosius in the East had subdued the barbarian peoples, had at last freed the Thracian provinces from the enemy and had made his son Arcadius his partner in the empire, Maximus—a man indeed energetic and upright and worthy of being Augustus, had he not risen up through usurpation against his oath of loyalty—was made emperor in Britain by the army, almost against his will, and crossed over into Gaul.

There, by a sudden attack, he terrified Gratian Augustus, who was planning to cross into Italy, trapped him by treachery and killed him, and drove his brother Valentinian Augustus out of Italy. Valentinian fled to the East, was received by Theodosius with a father's devotion, and soon was even restored to his throne.

In the year 1138 from the founding of the City, after Gratian had been killed by Maximus, Theodosius, the forty-first emperor, obtained the empire of the Roman world and held it for eleven years, having already reigned for six years in the regions of the East while Gratian was alive.

So, moved to civil war by just and necessary causes—since of the two Augusti, who were brothers, the blood of the one who had been killed demanded vengeance and the misery of the other in exile pleaded for restoration—he placed his hope in God and hurled himself against the usurper Maximus, superior in faith alone, for in every comparison of military preparations he was far inferior.

Maximus was then seated at Aquileia as a spectator of his own victory. His count Andragathius was directing the whole conduct of the war. He had, with an enormous force of soldiers and with outstanding planning that surpassed even the strength of such great forces, fortified all the approaches through the Alps and across the rivers to an incredible degree. Yet by an unspeakable judgment of God, while he was preparing to forestall and overwhelm the unsuspecting enemy by a naval expedition, he of his own accord abandoned the very barriers he had built.

So Theodosius crossed the undefended Alps without anyone noticing, let alone resisting, and arriving at Aquileia unexpectedly, he shut in, captured and killed, without treachery and without a struggle, that great enemy Maximus, a fierce man who exacted tribute and payments even from the most savage peoples of the Germans by the mere terror of his name.

Valentinian recovered Italy and took possession of the empire. Count Andragathius, learning of Maximus' death, threw himself headlong from his ship into the waves and was drowned. Theodosius, by God's arrangement, gained a bloodless victory.

See how, under Christian rulers and in Christian times, civil wars are carried through when they cannot be avoided. Victory was reached, the city was broken into, the usurper was seized. And this is not all. See, elsewhere, a hostile army was defeated and the usurper's count, more ferocious than the usurper himself, was driven to his death; such great plots were undone and frustrated, such great preparations brought to nothing.

And yet no one laid any traps, no one drew up a battle line, and finally no one, if I may say so, drew a sword from its scabbard. A most fearsome war was brought through to victory without bloodshed, and in the victory was concluded by the death of two men.

And so that no one may think this happened by chance, and so that the power of God, by which all things are both ordered and judged, may be declared by its own open testimony and may force the minds of those who clamour against us either to confusion or to faith, I shall tell of something both unknown to all and known to all:

after this war, in which Maximus was killed, many wars, both foreign and civil, have certainly followed upon Theodosius and his son Honorius down to the present, as we all recognize; and yet almost all of them, right up to the present day, have been brought to rest with either no bloodshed or very little, and indeed with the fruit of a simple and holy victory.

So the younger Valentinian, restored to his throne after the deaths of Maximus and of his son Victor, whom Maximus had left as emperor in Gaul, himself crossed into Gaul. There, while he was living in peace and the state was tranquil, he was strangled at Vienne, it is said, through the treachery of his count Arbogast, and, so that he might be thought to have brought about

his own death voluntarily, he was hung up in a noose. When Valentinian Augustus was dead, Arbogast soon dared to create Eugenius as usurper, and chose a man on whom he might put the title of emperor, while he himself, a barbarian, would wield the power. A man excessive in spirit, counsel, hand, daring and power, he gathered from all sides countless and unconquered forces, relying in some places on authority and in others on kinship, whether over Roman garrisons or barbarian auxiliaries.

There is no need to enlarge in words on a history known even to the eyes of very many, which those who witnessed it know better. That Theodosius always emerged victorious by the power of God and not by trust in man, this Arbogast is the outstanding proof in both cases. For he, when he served Theodosius, captured Maximus, who was equipped with such great forces, though he himself had very small ones; and now, when he overflowed against that same Theodosius with the gathered strength of the Gauls and the Franks, relying above all on the worship of idols as well, he nevertheless succumbed with great ease.

Eugenius and Arbogast had deployed their battle lines in readiness on the plains and had cunningly sent ahead ambushes to occupy the narrow flanks of the Alps and the unavoidable passes, so that even had they been inferior in numbers and strength, they would have been victors by the disposition of the war alone.

But Theodosius, stationed on the heights of the Alps, without food or sleep, knowing that he had been abandoned by his own men, though not knowing that he was shut in by the enemy's, prayed alone to the Lord Christ alone, who could do all things, his body stretched on the ground, his mind fixed on heaven.

Then, after spending a sleepless night in continual prayer, and leaving behind pools of tears, almost as witnesses, which he had paid out as the price of heavenly protection, he confidently seized his arms—alone, yet knowing that he was not alone. He gave the signal for battle with the sign of the cross and threw himself into the fight, sure to be victor even if no one followed.

The first way of deliverance was Arbitio, a count of the enemy side. Having caught the unsuspecting emperor in the ambushes set around him, he was moved to reverence for the Augustus before him, and not only freed him from danger but also furnished him with help.

But when they came to the space close enough for joining battle, at once that great and indescribable whirlwind rushed into the faces of the enemy. The javelins thrown by our men were carried through the air and, borne through the great void beyond the range of a human throw, were hardly allowed to fall anywhere before they struck.

Moreover, the unceasing whirlwind now beat against the faces and chests of the enemy by dashing their shields violently against them, now pressed the shields stubbornly upon them and shut them in, now tore them violently away and left them exposed, now kept their shields pushed against them and drove them backwards; even the weapons which they themselves had hurled with force were caught by the gust of wind, turned back and forced in the opposite direction, and pierced their own throwers to their misfortune.

The fear born of human awareness looked to its own safety; for at once, after a small band of their men had been routed, the hostile army prostrated itself before the victorious Theodosius. Eugenius was captured and killed; Arbogast struck himself down with his own hand. So here too a civil war was extinguished by the blood of two men—apart from those ten thousand Goths sent ahead by Theodosius whom Arbogast is said to have wiped out completely. To have lost them was certainly a gain, and to be defeated in this was to win.

I do not insult our detractors. Let them bring forward a single war since the founding of the City that was undertaken from so dutiful a necessity, finished with such divine good fortune, and laid to rest with such merciful kindness, in which neither the battle exacted heavy slaughter nor the victory a bloody revenge, and perhaps I shall concede that these things do not seem to have been granted to the faith of a Christian commander.

Yet I do not need to labour over this testimony, since one of their own, an outstanding poet indeed but a most obstinate pagan, has borne witness both to God and to the man in verses such as these, where he says: “O greatly beloved of God! For you the heavens wage war, and the winds, sworn allies, come at the sound of your trumpets.”
Thus heaven gave judgment between the side that, even without human protection, humbly hoped in God alone, and the side that most arrogantly presumed on its own strength and on idols.
Theodosius, having set the state in order and brought it to tranquillity, died while staying at Milan.

In the year 1149 from the founding of the City, Arcadius Augustus, whose son Theodosius now rules the East, and his brother Honorius Augustus, on whom the state now rests, began to hold the empire in common as the forty-second in the succession, with only their seats divided. Arcadius lived twelve years after his father's death, and when he died he handed the supreme power to his son Theodosius, who was still a very small child.

Meanwhile Count Gildo, who governed Africa at the beginning of their reign, as soon as he learned that Theodosius was dead, either (as some say) set about joining Africa to the eastern part of the empire, driven by some kind of jealousy,

or (as another view has it) judged that there would be very little hope in the young boys. After all, apart from these two, hardly anyone left as a child on the throne had ever survived to reach the maturity of manhood, and they are almost the only ones whom Christ's protection has brought through, divided and helpless as they were, because of their father's outstanding faith and their own. So he dared to seize Africa for himself, cutting it off from the fellowship of the state, content with a barbarian's freedom from restraint rather than puffed up by any ambition to claim the throne.

He had a brother, Mascezel, who shuddered at his brother's plotting of revolution. Leaving his two young sons with the army in Africa, he returned to Italy. Gildo, regarding both his brother's absence and his nephews' presence with suspicion, trapped the young men by treachery and killed them.

Mascezel, his brother, was sent against him to pursue him in war as a public enemy, since the fresh grief of his own bereavement promised that he would be fit to look after the interests of the state. Mascezel knew from Theodosius' example how much a man's prayer, made through faith in Christ, can obtain from the mercy of God in the most desperate circumstances. So he went to the island of Capraria and took with him several holy servants of God, who were moved by his entreaties. With them he spent days and nights continuously in prayer, fasting and psalms, and so earned victory without war and vengeance without bloodshed.

Ardalio is the name of a river that flows between the cities of Theveste and Ammaedara. There he pitched camp with a small force, that is, with five thousand soldiers, as they say, against seventy thousand of the enemy. After some delay he wanted to move from that position and pass through the narrow defile of the valley that lay before him.

As night came on, he seemed to see in a dream the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who had died a little earlier, making a sign with his hand, striking the ground three times with his staff, and saying, "Here, here, here." By a shrewd interpretation he understood that, by the merit of the one announcing it, this was a pledge of victory; that the word indicated the place, and the number the day.

He halted, and at last, on the third day, after a night spent awake in prayers and hymns, he went out straight from the very mysteries of the heavenly sacraments against the enemy, who surrounded him on every side.

While he was speaking dutiful words of peace to those who had met him first, a standard-bearer insolently stood in his way and was on the very point of starting the battle. Mascezel struck him on the arm with his sword, and the wound so disabled his hand that it forced him to lower his standard toward the ground.

Seeing this, the remaining cohorts thought that the front ranks were already surrendering, and they vied with one another in reversing their standards and giving themselves up to Mascezel. The barbarians, of whom Gildo had led a great multitude into the war, were left abandoned by the defection of the soldiers and fled in all directions.
Gildo himself also attempted flight. He seized a ship and put out to sea, but was then driven back to Africa, and some days later he died by strangling.

In recounting such great miracles we would run the risk of appearing to have the effrontery to lie, were it not that the knowledge of those who were present still runs ahead of our words. No plots were laid, no one was bribed; seventy thousand enemies were defeated almost without a fight. The vanquished man fled for a time, so that the victor in his anger might not dare anything further; he was carried off to another place, so that his brother would not know of the killing of the man by whose death he was avenged.

This same Mascezel, however, was carried away by the arrogance that success brings. He set aside the fellowship of the saints with whom he had previously fought for God and conquered, and even dared to violate a church, not hesitating to drag certain people out of it. Punishment followed the sacrilege. For while those whom he had dragged from the church to punishment survived and exulted over him, he alone was punished some time later. In his own person he proved that divine judgment is always watchful in both directions, since he was helped when he hoped in God and killed when he showed contempt for him.

Meanwhile the elder emperor Theodosius had entrusted the care and training of the young boys, together with each of the two palaces, to two of the most powerful men: Rufinus received the eastern court and Stilicho the western empire. What each of them did, and what each tried to do, was shown by how each ended. One aimed at royal power for himself, the other for his son; and so that, when affairs were suddenly thrown into confusion, the state's emergency might cover the crime of their ambition, the one let barbarian peoples in, and the other fostered them.

I say nothing of King Alaric and his Goths, so often defeated, so often hemmed in, and always let go. I say nothing of those unhappy events at Pollentia, when the supreme command of the war was entrusted to a barbarian and pagan general, Saul. Through his wickedness the most holy days and sacred Easter were violated, and the enemy, who was withdrawing out of religious scruple, was forced to fight.
