Then, as God showed by a swift sign both what his favor can do and what his vengeance demands, we conquered when we fought, and when we were conquerors we were conquered.
I say nothing of the frequent slaughter the barbarians inflicted on one another, when two divisions of the Goths, and then the Alans and the Huns, ravaged each other in various massacres.

Radagaisus, by far the most savage of all enemies past and present, flooded the whole of Italy in a sudden onslaught. For they say that there were more than two hundred thousand Goths among his people.

On top of this incredible multitude and untamed strength, he was a pagan and a Scythian, who, as is the custom of barbarian peoples of this sort, had vowed to offer the blood of the whole Roman race as a drink to his gods.

So while he was threatening the strongholds of Rome, all the pagans in the City came together, saying that the enemy was powerful, certainly because of the size of his forces, but above all because of the protection of the gods; the City, on the other hand, was left defenseless and would soon perish because it had lost its gods and its rites.

There were loud complaints everywhere, and immediately there was talk of restoring the rites and celebrating them. Blasphemies seethed throughout the City; everywhere the name of Christ was loaded with reproaches, as if it were some plague upon the present times.

And so, by the unspeakable judgment of God, it came about as follows. In a mixed population grace was owed to the godly and punishment to the ungodly; enemies had to be allowed in to chastise with harsher scourges than usual a city that in most of its people would not be persuaded and spoke against God, but not enemies who would wipe out everyone without distinction in unrestrained slaughter. At that time two peoples of the Goths, with their two most powerful kings, were running wild through the Roman provinces.

One of these kings was a Christian, closer to the Romans, and, as events showed, merciful in slaughter out of the fear of God. The other was a pagan, a barbarian and a true Scythian, who loved not so much glory or plunder as slaughter itself for its own sake, with insatiable cruelty. He had already been received into the heart of Italy, and from close at hand he was shaking a trembling Rome with terror.

So if the power of vengeance had been granted to this man, whom the Romans thought especially to be feared because he courted the favor of the gods by the devotion of his sacrifices, the slaughter would have blazed beyond all measure without any fruit of amendment, and the last error would have grown worse than the first. For if Rome had fallen into the hands of a pagan and idolater, not only would the remaining pagans have been firmly convinced that the worship of idols should be restored, but the Christians too would have been dangerously confused, since the latter would have been frightened by the precedent and the former confirmed by the example.

Therefore God, the just steward of the human race, willed that the pagan enemy should perish and allowed the Christian to prevail, so that the pagans and the blaspheming Romans might be confounded by the destruction of the one and punished by the coming of the other. This was all the more so because the admirable self-restraint and most holy faith of the emperor Honorius, a rare thing in a ruler, earned no small measure of divine mercy.

Against that most savage enemy Radagaisus, other enemies were indeed granted to help, inclined in spirit to aid us, with their forces. Uldin and Sarus, the leaders of the Huns and the Goths, came to the aid of the Romans. But God did not allow what was the work of his own power to appear the valor of men, least of all of enemies.

He struck Radagaisus with terror from heaven and drove him into the mountains of Faesulae. There, with fear pressing on them from every side, he shut up his two hundred thousand men (to follow those who give the lowest figure), destitute of counsel and of food, on a dry and rugged mountain ridge. Those hosts for whom Italy had lately seemed too narrow he thrust, in the hope of hiding, onto one small summit. Why should I linger over it?

No battle line was drawn up for war, no fury and fear brought on the uncertainties of combat, no slaughter took place, no blood was shed; nor, finally, were the losses of battle offset by the outcome of victory, which is usually counted as good fortune. While our men ate, drank and amused themselves, those enemies, so numerous and so savage, were worn out by hunger, thirst and exhaustion.

That would be too little, unless the Romans were to learn that the man they had feared had been captured and subdued, and could look down on that idolater of theirs, whose sacrifices they pretended to fear more than his arms, conquered without a battle, bound under the yoke and in chains. So King Radagaisus, seizing for himself alone the hope of flight, secretly deserted his men and fell into the hands of ours. He was captured by them, held for a short time, and then put to death.

The multitude of Gothic captives is said to have been so great that droves of men were sold everywhere for a single gold piece each, like the cheapest cattle. But God allowed nothing of that people to survive. For all those who were bought died at once, and what their wicked buyers had shamefully failed to pay in price they paid out mercifully on burials.

So ungrateful Rome had now felt the indirect mercy of God the judge, given not to indulge but to check the presumption of idolatry. In the same way she was soon to suffer God's wrath, though not in full, because of the godly remembrance of the saints, living and dead, in case she might perhaps be confounded and repent and learn faith through experience. Meanwhile she was granted a short respite from the onslaught of Alaric, a king and an enemy, but a Christian.

Meanwhile Count Stilicho, born of the race of the Vandals, an unwarlike, greedy, treacherous and crafty people, thought it a small thing to hold command under the emperor. He was striving by any means possible to set in power his son Eucherius, who, as many report, had been planning a persecution of the Christians ever since he was a boy and a private citizen.

For this reason he fostered Alaric and the whole nation of the Goths by a secret treaty, though they were humbly and sincerely begging for the best terms of peace and for any lands to settle in. Publicly, however, he denied them the chance of either war or peace, and kept them in reserve to wear down and terrify the state.

In addition, he stirred up other peoples, irresistible in their numbers and strength, by whom the provinces of Gaul and Spain are now oppressed: the Alans, Sueves and Vandals, along with the Burgundians, who were driven on by the same movement. He actively urged them to take up arms, and once their fear of the Roman name had been wiped away, he set them in motion.

For the time being he wanted them to batter the banks of the Rhine and to beat upon the provinces of Gaul. The wretched man hoped that under the pressure of this emergency he could wrest the empire from his son-in-law for his son, and that the barbarian peoples could be put down as easily as they had been stirred up.

So when the whole drama of these great crimes was laid bare before the emperor Honorius and the Roman army, the army rose up in the most just indignation and Stilicho was killed, the man who, to clothe one boy in purple, had given up the blood of the whole human race.

Eucherius was killed too, who, to win the favor of the pagans for himself, used to threaten that he would inaugurate his reign by restoring the temples and overthrowing the churches. A few accomplices in these great schemes were punished with them. Thus, with very little trouble and the punishment of only a few, the churches of Christ, together with their devout emperor, were both set free and avenged.
And so, after this great increase of blasphemies and no repentance at all, that final punishment, long held in suspense, overtook the City.

Alaric arrived; he besieged, threw into confusion and broke into trembling Rome. But first he gave orders that anyone who had taken refuge in holy places, and especially in the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, should above all be left unharmed and safe, and further that his men, though eager for plunder, should refrain from bloodshed as far as they could.

It also happened, which proved all the more that this breaking into the City was brought about by the indignation of God rather than by the strength of the enemy, that the blessed Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, was at Ravenna at the time. Like righteous Lot taken out of Sodom, he was removed by the hidden providence of God, so that he should not see the destruction of a sinful people.

While the barbarians were running through the City, one of the Goths, a powerful man and a Christian, happened to find a virgin consecrated to God, already advanced in years, in a house belonging to the church. When he courteously demanded gold and silver from her,

she, with faithful steadfastness, promised that she had a great deal and would bring it out at once, and she did. When she saw that the barbarian, as the treasures were laid out, was astonished at their size, weight and beauty, and even at the unfamiliar character of the vessels, the virgin of Christ said to the barbarian:
"These are the sacred vessels of the apostle Peter. Take them, if you dare; you will answer for the deed. As for me, since I cannot defend them, I do not dare to keep them."

The barbarian, moved to reverence for religion by the fear of God and by the virgin's faith, reported this to Alaric by a messenger. Alaric at once ordered that all the vessels should be carried back, just as they were, to the apostle's basilica,

and that the virgin, too, and with her all the Christians who joined her, should be escorted there under protection. That house, they say, was far from the holy shrines, with half the City lying between.

So, to the great wonder of all, the gold and silver vessels were distributed one to each person, raised above their heads and carried openly. The holy procession was guarded on every side by drawn swords.

A hymn to God was sung publicly, Romans and barbarians singing together. In the midst of the City's destruction the trumpet of salvation sounded far and wide, inviting and rousing everyone, even those hiding in secret places.

From every side they ran together to the vessels of Peter, the vessels of Christ. Very many pagans, too, mingled with the Christians, in profession though not in faith, and in this way escaped for the time being, only to be all the more confounded. The more the Romans flocked together in refuge, the more eagerly the barbarians surrounded them as their defenders.

O holy and unspeakable discernment of divine judgment! O that holy and saving river, which rose in a small house and, as it made its way along its blessed channel to the dwelling of the saints, swept wandering and endangered souls along with a godly force into the bosom of salvation!

O glorious trumpet of Christ's army, which, inviting all alike to life with its sweetest strains, left those whom it did not rouse to salvation, because they disobeyed, without excuse for their death!

This mystery, which took place in the carrying of the vessels, the singing of hymns and the leading of the people, was, I believe, like a great sieve. Through it, out of the assembled Roman people, as out of a great heap of grain, the living grains flowed out through every opening of their hiding places from the whole circuit of the city, moved whether by the opportunity or by the truth.

Yet all those that believed in present salvation were received from the granary of the Lord's provision, while the rest, like dung and chaff, already condemned by their very unbelief or disobedience, were left behind for destruction and burning. Who could ponder these things with sufficient wonder, or proclaim them with fitting praise?

On the third day after they had entered the City, the barbarians left of their own accord. They had indeed set fire to a number of buildings, but not even to the extent that the accident in the seven hundredth year of its founding had caused.

For if I were to review the conflagration that the emperor Nero staged as a spectacle for himself, there is no doubt that the fire now brought by the anger of a conqueror would bear no comparison with the one kindled by the wantonness of a prince.
Nor should I mention, in a comparison of this kind, the Gauls, who for the space of almost a whole year held possession of the trampled ashes of the City they had burned and overthrown.

And so that no one might doubt that the enemy had been permitted to do this to chastise a proud, wanton and blasphemous city, at the same time the most famous places in the City, which the enemy could not set on fire, were destroyed by lightning.

So it was in the year 1164 from the founding of the City that Alaric broke into it. Although the memory of this event is recent, anyone who saw the multitude of the Roman people itself and heard what they say would think that nothing had happened, as they themselves admit, unless perhaps he were informed of it by some ruins of the fire still standing.

In that sack Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius and sister of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, was captured by Athaulf, a kinsman of Alaric, and taken as his wife. It was as if Rome, by divine judgment, had handed her over as a special pledge and hostage; joined thus in marriage to a most powerful barbarian king, she was of great benefit to the state.

Meanwhile, two years before the sack of Rome, the peoples stirred up by Stilicho, as I have said, the Alans, Sueves and Vandals, and many others with them, overran the Franks, crossed the Rhine, invaded the provinces of Gaul, and pressed straight on as far as the Pyrenees. Checked for a time by that barrier, they poured back through the surrounding provinces.

While they were running wild through Gaul, Gratian, a citizen of that island, was made usurper in Britain and was killed. In his place Constantine, from the lowest ranks of the army, was chosen merely for the hope his name inspired, without any merit of courage. As soon as he had seized power, he crossed over into Gaul. There he was often tricked by the barbarians through unreliable treaties, and did more harm than good to the state.

He sent officials into Spain. When the provinces had obediently received them, two brothers, young, noble and wealthy, Didymus and Verinianus, set about, not seizing usurped power themselves against the usurper, but defending themselves and their country for the lawful emperor against the usurper and the barbarians. This was clear from the very way in which they went about it.

For no one seizes usurped power except in secret, after rapid preparation, and then arms himself openly; the whole point is to be seen in diadem and purple before anyone knows of it. These men, by contrast, spent a long time gathering only their own slaves from their estates and maintaining them at their own expense, and, making no secret of their purpose and without disturbing anyone, they made their way to the passes of the Pyrenees.

Against them Constantine sent into Spain his son Constans, who, alas, had been turned from a monk into a Caesar, along with certain barbarians who had once been received under treaty and enlisted into the army, and were called the Honoriaci. From this came the first ruin of Spain.

For after the brothers who were trying to guard the Pyrenean Alps with their private forces had been killed, these barbarians were first given leave to plunder the plains of Pallantia as a kind of reward for victory, and then were entrusted with the guarding of that range and its passes, while the faithful and useful watch of the country people was removed.

So the Honoriaci, having had a taste of plunder and being lured on by its abundance, betrayed the guard of the Pyrenees and threw open the passes, so that their crime might go all the more unpunished and they might have all the more scope for crime. They let in all the peoples who were wandering through Gaul into the provinces of Spain and joined them themselves.

There, after they had carried on great and bloody raids for some time, and after grievous devastation of property and people, for which even they themselves now feel some regret, they cast lots, divided the land among themselves, and remain settled in possession of it to this day.
I could now say a great deal about matters of this kind, if a secret conscience did not speak, in every human being, within each person's own mind.

The Spanish provinces were invaded and suffered slaughter and devastation. This was nothing new, for during the two years now past in which the enemy sword has raged, they have endured at the hands of the barbarians what they once suffered for two hundred years at the hands of the Romans, and what they underwent under the emperor Gallienus for nearly twelve years, when the Germans were laying them waste.

Yet who, aware of his own deeds and those of his family, or even of his thoughts, and fearing the judgments of God, would not admit that he has suffered all this justly, or has even got off lightly? Or as for the one who does not know himself and does not fear God, how has he not suffered these things justly, and lightly at that?

Even so, God's mercy, with the same kindness with which it had long before foretold it, arranged things so that, in keeping with his Gospel, in which he constantly warned, "When they persecute you in one city, flee to another," anyone who wished to leave and go away could make use of the barbarians themselves as hired servants and protectors.

At that time the barbarians themselves offered this of their own accord. Men who could have killed everyone and taken everything asked only a small payment as wages for their service and for carrying people's goods. And many people did in fact take advantage of this.

But those who did not believe God's Gospel, being obstinate, or who had not even heard it and so were doubly obstinate, did not give place to wrath, and were justly overtaken and crushed by the wrath that came upon them.

Yet soon after this the barbarians, cursing their swords, turned them into ploughshares, and they now treat the Romans who remain as allies and friends, so that there are already some Romans among them who would rather live in poverty and freedom among the barbarians than bear the anxious burden of taxation among the Romans.

And yet, even if the barbarians had been let into Roman territory for this reason alone, that the churches of Christ throughout East and West are being filled with Huns, Suevi, Vandals, and Burgundians, and with countless other peoples of believers, God's mercy would still seem worthy of praise and exaltation, since, even at the cost of our own ruin, such great nations would be receiving knowledge of the truth, which they could surely never have found except through this opportunity.

For what loss is it to a Christian who longs for eternal life to be taken from this world at any time and in any manner? And what gain is it to a pagan who has hardened himself against the faith in the midst of Christians if he draws out his days a little longer, when he must die some time or other and his conversion is past hope?

And since the judgments of God are beyond words, and we can neither know them all nor explain those we do know, let me put it briefly: the chastisement of God the judge, however it comes about, is justly borne by those who know it, and justly borne by those who do not.

In the 1165th year from the founding of the City, the emperor Honorius, seeing that nothing could be done against the barbarians while so many usurpers stood against him, ordered that the usurpers themselves be destroyed first. Command of this war was entrusted to Count Constantius.
Only then did the state realize both what benefit it had at last received from a Roman general and what ruin it had endured for so long while subject to barbarian counts.
So Count Constantius set out for Gaul with an army, shut up the emperor Constantine in the city of Arles, captured him, and put him to death.
From here on, to speak as briefly as I can

about the list of usurpers: Constans, the son of Constantine, was killed at Vienne by his own count Gerontius, a man more wicked than upright, who set up a certain Maximus in his place. Gerontius himself was killed by his own soldiers.
Maximus, stripped of the purple and abandoned by the Gallic troops, who were shipped across to Africa and then recalled to Italy, now lives in destitute exile among the barbarians in Spain.

Later Jovinus, the noblest man in the Gallic provinces, fell as soon as he had risen to usurp power. His brother Sebastian chose only this: to die a usurper, for he was killed the moment he was proclaimed.

What shall I say of the most unfortunate Attalus, for whom it was an honor to be killed among usurpers and a gain to die? In his case Alaric made him emperor, unmade him, remade him, and unmade him again, all of it done almost faster than it can be told, and he laughed at the farce and watched the comedy of empire.

Nor is it surprising if the wretched man was rightly made a mockery of in this pageant, since his shadow-consul Tertullus dared to say in the senate house, "I shall address you, conscript fathers, as consul and pontiff, of which offices I hold the one and hope for the other": placing his hope in one who had no hope himself, and certainly accursed, because he had put his hope in man.

So Attalus, like an empty phantom of empire, was carried along with the Goths as far as Spain. Departing from there by ship with some uncertain scheme in mind, he was captured at sea and brought to Count Constantius; then he was presented to the emperor Honorius, and was left alive with his hand cut off.

Meanwhile Heraclian, who had been sent as count of Africa, vigorously defended Africa against the officials sent by Attalus while the same Attalus was bearing the shadow of empire, and he gained the consulship.

Puffed up with pride at this, he chose as his son-in-law Sabinus, his chief of staff, a man of shrewd intelligence and skillful energy, who might have been called wise had he applied his powers of mind to peaceful pursuits.

With him, while he lay under suspicion of certain dangerous designs, he [?]; and after holding back the African grain supply beyond the proper time for a while, he at last set out for Rome himself with an immense fleet of ships, one truly incredible for our times.

For he is said to have had 3,700 ships at that time, a number that, according to the histories, not even Xerxes, that famous king of the Persians, nor Alexander the Great, nor any other king ever possessed.

As soon as he had landed and was making for the City with his column of soldiers, he was terrified by the advance of Count Marinus and put to flight; seizing a ship, he returned alone to Carthage, and there he was promptly killed by a band of soldiers. His son-in-law Sabinus fled to Constantinople, from where, some time later, he was brought back and condemned to exile.

This whole list, as I have said, whether of open usurpers or of disobedient generals, the emperor Honorius earned the defeat of by his excellent piety and good fortune, and Count Constantius carried it out with great energy and speed.

And rightly so, for in these days, by the command of Honorius and with the help of Constantius, peace and unity were restored to the Catholic Church throughout all Africa, and the body of Christ, which we are, was healed when its division was mended. The carrying out of this sacred decree was entrusted to the tribune Marcellinus, a man especially prudent and diligent and most eager for every good pursuit.

Count Marinus killed him at Carthage, whether spurred on by zeal or bribed with gold is uncertain. Marinus was at once recalled from Africa, reduced to private life, and dismissed either to the punishment or to the repentance of his own conscience.

In the 1168th year from the founding of the City, Count Constantius, stationed at Arles, a city of Gaul, with great energy in his operations drove the Goths out of Narbonne and forced them to withdraw into Spain, chiefly by forbidding and cutting off all passage of ships and all use of foreign trade.

At that time King Athaulf ruled the Gothic peoples. After the sack of the City and the death of Alaric, he had taken as his wife Placidia, the emperor's sister, who, as I have said, was a captive, and had succeeded Alaric on the throne.

As was often heard and was proved by his final end, he was a quite earnest pursuer of peace, and preferred to serve the emperor Honorius loyally and to spend the strength of the Goths in defending the Roman state.

For I myself heard a certain man of Narbonne, who had held a distinguished military post under Theodosius, a devout, prudent, and serious man as well, telling the most blessed priest Jerome at the town of Bethlehem in Palestine that he had been a very close friend of Athaulf at Narbonne, and that he had often learned from him, under solemn witness, what Athaulf, a man of overwhelming spirit, strength, and intelligence, used to say:

that at first he had ardently longed to blot out the Roman name and to make all Roman territory the empire of the Goths, and to call it so, so that, to put it in popular terms, what had been Romania would be Gothia, and Athaulf would now become what Caesar Augustus had once been;

but that once long experience had proved to him that the Goths could by no means obey laws, because of their unbridled barbarism, and that the state ought not to be deprived of laws, without which a state is no state, he had chosen at least to seek glory for himself by restoring the Roman name to its full strength and increasing it by the might of the Goths, and to be regarded by posterity as the author of Rome's restoration, since he had not been able to be the one who changed it.

For this reason he strove to refrain from war, for this reason he longed for peace, being moderated toward every work of good government chiefly by the persuasion and counsel of his wife Placidia, a woman of truly keen intelligence and of sound enough piety.
And while he was pressing most earnestly to seek and offer this same peace, he was killed at Barcelona, a city of Spain, through the treachery of his own men, as it is said.
After him Segeric was made king by the Goths, and though he too, by the judgment of God, was inclined toward peace, he was nonetheless killed by his own people.
Then Wallia succeeded to the throne, chosen by the Goths to break the peace, but appointed by God to confirm it.

This man, then, was greatly terrified by the judgment of God, because the year before, when a large force of Goths, equipped with arms and ships, was attempting to cross into Africa, it had been caught by a storm twelve miles out in the Strait of Cádiz and had perished in a pitiable

end; he also remembered the disaster suffered under Alaric, when the Goths, trying to cross into Sicily, were pitiably seized and drowned in sight of their own people. So he made a most favorable peace with the emperor Honorius, giving hostages of the highest rank; he returned to her brother Placidia, the emperor's sister, whom he had kept with honor and respect;

and he offered his own danger for Rome's security, undertaking to fight against the other peoples that had settled throughout the Spanish provinces, fighting for himself and conquering for the Romans.

And yet the other kings too, those of the Alans, Vandals, and Suevi, had bound themselves to us on the same terms, sending word to the emperor Honorius: "Keep peace with all of us and take hostages from all of us. We fight among ourselves, we perish to our own loss, we conquer for you, and it will be an everlasting gain for your state if we both perish."

Who would believe this if the facts did not prove it? And so now we learn from frequent and reliable reports that wars between these peoples are being waged every day in the Spanish provinces, and slaughter carried out by the barbarians on one another; and they say that Wallia, king of the Goths, is especially intent on bringing about peace.

On this basis I would grant, after a fashion, that Christian times may be freely criticized, if you can be shown anything accomplished with similar good fortune from the creation of the world until now.

We have made it clear, I think, and have shown that countless wars have been quieted, almost more by a word than by a finger; that very many usurpers have been destroyed; and that the most savage nations have been checked, confined, subdued, and exhausted, with very little bloodshed, without battle, and almost without slaughter.

It remains that our detractors should repent of their schemes and blush before the truth, and should believe in, fear, love, and follow the true and only God, who can do all things, all of whose works, even those they think evil, they have learned are good.

With Christ's help, and in accordance with your command, most blessed father Augustine, I have set out, from the beginning of the world to the present day, that is, over five thousand six hundred and eighteen years, the desires and the punishments of sinful men, the struggles of the world, and the judgments of God, as briefly and as simply as I could; yet I have set Christian times apart from that confusion of unbelief because of the grace of Christ, which is now more present.

So I now enjoy the sure and only fruit of my obedience, which is the one I ought to have desired. As for the quality of these little works, that is for you, who commanded them, to see: if you publish them, they must be judged by you; if you destroy them, they will have been judged by you.
